State every desired understanding as a full-sentence generalization asserting what the learner should conclude, never as a topic label or bare phrase.

State the understanding as a proposition or maxim summing up the overall conclusion drawn from many facts, using the stem "Students should understand that" to force a full-sentence answer and prevent falling back on a topic or concept.
Judge a design by the transfer it produces — the learner's ability to use what they know wisely and effectively in a new context — rather than by recall of what was taught.

Evaluate instruction by transfer rather than memory, because many approaches look equivalent when the only measure is recall and differences appear only when learning is tested on new problems and settings.

Recognize that performing autonomously with scaffolds and cues removed is the essence of transfer and that learners are rarely adequately equipped for it, so equip and assess them for exactly the situations where the conclusion is not obvious, the issues are murky, and it is ambiguous which knowledge is required.

Guard against losing sight of the whole while applying the design elements, since a design can produce successful short-term learning of many discrete facts while bypassing understandings and transfer tasks entirely.

Define learning as change in the learner — no change, no learning — and significant learning as a lasting change that matters in the learner's life; use that as the test for whether a stated outcome is worth designing for.
Design assessment evidence to match the objective: reuse exact taught facts for retention, but use meaningfully novel cases for conceptual transfer.
To assess transfer or cognition beyond remembering, use sufficiently novel material to prevent memorized reproduction without adding irrelevant knowledge demands.
When transfer is intended, teach and assess processes beyond recognition and recall; otherwise even conceptual or metacognitive content can be learned rotely.

In an integrated unit, state both disciplinary content and transferable practice explicitly, distinguish reusable learning from one-off products, and classify activities such as editing by their actual demand.

Ground the design in knowledge of how human beings learn — state not only what abilities are wanted but how they can be acquired — and draw only on the parts of learning theory that concern events an instructor can control.

Adapt only the general qualities of instruction — media and pacing — to learner abilities and traits, which are not readily altered by learning, while adapting content itself to the specific skills and verbal knowledge the learners possess.

Design the performance measures before the lesson materials, because a novice is more likely to stray from the objectives when writing tests than when preparing lessons, and a designer fresh from writing a lesson may inadvertently test content rather than performance — keeping the test focused on what the learner must do rather than what was read or presented.

Judge strategy adoption by a decrease in time and an increase in accuracy between the early applications while learning and the later ones after adoption — more informative than self-report or direct observation — since adoption implies the strategy is now part of the learner's information-processing repertoire and can be applied efficiently.

Select retrieval cues that past experience shows work for that particular learner, choose just enough varied examples to aid transfer, and conduct as many spaced reviews as that student needs for long-term retention.
Preserve evidence and lessons from evaluated instruction so future adaptations can reuse what is supported without assuming contexts are identical.
Use varied subject contexts to help learners recognize and transfer the underlying design process rather than memorizing one example.
Characterize meaningful learner variation before design and use familiar subject matter when the design process itself is the unfamiliar learning target.
Reuse lessons from systematically evaluated instruction when adapting it to new learners, settings, scale, or media, while revalidating the changed context.
Present authentic, vivid, explorable context containing the cues learners must interpret so they can recognize when and why to act and transfer the skill.
Trace every design, media, budget, and schedule decision to the intended behavior change, assign explicit learner advocacy, and use learner review to challenge the evolving solution.
Surface the conception of learning implicit in a design before critiquing its details: every design decision already encodes a theory of how people learn, whether or not the designer has stated one.

Do not design as if delivering information into the learner's memory. Knowledge is constructed by the learner and cannot be transferred intact, which is why the same message yields different outcomes for different learners.

Distinguish remembering from understanding in every objective and every test: remembering is reproduction or recognition measured by retention tests (quantity of learning); understanding is use in novel situations measured by transfer tests (quality of learning). Do not accept retention evidence alone as evidence that a design worked.

Keep learning, instruction, and assessment in view together — how people learn, how to help them learn, and how to determine what they learned — because a design decision in one constrains the other two.

Attribute extraneous processing to the design, not to the learner: it is processing that does not serve the instructional goal and is caused by confusing design, so the remedy is to change the material.

Assess load relative to the specific learner, not the lesson: capacity, prior knowledge, and strategies vary, so the identical lesson may overload one learner and not another. State which learner population a load judgement refers to.
Reject learning styles as a basis for design; customize instead on the learner's prior knowledge and work role, the individual difference that most influences learning.

Weight evidence by its fit to your situation: prefer studies whose learners, materials, and environments resemble yours, that measure application rather than recall when the goal is job performance, and whose results have been replicated.
Require the learned capability again in later course tasks so retention and transfer are exercised in service of new learning rather than as isolated review.

Recognize a behavioral design by objectives specified in measurable terms per component with techniques and evaluation tied to each, including learner self-evaluation, and note that a modern behavioral approach is broader than early programmed instruction in both topics and resources, covering attention and conceptual understanding.
Keep the design template to elements that specify what the finished design must contain, and put process moves that merely help produce a better design into a separate worksheet or tool.

Use the template as an intelligent tool that reinforces the habits producing designs for understanding and blocks the habits behind activity- and coverage-based design, not merely as a place to record ideas.

Treat "essential" as carrying three legitimate senses at once — essential for a lifetime of thinking, essential to the expert's view of the discipline, and essential to teaching this unit — and name which sense a given question is serving rather than assuming only the timeless sense qualifies.

Recognize the four senses of essential — broad timeless life questions, core disciplinary inquiries, questions needed for learning the core content, and questions that will most engage these particular learners — and note that answers to timeless questions are invariably provisional, with change of mind expected and beneficial.
Carry only a few genuinely essential questions per unit — two to five — because truly essential questions can by themselves establish priorities and uncover all the key ideas.

Separate essential information, for which certainty of learning is the concern of formal education, from information that is personally interesting but not essential — and place no limit on what a learner wishes to acquire out of interest.

Plan Stage 3 against the full WHERETO set, including tailoring the work to actual learners and organizing the sequence for maximal impact, not only the earlier where-hook-explore-rethink-evaluate elements.

Work the three backward-design stages in fixed order — identify desired results, determine acceptable evidence, then plan learning experiences — and defer method, sequence, and resource choices until the first two are settled.

Build the learning plan so it satisfies each WHERETO element — where and why, hook and hold, equip and experience, rethink and revise, evaluate, tailor, and organize — and code each key activity with the element it serves so the plan is auditable.

Use WHERETO as an analytic tool for checking a design's elements rather than a recipe or prescribed sequence, since design work legitimately emerges along many paths — including introducing a unit with the final task done in preliminary form.
Plan sequence within a unit separately from sequence across units, since units both frame and are framed by the course and programme they sit in.

Diagnose a weak design as one of the twin sins — activity-focused or coverage-focused — and treat their shared defect as the real fault: no explicit big idea guiding the teaching and no plan ensuring the learning.
Diagnose failure evidence carefully: do not condemn a delivery medium when weak instructional design may explain the observed result.

Interrogate an activity-oriented unit with four questions — to what ends is the teaching directed, which big ideas and skills are developed, do students know the learning targets, and does the collected evidence reflect worthwhile standards.
Where the basic concepts and skills are straightforward, ask specifically what in the unit genuinely requires uncoverage and which typical misunderstandings must be deliberately targeted.

Let pedagogy follow from the type of aim rather than from ideological assumptions about good teaching — an abstract concept must be inferred from well-designed experience, much knowledge can be learned from reading or lecture, and a skill needs modelling, guided practice, and feedback judged on actual samples.

Settle whether a topical question is genuinely essential by what students are asked to do with it in Stages 2 and 3 — whether activities make clear no simple answer is coming and assessments demand explanation and justification.

Ask the assessor's questions — what would be sufficient and revealing evidence, which performance tasks must anchor the unit, what evidence types the results require, against what criteria work will be judged, and whether the assessment distinguished real from apparent understanding — instead of the activity designer's questions about fun, student preference, and grade justification.

Teach discrete factual and procedural content by explicit instruction and reading followed by checks for understanding, and reserve guided inquiry and facilitated discussion for the unit's essential questions.

Work the favourite-activity entry point by answering the why question first — which big ideas the resource helps students understand and which standards it serves — and then revising the assessments and activities accordingly.

Diagnose a topic-activities-assessments unit as putting activities at the centre with no identified goals, no big ideas or essential questions, and no valid evidence — only a grading scheme — and read student reflections that name only the enjoyable mechanics as evidence that no enduring understanding was produced.

Use essential questions as the backbone of courses and programmes into which units fit, since they are overarching and recursive by nature and can be properly addressed only across many units or years.

Open the unit with an entry question connecting the topic to something students already care about, then introduce the essential questions and culminating tasks so the destination is known from the start, introducing key vocabulary as the activities require rather than front-loading it and using textbook reading to support those activities.

Split the activity decision into two questions — what the students will actually do, and what the teacher will do — and give this stage as much attention as the goals and assessment, because it shapes the nature and quality of the learning experience.

Have students work the fixed question sequence — which systems are involved, what we know, what we do not know, how to learn it, how to analyze and diagnose, what solution fits — because working the right questions in the right order is itself a major part of what is being taught, and the what-we-do-not-know step is how students identify their own learning issues.

Focus evaluation questions on four aspects: whether the course goals are being achieved, how effective particular activities and the overall strategy are, whether feedback and assessment are helpful and fair, and how effectively the teacher interacts with students.
When complex activity is a means to conceptual understanding, assess that understanding explicitly and teach any factual retention later required instead of assuming either from product quality.

Accompany each unit with teacher directions communicating the objective, the plan of student activities, the materials needed, and the test directions, so the teacher can see at a glance what needs planning and which instructional modes — small-group work, partners, tutoring — may be required and can advise the student on options.

Do not accept hands-on engagement or interdisciplinary theming as evidence of design quality; engagement is necessary but not sufficient, and rewarding students for engagement rather than understanding is a design error.
Keep learner engagement as a criterion distinct from disciplinary importance, since a question important in the grand scheme may have no apparent relevance to particular students.

Draw on the practitioner consensus about engagement — hands-on work, mysteries and problems, variety, personalization, real-world challenges, simulations, and real audiences — and about effectiveness — clear worthy goals, understood purpose, models and exemplars, public criteria for self-monitoring, limited fear with rewarded risk, concrete links beyond the classroom, and many chances to self-assess and self-adjust.
Exploit the overlap between engagement and effectiveness — genuine application to meaningful real-world problems, hands-on opportunities to do the subject, and helpful feedback each enhance both.

Accept that design tensions are inherent and inevitable, making the work inherently problematic rather than merely demanding, and that dilemmas of competing elements are negotiated rather than solved.
Treat interesting and engaging as necessary but not sufficient: the design must also address the goals and standards efficiently and effectively, making the work minds-on and not merely hands-on.

Gather the learner factors that change the design — life and work situation, professional goals, reasons for enrolling, prior knowledge and attitudes, learning styles — and treat the affective state students bring to the subject, such as anxiety about statistics, as a design input rather than a nuisance.

Calibrate design ambition to the teacher's honestly assessed skill: keep the design near the comfort zone when interaction, management, and design skills are still basic, and take on more challenging goals and more powerful strategies when they are well developed.

Treat the high behavioral engagement of games and simulations as no evidence of learning; the design problem is securing the psychological activity, since a game goal can be antagonistic to the instructional goal and produce fun without learning.

Distinguish purposeful survey from coverage: an overview is legitimate, but teaching by mentioning — checking off topics irrespective of whether students understand — is not, and its diagnostic fault is the absence of transparent purpose.
Define coverage as superficially teaching and testing content irrespective of student understanding or engagement, typically justified by framework demands or external testing.
Report a study's coverage honestly against its intended population, since even a large multi-site sample representing a great majority of schools may have omitted whole categories.
Use the textbook as a resource and never as the syllabus; let desired results, not the book's table of contents, define the content and sequence of instruction.
Treat the textbook as a platform to jump off from and return to in the course of inquiry, which naturally prompts consultation of other sources including other textbooks.

Treat a textbook as a reference manual that goes through topics divorced from meaningful use or overarching questions, and reject its unhelpful promotion into a sealed-off syllabus treated as both form and content.

Note that the critique of textbook-as-syllabus dates to 1935 and the situation has if anything worsened, with science texts front-loading vocabulary a well-educated scientist in another field would not need and chapter exercises amounting to regurgitating those words.

Define the job of design, instruction, and assessment as shaping a syllabus in light of standards, intellectual priorities, and student needs, since treating the textbook as the syllabus guarantees a lack of purpose and coherence and is akin to marching through an encyclopedia from A to Z.

Write the syllabus to carry what students need in order to do what is asked plus the ground rules: management information, course goals, structure and sequence with due dates, required reading, grading procedures, and policies on attendance, late work, make-ups, and academic misconduct.

Write an instructional guide to supply direct instruction where it is unavailable in published sources, often making it possible for the student to develop an intellectual skill necessary for further progress within the unit.

Do not treat accurate computation or a correct answer as evidence of understanding; check whether the learner grasped the meaning of the question and could use what they know to reach a contextually sensible result.

Anticipate the specific misunderstandings and rough spots a topic predictably produces, and design lessons and assessments that evoke and overcome them; knowledge and skill do not by themselves yield understanding.
Treat an understanding as a mental construct — an abstraction the mind makes to give sense to many pieces of knowledge — evidenced by the specific things a learner can then show and do.

Distinguish knowledge from understanding on six axes — facts versus their meaning, a body of facts versus the theory giving them coherence, verifiable claims versus fallible in-process theories, right-or-wrong versus degree of sophistication, knowing that versus understanding why, and responding on cue versus judging when to use what one knows.

Do not read a correct performance as understanding, since it may be accidental or rote; require the learner to explain why a given skill, approach, or body of knowledge is or is not appropriate to the situation.

Keep both senses of understanding in play: the verb sense of using knowledge and skill wisely and effectively, and the noun sense of a grasped unobvious inference that makes meaning of many discrete elements.
Do not equate greater factual knowledge with understanding: understandings can be missed by those holding the most knowledge.

Distrust the most readily available evidence: when students supply the answer the teacher was seeking it is easy to conflate recall with understanding, and a student who can answer only when the question is phrased just so does not understand it.

Guard against apparent understanding — teachers over-attribute understanding to correct, intelligent-sounding answers, and high-stakes testing gives students an incentive to appear to understand whether or not they do.

Treat misunderstanding as the plausible-but-incorrect mapping of a working idea onto a new situation — not as ignorance — since a learner must already have knowledge and some capacity to transfer in order to misunderstand.

Distinguish understandings, which are the constructivist result of the learner's own inquiry, performance, and reflection and must be comprehended, from knowledge, which summarizes straightforward facts and concepts and need only be apprehended.

Require inference about why and how backed by evidence and logic when assessing explanation, since a learner can state a theorem, know a phenomenon, or execute a technique without understanding the proof, the axioms, or the principles at work.

Do not accept the textbook's or teacher's official theory returned on a test as evidence of understanding; require the student to supply why the answer is correct and support their own opinion, using verbs such as support, justify, generalize, predict, verify, prove, and substantiate.

Edit essential questions into age-appropriate learner language, then verify with a survey or informal check that every student understands them and sees their value rather than assuming comprehension.

Make clear in the design that questions are not only the cause of greater understanding but the means by which all content accrues, and treat students as potential performers who experience how their own inquiries parallel experts' and how agreed understandings change over time.

Allow the desired understanding to be stated in technical adult terms novices never restate, and reject the misconceptions that goals must be simplistic for younger learners or that evidence of understanding requires stating it in words.

Treat learners as not blank slates: misunderstandings flow from prior experience and a plausible inference drawn from it, so old facts and habits of thought must be questioned and sometimes unlearned before new thinking can take hold, and able students may resist precisely because they are comfortable with the old view.

Review predictable misconceptions before teaching by asking what misinformation learners harbour and what rough spots always crop up, since identifying them also sharpens the designer's own grasp of the target understanding and its unavoidable impediments.
Aim for the shift in which learners see learning as an unending quest for understandings rather than a search for final facts handed down by authorities.

Elicit learner judgments made during genuine performance rather than responses to easily followed cues, and distinguish a genuine problem from a mock one by asking whether the question arises naturally in a situation and would provoke inquiry outside school rather than mattering only because a mark depends on it.

Describe understanding on a continuum from naive to sophisticated rather than as right versus wrong, and warn judges explicitly not to confuse factual-error count or writing quality with depth of understanding.
Judge interpretive work by the evidence that the student actually read and thought about the text, not by whether they thought about it as an adult would or matched an adult's correct answer.

Do not establish understanding by scoring correctness alone while ignoring how the student set up and solved the problem, since the best papers may reflect recall of formulas with no grasp of why they work.

Avoid doubtful inferences in both directions: wrong answers localized to a sub-skill or to language do not show absence of understanding when the student can explain the underlying rule, and a student can perform well without understanding or understand while jumbling key facts.

Expect evidence of understanding to be less direct and more complicated than objective-test evidence, since a right answer can come from rote recall, test-taking skill, or a lucky guess, and therefore ferret out the reasons behind answers and the meaning the learner makes of results rather than the percentage correct.

Close a unit by asking what changed in the learner's view over time, what their own misunderstandings were, and how they would teach the material for understanding, turning the ending into self-knowledge evidence.

Stay vigilant because teachers are prone to read correct answers as understanding while students want to appear to get it; that a few students get it and no one asks questions does not mean the rest understand, and answering on cue does not mean the knowledge can be used unprompted.
Keep informal checks for understanding ungraded, since their purpose is timely feedback on current conceptions and misconceptions and the instructional adjustments those imply.

Treat checks for understanding as as essential to teaching as any reading, lecture, or discussion, because they let learner and teacher know what is not being understood in time to adjust — understanding arising from repeated increasingly successful attempts coupled with feedback and guidance.
Use open-ended outcomes, tasks, and learner-generated evidence to recognise divergent or worthwhile unanticipated learning while judging relevance and quality against defensible criteria.

Respond to learner questions from the conceptual perspective that produced them, use convergent or divergent questioning according to the goal, and allow enough wait or asynchronous time for high-level reasoning.

Make two judgments about validity of an observed performance — whether it accurately reflects the objective and whether it occurred under conditions free of distortion such that the learner could not have memorised or remembered the answer — and treat the informal observations made right after learning as the same kind of thing as formally planned assessment, with no conflict between them.

Do not accept hands-on interactivity as evidence of learning. Behavioural activity does not guarantee cognitive activity — typing answers or driving a highly interactive simulation can leave the learner making no sense of the material.
Lay out feedback so the question, the learner's own response, and the feedback are visible together, and mark correct options beside the learner's answers.
End every case with a comparison of the learner's own action path against an expert's, so reflection targets the reasoning process rather than the final answer.
When the objective is verbal information, telling learners the answer to their questions is the correct form of learning guidance rather than a failure of guidance.

When a learner's hypothesis is partly but not wholly true, select a counterexample that satisfies their hypothesis while violating its predicted outcome, and generate hypothetical cases to force reasoning about situations that cannot easily be reproduced.

Trace the implications of a learner's answer until it contradicts another belief they hold, which forces consistent theory-building and demands deeper thought about the error than correct-answer or process feedback; it is especially useful for getting learners to abandon wrong hypotheses because they discover the inconsistency themselves.

When learners appeal to the teacher's authority or to a textbook for the answer, decline to supply it, say you may be wrong, and turn the question into an experiment or measurement the learner performs — having them decide what to measure before measuring it.

Suspend the current goal when an answer reveals a misconception, pursue the correcting subgoal, and return to the original goal once it is repaired; treat a learner's non sequitur as usable material for reviewing terminology or opening the next topic rather than as noise to suppress.
Tell learners that practice items resemble the test items and that consulting the answer before responding may leave them unable to recall the information when tested.
Accompany formal statements of a generality with questions that direct attention and force processing rather than allowing the learner to read past them.
Treat understanding as a family of six facets of transfer rather than a single goal, and deliberately develop them all when transfer is the aim.

Define transfer as using what one knows creatively, flexibly, and fluently in a different setting on one's own — not plugging in previously learned knowledge — and treat it as necessary because only a small fraction of any field can be taught.

Recognize that transfer depends on learning with understanding rather than memorizing facts or following a fixed procedure, and that covering too many topics too quickly may hinder both learning and subsequent transfer.
Make transfer likely by design rather than leaving it to luck or disposition, which requires explicit instruction in how to transfer plus assessments that constantly demand it.

Practise the second, Socratic direction of transfer as well — interrogating prior knowledge with why is that so, what justifies it, what is the evidence, what is assumed — so learners learn to distinguish knowledge from mere belief.

Treat evidence of misunderstanding as valuable feedback signifying an attempted transfer, and respond so as to reward the attempt without reinforcing the mistake or dampening future transfer attempts.

Make preparing students for flexible adaptation to new problems and settings a major goal, using transfer as an index of adaptive learning, since disconnected facts are insufficient and organizing information into a conceptual framework allows greater transfer.

Define understanding through observable, discipline-appropriate performance—such as explanation, adaptation, application, or changed action—and assess whether formal knowledge transfers beyond stock answers.
Set stage-appropriate levels of understanding and use SOLO to distinguish relevant detail from integration, coherent relation, and transfer to broader domains.

Recognise verbal information as an enabler of transfer: possessing information about one domain makes an analogy to another possible, after which cognitive strategies and intellectual skills can be brought to bear and new knowledge generated.
Promote transfer through an authentic new use of a learned strategy, and contextualize examples and diagnostic nonexamples with learner-relevant but coherent subject matter.
Teach strategic far-transfer skills as adaptable strategies, never as an invariant step sequence, because each work situation differs.
Identify the big ideas that give meaning and connection to discrete facts and skills, use them to prioritize the learning, and show students why those ideas are worth having.
In skill-focused courses, name the big ideas that govern wise use of the skill and give them plan time, rather than relying on discrete strategy instruction alone.

Do not equate understanding with progressive method or coverage with tradition: subject-matter knowledge is required for understanding and traditional approaches often produce it, so expand and target the teaching repertoire to fit the goal instead of adopting one tactic exclusively.

Make the design answer the learner's own questions from the start — how to read the material, what to look for, how to prepare, how to tell whether the work is effective, and what performance it heads toward — because opaque priorities produce confusion that students feel and teachers do not see.

Treat an understanding as a pattern inferred and projected onto the facts rather than contained in them, so different people may legitimately see different patterns and argue about which description is best.

Teach and assess pattern recognition explicitly, so students come to treat a new problem as a variant of problems and techniques they already know, through problem solving with big ideas and transferable strategies rather than plugging in formulas.
Awaken understanding by confronting students with a real problem for thought rather than a highly cued exercise in which what to plug in is unambiguous.

Justify unpacking pragmatically: since all the facts and skills of a topic can never be covered, clustering the specifics under big ideas and core tasks lets them — including what standardized tests assess — be taught in the context of exploring the larger ideas.
Make the chosen priorities visible to learners, so every student can say what is most important here, how the pieces connect, what to attend to most, and what the few bottom-line priorities are.
Use big ideas as conceptual Velcro that connects the dots, establishes learning priorities, and helps facts and skills stick together and stick in memory.
Identify a few big ideas and design carefully around them, resisting the temptation to teach everything of possible value for each topic.
Choose big ideas for their power to explain phenomena, which is what lets a small set of them survey a whole field.

Point understandings and essential questions beyond basic knowledge and skill to the core of the subject, because learning that does not reach what is vital about an idea yields abstract, alien, uninteresting lessons.

Test a candidate big idea against five criteria — it gives a focusing conceptual lens, it connects and organizes many facts and experiences as the linchpin of understanding, it points to what is at the heart of expert understanding, it requires uncoverage because its meaning is not obvious, and it transfers horizontally across subjects and vertically through later courses and out of school.

Judge an idea big by pedagogical power rather than intellectual scope: it must let the learner make sense of what came before and make unfamiliar ideas seem more familiar, functioning as a conceptual tool rather than another fact or a vague abstraction.

Recognize the eight forms a big idea takes in practice — concept, theme, ongoing debate or point of view, paradox, theory, underlying assumption, recurring question, or principle — and treat how it is framed as critical rather than a matter of style, framing it as what the learner should come to understand about it.

Do not present big ideas as settled facts, which makes them harder to grasp; they function as guiding conjectures subject to refinement as learners learn more, not as definitions to be memorized and filed away.

Require students to revisit the big ideas repeatedly and move gradually toward their core, and to ask and re-ask questions about those ideas in action, since an idea that works for a while can later prove inadequate.

Reject the belief that a skill-focused course contains no big ideas as confusing the purpose of the teaching with the means, since fluency is the wise use of many skills grounded in clear ideas about their value, why a skill works or fails, and when to use it.
Look for the big ideas of a skill-focused course in four places — the value of the skill, the underlying concepts, matters of strategy including when to use it, and the theory of why it works.

Teach that a working theory binds disparate and counterintuitive facts into a coherent account that predicts and illuminates, and that a theory wins over rivals by explaining, ordering, and predicting better — not by being obvious or cataloguing more facts.
Build units around questions, issues, and problems that demand student theories and explanations, as problem-based learning and minds-on science programmes do.
Give students substantial latitude in defining the problem or task if they are to relate their own ideas and experiences to it.

Teach students that their job is to uncover what lies beneath the facts and question them for meaning, since meaning cannot be taught but must be fashioned by the learner through artful design and effective coaching.

Interrogate the content deliberately so students see key understandings as products of connection and inference, since leaving content unexamined yields a hodgepodge of unprioritized facts that feel like random opinions.

Give students work that lets them have an insight equivalent to the one felt by the scholar who first reached the understanding, since that is how the pioneer came to understand — by asking questions and testing ideas.

Define an understanding as an important inference drawn from the experience of experts and stated as a specific useful generalization that uses discrete facts to focus on larger concepts and both derives from and enables transfer.
Remember that students can answer recall questions correctly without understanding, and that having lots of knowledge does not mean being able to use it.
Make visible to students and teachers how adults beyond school actually use or fail to use what is taught, and how discrete lessons pay off in higher-quality performance on worthy tasks.

Require a learning plan to be both engaging — thought-provoking and pulling learners into worthy intellectual effort centred on big ideas, not merely enjoyable — and effective, paying off in substantive value-added learning the students themselves recognize.

Make the goals clear to students, not merely to the teacher — demystifying the big ideas, essential questions, desired performances, and evaluative criteria — and supply a rationale identifying what is most important, what is not, and why it is worth learning.
Transform abstract key ideas into intelligible practical tasks and criteria the student can grasp as soon as possible, so the work is purposeful from the student's point of view.

Aim to tap intrinsic motivation rather than pandering to students' likes or making them fear bad results, on the principle that the best way to create interest is to render the subject worth knowing — making the knowledge usable beyond the situation in which it was learned.

Build understanding from an iterative mix of well-designed experiences, reflection on them, and targeted instruction in light of those experiences and the goals, since a big idea is a useless abstraction without an experience base in which it clarifies the experience.

Address the Why? and So What? questions early and often when teaching for understanding, and reject the belief that all basic facts and skills must be presented up front as not how effective long-lasting learning works.

Give the student experience with the phenomena that created the need for the idea, not only with the idea, so big ideas are seen for what they are — mental models that solve problems rather than facts.

Use the content dichotomy to route method — facts, discrete knowledge, definitions, the literal, the self-evident, discrete skills, and algorithms one way; concepts and principles, systemic connections, connotations, symbolism, the counterintuitive, strategy, and heuristics the other.

Do not sequence all discrete content before the conceptual: deriving understandings inductively requires the grist of particular facts and understanding facts requires seeing the problems that make them relevant, so the two work as a double helix requiring cycles of each teaching type with enough knowledge to get going without boredom or overwhelm.

Remember that discrete content is old understanding so internalized it has become fact, so advanced students apprehend by direct instruction what costs the less experienced great constructive labour — and that teachers, long past being novices, lose empathy for the objective difficulty of new ideas and are then most prone to covering content inappropriately.
Begin with challenging problems to develop understanding inductively whole-part-whole, as mathematics teachers in top-performing nations do.

Avoid beginning a course in a remote past unmoored from contemporary events, learner interests, overarching questions, and specific tasks, which makes students far less likely to do the subject or grasp the big ideas that transfer.

Negotiate the big-ideas-versus-specifics dilemma explicitly, since focusing on big ideas risks leaving students without essential know-how while focusing on discrete information leaves little meaningful learning or ability to apply it.

Answer how big a big idea should be only in relation to course and programme goals, letting the most conceptually general ideas anchor whole courses and programmes because no single unit could do them justice.

Consider building a whole school or programme on a small set of questions cast as habits of mind — whose viewpoint, how do we know and how reliable is the evidence, how are things causally connected, what is new and what is old, and so what — asked in every class and subject.

Pose the same recurring problem on the same messy data set each year, or one basic problem supporting answers at several levels of sophistication, which differentiates among students far better than items based on discrete facts and skills.
Hold that education should be useful and that it is useful because understanding is useful.

Consider leaving the so-called basics aside for a while and concentrating attention on what is not known — teaching the still-imponderable puzzles before the fundamentals — and treat every topic as requiring motivation, since the student's question of why they must learn this is thoroughly justified.

Take seriously the hypothesis that any subject can be taught effectively in some intellectually honest form to any child at any stage, since the basic ideas of the sciences and the basic themes of life and literature are as simple as they are powerful and command of them requires continual deepening through progressively more complex use.
Recognize that basic ideas are out of reach of the young learner only when put in formalized terms before the learner has understood them intuitively and had a chance to try them out.

Organize subject matter to move from problem to problem so knowledge increases in depth and breadth, moving between the known and the problematic — for without that movement no problems arise and problems are the stimulus to thinking — with the teacher designing related challenges so learning produces new ideas that ground further experiences.

Reject the hidden assumption that everything to be learned must be taught and that teaching key facts is what causes learning, since much of what students learn comes from well-designed work and their own effort to understand.

Note that advocating a rich body of shared factual knowledge does not entail teaching those facts didactically — an extensive curriculum can be delivered in a formal or informal school and must be paired with intensive study, since the mental models that make isolated facts cohere come only from detailed intensive study and experience.

Treat overly didactic teaching as a major cause of the documented student misunderstanding, since big ideas are abstract or counterintuitive to the naive learner and need intensive uncoverage, and define the job of teaching as optimizing student learning of what is worthy rather than covering a book or teaching, testing, and hoping.

Teach students to extract underlying themes and principles from their learning experiences and learn in multiple contexts, which is what develops flexible understanding of when, where, why, and how to use knowledge.

Treat big ideas as the meaningful patterns that connect the dots of otherwise fragmented knowledge and as the building material of understandings, and as linchpins without which students are left with easily forgotten fragments even when highly knowledgeable about facts.
Make the teaching theory shaping the learning environment explicit, then use evidence and a coherent framework to diagnose problems and adapt responses to local learners and constraints.
Keep programme and course outcomes few, integrated, relevant, and manageable; each must state what learners will newly do and how well, while grouping compatible topics under common performances.

Take the six categories of significant learning — foundational knowledge, application, integration, human dimension, caring, learning how to learn — as the goal-setting frame, each carrying a distinct value: a base for other learning, usefulness, intellectual power, human significance, energy, and continued learning.

Have students construct knowledge themselves and represent its structure — for instance by mapping the relationships among a unit's concepts — because self-construction produces meaningful rather than rote learning and surfaces that others may organize the same concepts differently.
Make students do during the course whatever the teacher wants them to be able to do with the subject after it.

Place an authentic practicum early rather than only at the end, because using ideas while learning them shows students the relationship between theory and practice and makes them see why the later courses in the curriculum are needed.

Build the thematic structure from four to seven major concepts, issues, or themes, sequenced so each builds on the last — chronologically, simple to complex, or fundamentals first — with the test being whether a student who understands those topics has a good grasp of the subject and a foundation for future learning.

Make how-knowledge-is-constructed visible by having students analyze the same material through several disciplines' methods and then close each unit by discussing both what was learned and how it was learned.

Consider deliberately delaying foundational knowledge until students have a strong internal sense of what they need to know and why, by first surfacing their own beliefs and assumptions and having them generate the key questions before the literature is introduced.

Make the primary criterion for evaluating teaching whether a major proportion of the students had a significant learning experience, with teacher expertise, lecturing ability, and rapport as important but secondary.
Sequence the four to seven major ideas so they build on one another and, where possible, culminate in a project that integrates them.
Connect selected facts into accurate conceptual structures so learners can reason with them and transfer them beyond the original classroom context.

Aim the design at aiding the learning of the individual student, not at mass opinion change or diffusion of information; grouping learners does not change the fact that learning occurs within each member.

Plan a lesson in four steps: classify its objectives by learning type, list the instructional events needed, choose a medium capable of providing those events, and write prescriptions incorporating the appropriate conditions of learning for how each event will be accomplished — allocating events among learner, materials, and teacher.

Structure a course of study on its intellectual skills, because they determine what the student can do and so define the learning outcomes, and because they build on each other predictably, which makes them the most useful model for sequencing.

Treat students' attitudes toward attending, cooperating, attending to communications, and toward learning itself as of great significance in determining how readily they learn, and expect general learning principles to apply across attitudes because all of them function to affect approaching or avoiding.

Gain attention by stimulus change or, more fundamentally, by appealing to the learner's interests — and accept that no standard content can be prescribed because every student's interests differ, so skill at gaining attention rests on insightful knowledge of the particular students.

Let the materials and the learners carry more of the events in higher grades: where successive units are structurally similar the objectives may be evident and need not be communicated, and for reasonably well-motivated students no special provision for controlling attention may be needed.

Hold both teacher-led and mediated lessons to the same four themes: classify objectives by the taxonomy of learning outcomes, sequence them to take account of prerequisites, include the appropriate events of instruction that apply to all domains, and incorporate into those events the particular conditions of learning relevant to the objectives' domains.

Have students number the discrete points in a passage and elaborate each to themselves by associating it with familiar ideas, elicit the performance without word-for-word repetition, and verify learning and retention in meaning units rather than verbatim wording.
Represent essential mental operations and decision branches, teaching decision criteria only when learners lack them and showing every materially different path unambiguously.

Have learners formulate the generalities themselves from observation of varied cases, and let questions supply the focus and direction of the instruction, since the aim is depth of processing and the development of higher thought processes and independence of thought rather than content knowledge alone.
Attach supporting information about real-world uses, history and manufacture at remember level to the lesson whose principles they depend on rather than teaching them as separate topics.

Use theories as analytic instruments as well as design guides: they supply a systematic way of conceptualizing a situation and identifying the conditions and variables most pertinent to effective, efficient and enticing instruction, and can reveal that different problems share common features and possibly common solutions.

Write curriculum as a blueprint derived from desired results — what the learner should have achieved on leaving, what they must do to achieve it, and what the teacher must do to bring it about — rather than as a list of topics, facts, and skills.

Recognize that big ideas, core tasks, and developmental rubrics are not sufficient to build a powerful curriculum: scope and sequence matter far more in a macro framework than many educators realize, and cultivating reflectiveness — leading learners to redefine, reshape, and reorder what they met — is one of the great problems in devising curricula.
Take the teacher's philosophy of teaching as given while designing a specific course and shape the design around it, reserving examination and revision of that philosophy for the longer term.

Build an instructional curriculum map by starting from the target objective and asking what other objectives — essential or supportive — relate to its attainment, connecting same-domain objectives with solid lines and marking cross-domain links so the domain shift is recognised, because it implies different conditions of learning will be needed.

Write a lesson plan containing the objectives, the list of instructional events, the media, materials, and activities by which each event is accomplished, and notes on the teacher roles and communications required.

Carry on the lesson planning sheet the objective and its outcome-domain classification, the instructional events to be employed, the media, materials, and activities accomplishing each event, and notes on teacher roles and activities as prescriptions — writing the script from the sheet afterwards.

Separate assessment from evaluation: assessment gives and uses feedback against standards to enable improvement, evaluation is summative and credential-related, so not everything assessed needs a grade.

Test Stage 2 against its standard — the assessments are fair, valid, reliable, and sufficient; understanding is exhibited through authentic performance tasks judged by criterion-based tools; varied formats supply additional evidence; and assessment feeds back to students and teachers as well as evaluating.

Watch for the tell that an assessment misses the point of the unit — a grade turning on effort rather than on the key ideas, or testing what is easy to test rather than the deeper goal — and treat grading-driven assessment as a cause of students focusing on grades rather than learning.

Treat performance assessment as a necessity rather than a luxury, because ordinary usage says a learner understands only if they can teach, use, prove, connect, explain, or defend it — which quizzes and short-answer tests can only suggest.

Note that all formal tests are standardized but an assessment is not: the administrator may vary the questions, tasks, order, and time allotted in order to be satisfied the results are fair, valid, and reliable.
Separate assessment into criteria, evidence selection, and judgement, and involve learners in each where doing so develops assessment literacy and professional quality judgement.
Treat criteria and standards as the precondition for the rest of educative assessment: feedback, forward-looking assessment, and self-assessment cannot be done properly without them.

Accept that beyond foundational knowledge and application the available assessment procedures are valid but less consistently reliable, and separate what is assessed for feedback from what is graded — caring and human-dimension goals may be highly desirable yet unsuitable as a basis for the course grade.

Combine the four institutional levers rather than picking one: professional development inside the evaluation system supplies incentive and time, learning-centered teaching evaluation focuses attention, a development center supplies ideas, and prepared students supply cooperation and reward.

Change the assessment procedures themselves if assessment is to enhance learning as well as audit it, using clearer criteria and standards as the lever that makes grading an integral part of the educational process.
Derive assessment directly from the statements of the objectives, which describe the domains from which observations and test items are drawn, and measure outcomes criterion- (objective-) referenced.

Distinguish learner assessment from instructional evaluation, using formative assessment to improve learning, staged formative evaluation to revise development, and independent summative evaluation to support post-completion decisions.

Gather evidence of understanding by many methods over time — observations and dialogues, quizzes and tests, performance tasks and projects, and student self-assessments — with far more weight on formative and performance assessment than is typical.

Separate Stage 2 evidence into authentic performance tasks with explicit judging criteria and provision for self-assessment, and other evidence such as quizzes, prompts, observations, homework, and journals.

Craft assessments to evoke transferability — whether students can take their learning and use it wisely, flexibly, and creatively — since understanding is a flexible performance capability that copes with ambiguous challenges not arriving as a cue.

Translate the complex processes and performance mastery that published standards demand into actual programme and course objectives, since educators have been slow to do so and student performance suffers for it.
Develop the understanding behind a skill through activities other than exercising the skill itself, such as analysing exemplars and critiquing real cases.
Give students firsthand knowledge of how disciplinary understandings are built and refined from the inside, since that is what education for autonomous adult intellectual performance requires.

Treat the test of understanding as appropriate application of concepts and principles to newly posed questions rather than repetition of learned information or performance of mastered practices, using new problems followed by open-ended interviews or careful observation as the best evidence.
Make performance-based learning that culminates in authentic tasks the spine of the application facet, supplemented by conventional tests rather than replacing them.
Teach and assess self-reflection deliberately, including ongoing self-assessment of intellectual performance and explicit attention to how knowledge differs from belief and opinion.

Reach a curricular understanding by scholarly method — consider the matter in light of what experts say, reach one's own understanding, submit it to review, then hold it while staying open to revision — and owe students both the experts' understandings and practice in reaching, verifying, and criticizing them.

Check what a task actually required the student to do, since an assessment can produce evidence of a lesser achievement than the standard it claims to measure, and work prepared at home yields inadequate evidence of what the student can do unaided.

Recognize that an activity capturing imagination can still yield little in the way of big ideas given the time available, and that an exam format can contradict the stated course goal — a failure of alignment rather than of item quality.

Build assessment as a scrapbook rather than a single snapshot — evidence gathered along the way by varied methods and formats — because understanding develops through ongoing inquiry and rethinking rather than arriving at one end-of-instruction moment.

Place each assessment on the continuum from informal checks through quizzes, tests, and open-ended prompts to performance tasks and projects, noting how they vary in scope, time frame, setting, and structure.

Base assessments of understanding on real problems rather than exercises using discrete facts in isolation, since all doing of a subject involves problem solving, and note that nearly every conventional test is a set of exercises requiring only the correct move on cue.

Treat selected-response formats as generally insufficient and sometimes misleading evidence about understanding, and prefer oral assessments, concept webs, portfolios, and constructed-response items that let students show their work and reveal their thinking.
Use self-assessment as the only route to full insight into how sophisticated and accurate students' views are of the tasks, criteria, and standards they must master.

Build in portable self-knowledge devices — the same question as first and last assignment with a progress postscript, portfolio review with reflective prompts, a dispassionate postscript on strengths and gaps, and self-assessment against the grading rubric with its accuracy counting for a small part of the grade.

Include the explanation facet in any task targeting the other five, since the assessor needs to know why students performed as they did and what justifies the approach, and require reflection, explicit self-assessment, and self-adjustment with reasoning made evident.
Avoid the common pattern of relying on one or two assessment types and concentrating on the curriculum most easily tested by multiple-choice or short-answer items.

Reject the misconception that reform requires exclusive reliance on authentic assessment: objective quizzes, tests, and observation checklists often suffice for discrete knowledge and skill, and method choice should follow the evidence needed with no philosophical axe to grind.

Reject the twin assumptions that evidence gathering requires formal summative testing and that everything assessed must be graded, since ongoing formative assessment is what reveals understanding and misunderstanding.

Use cheap recurring checks — the one-minute essay on the big point learned and the main question remaining, and a routine of student-brought written questions discussed and summarized — to get immediate feedback on the extent of understanding and to make inquiry the class structure.

Count evidence of understanding as coming from a variety of formal and informal assessments across a unit — observations, dialogues, quizzes, tests, tasks, projects, self-assessments — not only end-of-teaching tests or culminating tasks.

Treat testing what is easy to test rather than what is most important as a design failure, and recognize that using assessment mainly for grading can itself drive students to focus on grades rather than learning.
Do not grade each piece without clear criteria and weighting and then average over time, since averaging initial and final comprehension misrepresents the learner's understanding.
Treat daily teacher checks rather than formal summative assessment as the vehicle through which understanding is actually monitored, given its iterative nature and the likelihood of misconceptions.

Ensure students understand what the learning eventually requires them to do, since knowing the topic, readings, activity directions, and that a test is coming does not suffice to focus attention and guide effort, and give them the key questions and performance specifics as early as possible.

Open a unit with the culminating challenge, its rubric, and a framing question so students have a purpose and context from day one, rather than distributing the material with a reading syllabus and grading requirements.
Ask where the learners are coming from — prior knowledge, interests, styles, talents, and possible misconceptions — which makes diagnostic assessment early in the learning plan essential.

Treat self-understanding as arguably the most important facet for lifelong learning, resting on honest self-assessment of what one does and does not understand, since the most successful people self-monitor and self-adjust proactively while working.
Train students to evaluate work the way exam readers are trained, which makes them more accurate peer reviewers and self-assessors and more inclined to think like assessors in their own work.
Treat self-assessment as a graded enabling ability in its own right, grading early attempts at complex performance on the student's self-assessment and improvement plan rather than on the product.

Introduce the assessment tasks, criteria, and rubrics early so students see the purpose of the particulars they are learning, and build peer review with time for revision into the culminating task rather than leaving feedback to the grade.

Use the textbook for what it does well — organizing information and supplying reinforcing exercises — and compensate for what it does poorly: framing work around ongoing questions and complex assessments, and offering different perspectives.
Assess aggressively while teaching, uncovering understandings and misunderstandings along the way rather than restricting assessment to culminating tasks and final exams.

Aim early at the desired performance even in simplified or scaffolded form, build performance progressively, revisit the fundamentals repeatedly, and eventually remove the cues and tools to see whether students can perform on their own.

Ask students directly on a recurring form whether the work focused on big ideas rather than unconnected facts, whether goals and quality standards were clear, whether they had enough freedom in how to reach them, and whether the assessment was a fair test of their learning.
Frame content-packed courses through strategy-flexible assessment tasks that cast the student in a real professional role with a real audience and product.

Require course syllabi of all teachers as a public document available to students, parents, and colleagues, specifying the essential questions and core problems, the core performances, the rubrics and scoring systems, a justification of assessment and grading policies against goals, a week-by-week calendar of learning goals rather than topics, and built-in flexibility to adapt to feedback.

Start a team with concrete moves — unpacking standards into understandings and essential questions, prioritizing standards and textbook content with the three-tier tool, developing core performance tasks and common rubrics, jointly evaluating student work to select shared anchors, and analysing achievement data to target intervention and action research at diagnosed weaknesses.

Pair the performance tasks and other evidence with explicit student self-assessment and reflection items, including reflection on whether the student's own behaviour changed over the unit, and list Stage 3 activities in sequence coded to the WHERETO element each serves so the plan is auditable.

Build the rethink-and-revise element into an ordinary assignment through peer assessment against a criteria list followed by permitted revision, and model how to read and interpret a technical artifact before students practise on real examples rather than assuming the skill from a description.

Place an academic prompt between an authentic task and a short-answer quiz — an open-ended written performance test that is not authentic because school constraints bind time, resources, and consultation.

Treat assessment in its root sense of sitting beside — thoughtful observation, disinterested judgment, and clear helpful feedback — and balance techniques because each is limited and prone to error, remembering that strengths and weaknesses can be assessed without placing a grade on the performance.

Distinguish five kinds of desired result — declarative knowledge, skills and processes, understandings, habits of mind, and attitudes — and cast them in measurable terms despite their complexity, since any valid assessment measures the degree to which the learner's work hit the target.

Note that most real problems are ill structured and most test items are not, so well-structured items validly assess elements of knowledge but not the ability to judge which knowledge and skill to use when.

Focus an outcome-based approach on desired outputs rather than inputs — asking what students will know and be able to do as a result rather than which methods and materials to use — and require agreement on the specific measures, criteria, and standards to determine whether outcomes were attained.

Distinguish a performance assessment, which involves more than one test and may include surveys, interviews, observations, and quizzes, from a performance test, and note that in a test of performance the student must put it all together under ill-structured or unpredictable conditions rather than recall isolated bits.

Define accurate self-assessment as understanding what one does not understand with clarity and specificity, and recognize that understanding is not simply received — ways of thinking and categorizing are projected onto situations and inevitably shape what is understood.

Meet the WHERETO elements as specified — students themselves can say where the work is headed, why, what their obligations are, and by what criteria they will be judged; explore-and-equip supplies both experiences to pursue leads and instruction that equips for the final performance; rethink digs deeper through the facets and guides self-adjustment on feedback; evaluate involves a final self-assessment identifying remaining questions and future goals; and tailor differentiates without compromising the goals.
Design from explicit learning outcomes, require learners to enact the corresponding performances, and align activities and assessment to the same forms of learning at course and programme levels.
Make assessment reveal the depth, structure, and relationships in understanding rather than sort students or reward isolated reproduction; redesign incentives that permit low-level shortcuts.
Investigate teaching through an iterative evidence cycle: frame an observable learning problem, use theory and student evidence to plan a change, apply it, evaluate results, and revise.
Prepare learners for independent learning by giving meaningful choices and teaching them to monitor progress, identify error patterns, and adjust their own strategies.

For every outcome, decide whether learners must know about, act with, or integrate knowledge; teach and assess professional application directly, increasing functioning emphasis as practice approaches.

Separate judging each performance from combining evidence into a final grade; use explicit qualitative categories for integrated learning and calibrate their highest standard progressively across programme stages.
In large classes, establish stable peer support, gather rapid formative evidence, and embed work-along or note-revision activity so learners' reasoning becomes visible.

Use self-assessment, peer assessment, critical-incident reflection, diaries, and portfolios as structured activities for developing professional self-evaluation, not merely for assigning marks or archiving experience.
Use authentic assessment backwash deliberately: make anticipated tasks represent the outcomes so strategic preparation rewards complete, well-reasoned learning rather than superficial mark tactics.

Choose assessment format by the performance it can validly elicit: use extended prose for structured higher-level declarations, objective items for suitable narrow outcomes, and timed exams only when speed, breadth, accuracy, or secure conditions matter.
If an examination is retained, design it for integrated understanding, prepare learners for efficient resource use, and supplement convergent questions with routes for relevant divergent evidence.
Moderate essay assessment by clarifying relevant criterion families, defining grade-level performances, calibrating on shared samples, and resolving disagreement through evidence-based discussion.

For large classes, choose rapid formats that still elicit intended structure or functioning, and use group evidence only with visible contribution, whole-task understanding, individual reflection, and safeguards.
Calibrate self- and peer assessment through explicit criteria, examples, discussion, and practice; moderate more heavily for novices, divergent work, and consequential decisions.

Evaluate alignment with targeted questions about outcomes, standards, activities, and assessment, triangulate across consultation and learning evidence, and orient learners explicitly when system-wide change alters their expected role.
Use student questionnaires formatively for specific course decisions and triangulate them with learning evidence; do not equate charisma, liking, or generic ratings with teaching effectiveness.

Map each activity to its primary and secondary outcomes, then make retained lectures active, use tutorials for varied application, and align supplementary support with both disciplinary difficulty and self-learning capability.
Use rapid-response questions and brief unresolved-point notes to expose understanding in large classes, then close the loop while teaching can still be adjusted.

Assess collaborative learning through preparation, relevant literature, substantive contribution, and shared problem solving, and structure discussion around reasoned agreement, disagreement, questions, solutions, and implications.

Use outcome-indexed learning logs to make learners track how activities affected learning and to keep instructors explicit about weekly outcomes; pair collaborative fieldwork with individual reflection when both forms of learning matter.

Permit learner-prepared study aids when selecting and organising knowledge supports higher-order examination performance, and reserve high standards for coherent original analysis, synthesis, and relevant understanding.

Adapt constructive alignment to local context while preserving its core relationship: derive performance outcomes from course aims, select declarative and functioning complexity deliberately, and use each outcome's verb, content, and context to align activity and assessment.

Link design components to each other rather than adopting them singly, because the power of an instructional idea comes from its connection to the others — experiential work paired with reflective dialogue, authentic assessment paired with self-assessment.

Build educative assessment from its four components — forward-looking assessment, criteria and standards, self-assessment, and FIDeLity feedback that is frequent, immediate, discriminating on clear criteria, and delivered supportively — because together they let students begin monitoring their own learning.

Give students practice at self-assessment inside the course, because the criteria are new to them and because after the course they are the ones primarily responsible for judging whether their own work is worthwhile.

Write assessment tasks forward-looking rather than backward-looking: instead of asking whether students got topics X, Y, and Z, put them in a situation where people actually use that knowledge and require them to act with it.

Build self-assessment capability in three ordered steps — acquire or develop the criteria, practise applying them to other students' work, then apply them to one's own work and improve on that basis — because the ability does not develop automatically.

Evaluate the course and one's own teaching beyond the means of end-of-course ratings: collect at midterm as well as at the end so concerns can be addressed while those students still benefit, and draw on multiple sources — questionnaires, class or sample interviews, session recordings, patterns in test responses, and observation by a colleague or consultant.

Match the assessment procedure to the kind of learning: personal reflections, portfolios, and problem-based performance for learning how to learn; interest, attitude, or value questionnaires for caring; before-and-after self-confidence instruments and teammate reports for the human dimension; concept maps, interdisciplinary cases, and capstones for integration; and simulations, demonstrations, team projects, and case studies judged against clear criteria for application.

Start self-assessment with a public criteria-generating exercise: all groups display their artifacts, the class discusses and generates the criteria and procedure, every group assesses every artifact, and the grade reflects both the group assessments and the instructor's — and make the artifact one students must rely on later, which is what makes the exercise feel relevant.

Evaluate a redesign with colleagues who have assessment and data-analysis expertise, gathering student performance data, students' perceptions of their own performance, and student assessment of the course — treating student self-ratings as suggestive rather than decisive evidence.

Assemble the full authentic-assessment package for performance learning: real performance situations, recording, frequent oral and written teacher feedback, peer feedback, written self-assessment against the recording, and clear specific criteria and standards.

Diagnose perceived competence through observable behaviours — explaining complex material well, managing the classroom, answering questions, referencing significant works of others, communicating well, being able to do what is taught, and holding a broad base of information — since these are specific and often easy to change.

Plan the evaluation by naming the specific questions first — about goal achievement, the effectiveness of particular activities, and interaction with students — then identifying which sources can answer them: session recordings, student interviews or questionnaires, outside observers, and test results.
Interpret achievement results in terms of the knowledge and cognitive processes actually sampled by the assessment.
Distinguish recognition from recall in assessment design, and calibrate cues and learning-assessment similarity to the intended retrieval demand.
Infer an assessment's real cognitive demand from its questions, scoring criteria, and timing as well as its label, and flag speed when it may be construct-irrelevant.

Provide access to intellectually substantial material through conceptual bridges, paraphrase, examples, performance, and structured comparison rather than lowering expectations solely from prior attainment.
Before grading learner choice among project options, calibrate options for cognitive demand, workload, required knowledge, support, and scoring, and explain those differences before selection.
Plan long-developing concepts, strategies, and fluency across grades with deliberate introduction, revisiting, and increasing independence, recognizing that automaticity may remain context-bound.
At the start of a multistage task, provide the culminating performance, process, timeline, and scoring criteria, then have learners restate the criteria to verify usable understanding.
Use common criteria across self, peer, and teacher feedback; keep helping assessments ungraded, grade reusable process separately when it is an objective, and explain judgments with evidence.

Classify assessment purpose by how evidence is used: employ timely evidence for reversible instructional adjustment and stronger evidence for high-stakes judgment, linking feedback to revision before grading.
Build reusable assessment prototypes by knowledge-process combination, but recheck wording, content, point weights, and instructional-time proportions because small changes can alter the construct.
Assess only the taught portion of a long-range objective and label it partial evidence; where possible, choose assessment from worthwhile objectives rather than redefining aims around easy tests.

For consequential assessment, independently align objectives, taught substance, and assessed substance on both knowledge and process, while using only limited format practice to remove irrelevant unfamiliarity.

Prepare learners for performance assessment by teaching validated criteria, sharing the guide without answers, and practicing on structurally equivalent tasks while reserving comparable tasks for independent evidence.

Run formative evaluation in three levels — one-to-one trials with representative learners, a small-group tryout with six to eight students, then a field trial of the revised instruction with a whole class — using the one-to-one stage to surface structural and logistic problems by interview or think-aloud and the small-group stage to see how much help is requested so the lesson can be made more self-sufficient.
Assess verbal information by whether the learner can communicate it — an oral or written statement normally, and simple oral questions or pointing to pictures and objects in the early grades.

Recognise that text-based homework leaves practising the appropriate performance and judging its correctness to the learner, since the text can aid selective perception through bold print and headings and supply a meaningful context for encoding but nothing more — which is why an important part of studying is practising the performance, restating information in one's own words, applying a rule to examples, or originating solutions, rather than merely reading.

Measure productive thinking with items asking students to invent hypotheses, questions, and answers beyond the lectures and text — predicting consequences of an unusual event, writing an imaginative sentence using specified new concepts, stating a novel hypothesis, titling a data table, drawing conclusions from a graph — using ten to fifteen items and two raters, who agree highly after short training.

Recognise that assessing verbal information typically means measuring quantity — how much the student knows about a topic — with items drawn from a domain that may be precisely defined as a passage or loosely as the declarative knowledge expected from lectures, text, and references, while treating depth-of-knowledge measurement as awaiting further research even though prose analysis can distinguish main from subordinate ideas.

Understand what item-analysis refinement does to a test: discarding items most students pass and items few pass makes it increasingly measure problem solving and other cognitive strategies and, in part, intelligence rather than what was directly learned.

Make assessment with corrective feedback as frequent and regular as possible, since the more frequent it is the better the learning outcome — regularly scheduled quizzes after segments of study material being considered the most valuable feature of some computer-managed college courses, where computer assessment achieves a precision impossible for the teacher of a large group.
