Recognise that when recitation follows homework, control of attention, learning the objective, encoding, and corrective feedback are all left to the student during the homework — so good study habits become the determiners of effective learning.

Key diagnostic and placement tests to a sequence of objectives and key those objectives in turn to the materials available for each, held in files the students have learned to use and to return materials to — that chain is what makes an individualised classroom run.

Build college-level individualisation coarser than elementary: combine large-group lectures, smaller quiz sessions, and independent study economically, use tests to route students to the most appropriate activity, adopt mastery learning within the limits of academic-term policy, have students concentrate where progress checks show the most work is needed, make less use of small-step materials, and provide laboratory assistants for tutoring when other methods fail — yielding a precision intermediate between large-group and elementary individualised programs at reasonable cost.

Treat day-to-day mastery assessment as the informal probing every teacher does rather than as formal testing, distinguished not by formality of administration but by the preestablished criteria the teacher or student uses to judge when mastery has been achieved.

Make summative evaluation far more formal than formative: use carefully constructed attitude questionnaires that can be validly compared with the previous year's students, and assess mastery of each objective systematically to give a quantitative indication of the whole course's accomplishment.

Match the assessment method to each support variable — questionnaires for what parents do about homework, counts of books and reference sources for material availability, systematic observation schedules for classroom climate, and readily available records for class size or pupil-teacher ratio.

Measure feasibility of program parts by asking teachers to judge the appropriateness of materials for fast, medium, and slow learners, since such judgments support elimination or revision of program elements.
State the goal as observable, measurable, bounded learner performance with relevant content and tools, and validate its interpretation with colleagues and intended learners before analysis.

Use learner assessment to measure achievement, formative evaluation to improve work in development, and summative evaluation after completion to support adoption, maintenance, or adaptation decisions.
Diagnose recurring gaps with a common authentic task and cross-role review, and trace every resulting instructional goal to a specific evidence pattern.

Keep internal traceability in design records while presenting learner-facing aligned assessments without unnecessary codes, and use whole-task and subordinate-skill pretests to support fair branching.
Evaluate every learning event for meaningfulness, memorability, motivation, and measurable performance.

Interleave assessment with learning, define authentic criterion tasks from objectives, and prefer delayed real-performance evidence over immediate post-test recall when judging durable capability and behavior change.
Do not rely on learners to judge what they know: calibration correlations are near zero, self-assessment does not improve with seniority, and poor performers overrate themselves by 30 to 40 points.

Require additional instances of the performance beyond the first elicitation, both to establish that the learning has reasonable stability and to supply further practice, while recognizing that assessment is a testing prescription rather than an instructional one.

Have learners predict how many items they expect to get right before attempting them, give them the typical success rate of students who complete the segment, and provide a per-item scorecard, so the standard is personal, calibrated by a realistic norm, and visible.
Expect to adjust the design mid-course when feedback shows the desired results are at risk, rather than treating the plan as fixed.

Plan for adjustment in light of goals, feedback, and predictable problems, since a plan impervious to feedback is not a virtue and excellent results are unreachable without improved diagnostic skill and adaptive planning.
Handle design dilemmas by aggressively seeking feedback while working — try something, see how it works, and adjust against both the desired results and the design standards.
Hold the design as a plan that must stay flexible and change as it is implemented.
Plan within constraints, retain contingency for expected surprises, and spend limited resources on the improvements with greatest expected learning impact rather than on perfection.
Treat the framework as a conceptual scaffold with multiple entry points and design standards rather than a step-by-step recipe, since a prescriptive recipe is antithetical to good design.

Treat the value of the framework as residing in the process, template, tools, and design standards that make good results likely by design rather than in the backward-design idea itself, which is old.

Design at the unit level rather than the individual lesson, because a single lesson is too short to develop a big idea, explore an essential question, or support authentic application; let lesson plans flow from the unit plan.
Think like an assessor before designing lessons: frame the unit in terms of the evidence needed to document and validate the desired learning, not as content to cover or activities to run.

Start from an established content standard when one exists, then decide what students should take away from the unit, and name the desired understandings so teaching and limited class time focus on what is truly important.

Resist the natural jump to lesson and activity design before asking what performances and products the teaching must aim at, since designing only as an activity designer leaves any resulting understanding to luck.

Accept that no step-by-step recipe for unit design exists — design is more like graphic design or sculpture, reflecting the designer's own interests, talents, style, and resources — because instructional design contains irreducible uncertainty and not every aspect of thought and behaviour can be articulated.

Keep the unit as the design focus — small enough to guide day-to-day teaching, large enough to avoid isolated lessons — while designing course syllabi and programme frameworks backward with the same elements so they serve as a blueprint for all units and their connections.

Adopt the understanding-oriented lesson pattern — pose a complex thought-provoking problem, let students struggle, have various students present solutions, summarize the class's conclusions, then practise similar problems — in preference to the skill-acquisition pattern of instruct, demonstrate, then practise individually.

Adopt the lesson-study model in which small teams develop, teach, and refine one research lesson per year and share results at regional fairs, since attributing emergent problems to the group's lesson rather than the individual makes it possible for teachers to be critical while providing a benchmarking process for gauging one's own skills.
Set the local challenge as designing rich units that ultimately address all the standards while clearly signalling the priorities to students, not as designing a lesson per indicator.

Have students design a teaching and learning unit for the students one level behind them, since reasoning about goals, activities, and feedback for others simultaneously makes them conscious of those issues in their own learning while deepening their grasp of the content.
Use coherent unit-level planning to connect lessons to larger purposes, provide repeated practice for complex objectives, and preserve time flexibility for learning pace and unexpected events.
Keep immediate lesson planning and long-range design as separate tasks, and supply the products of long-range design (texts, guides, aids) to ease the teacher's immediate planning.

Apply the same design process at every scale — national curriculum project, course, unit, or single lesson — since the process has common features at all levels and every stage of any model falls into identifying outcomes, developing instruction, or evaluating effectiveness.

Design instruction differentially for each objective in a course, because a single course normally carries objectives of several kinds and the most important difference among them is that each requires a different plan for its achievement.

Group specific objectives into lessons rather than giving each its own, since teaching a single objective may take very little time even though each outcome type requires different conditions, and set lesson length by audience because attention span varies with age.

Design a lesson in order: first ensure the events of instruction are provided for, then classify the objectives and arrange the specific events in a sequence appropriate to attaining them, and only then write the content of the events as instructional prescriptions.

Accept that teachers often design as they teach, planning only in enough detail to be ready and improvising the rest, which is not entirely undesirable because it preserves flexibility to redesign on the spot in response to the situation and to learners.
Attend to a single-objective lesson's prerequisites and provide for transfer to subsequent objectives, since its purpose is to supply part of the instruction for the unit's integrated goals.

Design individualised instruction by the same planning processes as conventional group lessons — performance objectives, learning hierarchies, sequencing, instructional events, and conditions of learning all apply — since it is the delivery system that primarily distinguishes module design from lesson design.

Make lesson content depend on the learners' entry level as well as on the objectives and the terminal algorithm, state the assumed entry level explicitly, and expect an implementing teacher to adapt the design to their specific conditions.
Do not read a demonstration's variety of methods and delivery systems as a design recommendation: an integrated lesson would not use such variety, and it is present only to display the range.
Apply the depth-for-understanding apparatus only where in-depth understanding is genuinely the goal; going into depth on everything is neither possible nor desirable.
Treat designing for understanding as compatible with content standards and state testing, since most standards identify or imply big ideas meant to be understood rather than merely covered.
Subject designs to explicit design standards for quality control, and share validated designs through a common searchable repository instead of each designer working in isolation.

Design under the real constraints — external standards, student interests, developmental level, class size, prior achievement — while still being able to state the desired understandings independently of those constraints.

Give designers the design standards and models before the work starts, so the standards act as a performance target rather than an after-the-fact judgment — the same practice recommended for students.

Read content standards as an attempt to prioritize the work and avoid defining aims as hundreds of apparently equal discrete objectives taught and tested out of context, whatever the quality of specific standards.

Expect three recurring problems when planning from content standards — overload, the Goldilocks problem of standards too big or too small, and vagueness that different teachers interpret differently — and recognize that overload is a function of treating knowledge and skills as discrete and disconnected, not merely of their quantity.

Unpack standards into the big ideas and core tasks they contain: reframe an over-broad standard as a transferable generalization with a companion essential question, and satisfy a narrow fact-level standard as a particular case under that broader idea.

Convert goals and content standards into questions, which signals both what the big ideas are and that continued inquiry into their meaning is part of the learner's job, since naive thinking matures through provocative questions and performance challenges that test and refine ideas.

Reframe a content standard as a question that opens its underlying purpose, and treat knowledge and skill as the means of addressing questions central to the subject rather than as stuff to be covered.

Judge essentialness by examining the whole design — assignments, assessments, and envisioned follow-up — rather than the wording or even the designer's stated intent, treating it as a matter of alignment.

Expect content standards to vary widely in form — discrete lists, broad statements, so-called understandings that are actually facts, and unhelpfully vague statements — and operationalize any of them by pairing the standard with an explicit understanding statement and a derived essential question.

Earn understandings through carefully designed experiences that uncover the possible meanings of core content, since big ideas are unobvious and abstract and well-designed experience is the only way to make them real.

Treat standards as building codes and local design as architecture — the goal is not slavish compliance but something practical, pleasing, and stylish that also meets the codes — noting that most standards actually stress in-depth understanding and complex performance, so a big-idea focus with robust assessment makes meeting them likely.
Keep grades, transcripts, and admission standards, but require that the grade correspond to a valid assessment of understanding so the grading system can be articulated and justified.

Set a valid performance standard by asking at what level of performance the student would be appropriately qualified or certified, and lend the scoring substance and credibility by equating internal standards to an equivalent worthy level of achievement in the outside world.
Keep academic grades as evidence of learning quality and handle lateness or conduct through separate transparent processes.
Treat scale and constrained formats as design problems, but treat mandatory norm-referenced grading as a policy incompatibility when grades must certify individual outcome attainment.
Keep non-academic conduct out of the academic-quality grade unless that conduct is explicitly an intended professional outcome with published criteria.

Protect criterion-based outcome judgement from administrative constraints: separate relative selection from achievement, use valid supervised performances when invigilation is mandated, and convert qualitative grades to required numbers only after substantive judgement.

Prefer criterion-referenced grading against predefined standards using performances and portfolios, with continual assessment of instruction, over norm-referenced grading on a curve judged by end-of-course ratings.

Make self-grading workable by publishing the criteria with the assignment, taking a self-declared grade with justification, accepting it within one level of the teacher's, and requiring a conference and re-justification beyond that.
Make feedback discriminating by naming which criteria were met and which were not; a bare OK or a letter grade tells the student nothing they can act on.

Build the grading system to be fair and educationally valid: diversify the graded items because students differ in how they best show what they know, reflect the full range of goals and activities, and weight each item by its relative importance.
Grade at least one instance of every kind of learning the teacher wants students to retain, while leaving individual activities ungraded as needed.
Treat teaching as a client-centred design profession: the students are the primary end-users, and a design's effectiveness is judged by whether they achieved the desired learnings.

Treat shared design work as rich professional development in itself, since unlike one-size-fits-all sessions it concentrates on teaching and assessing specific content and yields tangible products of immediate value, with conversations focused on the profession's core questions.

Treat by design as meaning through thoughtful planning rather than accident, holding that what happens before the teacher enters the classroom may be as or more important than the teaching inside it, and use design standards so teacher work is assessed the way student work is — guiding review and validating designs.

Design service learning as a whole: pair living and working alongside the community with substantial theoretical reading and with journals, reflective essays, and frequent discussion, and have students give something back to the host community in a form that demands collaboration and creative work.

Design instruction as the whole set of events that support learning, allocating each event to whichever agent can perform it — teacher, materials, media, or the learner — rather than scoping the design to teacher behaviour.

Follow the same stages whether a team designs a curriculum or a teacher designs a course, up to lesson design — at which point teachers must consider what they personally bring and what role they will play, while designers of mediated materials must decide how to provide the needed activities in a preplanned lesson.
Clarify the desired results first, because without them there is no way to tell whether a design is appropriate or arbitrary, or to distinguish merely interesting learning from effective learning.

Remember that ambitious goals without more powerful learning experiences produce only frustrated expectations, and that a good design creates the possibility of a significant learning experience but is a necessary rather than a sufficient condition — it still has to be implemented.
Judge instructional theories and the designs built on them only by how well they facilitate learning for actual students, whatever rationale guides them.
Reject the content-first sequence — pick a topic, pick a resource, pick methods, invent the assessment last — as design by hope rather than by design.

Design the assessments before the lessons, because they act as teaching targets that define what students must understand and do, sharpen instructional focus, and settle which content deserves emphasis.

Reject a linear march through content when overarching questions and recurring tasks anchor the curriculum, since students cannot master complex ideas encountered only once; make the unit's flow iterative, with students aware of the need to rethink and the work following the trail back to the original ideas.

Treat sequence as a real design decision rather than a default, since the typical march through content — especially one dictated by the textbook's organization — is rarely the best choice for engagement or understanding.

Accept that content and methods can both be excellent while the course fails because the sequencing was wrong, making sequence as important as the quality of the elements — perhaps more so when engagement, understanding, and productivity are the criteria.

Before a formative review, agree its focus, evidence, feedback, and logistics; then use minimally disruptive observation, video, guides, or material review only insofar as each method fits that focus.

Do the analytic work long before the lesson begins, since what distinguishes a structurally analysed design is the precision of content selection and sequencing, its fit to learner need, and the validity of the supporting test items.
Recognize that a content-selection theory prescribes content and sequence but not method, and that the resulting design is only as complete and useful as the analysis it derives from.
Make Stage 1 an act of prioritization rather than an undifferentiated goal list, since there is always more content than the available time can address.
Read the Stage 2 criteria off the Stage 1 goal's own wording, since any explicit goal implies its criteria before a particular task is designed.

Scope the framework honestly — it covers the elements of the goal of understanding and how to design for it, leaving the wider change management of preparing students, parents, and staff outside its remit — while treating its design argument as applying across the whole K-16 range.
Treat specific context as always design-relevant: class size, course level, length and frequency of meetings, and delivery mode all bear on the key decisions.

Expect on first application to discover that what you previously judged effective teaching for understanding was not, and that specifying the intended understandings and what they look like in assessment is harder than anticipated.
Treat inability to document a competence once the circumstances of testing are slightly altered as showing that understanding in any reasonable sense was not achieved.

Expect widespread weakness in understanding validity, and expect teacher-made tests to focus on accuracy of knowledge and skill rather than transferability, which is why performance assessment is needed for evidence of understanding.

Expect less telling to yield more and better learning when the assignments and assessments are well designed and the teaching is judicious, well timed, and goal directed, since many secondary and collegiate classrooms have too much front-loaded direct instruction rather than too little.

Expect a learning-how-to-learn goal to force a prior question the teacher has never had to answer explicitly — what counts as knowledge in this field — and settle that question before proceeding with the design.

Make goals and standards concrete as assessment evidence at the start of planning, rather than writing assessments near the end of the unit or borrowing publisher tests that may not measure the intended standards.
Expect favourite activities and projects to require modification in light of the evidence the targeted standards demand, rather than being carried over unchanged.

Accept that no assessment task is uniquely perfect for an understanding target while still specifying what counts as appropriate evidence, or the designer will settle for a factual test where only a complex inquiry with a defence of method and result would do justice to the standard.

Put the core task in Stage 1, since it is not a specific test but a summary of related performance demands across varying situations that embodies the key standards, and let it specify the conditions any Stage 2 assessment must meet so arbitrary projects are ruled out.

Allow entry at any stage — an existing unit, a key resource, a planned assessment — provided the result is coherent, and require the designer to justify even an apparently worthwhile text by linking it to specific purposes, big ideas, and standards.
Negotiate the individual unit against larger goals, since each unit must stand on its own as a logical design while honouring all local programme goals and content standards.
Assess learners against outcome-derived standards through direct performance where feasible, while allowing valid evidence of worthwhile unanticipated achievement.
Set objective specificity to its planning level, decomposing broad goals enough to guide units and lessons without fragmenting their integrated meaning.

Choose representative samples of objectives within each outcome domain at intermediate planning levels rather than listing complete performance objectives everywhere, while recognising the fuller procedure can be followed and is sometimes desirable.
Treat the first goal analysis as a draft; calibrate step size to learners and revise extraneous, misplaced, underspecified, or excessively detailed steps.

Discover and validate goal steps through the intended assessment, competent self-performance, multiple performers, workplace observation, expert and incumbent interviews, standards, and authoritative procedures.

When goal steps are unclear, draft the goal assessment and triangulate its required actions, cognition, and decisions through self-performance, multiple competent performers, workplace evidence, job analysis, and authoritative procedures.
Apply the backward-design logic regardless of learner or goal — including adult professional learning — by determining the evidence of attainment before planning activities.

Use a backward design template to build a productive mental model for planning that avoids activity-oriented and coverage-oriented curricula, which is particularly valuable for new teachers not yet reliant on a file of favourite activities or on textbooks.

Walk the talk by using backward design to plan the adoption of backward design, with administrators learning it by codesigning a unit with a teacher or by planning professional development with the same template.

Understand backward design as called backward only because many teachers begin with the means, and follow its order — desired results, then the evidence needed to determine they were achieved, then the enabling knowledge and skill, and only then the teaching — since objectives become the criteria by which materials, content, procedures, and tests are chosen.

Work backward in three moves: ask what learning should still be there and have value one or two years after the course, then what students would have to do to convince you they achieved it, then what they need to do during the course to do well on that.

Note the convergent evidence for backward design: an independently developed school-level model reaches the same principle — develop a good set of learning goals then design that quality into the experience — and its facets of understanding closely resemble the taxonomy of significant learning.

Separate instructional from non-instructional goals before designing, because some desired states of affairs cannot be reached by instruction at all, and make any global instructional goal more specific before attempting to design for it.
Work backward from the expected outcomes, beginning by identifying the human capabilities the instruction is to establish, rather than forward from the content to be covered.

Agree across teachers on the evidence that counts for a shared standard, since widely varying assessments make it impossible to tell which students achieved what and forfeit curricular coherence and reliable evaluation.

Reject both failure modes of standards writing — the too-global standard that gives no usable guidance on what to teach or assess, and the factlet standard that is measurable but misses the discipline's big ideas and signals that school learning is memorization.
Treat a nebulous standard as guaranteeing divergent interpretation by different teachers, which defeats the whole point of having standards.

Treat the documented courses as convergent support rather than proof: teachers who were not following this model arrived at consistent goals, activities, and results, and the sample's feedback-and-assessment component could not be analysed because published descriptions rarely report it.
Expect backward design to feel unnatural, awkward, and slow on first use, and do not treat that discomfort as evidence the method is wrong.
Do not treat use of the backward design process as sufficient: the design must additionally be coherent and focused on clear and worthy intellectual priorities.

Derive assessment evidence from the outcomes sought rather than treating assessment primarily as a means of generating grades, which is where backward design departs most sharply from conventional practice.

Test ideas against the backward design logic and standards while playing with them rather than filling the template box by box, which skips the revising and aligning a coherent plan requires; the best designers both play creatively with ideas and test them before and during use with students.
Keep a one-page view of the design so the whole can be grasped at once and alignment between Stage 1 goals, Stage 2 assessments, and Stage 3 activities can be checked quickly.
Write the template from the designer's perspective and treat Stage 3 as the job of translating those Stage 1 results into learning that is intelligible and engaging to the learner.

Shift the Stage 3 frame from what the designer wants to accomplish to who the learners are and what they need to reach the results and perform the tasks, treating the design as needing to be user-friendly as well as intellectually defensible.

Work the existing-unit entry point by placing current lessons and assessments in the template, checking alignment across the three stages, asking whether the lessons relate to the richest aspect of the goals, and revising to do justice to a clarified Stage 1.

Before broad rollout, build a shared need and conception among affected participants, translate it into outcomes, activities, assessment, and grading decisions, and align surrounding policies with the design.

Answer the five design questions in order — situational factors, the full set of learning goals, feedback and assessment, teaching and learning activities, and whether all components connect and support each other — rather than starting from content or activities.

Use a four-column worksheet — goals, feedback and assessment per goal, learning activities per goal, and resources — to produce a design that is more ambitious than the original yet internally cohesive and demonstrably doable.

Record in Stage 1 the established goals, the understandings phrased as "students will understand that", the predictable misunderstandings, and what students will know and be able to do — big ideas and discrete knowledge together.

Write Stage 1 essential questions as provocative questions that foster inquiry, understanding, and transfer, deriving them from the stated understandings so both together set the context in which the unit is nested.

Test Stage 1 against its standard — targeted understandings are enduring, transferable, at the heart of the discipline and in need of uncoverage; essential questions are provocative and arguable rather than inviting a pat answer; and valid unit-relevant knowledge and skills are identified.

Test Stage 3 against its standard — students know the goals, why the material matters, and the evaluative criteria; are hooked into the big ideas; get adequate exploration and equipping; get sufficient rethinking and revision on timely feedback; and evaluate and set goals, with the plan tailored and organized for engagement.
Begin Stage 3 by identifying the enabling knowledge and skills students need to demonstrate the targeted understandings in performance, treating teaching as enabling performance.

Do not assume that aiming at understanding daily means the goal is well understood; "understand" and "teach for understanding" are ambiguous terms that must be operationalized before they can guide design.
Keep the Stage 1 and Stage 2 questions categorically apart: Stage 1 asks what students should come away understanding, Stage 2 asks what performance and products would acceptably embody that goal.

Separate five distinct kinds of Stage 1 result — established goals, understandings, essential questions, knowledge, and skills — because several kinds of aim are always simultaneously in play and goals are less clear than they seem.

Name three kinds of Stage 1 knowledge and skill — the building blocks of the desired understandings, what the established goals state or imply, and what is needed to perform the Stage 2 tasks — and do not leave the enabling skills behind a complex performance unplanned, since stating the performance requirement neither prepares students nor makes the result fair.
Keep the field-level question of what the most important tasks and challenges are in Stage 1, distinct from the Stage 2 question of which specific assessment tasks students will face.

Ask in Stage 1 which questions students should eventually be able to address well, irrespective of whether they can handle them now, since the ability to ask and consider such questions is itself a desired result rather than a teaching ploy.

Disambiguate "students will understand how to": when it names a discrete skill it belongs in the Knowledge and Skill fields, and only when it names an array of skills requiring attention to underlying concepts does it denote an understanding.

Write Stage 1 for the designer rather than the learner: the desired understanding is a blueprint for building the learning plan, not text the student must recite, with the learner's own understanding revealed in Stage 2 and caused in Stage 3.

Differentiate to accommodate developmental needs, learning styles, prior knowledge, and interests while keeping the Stage 1 desired results constant for all students, since the standards and understandings are targets for everyone.
Identify prerequisite knowledge and skill by working back from the culminating task, keeping resultant knowledge in Stage 1 as the goal and weaving the prerequisites into the Stage 3 learning plan.
Act as a coach of the students' ability to perform with understanding rather than as a teller of one's own understanding from the sidelines.

Make coaching central when the goal is skill development while still facilitating understanding of the strategic big ideas, and use much facilitated inquiry when the goal is a counterintuitive idea — with lectures placed after the experiences to solidify learning.
Use the template to review existing units as well as to build new ones.

Track design status explicitly on the unit cover page — which template stages are complete, task blueprints, rubrics, directions, materials, accommodations, extensions — and review status from initial draft through peer review, content review, field test, validation, and anchoring.
Include performance-grounded assessment whenever understanding is the aim, because only performance evidence shows transfer.

Grade an assessment's transfer demand by the cueing it supplies — far transfer with no cues, near transfer with narrowing clues, recognition of which known rule applies, or mere direction-following — and use that scale to self-assess and peer review any task claiming authentic application.
Use mandated examinations only for performances they validly elicit and protect space for authentic project or direct-performance assessment of functioning knowledge.
Collect input and process measures as well as the measures that directly assess outcomes, since evidence of learning outcomes cannot be interpreted without them.
Verify that an external assessment validly represents target standards before interpreting low scores as a learner-performance gap.

Evaluate impact only after target learners can perform in context, gathering unobtrusive workplace evidence about need resolution, capability use, and performance change, then report it as decision evidence.
Repair relevance by grounding examples and practice in the authentic goal, use only fair taught distinctions in distractors, and provide immediate self-checkable feedback during embedded assessment.

Use design standards in three distinct roles — a reference checked periodically during design, criteria for self-assessment and peer review of drafts, and independent quality control validating completed designs before distribution.
Subject teacher-designed units and assessments to structured peer review, which improves the product, helps designers internalize the qualities of good design, and exposes them to alternate models.

Test your own assessment design once it is fleshed out, since few teachers do and such self-testing is key to better results and to fairness; peer review of assessments against design standards further improves quality.

Prefer design criteria generated by the participants themselves, since they are more credible and acceptable as a basis for making the traditionally private work of design public and subject to scrutiny.

Recognize the six entry points — content standards, desired real-world applications, a key resource or favourite activity, an important skill, a key assessment, and an existing unit — and check the emerging design routinely against the design standards whichever is used.
Establish a self-assessment and peer-review protocol against explicit design standards, which provides quality control while promoting continuous improvement of curriculum design.

Distinguish three kinds of standard — content standards for what students should know and do, performance standards for how well, and design standards for what worthy work students should encounter — and supply design standards locally, since most official documents identify only content standards.
Reject the norm that hard planning work implies a good design; substituting designer effort for design quality is exactly what explicit design standards exist to break.
Expect design reform to be difficult and to require constant revision, and to be particularly difficult for teachers who must unlearn prior practice.
Apply coherence as the overall design standard: the elements of all three stages must be aligned with one another, not merely defensible in isolation.
Read the three stages as the logic of the finished product, not as a step-by-step procedure; where the designer starts does not matter provided the result is coherent against that logic.
Provide scaffolds — prompts, organizers, idea sheets, and worked examples — to designers, because design work is genuinely hard and scaffolding raises the quality of the result.

Use authentic design-and-build projects to integrate intended professional performances, assess the several products needed to represent them, and require reconciliation between theoretical prediction and observed results.

Scaffold generative performance from transforming supplied examples to independent creation, support execution with concise criteria, and show multiple representative solutions when several answers are valid.
Expect routine use of the tools to build an internal mental template of the key ideas, after which explicit use of the tools becomes unnecessary.
Use intelligent tools that put abstract ideas and processes in tangible form and enhance performance on cognitive tasks, since routine use builds a mental template of their key ideas.

Choose a tool the prototyper already knows that can rapidly and faithfully represent the intended experience; check that templates, presets, or linear affordances are not silently selecting the pedagogy.

Expect even a highly detailed theory to leave many ways of implementing its prescriptions, supplying the context within which specific procedures are planned rather than the procedures themselves; a macro theory deliberately does not specify how instruction is presented, and the sequence it produces depends on the subject matter.
Test whether an idea is worth anchoring a unit by asking whether an authentic, lifelong need applies that knowledge.

Require both senses of enduring — the understanding has endured over time and across cultures because it proved important, and it should endure in the student's mind past the unit and the test — and run candidates through a worthiness filter of prompts about universality, underlying concept, and real-world application.

Qualify a task as authentic only if it is realistically contextualized, requires judgment and innovation on a relatively unstructured problem, asks the student to do the subject, and replicates situations in which adults are genuinely tested — with the learner having to figure out the nature of the problem and develop a plan rather than respond to a cue.

Choose teaching methods and resources last, asking which strategies will be most effective for reaching these targets with these particular students rather than which strategy is currently in favour, and let the textbook become a selectively used support rather than the primary resource.

Resist falling back on comfortable familiar techniques and instead ask which approaches, resources, and experiences the desired results actually require, testing every proposed activity including teaching against the particulars of Stages 1 and 2 regardless of the teacher's preferred style.

Choose approaches by what learning needs rather than what teaching finds comfortable, expecting the right proportions to be a ratio one is not in the habit of using, and knowing each preference's failure mode — overlecturing, underinstructing, confusing discussion, cut-off inquiry, overdrilling, or underdeveloped core skills.
Apply the self-knowledge facet to the teacher when planning, since teaching for understanding demands routine use of all three teaching types in ways that may challenge comfortable habits.

Treat the teacher's job as using resources so learners understand important ideas and can use knowledge in performance rather than as explaining the textbook, since making the textbook the course makes overlecturing more likely.

Take the comparative finding that covering fewer topics produces better results, driven by teachers whose stated aim is conceptual understanding and whose lesson goal is developing thinking rather than acquiring a specific procedure.
Treat course design as the highest-leverage change available to most teachers, and prefer redesign over exhortation, penalties, or polishing delivery when a teaching problem appears.

Locate the improvement target among the four aspects of teaching — subject-matter knowledge, design of instruction, teacher-student interaction, and course management — because subject knowledge is rarely the bottleneck, interaction is the bottleneck for some teachers, and design is the most common bottleneck of all.
Review mid-unit student work specifically for misunderstandings needing instructional attention, not only to award marks.
Probe beyond tests and discussion, because even the best students can appear to understand and then reveal significant misunderstanding once follow-up questions or application are required.

Build quick pre- and post-assessments targeting the key misunderstandings regardless of what other tasks are in use, using short scenarios that expose whether the learner grasps the underlying principle.

Insert a rethinking move by following authoritative guidance with a question that unsettles it, and collect group work products specifically to look for misunderstandings needing instructional attention rather than only to grade.

Direct struggling learners to complete as many items as they can unaided and then review the specific sections, and after scoring have successful learners work out why any missed item was wrong while others restudy and seek help from a teacher or another student.
Build each performance task with a real audience, purpose, and product, and include a constraint or modification that forces judgment, rather than asking for recall of the content.

Map the general type of performance implied by the goal before designing the particular task, since some performances such as comparing and contrasting or summarizing key ideas reveal understanding regardless of content.

Build a problem with a clear statement but few cues, several possible approaches, a needed strategy, and a realistically noisy setting with competing variables of audience, purpose, and criteria — unlike an exercise, whose setting is simplified so the only variable is the targeted skill.

Build authentic performance tasks with a real-world goal in a realistic context, a tangible product for an identified audience, and evaluative criteria and performance standards known to the student in advance.
Create products from ephemeral performances so the assessment is documentable and open to review and oversight in scoring.
Develop complex products iteratively through an initial plan, feedback against shared criteria, rehearsal or revision, and final production for an audience.

Distinguish an item that merely elicits recall of the stimulus material from one that elicits the target performance; only the latter satisfies the elicit-performance requirement, and concept performance must be elicited on previously unencountered instances as well as taught ones so classification rather than recognition is tested.
Write a complete performance objective that states the situation, the learned capability, the object, the action, and the tools or constraints, and communicate its essential elements to the learners.

Run each design stage as the same four-step cycle — start from the key design question, narrow by intelligent priorities, self-critique against explicit filters, and end with a product meeting the design standards.

Apply the stage-specific filters — big ideas and core challenges for Stage 1; validity, reliability, and sufficiency for Stage 2; engaging and effective on WHERETO for Stage 3 — to the considerations that feed each stage.
Apply the stage-appropriate filters — WHERETO for Stage 3, and focus on big ideas plus validity, reliability, and sufficiency for Stage 2.

Expect the design process to be always iterative, with designers revisiting what they are after, how to assess it, and how to teach it, and rethinking earlier units in light of later designs and results.

Separate genuinely distinct design-performance criteria without fragmenting an integrated whole, and make higher levels require relational understanding, critical judgement, and open-problem solutions rather than additional recall.

Run the design as a systems approach: begin with analysis of needs and goals, base each step's decisions on empirical evidence as far as it is available, feed each step's output into the next, and check each step against evidence fed back from later steps.
Expect the design process to be iterative and to require reworking earlier products in light of what later stages uncover, rather than running straight through from analysis to delivery.

Treat comprehension monitoring as a capability distinct from decoding and vocabulary, since knowing every word and following the sequence is compatible with not understanding; teach learners to notice when they are not getting it and to change strategy.

Teach comprehension monitoring as the capability of setting learning goals, estimating success against them, and selecting alternative strategies to meet them — students have been taught to generate their own statements and questions to guide and control prose comprehension.

Treat reading comprehension as the learner characteristic that decides media with least doubt, since low scorers will have difficulty with print and — because the ability correlates with oral language understanding — are also likely to learn poorly from semantically complex speech.

Recognize that no additional fact tells the learner which fact to use when — that requires understanding of essentials, purpose, audience, strategy, and tactics — so drill and direct instruction can build automaticity but cannot by themselves make a learner able.

State a skill-area understanding as the strategic and tactical principle governing when to use which skill, since skills join a fluent flexible repertoire only through that insight and not through drill alone.
Prefer understanding-based teaching of skills, which research and practice indicate develops more fluent, effective, and autonomous proficiency than rote and drill-and-practice alone.

Do not require novices to learn the expert's technical vocabulary without experience that gives it meaning, since information that cannot be organized into the learner's existing experience becomes mere words calling out mechanical reactions.

Treat direct instruction as only one aspect of causing learning and the design of work as at least as important as any articulate sharing of the teacher's knowledge, since only experts or highly gifted thinkers can do all the constructivist work in their heads without experiences, tools, tasks, and feedback.

Teach novices explicit hypothesis-and-evidence reasoning, require multiple evaluated resources, and retain explanatory theory so problem practice does not become imitation or unexamined apprenticeship.
Use conceptual patterns, procedures, metacognitive choice, and direct retrieval practice as explicit means to a fluency target rather than equating memorization with drill alone.

Recognise that three irreconcilable models of problem-solving instruction coexist — general skills teachable directly and generalising, general skills developing only indirectly from task-specific strategies, and direct instruction yielding only weak broadly generalisable strategies — while dependable evidence exists that task-specific strategies can readily be acquired.
Identify and teach the skills that make the desired choice possible, since a learner cannot choose an action he lacks the skill to carry out.
Require a sequence of varied, divergent problems; applying knowledge to only a single problem, or to a non-divergent example set, is insufficient for learning a cognitive skill.
Use non-interactive instruction only when the task is familiar, simple, clearly demonstrated, easy to judge, and safe; construct guided learning events for complex or challenging proficiency.

Treat drill-and-practice reinforcement as limited rather than wrong: it can strengthen a specific response but does not account for complex conceptual learning, so do not use it as the model for teaching understanding.

Set practice quantity from task criticality and the automaticity requirement, weighing learner time — extra practice cost lower-ability learners 75 percent more time for a small gain — and avoid over-learning where it is not needed.

Recognize that expert operations differ from novice operations in format and regulation — running simultaneously and actuated by the problem's own conditions rather than by self-instruction — so teaching the operations does not by itself produce the expert format, which conventional instruction leaves to spontaneous lengthy experience.
Avoid inert ideas — ideas received without being utilised, tested, or thrown into fresh combinations — by keeping the main ideas few and important and putting them into every possible combination.

Do not count a task as a transfer problem if it differs from classroom examples only in quantities or symbols; it is new only if the student must modify the problem statement, cast it into a model, or search memory for the relevant generalizations.

Treat problem solving as an activity that combines previously acquired concepts and rules rather than as a generic skill: mathematics problem solving does not automatically transfer to mechanical problems, and problem solving in a task class is improved by adding the intellectual skills relevant to those tasks — because no learner can acquire all the rules every situation needs.

Assure transfer by setting new tasks that require applying what was learned in situations differing substantially from the learning situation — varying the whole situation rather than merely the items within the same task format.

Use different examples in the test from those used in teaching, so the correct response cannot be produced by copying a value or remembering a previously worked problem instead of by the intended intellectual process.

Treat failure to transfer a taught rule once its cues are removed as evidence that it was taught as a fact for cued calculation, and reject drilling for state tests as a strategy, since those tests demand the transfer decontextualized drill does not produce.

Treat the knowledge/understanding boundary as learner-relative and developmental — what once required a chain of reasoning is later simply known — so classify a target for the actual learners rather than in the abstract.

Teach a specific topic or skill inside its context in the field's broader structure, because understanding something as an instance of a general case supplies a model for understanding other things like it and is the main road to transfer.
Classify learning targets rather than listing them uniformly, since they differ in nature, in the specificity of their description, and in what they imply for teaching and assessing.

Include some history of ideas — the competing notions and arguments the field passed through before consensus — so students see understandings as hard-earned constructions rather than ready-to-grasp knowledge.

Treat the fact/understanding boundary as learner-relative, since a difficult inference becomes an obvious fact over time and many things treated as facts are hard-won understandings most people have never personally verified.

Frame targeted understandings as specific propositions describing a relationship among concepts — principles, generalizations, axioms, laws — rather than as phrases referring to the topic or content standard, and let a rubric answer what understanding or proficiency for that result looks like so both assessor and student can judge it.
Use learning theory as a context-sensitive instrument for interpretation and revision, not as a source of one prescribed method or an end in itself.

Teach the underlying conceptual structure of the subject, not only its facts: a powerful command of foundational knowledge means being able to explain and predict with the concepts, which is a different target from performing the calculations in routine exercises.

Recognize the paradigm a course is being designed under: answering what students should learn with a list of topics expands the course along one dimension into an unwinnable coverage race, while answering with kinds of learning expands it into multiple dimensions without abandoning content, which is renamed foundational knowledge.

Anchor the structure of a course on its intellectual skills, on the practical grounds that they must be learned rather than told, are acquired in short periods, accumulate cumulatively through transfer, and are readily and operationally observable — not on a claim that they matter most.
Assume and verify that the component concepts of a rule, including its relational concepts, have been previously learned and are readily recalled before teaching the rule.

Treat the ideal learning structure for a subject as known only vaguely and existing representations by teachers, curriculum specialists, and textbook writers as partial and inadequate, and hold any method for describing learning structures open to empirical verification, revision, and refinement.

Choose induction or deduction by concept type and learner: for concrete concepts present a variety of examples before the definition, whereas for older learners acquiring a defined concept a simple definition may come first followed at once by an example — provided the component concepts are already understood.

Recognise learning guidance as where adapting instruction to the learner's needs has its clearest meaning, since the tutor can try one means of encouraging semantic encoding after another until one works best.

Adopt the knowledge-construction conception of learning — the learner as active sense-maker, the message as cognitive guidance — over the response-strengthening (drill) and information-acquisition (delivery) conceptions, whenever the goal is understanding.

Target the process of applying knowledge, not only the knowledge itself, because students who possess a body of knowledge are often unable to think, reason, solve problems and decide with it; doing so requires knowing the composition and structure of the cognitive operations involved and how to develop them.

Distinguish the cognitive families by their emphasis: dialogue technique starting from terminology before higher understanding; structural analysis of the subject matter to identify the rules to be learned, whose technical sense of rule must not be conflated with the casual one; and an algo-heuristic focus on the procedural cognitive operations of learning and using knowledge, teaching expert practice as algorithms plus the heuristics used where no set procedure applies.
Choose big ideas that handle whole classes of problems across settings rather than familiar instances, since a well-chosen idea transfers across an entire domain.
Design lessons that bring abstract concepts to life, or they remain empty phrases to be memorized and learners never discover that ideas have power.

Give students far more direct or simulated experience of abstract ideas than textbook-driven courses allow, since the absence of such experience may explain why important ideas are misunderstood and learning is fragile.
Design work deliberately to ferret out predictable unhelpful ways of thinking, because without it students' preconceptions remain untouched by instruction.

Name the Expert Blind Spot as the confusion of what the teacher talks about with the meaning-making the learner must do, expressed in the belief that clear coverage produces retention and more coverage means more learning.

Name the Expert Blind Spot as the failure to grasp that key lessons involve understandings that must be engineered rather than facts to be transmitted, and reject as naive the assumption that older students find expert knowledge self-evident once presented.
Guard against the Expert Blind Spot's institutional form — the belief that what worked for the educator will work for most others.

Name the teacher's blind spot — I taught it so they must have learned it, and more teaching means more learning — as the reason that, left to themselves, teachers find the habit of coverage more defensible than it is, and require teams to ask each year which approaches actually yield the greatest learning regardless of their own habits.

Require action research that keeps teachers inside how learning works, since the blind spot hides the pain of all learning and real learning is frightening and frustrating regardless of age or talent; teachers who never occupy the learner's position miss the chance to make education honest and self-correcting.

Reject coverage as uneconomical on three grounds: it makes generalizing to what comes later exceedingly difficult, it offers little intellectual reward, and unstructured knowledge has a very short half-life in memory.

Recognize that coverage leaves students without the sense of the whole that is obvious to the expert, so all but the most able get lost and perhaps alienated, and that it does not even optimize external test performance.

Reject the standard justifications for coverage — external standards, textbook obligations, standardized testing — since teaching by mentioning cannot yield learning that culminates in competent performance, and recognize the hurried tour as the Expert Blind Spot confusing teaching with resultant learning.

Distinguish depth — getting below the surface to how something works and how to diagnose and fix it — from breadth, which expands a topic to its connections and larger implications, and reject excessive exclusive depth as no better than excessive coverage.
Recognize that superficial disconnected teaching of information cannot yield optimal results on any test, since that expectation again confuses the teaching with the learning.

Use exclusion rules to keep media inappropriate for learning out of consideration and inclusion rules to identify those best suited, making the practical choice from the resulting short list on feasibility, availability, and cost — because every neglect of how learning takes place may be expected to result in a weaker procedure and poorer results.
Watch for the three pathologies of mislearning that conventional teaching abets — amnesia, fantasia (not understanding that we misunderstand), and inertia (being unable to use what was learned).

Expect learners to project categories, assumptions, and priorities onto reality and then find ways of proving their instinctive ideas true, so misconceptions are durable and can survive successful formal instruction and later revert.

Design for three kinds of uncoverage — students' potential misunderstandings, the questions and grey areas beneath surface accounts, and the non-obvious core ideas — because concepts are results of inquiry and argument and their value has to be uncovered rather than stated.
Do not read persistent misunderstanding as an indictment of the teaching method, since big ideas are rarely obvious and are often counterintuitive.
Ferret out student conceptions and misconceptions and keep them in mind when designing learning, which cognitive researchers identify as key to better results.

Before teaching, be able to describe what the understanding looks like when present and absent, how apparent understanding differs from genuine, which misunderstandings are most likely, and whether the design is making headway against them.

Guard against the Expert Blind Spot at every step, since once teachers see a big idea clearly they become prone to assuming it is obvious to learners, and core ideas of modern subjects are typically abstract, non-obvious, and counterintuitive.
Make attention to likely student misunderstanding central to the design, because big ideas cannot be grasped through telling and reading alone and are likely to be misunderstood on first encounter.
Ask explicitly during Stage 1 which ideas in the unit require deliberate in-depth uncoverage rather than assuming exposition will suffice.

Confront students with new facts, phenomena, or problems when assessing explanation, so they must on their own subsume the information under the correct principle and dispose of apparent counterexamples.

Acquire understandings by uncovering — developed inductively and coconstructed by learners doing the subject on real problems — with students emulating what practitioners do when generating new understandings: consider, propose, test, question, criticize, and verify.
Select for uncoverage the concepts and principles most prone to misunderstanding — the non-obvious and counterintuitive ones students predictably get wrong.

Choose hooks from puzzles, real-world problems, perspective role-plays, far-out theories, paradoxes, incongruities, anomalies, and mysteries whose answers raise essential questions, since mystery is central to awakening inquiry and to teaching students that their job is to inquire.

Give learners an explicit inference organizer that asks them to add up given facts and state the big idea, which supports inductive meaning-making and hands them a cognitive tool transferable across subjects; using the same organizer for teacher planning and student work yields the transparency designers should seek.
Treat uncoverage as the way to make any idea accessible and real regardless of instructional method, not as a type of teaching or a philosophy of education.
Make the challenge of working with textbooks understanding what they conceal rather than only what they reveal, since to uncover is to reveal what would otherwise remain hidden.

Contrast the two uses of a text: under uncoverage it is one resource among many including primary sources, read in a sequence serving the goals, with its summaries treated as accounts to be analysed; under coverage it is the syllabus, read in page order, with its summaries taken as givens.

Treat uncoverage as vital rather than optional, since all big ideas are counterintuitive and abstract and no effective transfer via them is possible unless the student is helped to uncover their meaning and interconnection.

Recognize that presenting big ideas as obvious things to be apprehended rather than comprehended abets misunderstandings and encourages students to keep them hidden, and make uncovering student misunderstandings and persistent errors a key teacher role — teaching that such mistakes are unavoidable and are key episodes in gaining understanding rather than shameful.
Put designed learning of how to question the material at the heart of uncoverage, since important claims must be tested rather than merely mentioned if they are to be understood.

Distinguish an appropriately simplified account from an overly simplistic inquiry-ending one that hides the uncertainties, arguments, and subtleties central to understanding, and treat lurking and emergent questions as essential rather than a tangent to drop when time is short or reserve for gifted students.

Use a repertoire of cheap checks — a two-sided card naming a big idea understood and something not yet understood, an anonymous question box for students uncomfortable admitting confusion publicly, and a visual representation that reveals whether relationships among a topic's elements are grasped.
Include in uncoverage the idea that students should experience authentic inquiry and sometimes re-create how knowledge was developed, without endorsing recapitulation as an educational theory.
Provide uncoverage through sustained inquiry for enduring understandings, since they are abstract and not obvious and a teacher who treats one like a fact makes it unlikely the student will get it.

Reserve uncoverage for three kinds of content — principles and theories meaningful only when the learner can verify or justify them, counterintuitive or easily misunderstood ideas, and the conceptual or strategic element of any skill — and uncover a skill's strategic element by clarifying effective and efficient means given its ends, which yields greater purposefulness and less mindless technique.

Split the evidence question in two — where to look, a validity question about which student work must be seen done well, and what to look for in the performance regardless of approach, an evaluation question answered by criteria.

Answer the three Stage 2 assessor questions — what evidence can show the Stage 1 results were achieved, what tasks and other evidence should anchor the unit and guide instruction, and what to look for to judge the extent of understanding.

Do not confuse a standard with a performance indicator: the standard is a goal belonging to Stage 1, while the bulleted indicators under it represent possible assessment evidence and sometimes name activities belonging to Stage 3.
Place performance indicators, benchmarks, and performance goals in Stage 2 where they speak to evidence rather than to the standard itself, since many official documents blur that distinction.
Present a situation that is new or contains new elements when assessing application, ideally testing contextualized practical use of the abstraction.
Anchor assessments in the prototypical core-task performances of the field and build curriculum frameworks around those core tasks alongside the big ideas.

Define a core task as the most important kind of performance demand in the field, set in authentic challenges whose context is as faithful as possible to real-world opportunities and difficulties including their messiness.
Use core tasks to move past the factual content to what professionals and laypersons actually do with the knowledge, which clarifies the goals and suggests the assessments.
Use all three mechanisms for staying focused on big ideas — essential questions, specified desired understandings, and key performance tasks — rather than relying on any one.

Require more than a once-a-year external test as evidence of achievement, adding high-quality application-focused performance tasks built around the six facets to the local plan, since most frameworks ignore assessment even though specifying a curriculum requires clarity about the performance targets embodying its goals.

Pull the two central levers for improving performance while preserving intellectual engagement — teaching and assessing for understanding of big ideas and core tasks, and applying design standards to review and refine local curriculum as ongoing research embedded in the job.

Anchor assessment in authentic tasks — realistic, demanding judgment and innovation on an unstructured problem, requiring the student to do the subject, replicating a real context with its constraints, purposes, and audiences, and exercising a whole repertoire rather than isolated elements — because authentic tasks supply direction, coherence, and motivation for daily work.

Anchor learning in real-world, whole-task problems that are representative of the tasks the learner will face after instruction, instead of teaching task components in isolation before the whole task (topic-centered).

Replace narrow prompts eliciting the correct answer to a familiar question with tasks that test whether a student can recognize what in their repertoire is useful in a novel situation and use it effectively.

Recognize that a diet of coverage and right-answer expectation teaches students that only the foolish have questions, and that a stream of leading questions reduces their questions to procedural ones about tests, teacher preferences, and length requirements.
Recognize that when learning the answers is the only goal, instruction covers up the vital questions that naturally arise in the work, diminishing both engagement and understanding.
Disambiguate concurrent perspectives in prompts—for example, an author's intended effect versus the learner's personal reaction—so valid answers are scored against the process actually requested.

Vary the amount of guidance with the capability: for an arbitrary matter such as a new name, telling the answer is the correct guidance and indirect hinting wastes time; where discovery is a logical route to the answer, less direct prompting is appropriate and may yield more permanent learning.

Develop cognitive strategies through variety and novelty in problem-solving tasks introduced systematically and interspersed with other instruction, and make the general nature of the expected solution clear when presenting a novel problem, since a practical solution differs from an original one and the student's performance is easily affected by that difference.

Gain attention with a rapid stimulus change matched to the delivery form — gesture and vocal variation for groups, changing displays for computer-assisted instruction, novel situations for individualized study — and for problem-solving outcomes raise curiosity with a hypothetical situation or rhetorical question instead.
Run inquiry dialogue with groups as well as individuals, since fostering multiple competing hypotheses and argumentation among a group can make the method more effective.

Design even conventional tests with misunderstanding in mind, following the model of misconception-targeted instruments used as pre- and post-tests to measure progress against persistent misconceptions.

Identify the predictable misconceptions students bring to a topic, make dispelling them an explicit unit goal, draw on published misconception research as a design input, and then check empirically with an early quiz or informal check whether this year's students actually hold them.

Use pretesting and ongoing misconception checks to determine which side of the fact/understanding boundary a claim falls on for this group, applying the inferential-load test: the more inference, uncoverage, and misconception-overcoming a claim needs, the more it is an understanding.

Use K-W-L for an immediate read on prior knowledge and potential misconceptions, with the Want-to-learn column revealing interests and yielding student-generated essential questions, and pair a nongraded pretest with a matched post-assessment targeting key misconceptions to evidence growth.

Present a common predictable misconception and ask students to agree or disagree and explain, which surfaces the misconception directly rather than inferring it from errors, and convert any answer into evidence with follow-up probes about reasons, meaning, supporting data, and examples.
Pair each desired understanding with its documented key misunderstandings in the curriculum resource itself, as science benchmark projects do.
Design assessments to supply conceptual benchmarks as well as performance evidence, taking account both of the big ideas and of the likelihood that they will be misconceived and resist correction.

Expect validity problems to be very hard to see unaided, since most designers do not self-assess against any design standards and consequently draw invalid inferences, while disciplined self-assessment plus quick peer review solves most of them.

Analyse familiar time-tested drills against explicit design elements, which can reveal that some are badly ineffective and gives practitioners an analytic frame that transfers to designs never explicitly demonstrated.
Design assessment with outcomes and learning activities, using direct or authentic performance and a varied programme of tasks only where each contributes distinct valid evidence.
Treat the first design as a testable approximation; balance targeted analysis with early alternative designs, learner involvement, and low-cost experimentation before expensive commitment.

Anchor decisions about what to teach, omit, emphasize, and minimize to agreed long-term exit-level priorities, since without them there is no perspective and no check on teaching to short-term content objectives.

Delay the selection of teaching strategies to the last phase, since a discussion of strategy is premature until the desired results, implied assessments, and required activities are specified, and the right teaching moves follow from what learning requires.

Where an essential question recurs and has no final resolution, make the desired result the serious pursuit of the question, which commits the designer to genuine inquiry — discussion, reflection, problem solving, research, and debate — instead of coverage.

Qualify a question as essential against six criteria — it causes genuine inquiry into big ideas and core content, provokes deep thought and new questions, requires students to weigh alternatives and justify answers, stimulates rethinking of assumptions and prior lessons, sparks connections with prior learning and personal experience, and naturally recurs to enable transfer.

Treat an essential-sounding question as merely rhetorical whenever no deliberate inquiry follows, whenever it is a warm-up before teaching that proceeds as if the discussion never happened, or whenever student responses cannot affect the direction of the class or the work.

Derive essential questions from content standards by turning the recurring key nouns and the declarative statement into an interrogative, and from a stated enduring understanding by turning it into its companion question.

Expect that simply posting an essential question may generate no interest, rewrite a question that fails to resonate in the students' own idiom using their suggestions, and revise the design when working with the topic reveals the standard's real big ideas differ from the original question — retaining that question as a hook.
Introduce the essential question immediately or engineer it to arise later and inductively after focused problem solving or instruction, as the design requires.

Define an essential question as one lying at the heart of a subject that produces different plausible responses about which thoughtful people may disagree, and allow it to be either overarching or topical in scope.

Distinguish a skill — a technique or procedure developed by guided practice and coaching — from a long-term performance goal such as writing powerful essays, which needs many units and several integrated skills.

Separate the conceptual element of a skill from its technique — the purpose of the genre, the criteria of effectiveness, and the strategies likely to work with a given audience — and do not read competence in a fixed format as evidence of understanding the underlying idea.

Test every knowledge and skill goal by asking what important capacities the content will actually equip learners for, not merely what knowledge is potentially important, and let overarching performance goals decide what to emphasize and omit as they do in drama, athletics, and carpentry.

Treat skills as means rather than ends — the aim is fluent flexible performance requiring judgment about which skill to use when, how, and why — and recognize that skill areas only appear to lack essential questions because their usual assessments require no transfer or judgment.

Include desired understandings in skill-development units, covering the skill's underlying concepts, why it matters and what it accomplishes, which strategies maximize its effectiveness, and when to use them.

Name the criteria that separate novice from competent performance for any skill goal, because the goal of skill-focused learning is to move learners along that continuum and the continuum has to be described before it can be taught or assessed.

Infer a motor skill only from performance across a variety of contexts — different tools, surfaces, and sizes — never from a single instance, and remember that motor performances themselves enter into further learning.

Classify a task as a motor-skill objective only when precision, timing, and coordination of muscular performance are genuinely involved; where the learner already has the requisite motor skills and is merely following a procedure, the outcome is rule learning.
Require observable performance, sufficient practice, and performance feedback before concluding that a skill has been acquired.
Treat content mastery as a means rather than the aim: content knowledge is the tools and material of intellectual competence.

Avoid framing content goals as factlike sentences to be learned by direct instruction, which promotes coverage and hides two facts about learning — that understanding derives from inquiry, and that meeting intellectual standards requires questioning expert opinion rather than only absorbing it.

Aim in every subject at being able to do the subject with understanding — knowledge and skill as means for handling key tasks in the field — through many part-whole-part cycles of trying it out, reflecting, and adjusting, learning just enough content to use it and then tackling more complicated ideas.

Aim at maximal transferability — the effective use of content rather than merely learning it — so performance needs dictate the timing and approach of content learning and the sequence is framed by the key performance tasks rather than by a table of contents, with the main ideas kept few and important and thrown into every possible combination.

Include content mastery in the goals but go beyond it, and aim for as many of the six kinds of learning as the course can genuinely support, since more kinds make the experience more worthwhile and each kind happens more fully.

Keep content expertise out of goal-setting and apply it later, in building the course structure and the learning activities within it; only after the intended learning is described can the supporting activities and assessment be chosen.
Treat mastering the content as chiefly a means to the second task of learning to use it, and move initial content learning out of class because that is what frees the time the second task requires.

Maintain the knowing-how versus knowing-that distinction: an intellectual skill is procedural knowledge exercised through symbols and conceptualisations, verbal information is declarative, a learner can acquire either without the other, and the distinction must hold even when one unit teaches both.
Grant content and method control on prior knowledge and metacognitive skill: novices with weak self-regulation do better under program control, especially in complex courses.

Treat objective overload as a long-standing structural problem, not a new one: aims lists so extensive that no reasonable instructional programme can be built around them were already being reported in the 1930s.
