Use the recurring nouns, adjectives, and verbs of a standards document as the practical handle for identifying its priorities.

Work the standards entry point by grouping related standards, mining key nouns for big ideas and key verbs as a blueprint for performance assessments, deriving essential questions, then listing enabling activities and refining for alignment.

Standardize terminology, text and media formats, scenario and assessment structures, editing, and approvals before distributed production, and mature prototype breadth, depth, media, and logic only as decisions warrant.
Organize information into a conceptual framework, since that is what allows greater transfer and learning with understanding promotes transfer better than memorizing from a text or lecture.

Teach the structure of a subject — how things are related — because grasping structure is what lets a student recognize that new problems are not new at all, and thorough understanding of a discipline's characteristic concepts economizes learning effort.
Treat understanding as at risk in any sequence giving one tour of each topic in a flow dictated by the content elements rather than by learner performance goals.
Treat broad formats as settings, select different learner activities for different outcomes, and use lectures selectively for distinctive live value rather than routine information transfer.
Move foundational information before class where feasible, diagnose confusion, and use class time for novel problems, peer explanation, reconsideration, and timely feedback.

Link the foundational-knowledge activity in a structured, sequenced way to the activities promoting other kinds of learning, because that linkage is what supplies the energy for multiple kinds of learning at once.
Separate knowledge of a disciplinary method from successful use, and use organized principles and theories to support explanation, prediction, and action.

Use organising strategies to impose a framework — categorising word sets, tabulating relations so spatial cues aid recall, or outlining and regenerating the organisation of prose ideas as comparison, collection, or description.

Distinguish three verbal-information situations for design — learning labels or names, learning isolated single facts, and learning organised information — because they vary in amount and organisation and call for different treatment.

Organise bodies of knowledge so they can be readily retrieved and have learners organise during learning, because that supplies retrieval cues and because the more highly organised a learner's prior information the easier any related new fact is to acquire and retain.

Tell learners what to look for or what to remember before learning begins — directly, through questions inserted in the text, or through an advance organiser that orients them to what follows — because this can activate a cognitive strategy for learning.

Reduce learner diversity to a manageable number of dimensions that carry different implications for instruction, then design for those variations shown to make a difference in learning results — attending to the characteristics that affect the whole information-processing chain from sensory input through storage and retrieval to response organisation.

Anticipate the schemas learners bring to a topic and design the new instruction to fill out their slots, since a schema organises a large set of meaningful information about a general concept, learners arrive with schemas already in memory, and those schemas differ across individuals in comprehensiveness and stored detail.
Take prerequisite skills to mastery so they are easier to recall and more accessible for the new learning, and embed them within an organised schema so more cues are available to the memory search.

Have the component concepts and rules recalled just before the new learning, since most new learning is the combining of previously learned ideas and they must be highly accessible at that moment — using a recognition or, better, a recall question, and a chain of such questions to lead the learner toward the new rule.

Employ both factual-information sequencing procedures: present an organiser passage naming the major categories of description beforehand, and use prior questions or statements identifying the categories of fact for which learning is desired — matching the pre-questions to the target category, since prior experience with questions of a given kind facilitates learning and retention of that kind of information.

Arrange verbal-information lessons by subtype: for names, recall of verbal associations plus student encoding relating the name to an image or meaningful sentence plus use of the name in context; for facts and organised knowledge, recall of the related meaningful context, performance reinstating the new material within that larger context, and using it by relating it to other facts and bodies of knowledge.

Identify exactly what information is to be learned and retained — a list of names or dates, or the substance of a passage — and make it equally apparent to the student, which is what makes learning for mastery feasible, fair, and reasonable.

Provide or activate an organizing structure or mental model for the new knowledge: supply a structure when the learner's existing model is insufficient, encourage the learner to activate their model when it is adequate, and keep any motivational themes relevant to the content.
For verbal-information goals, identify and meaningfully organize information clusters without implying a procedure that recall does not require.
For verbal-information outcomes, organize what learners must recall through a meaningful inherent relationship without treating recall as symbolic manipulation.
Build cognitive guidance into the message, not just content: tell the learner what to attend to, how to organise it, and how to relate it to prior knowledge.

Activate relevant prior knowledge explicitly: knowledge in long-term memory only helps when it is brought into working memory, and it is what lets the learner bridge steps the presentation leaves implicit.
Present corresponding verbal and visual material together rather than separated, so the learner can integrate them in working memory.

Schedule a hands-on operation before the explanations that use its concepts, so learners gain direct experience of the concept and its name then becomes a stimulus later responses can be associated with.

For a conceptual course, organize the concepts into structures showing superordinate, coordinate and subordinate relationships, then sequence the most important structure top-down from the most general and inclusive concepts to progressively more detailed ones.

Use an analogy to relate new information to a more familiar body of organized knowledge the learner already holds, reminding them of something concrete in their experience to prepare them for a more abstract idea.

Recognize the expert-novice difference in problem approach: experts first seek to understand the problem in terms of core concepts, while novices search for correct formulas and pat answers fitting everyday intuitions.

Distinguish basic from core: basic ideas are definitions, building-block skills, and rules of thumb, while core ideas are the hard-won results of inquiry and the expert's ways of perceiving — non-obvious, often counterintuitive, and prone to misunderstanding.
Decompose adaptive problem solving into problem recognition, relevant conceptual knowledge, procedure selection and use, monitoring, and evaluation, then teach the missing components.

Temper the value assigned to teaching general problem-solving strategies with the expert-novice finding that experts do not necessarily use better strategies than novices but approach problems with larger and better organised knowledge bases of both verbal information and intellectual skills.

Judge a method's fit against the specific audience and content rather than in the abstract: an approach that suits novices exploring a domain can be a poor fit for expert practitioners acquiring a specific established technique.

Apply the curriculum test — is the material worth an adult's knowing, and does having known it as a child make a better adult — and treat a negative or ambiguous answer as showing the material is clutter.

Reach core ideas slowly through teacher-led inquiry and reflective student work, alternating between the text and the learners' own experience of the idea, and remove text-access barriers so literacy difficulty does not block conceptual access.
Make bringing a text to life the teaching challenge for interpretation — showing through study and discussion how it speaks to learners' own concerns.

Develop student-focused teaching by changing conceptions and actions together: surface discrepancies between espoused theory and observed practice, examine learner and context perceptions, and use inventories only as prompts alongside contextual evidence.

Build in time to reflect, because a new experience or idea acquires an initial meaning that may remain unconscious and be limited or distorted, and only conscious reflection can change it; without reflection students have learned something but not made it meaningful.
Subsume technical concepts and skills under a transferable big idea, since a student who can define or compute a term without discussing the underlying idea does not understand it.

Generate candidate big ideas with three further devices — existing lists of transferable concepts, probing questions of the topic (why study it, so what, what larger concept underlies it, how is it applied in the wider world), and suggestive pairs of contrasting concepts that indicate the kind of inquiry required.

Assume that what counts as a big idea to the expert is frequently abstract, lifeless, confusing, or irrelevant from the novice's point of view, and treat making the field's big ideas big in the learner's mind as the core challenge rather than presenting them.

Focus a unit on a small number of transferable big ideas with stated understandings — otherwise there are no priorities at all — and state those understandings in clear unambiguous terms as specific insightful generalizations despite their abstraction.

Sort content into three nested priority tiers — worth being familiar with, important to know and do, and the innermost big ideas and core tasks — because a course always contains more content than can reasonably be addressed.

Assign the outer tier only broad-brush encounter with knowledge assessed by traditional quiz or test items, and reserve fine-grained decisions for the innermost tier of anchoring ideas and transfer tasks.

Use the priority tiers as a curriculum audit at course and programme level, which reveals whether the curriculum concentrates on transferable ideas or merely covers information and lets teachers drop always-taught content that belongs in the outer tier.
Organize programmes, courses, units, and lessons around the essential questions so that the content becomes the answers to questions.

Build a course-level plan pairing course understandings with matched course essential questions and a list of course skills stated as analytic capabilities — interpreting sources, connecting past to present, distinguishing relevant from irrelevant, separating fact from opinion, defending positions — rather than as content coverage.

Recognize that content-driven curricula reveal no genuine priorities — every topic appears equal and the flow is impervious to performance need or learner misunderstanding — so priorities must be made tangible as recurring questions tied to key performance goals, set apart from the textbook as a coach frames goals separately from any resource.

Do the course-structure step even when the teacher already knows the full topic list, because it forces identifying which topics are major and absorb the subtopics, and lays out the thematic structure of the whole course.
Make curriculum priorities explicit when intended content exceeds available time, and use the taxonomy map to reveal the consequences of those choices.
Organise a course from the top downward, from general to more specific objectives, using the functional relationships among the types of learning.
Keep the unit-level outline broad, specifying only the major objectives, because each may have a great many subordinate essential and supportive prerequisites and the detail can get out of hand.

Flesh the other content types and the learning prerequisites onto the organizing sequence at the point where each is most relevant rather than letting them form the skeleton, and record the result as a blueprint showing per lesson the organizing content, its elaborations, and the supporting content and prerequisites attached.

Order within a lesson by the organizing content type: easiest and most familiar concepts first for a conceptual organization, steps in performance order for a procedural one, simplest organizing content first for a theoretical one.

Place supporting content immediately after the organizing content it relates to, place each learning prerequisite immediately before the content that requires it, group coordinate concepts together, and teach a principle before the procedure it explains.

Break supporting content into concepts, procedures, learning prerequisites and information — not strictly necessary but it reduces the chance of overlooking something — and keep prerequisites as their own category to force identification of prerequisites for the supporting concepts and procedures as well as for the organizing content.
Treat a shift of perspective that is prerequisite to a later concept — such as unitizing before place value — as a big idea in its own right rather than as an incidental step.
Read the middle tier two ways — as knowledge and skill with connective and transfer power, and as the prerequisite enabling knowledge students need to accomplish the unit's complex performances.

Anchor an understanding-focused unit with performance tasks or projects showing knowledge used in context, and round out the picture with traditional quizzes and prompts assessing the enabling knowledge and skill.
Resolve broad objective language into the specific knowledge subtype and cognitive process that successful learner performance actually requires.

Require students to select and justify among alternatives rather than define terms, because the choosing-and-justifying task demands a qualitatively different grasp and, when the outcome matters to them, stimulates interest in the underlying distinctions.

Build confrontation with alternative theories and diverse expert points of view into the coursework and materials rather than leaving it to spontaneous student disagreement, since every discussion of content requires weighing its meaning from different points of view if coverage is to be avoided.

Differentiate process by varying reading level, presenting information orally, visually, and in writing, and offering options in how students work and communicate learning — and where product choice is offered, evaluate all results against common criteria so diversity does not cost validity or scoring reliability.

Use differentiation to extend as well as support — making the same task more demanding for advanced students by shifting its audience or adding constraints, while allowing non-writers to demonstrate the same understanding orally.

Choose the focus of a caring goal deliberately among the five available — the phenomena studied, the ideas studied, the student's own Self, the Others encountered, and the process of learning itself — rather than leaving get-them-excited unspecified.
Do not replace complex or contested educational aims with simpler objectives merely because the simpler outcomes are easier to state or measure.
Give learners information about the possible alternative choices first, because a common obstacle to changing an attitude is simply that learners do not know the options available.

Recognize the reasons theories are actually chosen — the philosophical views attached to the theorist, ease of analysing local components, presumed goal compatibility, and preference for particular classroom activities — and that selection problems come from considering too few features rather than too many, since most practical situations involve more variables than any one theory addresses.
Read the descriptive prose that precedes the enumerated standards, since that is where big ideas are stated or implied, rather than working only from the numbered list.

Establish priorities not only from big ideas but also by organizing schoolwork around transfer tasks derived from authentic challenges in the field, since the goal of schooling is fluent effective performance in the world rather than response to narrow prompts.

Acknowledge the weak spot honestly: strategies for highly novel problems are often the primary interest of educational programs, yet knowledge of how to ensure their learning is the weakest part of the field.
Define successful transfer as performing well with minimal or no hand-holding, guiding, or cueing from teachers.

Treat inability to transfer as a teaching need rather than a learner deficit, since instructors who complain about it have usually planned no coaching in how to transfer knowledge to varied situations.

Define transferability as using knowledge appropriately and fruitfully in a context different from the one in which it was learned, and to understand as making sense of what one knows, knowing why it is so, and being able to use it across situations.
Interpret transfer as the interaction of instructional relevance and practice, learner ability and motivation, and workplace opportunity, feedback, accountability, support, and incentives.
Establish with valid posttest evidence that learners acquired every main goal performance before interpreting absent workplace behavior as a transfer failure.
Reject goals conceived only as lists of facts and skills, since design and instruction then degrade into inert out-of-context bits and transfer is bypassed entirely.
Reject covering the content as a learning goal, since it states what the teacher does rather than what students will be able to do, and require it to be restated as a student capability.

Reject candidate performances that a lesser capability would satisfy: understanding a concept is not shown by stating what it is, which could be mere verbal information, nor by distinguishing instances from non-instances, where the learner may be cueing on a surface feature — it is shown by using the rule in one or more specific situations.

Treat task analysis as conceptually identical with backward design but hobbled in practice by an excessively behaviouristic and atomistic view of goals, and work backward from complex ideas and messy performances rather than from easy-to-manage measurable behaviours.
Reserve detailed task analysis for high-priority work and identify each selected task's elements, relationships, tools, conditions, and success standards.
Treat understanding as several distinct achievements each revealed by a different kind of evidence, not as a single achievement with one indicator.
Combine achievement with structured and open learner reactions, investigate reported ambiguity, and map each diagnosed issue to an evidence-supported revision.

Accept that understanding sometimes demands critical detachment and sometimes empathic solidarity, that these are opposite and both legitimate, and that failures of interpersonal understanding usually come from not imagining another point of view rather than from lack of knowledge.

Recognize that understanding involves matching ideas and actions to the concrete situation — tact — which is distinct from theoretical understanding of the domain, so assessing application requires new problems and diverse situations rather than repetitions of practised ones.

Define empathy as a disciplined attempt to feel and see as others do — not sympathy or uncontrolled affect — and distinguish it from perspective, which is cool analytic detachment aimed at objectivity.
Require intellectual empathy for ideas one is inclined to reject, since deriding a predecessor's theory guarantees failure to understand their world.
Read inability to go beyond rote and routine thought and action as a signal of lack of understanding, since understanding shows itself in flexible performance.

Look for empathy in the assumption that an apparently odd or obscure text or person may contain insights worth the work, and for self-knowledge in recognizing one's prejudices, sorting strong belief from warranted knowledge, admitting ignorance, self-assessing accurately, and accepting criticism without defensiveness.

Continue the continua for the remaining facets — perspective from uncritical and ad hominem to making one's own view more plausible by fairly weighing others'; empathy from egocentric and threatened to actively seeking out the odd and alien; self-knowledge from innocent of one's own bounds to wise recognition with the integrity to act on it.

Accept that an understanding can never be covered if it is to be understood, since it sets an end goal demanding the right experiences, discussion, and reflection, and since an idea told to someone arrives as another given fact rather than as an idea.

Define empathy as a learned ability to grasp the world from someone else's point of view — the discipline of using imagination to see and feel as others do and to imagine that something different might be possible or even desirable.

Define the six facets operationally — explain with justified systematic accounts, interpret through meaningful stories and apt translations, apply in diverse contexts, hold perspective, empathize, and possess metacognitive self-knowledge including awareness of what one does not understand.

Treat the facets as manifestations of transfer that work like several criteria judging one complex performance — each different and somewhat independent — so evidence of one facet must never be read as evidence of the whole.
Use the facets as windows that guide the selection and design of assessments, treating full development of all six as an aspiration for teaching for transfer rather than a requirement of every unit.
Let the six facets permeate all three design stages, clarifying the desired understandings, the necessary assessment tasks, and the learning activities alike.

Use the six facets as a question generator, with each facet supplying its own starters — including perspective starters that interrogate viewpoints and evidence quality, and self-knowledge starters that ask how one knows, what one's limits and blind spots are, and how one's views are shaped.

Use the six facets as the Stage 2 assessment blueprint, completing the stem "A student who really understands" with each facet's key verbs to generate the kinds of task needed regardless of topic or age.

Look for facet-specific indicators — the explainer gives credible theory-based reasons, makes fine distinctions, argues for what is central and predicts well; the applier works in messy authentic contexts, extends knowledge novelly, and self-adjusts; the perspective-holder critiques a position as a point of view, infers assumptions, knows an idea's limits, and sees through ideological language.

Build facet-specific task types — explanation tasks that require stating the big idea in one's own words and inducing theory from data, interpretation tasks that make sense of texts and data or translate across media, application tasks set in authentic contexts with real audience and constraints, and perspective tasks comparing competing accounts and defending or opposing their use.

Draw criteria from each facet's own family — explanation judged accurate, coherent, justified, systematic, predictive; perspective credible, revealing, insightful, plausible; empathy sensitive, open, receptive, perceptive, tactful; self-knowledge self-aware, metacognitive, self-adjusting, reflective, wise.
Allow two learners' facet profiles to differ while both count as sophisticated, since individuals can hold diverse but equally valid understandings of the same ideas.

Describe each facet on its own naive-to-sophisticated continuum — explanation from unexamined hunch to fully supported account beyond the information given; interpretation from mechanical decoding to illuminating account of significance; application from scripted plug-in to fluent transfer in difficult contexts.

Produce paired evidence by working a desired understanding through the apply and explain facets — a performance that applies the idea plus an artifact in which the student justifies why the analysis holds.

Use the six facets as a Stage 3 activity generator as well as an assessment blueprint, and deliberately force the facet that feels unnatural for the content area, which teachers report produces energizing designs by pushing them outside habitual patterns.

Generate activities facet by facet — asking what artifacts and events students must explain to practise sound inference, how to arrange materials so students both generate and critically evaluate multiple points of view, what direct or simulated experience would make them viscerally connect with others, and which experiences will surface their own habits of mind and biases.

Treat a facet as a criterion in performance assessment rather than a learning style — it concerns how teachers judge whether understanding is present, not learner preference — and as a framework rather than a quota, since self-knowledge and empathy are often not at stake in evidence of many mathematical concepts.
Read a weak explanation as naive, simplistic, or incomplete rather than factually false — unqualified and unsupported by data — and grade it on that dimension.
Target meaning rather than a merely plausible account when assessing interpretation, and treat word-perfect translation without grasp of meaning as failed interpretation rather than failed knowledge.

Hold both halves of interpretive rigour: interpretations are always contestable, multiple, and context-bound, yet one reading is stronger than another by its coherence, thoroughness, and documentation.

Distinguish explanation from interpretation in kind — theory is general and expected to converge on one surviving account, interpretations are contextual and legitimately as numerous as thoughtful interpreters — since a theory must be true to work while a story need only have verisimilitude and illuminate.

Do not hand students prepackaged interpretations or statements of significance without letting them work through the issues, which is futile and misleads them about the arguable nature of all interpretation.

Have students rather than only teachers and textbook writers develop the interpretations, with feedback that forces continual testing and revision, and give them activities that require interpreting inherently ambiguous matters rather than right-answer testing.

Reject four non-understandings — a bare topic phrase, a straightforward fact, a truism or global pronouncement, and a bare list of skills — because none asserts a specific proposition of general significance requiring inquiry.

Treat merely stating the understanding — by teacher or textbook — as the cardinal mistake of coverage, since it turns a complex inference into words to be taken in rather than a problem to be solved by good design.

Trace complaints of too-literal reading to two design flaws — assignments rarely involve genuinely ambiguous readings, and no instruction was designed to help students judge, absent obvious clues, what kind of reading requires what kind of response.
Watch for foundational distinctions buried as unexplained asides long after the concept was introduced, which leaves neither students nor most teachers able to appreciate their significance.
Identify the deeper incoherence of standard texts as throwing a welter of concepts and terms at students in confusing order, opening with assertions incomprehensible to most learners.

Recognize that interpretation carries more inherent subjectivity and tentativeness than explanation — even knowing the facts one must still ask what it all means — and that handing students prepackaged interpretations produces sham understanding and quickly forgotten knowledge.

Define application as using knowledge effectively in new and diverse realistic contexts, deciding where present competencies suffice and where new skill is needed — distinguished from comprehension by the absence of a prompt about which knowledge to use and by the unfamiliarity of the problem.

Take seriously the stronger claim that many so-called application problems are not truly novel and therefore do not indicate understanding, with true understanding shown by new spontaneous applications amounting to reinvention.

Do not conflate the three meanings of application: developing a particular skill, learning to manage a complex project, and learning a kind of thinking each require different activities and different criteria.
Classify endless plugging-in and fill-in-the-blank exercises as pseudoperformance rather than application.
Approximate the situation in which a scholar, artist, engineer, or professional attacks such problems — including the time allowed and the conditions of work — when setting problems for students.
Judge a final product on three grounds — its effect on the reader or audience, how adequately it accomplished the task, and evidence about the adequacy of the process that produced it.

Keep a clear performance goal in the learner's constant view, as the law case method and problem-based medicine do, and require constant self-assessment against standards so that working hard, following directions, and turning in a product does not count as being done.

Keep an ongoing personal record across the unit that supplies the raw material for a final self-assessment of change, and conclude with the learner self-evaluating against that record and producing a personal action plan — turning the self-knowledge facet into a product.

Use a standards model for attainment: judge multidimensional performance holistically against public criteria, avoid false percentage precision and forced distributions, and permit every learner who meets a standard to receive its grade.

Define perspective as the mature recognition that any answer to a complex question involves a point of view and is one of several plausible accounts, shown by alertness to what is taken for granted or glossed over and by making tacit assumptions explicit.
Treat perspective as a mature achievement: novices may hold a revealing point of view but by definition cannot deliberately take and weigh multiple perspectives.
Practise the discipline of asking how the matter looks from another point of view, including how one's critics would see it, recording every contrary fact at once as Darwin did.

Extend critical reading to the teacher and textbook themselves — what those authors treat as true and important, what questions and assumptions informed them, what blind spots they carry, and how far simplification distorts the original thinkers.

Tailor high-level content for limited readers with audio and video of key passages, reading and writing assistance, and abridged versions, without changing the essential questions, and introduce key definitions at the teachable moment the conversation creates rather than before it.

Recognize that textbooks by design summarize and simplify expert knowledge to suit student levels and competing constituencies, which can hide the true nature of the subject and of scholarship, and that few help students understand the inquiries, arguments, and judgments behind the summaries.

Weigh the review evidence against textbooks — a highly simplified view of reality with no insight into how facts were gathered, unsatisfactory ratings for covering too many topics and developing none well, activities irrelevant or unconnected to the key ideas, and failure to take documented student difficulties into account.

Recognize that textbook simplification hides exactly the questions, issues, and inquiries the learner needs in order to understand, presenting only the cleaned-up residue and thereby distorting how understanding actually develops.

Accept the text where it usefully simplifies but question it where it oversimplifies a big idea, and know exactly what students will gloss over and misunderstand so lessons can deliberately require them to find the issues, gaps, and inconsistencies hidden in those accounts.

Note that a text can simplify an argument for younger readers without making a simplistic claim, leaving a genuinely debatable question open — but even then the teacher must supply the research materials and direction the inquiry requires.

Identify the big ideas and revisit them via problems of increasing sophistication as the work unfolds, whether or not the textbook is organized to do so, since the lesson that good assumptions have limits and every simple starting point hides deeper issues transfers to all walks of life.

Recognize the danger of a textbook-based syllabus as leaving a single simplistic representation unchallenged, teaching students that there is one official viewpoint to be taken in for recall; after learning to keep their facts straight they must learn that experts disagree widely on how those facts are to be interpreted.

Weigh the large-scale evidence that interactive teaching — teacher as guide or coach, students asking questions and developing strategies, students explaining how they reached conclusions, mastery assessed through discussion and extended writing — was associated with more learning in both reading and mathematics, with the process of developing the answer counting in the judgment of quality.

Test real understanding by presenting another nation's or tradition's account of the same events, since only understanding rather than accurate recall lets a student cope with the historiographical issues that raises.

Recognize that reducing understandings to information, and assessments to recall or plug-in items, teaches students the misconception that their job is to memorize understandings as if they were facts.

Identify enduring understandings by asking what students should understand and be able to use years from now after they have forgotten the details, since such an understanding is a conceptual unifying lens for recognizing the significance of one case and examining new ones.

Use observing experiences to let students meet the reality of the phenomenon, since a strong direct observation produces two discoveries at once — that the subject is real and significant, and that the course's tools let the student make sense of what they encounter.

Apply inquiry to a procedure by having learners invent it through considering what could go wrong at each step, and to history only where the causal links between events are known well enough to have learners predict how events unfolded.
Treat What of it? What is assumed? and What follows? as essential rather than extra-credit questions that all coursework should ask and answer.

Give each essential question its own concrete exploratory activities, sequence the questions so they lead naturally from one to another, and allot enough time to unpack subquestions and probe implications given student age and competing obligations.
Supply the specific propositions yourself, since content standards typically name the area of concern without specifying the particular understandings students should acquire.

Meet the W standard only when students can answer with specificity what they must understand and what it looks like, what their final obligations are, what resources support them, how today's task serves the overarching obligation, how to allot time and set priorities, and how their work will be judged and improved.

Settle feedback and assessment before choosing teaching and learning activities, because doing so greatly clarifies which activities are needed — while acknowledging a course can be designed successfully in either order.

Surface the external expectations that constrain the course — what society needs from graduates in the subject, accreditation and licensing requirements, and institutional or departmental curricular roles such as writing across the curriculum or filtering majors — before setting goals.
Use role-play of a historically unfamiliar position and its argument to make once-bizarre views intelligible without requiring students to endorse them.

Aim empathy tasks at better understanding the diversity of thought and feeling in the world rather than at getting students to accept the ways of others, using role-play debates, writing from inside another position, and reading discredited work to see why it was plausible at the time.

Use thought provocations that make the strange familiar and the familiar strange, appealing at gut level rather than through argument, and personal-connection inquiries that open onto the unit's universal themes; a deliberate shift of perspective nudges students out of their comfort zone and stimulates deeper thinking.
Assess whether students have overcome egocentrism, ethnocentrism, and present-centeredness in their answers and explanations.

Define self-knowledge as the wisdom to know one's own ignorance and to recognize how one's patterns of thought both inform and prejudice understanding, and treat the immature mind as unreflective rather than merely ignorant.

Do not treat prejudice as always wrong or harmful, which is itself a prejudice; self-conscious exposure of one's prejudices may be the key to insight, and self-knowledge demands the discipline to seek out blind spots and the courage to face the inconsistency beneath confident worldviews.

Expect intellectual blind spots to drive rationalization — assimilating experience to favoured models that feel like objective truths — and treat either-or dichotomous thinking as a common habit in which the categories are not seen as narrow projections.

Apply the same scrutiny to educators' own categories and metaphors — the brain as computer, education as delivery of services, behavioural objectives — whose limits and subjectivity are seen only long afterwards.
Specify and classify every educational objective as a cognitive process acting on a defined type of knowledge.

Make the meaning of certain facts and skills a problem rather than a glib solution when understanding is the aim, using designed puzzlement — a text whose words are known but whose meaning is not, an unexpected result, data the formulas do not fit, or two accounts that disagree.

Write essential questions that are not answerable with finality in a brief sentence and that burst through the boundaries of the topic, since deep and transferable understanding depends on framing work around such questions.
Frame an activity-heavy unit with a set of provocative questions to supply the intellectual focus and impetus for depth that a smorgasbord of activities lacks.

Point the hook toward what is essential rather than merely entertaining, and use the five conditions that pique intellectual interest — instant immersion in a wits-demanding challenge, thought provocations such as anomalies and counterintuitive ideas, experiential shocks, personal connection, and a deliberate shift to differing points of view.

Create conditions for deep engagement by showing conceptual structure, limiting overload, allowing time, supporting mistakes and dialogue, and eliciting application or theorising through questions and problems.

Organize activities under three components — getting information and ideas, experiencing (splitting into doing and observing), and reflecting — and require an effective set to include activities from all three.

Use questions as doorways to the big ideas — posing dilemmas, subverting canonical truths, and forcing incongruities on attention — and shift the focus onto the reasoning used to reach and defend an answer rather than onto whether it is right.

Treat each academic field as definable by its essential questions, and prefer questions that are alive outside school — that people actually argue about — since these signal that inquiry and open-mindedness are central to expertise.
Pose live open questions from the current frontier of the field at some level throughout schooling, since school should be relevant and empowering.

Recognize that typical frameworks emphasizing lists of discrete knowledge and skills subtly encourage mechanistic didactic coverage, whereas framing curriculum around essential questions makes connective, thought-provoking, recurring inquiry central.
Let cross-disciplinary questions recur over the years, since they demand transfer beyond the topic where they were first met and thereby promote conceptual connections and curriculum coherence.

Distinguish topical questions, which refer to unit content and are provisionally settled by the unit's end, from overarching questions, which point beyond the topic to transferable understandings cutting across units and courses.

Build units on related sets of paired topical and overarching questions rather than a single question, and use overarching questions as the conceptual pillars framing whole courses and multiyear programmes.
Make the questions publicly visible — posted, used to organize notebooks, and shared across the faculty — so their priority for study is evident and cross-subject coherence becomes more likely.
Link each unit-level essential question upward to a programme-level question that can be re-asked in every course and pursued over time through recurring assessments.

Treat the tendency of essential questions to jump curricular boundaries as a virtue, since question-framed curriculum makes fruitful cross-disciplinary connections more likely even when that was not the aim.

Measure coherence by its threats — frequent topic switching and outside intrusions — noting that lessons with significantly more topics and switches, only one-fifth of topics with developed rather than merely stated concepts, and roughly twice as many definitions, amount to learning terms and practising procedures with little underlying rationale.

Allow that a question may be essential even though its power is not grasped on first hearing, but treat prolonged failure to signal useful inquiry as a sign that a narrow focus on it is counterproductive; conversely, liveliness alone does not qualify a punchy question as essential.

Treat making an objectively essential question accessible as a Stage 3 translation problem, solved by provocative experiences or concrete entry questions rather than by weakening the Stage 1 question.

Write an entry question for maximal simplicity in student-friendly language with provocation value pointing toward the larger questions, and design so the essential and unit questions arise naturally from those entry questions, problems, and activities.

Judge a question by its powers in context — purpose, audience, and impact — not by inherent properties, since the same wording is essential or not depending on why it is posed, how students are meant to tackle it, and what follows from it.
Do not impose a hard rule against yes/no or who/what/when phrasing, since many such questions spark curiosity and reflection depending on how they are posed and what follows.

Frame skill-area essential questions around four categories — key concepts, purpose and value, strategy and tactics, and context of use — and pose them only in a context of genuine performance challenges requiring ongoing judgment.

Where essential questions seem too conceptual for a skill-focused course, identify instead the questions or problems tied to key performance challenges that require intelligent use of those skills — two questions can frame an entire curriculum provided a carefully designed matching set of problems accompanies them.
Frame impact questions from organizational, job, and learner outcomes; build trust and access, explain that training rather than participants is under evaluation, and tailor methods to each site.
Exclude from Stage 1 any question meant to culminate quickly in a fact or settled conclusion, and place leading questions — legitimate but recall-oriented — in Stages 2 and 3 where they belong.
Keep leading questions in the repertoire for teaching and checking understanding while marking their different purpose, since calling a question leading is not to condemn it.
Cross intent with scope to generate four question types — open and guiding, overarching and topical — and use that chart as a design tool for producing a balanced mix.

Avoid all three single-type failure modes — only topical questions cannot ensure transfer however provocative, only overarching open questions risk aimless discussion untethered from standards, and only guiding questions deny students the freedom to ask their own and lose uncoverage.

Accept that not every good question can feasibly be explored and choose a focus, but ensure a mix of topical and overarching questions is present, since without a question-framed focus the student is left passive amid unconnected activities and the twin sins return however lively the lessons.

Exploit essential questions as natural accommodation, since their open-endedness lets students with differing prior knowledge all engage while some answer in greater depth, and address diagnosed gaps by targeted small-group instruction rather than by lowering the goal.

Match each topical question explicitly with a related overarching question, which is what earns it its essentialness and signals to learners that answers lead to further questions and new inquiries send them back to revisit earlier answers.

Generate topical questions by inverting the content — treat the textbook material as the answer and ask what important question about a big idea it answers well — then push outward to broader questions with transfer value that still require the core content.
Never state a question you do not intend to actively investigate through discussion, research, problem solving, or other means.

Select or design the assessment tasks up front and link them explicitly to the essential questions, so tasks and performance standards clarify what acceptable pursuit of and answers to those questions look like.

Use the GRASPS elements — Goal, Role, Audience, Situation, Product or Performance, and Standards — to design at least one core performance task per major unit or course, and to recast existing assessments and engaging activities into performance tasks.
Check assessment adequacy against the unit's essential questions: the performances should directly or indirectly require students to address them.

Move from question to task by first treating the essential question as a final essay prompt and then recasting it as a GRASPS scenario; where that would be contrived, use a traditional prompt built on the question, which makes assessment less mysterious and arbitrary.

Choose criteria that highlight the most revealing and important aspects of the work given the goals rather than what is easy to see or score, make them a set of independent variables affecting quality that define the task requirements operationally, and derive them from the goals as the assessments themselves are derived.

Work the external-assessment entry point by clarifying the goals the assessment serves and the transferability it seeks, then inferring the big ideas needed to meet the standard and developing parallel performance tasks.
Agree the core ideas and assessment tasks at district, department, or grade level, which lightens the unit designer's load and removes the incoherence that results from units designed in isolation.

Treat the essential questions as the general specifications for any particular assessment, and tell students of any age up front and throughout that the course's questions will be considered from various points of view and addressed in various projects.

Record on an assessment task blueprint which understandings the task assesses, the criteria implied by the standards regardless of task specifics, the task overview, the student products, and the criteria for evaluating them — keeping the standard's demands visible even as the task changes.

Ask of validity whether the test measures what it purports to, whether results correlate with other valid results, whether the sample represents what was taught, and whether results predict future success — while noting that one task does not license inference to other task types, so the few tasks in performance assessment often provide an inadequate basis for generalizing.

Design the assessment programme as an evidence system: use synoptic tasks where outcomes integrate, complementary tasks where one sample is insufficient, and weights and workload proportional to educational importance.
Scale the breadth and diversity of assessment tasks to the breadth and complexity of the objective, and limit conclusions to what the task sample supports.
Make representative assessment demands visible because consequential concrete tasks often define the operative curriculum more strongly than abstract objective statements.

Use the objective to set up the assessment situation directly, since it describes what must be observed to verify the learning and can equally ground a teacher-made test or a student self-test, and treat objectives as both the guideline for developing instruction and the basis for the measures that determine whether they were reached.
Make assessment tasks parallel to the objectives and select evidence forms that match the actual target performance.

Treat questioning as what makes an object and its possibilities fluid against the fixity of opinion, and skill in questioning as the ability to keep questions from being suppressed by the dominant opinion.

Use the essential question as a criterion for judging progress, asking whether the class is making headway on it, and treat a negative answer as obliging a mid-course adjustment as coaches and athletes make.

Keep essential questions in Stage 1 because they frame the goals and oblige both teacher and learner, leaving the more teacherly questions to Stage 3; unit-framing questions are different in kind from questions a teacher improvises in class and require separate deliberate design.
Frame Stage 1 questions as the field would frame them for the designer, then edit and adapt them into learner-facing versions when the student materials are built.
Leave the second part of a unit deliberately open so students frame and pursue the inquiry from the questions and clues remaining at the end of part one, as case-method and problem-based courses do.
Specify both topical and overarching understandings, since the overarching one answers the student's So what? about work that seems to have no larger purpose.

Treat the topical/overarching boundary as elastic — set by content scope, subject priorities, student age, and time — and identify the overarching understanding as the transferable insight eventually sought, tested by asking how far the unit's insight generalizes to give connective power elsewhere.
Ask students routinely to show their work, give reasons, and connect answers to larger principles, since a single application may not link to the larger goals.

Treat timing rather than overreliance on one approach as the major mistake, asking of lecturing when to answer versus question, advocate versus present alternatives, state the purpose versus let it be inferred, and do the research versus have students do it.

Treat both topical and overarching understandings as requiring inference from facts rather than treating topical understandings as facts, and note that even an understanding-how-to target still requires specific insights that enhance the performance.

Treat facts as the data and the understanding as a conclusion based on evidence and logic: a fact requires only apprehension, an understanding requires comprehension — questioning the facts, connecting them, and applying them.

Do not judge by syntax: a fact and an understanding can read almost identically while the fact is true on inspection and the understanding is an inference made valid through proof, which is why uncoverage demanding analysis and synthesis in the learner's own words is necessary.

Define a fact as the verbal statement expressing a relation between named objects or events rather than the referent it describes, and require as evidence of learning a stated relation having the syntactic form of a sentence.
Catch the restated-topic failure: naming a subject states no proposition, and narrowing the content focus does not fix it — the designer must say what the student should conclude.
Treat full-sentence form as necessary but not sufficient, since a trivial or hopelessly vague proposition still fails to warrant a unit.

Introduce vocabulary, criteria, and definitions at the point where they clarify experience the design has already produced, since presenting them up front leaves learners able to recite but unable to use them to craft and evaluate instances.

Establish a rationale for what is to be learned before designing: return to the original sources of the recognised need, agree goals through a responsible group, weigh available resources and constraints, and define needs as documented gaps between the desired and the present state.
Apply evaluation to the design effort itself first, seeking evidence for revision (formative), and only later seek evidence of the learning effectiveness of the finished design (summative).

Build a defined-concept demonstration from the component concepts and the relation among them, and reject an assessment item that a learner could answer by plugging values into a formula in favour of one requiring identification of those components and their relation.
Translate objectives written to communicate unambiguously to teachers and designers into words or pictures the students themselves can readily understand before communicating them in a lesson.
Preserve design products from front-end analysis through revision so reviewers can trace decisions, and let novice developers first take direct responsibility for every instructional component.

Design instruction to build observable capability and application, with experiences that are meaningful, memorable, and motivating; treat knowledge exposure as supporting means rather than the endpoint.

Begin with readily available evidence about the performance need, audience, support, delivery, prior work, content, constraints, contributors, and expectations; add interviews, observation, and harder research as design questions reveal their value.

Involve recent and representative learners while fundamental changes remain affordable; let them experience rough prototypes authentically, explain incompleteness only as needed, and shift review focus from treatment to wording, media, interface, navigation, and feedback as fidelity rises.

Present a concrete worked illustration with commentary before the detailed abstract description when introducing a framework to newcomers, and have learners predict each annotation before reading it for deeper understanding at the cost of extra effort.
Present a variety of examples when introducing a concept, because without that variety learners fail to recognize the many different forms in which instances occur.

Decompose a concept's definition into its separate necessary attributes and teach each against examples, rather than presenting the definition as one undivided sentence; when the number of criterial attributes is large for the audience, treat the attributes individually as a shaping treatment and defer whole-concept recognition to the last stage of practice.

Introduce a concept only after learners have experienced the phenomenon it names, and open the section with a question arising from what they have just observed, so the definition labels something already seen and the new content is motivated by a discrepancy in their own experience.

Introduce a representational device as the vehicle for a new concept and let learners read the concept off the drawing, then have them explain an earlier empirical finding in terms of the representation to test that model and observation are connected.

Build an expository use-concept segment in order: reference example, definition, elaboration, matched example-nonexample pairs each with attention-focusing help, classification practice, then helped feedback.
Build a use-principle presentation as the proposition, several different explanations of specific applications, then practice explaining or predicting in additional instances.

Compare a demonstrated application's subject matter, objectives, processes and learning tasks against your own before borrowing from it, since a designer's approach depends on the subject matter as well as the theory, each application is only one of many ways the theory could be used, and demonstrated plans are tentative and precede formative evaluation and revision.

Treat a theorem or comparable result as an understanding rather than a fact, since it is not obviously true on inspection and needs proof, and note that a graphic can mislead by making a claim seem true by inspection when it is true by argument only.

Recognize that treating unobvious big-idea understandings as facts makes amnesia, inertia, and fantasia far more likely, and counter it by making the interconnected sub-claims behind the big idea explicit — what it holds for, why it matters, what it makes possible, and why proof rather than inspection settles it.
Treat every understanding as somebody's and fallible — an inference from limited evidence, experts included — so no theory is a fact and major understandings can be overturned within living memory.
State the corrective for an intuitively plausible misconception in terms of the underlying principle it violates rather than as a bare rule.

Treat an unexplained boundary condition as a gap in the account, not a nuisance: the obligation to explain when a principle fails is what disciplines the theory and what tells a practitioner where the principle will not carry.

Include common misconceptions and cases where the principle does not apply among the illustrative explanations, so learners become discriminating in applying it; and prefer practice that asks for a prediction over practice that asks the learner to choose between an appropriate and an inappropriate application.

Where the field holds no single agreed answer, make the absence of a settled understanding the desired understanding and state it specifically by naming the competing accounts — while insisting that no-single-right-answer does not make all answers equal, since some are better by argument.
Do not read content standards as asserting a timeless official set of unchanging understandings; enduring must not mean indifference to feedback and resistance to change.
Presume a student does not understand until proven by a preponderance of evidence that is more than circumstantial, as a jury treats the accused.

Distinguish the four evidence types by their defining properties — authentic non-secure performance tasks with known criteria; open ill-structured academic prompts under exam conditions with judgment-based scoring; convergent secure quiz and test items; and ungraded informal checks that feed back to teacher and student.

Treat validity as concerning the meaning that can properly be made of specific evidence — which events or data yield the most telling evidence of the general ability claimed — and as a property of the inferences drawn rather than of the test itself.
Use a mix of different evidence types over time, following the maxim that it does not matter which tests are used as long as they are varied and many.

Keep most multiple-choice tests secure to protect their validity, since they rely on a small number of uncomplicated questions, while recognizing that many valid performance assessments are not secure at all and that in a non-secure performance assessment the teacher appropriately teaches to the test of performance.

Express legitimate professional requirements as outcomes and valid evidence rather than inherited proxies such as coverage, harsh marking, fixed distributions, or exam quotas, and keep a proportionate route for evidence-driven programme revision.

Model the real-world conditions of performance, where there is little secrecy about goals or success criteria, asking the examiner questions is advantageous, and ongoing feedback from colleagues is available.

Treat conventional items as sideline drills sampling isolated bits, and remember that performance is always more than the sum of the drills, so authentic tasks must assess use of a whole repertoire across a complex multistage task.

Use the whole-to-part practice flow — discrete skill, game-like, game conditions, game, then back to the discrete skill at higher demand — as a transferable sequencing model, and require every drill rather than only every session to exercise the full set of target elements.

Move part to whole and whole to part, between content and performance and between discrete skill and strategy, letting feedback from whole-performance results send the performer back to targeted drill in a constant recycling among elements, chunks, and the whole.

Maximize learning with cycles of perform-feedback-revise-perform producing known high-quality products judged against public standards, and let secure testing coexist with transparent assessment rather than leaving room for mystery testing.

Be cautious evaluating process skills separately from the product, keeping the emphasis on whether the final product met the standards set, and treat a product as valid evidence only to the extent that success in producing it reflects the knowledge assessed and samples appropriately from the curriculum's relative importance.
Use authentic, transparent standards to make improvement controllable by learners rather than dependent on who else is assessed.

Give students opportunities to rehearse, consult resources, get feedback, and refine, and run learning as cycles of performance, feedback, revision, and new performance; the secure secret test retains a role but must coexist with educative assessment if performance is to improve.

Distinguish exercise from problem: an exercise executes a move out of context, while a problem is a demand within performance requiring thought about the choices and challenges a performer faces in context.

Judge a problem by the justification of the approach and solution mindful of competing requirements and trade-offs, whereas an exercise is judged by the accuracy of the single right answer and choice of the correct approach.
Require the performer to decide which approach and which facts to use without simplifying prompts, since that self-directed selection is transferability revealed.
Treat exercises as necessary but not sufficient for competent performance and as unreliable indicators of the ability to perform.

Distinguish exercising from forward-looking assessment: repeating a taught protocol with varied parameters gives useful early practice and familiarity, but it is not assessment of readiness to act, and students find realistic tasks more motivating.

Eliminate every medium except those on which the performance can be directly practised — the actual equipment or a simulator — when errors in the target performance are dangerous, since a lecture or television program may set the stage but is inadequate for learning such a skill.

Do not initiate instruction without a valid performance discrepancy; after training is plausible, triangulate evidence to define the standard, current performance, capability gap, tracking measure, and instructional goal.

Treat practice as necessary but not sufficient: only deliberate practice builds expertise — effortful, intrinsically motivated, targeted at weaknesses just beyond current reliable performance, fed by feedback, and sustained over time.

Keep the Stage 2 goal as appropriate evidence rather than interesting projects: a fun project can supply too little evidence — especially with collaboration and free choice of approach — and a less engaging exercise can yield more conclusive evidence, so design the task backward from the evidence needed rather than from learner interest.

Do not let complexity and interest make evidence appropriate: a beloved project can sample only a small slice of the standard and bypass its core demand, which is the common error of confusing an interesting activity with a valid assessment, and the aim of Stage 2 is good evidence rather than engaging work.

Collect the learner's thought process alongside the answer — why they did what they did, what supports the approach, how they reflect on the result — because answers without reasons and support are insufficient to establish understanding, as the dissertation-plus-defence model recognizes.
Model a critical stance that employs both criticism and belief — believing when others doubt and doubting when others believe.

Assemble a coherent package in which each instrument carries the evidence load it is suited to — an authentic task for the understanding, quizzes for prerequisite knowledge, and a test for grasp of consequences.
Guide judgment with criteria wherever there is no single correct answer or solution process, since criteria are what make a judgment-based evaluation consistent and fair.
Use criterion-referenced judgement for learning and reserve norm-referenced ranking for genuinely selective decisions; train learners to apply criteria while retaining appropriate moderation.
Make standards-based judgement dependable through explicit outcomes, admissible evidence, learner-usable rubrics, assessor calibration, and checks of within- and between-judge consistency.
When essay assessors disagree, first calibrate criteria, priorities, and the structural framework before concluding that reliable judgement is impossible.
For consequential creative judgement, use several knowledgeable, diverse judges with shared criteria and reasoned consensus; use learner-defined criteria only after guided meaning and evidence work.
Require explicit criteria for evaluation, using internal consistency for checking and external standards for critique, and identify strengths and weaknesses before judgment.
For each consequential decision in a goal, determine whether learners already possess the judgment; if not, teach its criteria and every materially different downstream path.

Watch for the predictable failure modes of easy-to-see criteria — high scores for footnote count rather than well-supported research, understanding inferred from wit rather than thoroughness, exhibits judged effective for being colourful rather than accurate.

Build a rubric as a criterion-based guide with a fixed scale plus descriptions of each score point along a continuum of quality, answering by what criteria to judge, where to look and what to look for, and how the levels differ — using a checklist instead when only a yes/no determination is needed.

Prefer analytic to holistic rubrics when assessing understanding, since a single score compromises feedback quality and misleads readers into treating two very differently flawed performances as the same; balance appropriately varied criteria against feasibility.
Derive rubric descriptors from review of many concrete samples of student work, and treat a rubric as incomplete until it has been used on real work and that analysis has sharpened the descriptors.
Manage rubric proliferation by framing multiple rubrics around the fewest key differing aspects of understanding, knowledge, and skill.

Build a rubric from student work in six steps — gather diverse samples, sort into stacks while writing down the reasons, cluster the reasons into traits, write value-neutral trait definitions, select anchors for each score point, and refine continuously with use.

Apply validity scrutiny to rubrics as well as tasks, since scorers commonly presume greater understanding in the student who knows all the facts or writes elegantly even when the flawed paper's findings are the more insightful.
Treat criteria and rubrics as not yet ready if the criteria could be met without deep understanding or could go unmet by a performer who nonetheless shows understanding.

Let core performance tasks drive selection of companion rubrics, and maintain a shared bank of criterion rubrics used consistently across a district — amended with task-specific indicators while the general framework stays intact — so students get a consistent message about quality.

Write a rubric to carry both formal descriptors for the teacher and learner-facing bullets translating each score point into the terms of the specific task and age group, and give students examples of work at each score point so the rubric supports self-assessment and makes the final judgment intelligible.

Attach work-sample anchors to each rubric level, since a rubric without them is far too ambiguous to set a clear standard and anchors are what give phrases like sophisticated and persuasive concrete stable definition, contributing significantly to scoring reliability.
Use a small scoring scale of about four to six points, since each point must correspond to a specific criterion or quality and a scale of many discrete numbers reduces scoring reliability.

Set pass and mastery standards from minimum acceptable qualitative performance, make ordered rubrics public, calibrate assessors on whole examples, and allow bounded reassessment when mastery rather than selection is the goal.

Map every assessment and weighting to outcomes, state standards separately for each outcome, and define rubric levels as qualitative changes from partial execution toward accurate, justified, integrated performance.

Apply the five marks of a good course as a review checklist: significant kinds of learning, active forms of learning, a teacher who cares about subject, students, and the process, a teacher who interacts well, and a good system of feedback, assessment, and grading.

Build a rubric by Primary Trait Analysis: clarify the objectives for the assignment, identify the traits that will count, construct a two- to five-point scale per trait with descriptive statements of good and poor versions, and try the scale out on students or colleagues and revise.

Write each standard on a rubric scale as a description of what performance at that level looks like rather than as a bare numeric label, and derive the criteria from the verbs in the learning goal — an application goal naming design, construct, and assess yields three criteria clusters, each with its own multi-point standards.
Let learners help generate quality criteria when useful, then organize the criteria into a substantively faithful scoring guide written in language they can use.
Audit every rubric criterion and its weight against the objective, validating learner-generated criteria before using an aggregate score as mastery evidence.
Classify each rubric criterion independently by the knowledge and process it demands, accounting for whether the underlying production procedure was taught.

Score at least two distinct traits — one for understanding and one for the qualities of the performance in which it was displayed — keeping mechanics, craftsmanship, and organization separate from understanding.

Start small when overwhelmed by traits — quality of the understandings and quality of the performance, adding a third for process when appropriate — and later use only the parts of a larger set that fit each assignment.
Keep trait definitions value-neutral by describing what the trait is about, putting descriptions of good performance in the highest rating rather than in the definition.
Distinguish analytic-trait scoring, which assesses a performance several times through separate criteria, from holistic scoring in which the judge forms one overall impression.

Allow multiple holistic scores for a multifaceted task involving several standards — separate scores for an oral presentation and a written report — without breaking each mode into analytic components.

Understand abilities and traits as producing an aptitude complex that engenders purposive striving — abilities affecting the quality of learning and personality traits the quantity in effort and persistence — whose combination determines engagement and hence achievement.

Score a problem-solving product against a prepared list of features rather than a verbatim key, since mechanical scoring is not feasible: where several teachers share the objective they should jointly define the criteria and how many rules must be synthesised, marking some mandatory and others optional, and treat their agreement in applying the checklist as what determines the measure's reliability — not a count such as eight of ten correct.

State the students' aptitude level — average score and a dispersion measure — when reporting whether objectives were met, since the same course may meet a much larger share of its objectives with a higher-aptitude group, and try the entity out in several schools differing in the range of student aptitude and in support characteristics.

Have students study exemplary and weak work samples and identify what makes each strong or weak, which gives them a map of the unit and makes the criteria usable to them rather than only to the grader.

Bracket the unit with a definition written at the start and a more sophisticated one at the end plus a journal entry on the strengths and weaknesses of the method used, and have students compare their own interpretation against the published expert account so that account stays contestable rather than authoritative.

Maintain a searchable database of validated units so teachers work smarter rather than reinventing the same wheels, concentrating energy on one or two high-quality units and raising design standards and skill over time.

Treat all unit and test design as sampling from a vast domain, asking which feasible and efficient set of tasks will support valid inferences about overall performance given that the student cannot be tested on everything taught.

Generate criteria by contrast: ask the teacher to describe how a student who cannot do the task well behaves and then how one who can does, and take the difference as the criteria, giving each a short scale of quality standards.

Separate conceptual grasp from correctness and from communication in a complex performance, as a five-criterion scheme of insight, reasoning, effectiveness of solution, accuracy, and presentation does, and score reasoning on the methodicalness and justification of the plan — including whether counterarguments and implicit premises are explicated — independently of whether the knowledge used was accurate.

Expect performance evidence to complicate judging — parts of a complex performance may be shaky while the content insight is clear, or the result fine although little insight was required — and counteract that messiness by pairing the task with parallel assessments of the same content in a different format.

Follow the comparative evidence that better-performing systems develop key ideas through problems and discussions with the problem presented first and direct instruction following, rather than merely presenting terms, rules, and tactics.

Build performance tasks that elicit the target understanding directly — asking students to correct a common present-day misunderstanding, or posing a problem where the technically optimal answer is not the best practical solution so that judgment becomes assessable rather than merely asserted.

Settle criteria before designing the task, since designing an assessment of critical thinking requires knowing beforehand what its indicators are, and decide the relative weight of each criterion rather than treating them as equally important.

Use analytic components formatively for diagnosis, but judge integrated performance holistically, preserve non-negotiable components, and make assessor reasoning examinable through an appropriate conceptual framework.

Assess functioning knowledge through direct contextual performance or a valid simulation, allowing varied solutions while judging intelligent framing, resource use, constraints, contingencies, and effectiveness.

Infer cognitive-strategy performance indirectly — from the quality of performances that call on other intellectual skills, or by asking learners to think aloud while learning, remembering, or solving problems — since it cannot be observed directly.

Judge an objective precise when it communicates to another person what would have to be done to observe that the purpose has been accomplished, and imprecise when the reader cannot think how to carry out that observation — which is why mentalistic wording such as realises that fails where demonstrates that succeeds.

Assess a cognitive strategy by a longer chain of inference than the performance alone supports — adding observations such as the order of responses and the efficiency of the performance, or think-aloud reports — because the same successful performance could have been produced by a different and less efficient strategy, and use several lengthy problem-solving tasks so prior information and skills can be disentangled from the quality of original thought.

Do not extend mastery decisions to cognitive strategies: what is assessed is the quality of the mental process rather than its presence or absence and a novel problem may have many solutions, so assessment becomes judging how good the solution is and a pass-fail decision is unlikely — though judgment-based assessment of novel contribution is workable, as the consensus judgment of a dissertation's originality shows.

Elicit the performance in the form the outcome requires: paraphrase in the learner's own words for verbal information, application to previously unencountered instances for an intellectual skill, an unfamiliar problem for a cognitive strategy, and a real or simulated choice for an attitude.

Sort until no new attributes are added, since the qualities articulated while sorting are what reveal the important criteria indicators, and treat difficulty placing a paper because it is strong on one trait and weak on another as the signal that analytic trait scoring is needed.
Supply more than one anchor example per level, since showing students a single example of good work invites imitation or copying.

Check the three ways a score can be invalid — items unrepresentative of the domain, items loading on an unintended ability such as language comprehension, and items of very different difficulty weighted equally.

Apply two self-test questions to expose an invalid assessment — could a student do well without demonstrating the understandings sought, and could a student do poorly yet show significant understanding elsewhere — and treat a yes to either as meaning the evidence is probably not valid.

Run the full assessment self-test in both directions — how likely a student could score well by guessing, parroting, effort, lovely products, or articulateness without understanding, and how likely a student could score poorly despite deep understanding because the task is irrelevant or the criteria arbitrary — aiming for every answer to be very unlikely.
Accept that there are no rules or recipes for validity and that the designer must sometimes make a thoughtful judgment mindful of their own fallibility.
