Validate designs against explicit standards rather than assuming they are sound because the designer worked hard or the students enjoyed the activities.

Distinguish reliability of the performance — confidence that a result reflects a pattern rather than an anomaly — from inter-rater reliability, since judges can score one event consistently while that day's performance is untypical.

Accept that measurement error is unavoidable and aim to minimize it to tolerable levels, addressing the two reliability problems — generalizing from few performances, and judges seeing the same performance differently — with multiple tasks for the same outcome and well-trained supervised judges working from clear rubrics and specific anchors.
Require transfer of an explanation to a new problem, situation, or issue, because an articulate explanation can be a function of verbal ability rather than real understanding.
Assess explanatory understanding by requiring learners to operate a cause-and-effect model through prediction, troubleshooting, redesign, or counterfactual change.
Tap several facets at once — pairing a hands-on application with interpretation and self-assessment — so the final product is not overvalued.

Build feedback and the opportunity to use it into the plan, since learners will predictably misunderstand key ideas and make performance errors that are not necessarily signs of poor teaching, and both teachers and learners need feedback to rethink, revise, and refine.

Work in a back-and-forth rhythm between creative brainstorming and careful critical testing against the design standards, seeking early and frequent feedback — which also shows the teacher-designer first-hand why ongoing assessment is vital to performance success.

Keep design feedback frequent, timely, helpful, and nonintrusive and distinct from official course evaluations, asking what worked and what did not rather than what students liked — which signals nothing personal is at stake and makes students less fearful and more honest.

Overcome the reluctance to solicit feedback from students, peers, supervisors, and outside experts, since that fear is counterproductive, and make collegial collaboration on design with feedback against standards a regular part of the job with training and time allocated to it.

Recognize that planning increases rather than reduces spontaneity — clear goals sharpen attentiveness to purposeful teachable moments — while noting that even the best teachers can dismiss comments threatening an excellent plan's flow, and that winging it rationalized as student-centred makes the teacher a passive victim of whatever comes up.

Recognize that habits and misunderstandings are rarely overcome by argument alone: claims must be locally uncovered, tested, argued, and explored in one's own setting to be accepted or rejected on rational grounds, and improvements are most successful when developed in the classrooms where teachers teach, with ideas from afar tested and adapted locally.

Evaluate teaching competencies and presentation only by how, when, and why they support learners' achievement; when outcomes are missed, investigate changeable features of teaching before assigning fixed learner deficits.
Make formative feedback timely, two-way, and gap-closing: expose current performance and the intended standard, combine informed sources, and let teachers adapt while learners can still revise.
Build frequent, usually ungraded feedback into the learning process itself, so students can improve the quality of their learning while the teacher gauges which strategies are working.

Build self-direction with concrete moves — use learners' existing knowledge structures, encourage deep-level learning, increase learner questioning, develop critical thinking, strengthen reading, and strengthen their monitoring of their own learning — and expect learners to pass through stages from dependent to self-directed with the teacher's role changing at each.
Conduct feedback as dialogue rather than announcement — the giver needs a response to know the message landed — and draw it from peers and outside experts as well as the teacher.

Keep feedback and assessment functionally distinct: feedback stays out of the grade and runs as dialogue in which the teacher shares an evaluation, learns what the student thought and which criteria they used, and explains how the teacher's criteria applied — putting the giver in the role of coach.
Make feedback frequent (every class where possible, at least weekly) and immediate (ideally in the same session), because delayed feedback leaves students asking only what they got rather than why.

Plan feedback and assessment goal by goal: what information reveals each student's individual progress and how the class as a whole is learning, which goals need only paper-and-pencil evaluation versus reflective writing or performance assessment, and what feedback would enhance learning rather than only support the grade.
Teach strategy use conditionally: learners should plan, monitor, and repair with tools matched to the task, domain procedures, context, and their own limits.
Use shared conceptual criteria in recurring teacher and peer critique so learners can revise both content and organization before final production.
Make tutoring feedback precise in content rather than merely in timing: tell the learner accurately what is right or wrong with his performance and give directions permitting correction.

Treat teachers' estimates of a lesson's effectiveness as indirect and weaker evidence about process than direct indicators — how many exercises were attempted, how long was spent on each, what feedback was given — while accepting them as possibly the best obtainable when the program does not make its intended process variables explicit.

Provide feedback and coaching during application (including error detection, correction, and avoidance) and gradually withdraw it as competence grows; feedback is a necessary condition for learning and the most important form of learner guidance.
Review goal steps from the uninformed learner's perspective, separating learner performance from teaching activity and retaining only the complete, necessary, well-sequenced, nonredundant set.

Inform learners of the objective in the form the outcome requires — stating what they will be able to say, describing and demonstrating the activity, clarifying the expected solution, or demonstrating the performance — because the objective creates an expectancy that is confirmed by the closing feedback.

Make feedback inform the learner of the degree of correctness of their performance; its delivery may be built into the medium, learner-initiated and immediate, or supplied later by an instructor, but the correctness information is not optional.

Make early practice feedback immediate and precise — naming steps omitted, steps performed correctly, and decisions omitted or incorrect — then let the consequences of the learner's own actions supply the feedback in later practice.

Use a recurring response journal asking what was most important and what remains the most important unanswered question, which supplies comprehension evidence and trains students in the strategies of effective readers.
Leave room in the syllabus for adjustments based on gathered feedback, treating that built-in flexibility as a key aspect of effective instructional design.
Design instruction as an interacting, feedback-controlled system; analyze all relevant components and revise the system when outcomes miss the goal.
Design instruction as a dynamic system whose interdependent people, materials, activities, delivery mechanisms, and environments are monitored and revised from outcome feedback.

Recognize four overlapping audiences for instructional-design work — researchers, theorists, designers, practitioners — where the first pair care about rationale, variables and measurement and treat implementation detail as low priority, while the second want a sound basis for practice but care primarily about the roles and activities for instructors and students and expect every facet of their setting to be addressed.
Note that pressure to improve instructional quality has brought instructional theory and design into decisions where they were previously absent, including textbook selection.

Treat needlessly dull schoolwork — mind-numbing worksheets and passive listening divorced from interesting problems and worthy challenges — as a design failure, since reaching higher intellectual standards requires improving the ability to provoke thought, curiosity, and drive.
Establish the practical use of intrinsically dull material and why the skill matters before teaching it, because motivation for such content does not otherwise exist.
Organize courses around controversies or opposing arguments, which a multiyear examination of undergraduate education found characterized the most engaging and effective courses.

Follow the survey evidence that courses emphasizing application, judgments about the value of information and arguments, and synthesis into complex interpretations are highly related to educational and personal gains, as are quality of faculty relationships and frequency of prompt feedback.

Stop front-loading information before an application task or question has created the need for it, delivering instruction just in time so class hours go to facilitated inquiry and coaching, and consider supplying direct instruction only on demand with the performance challenge driving the sequence.

Place direct instruction while and after learners perform, as a way of deriving understanding from the attempts, since would-be performers profit little from lengthy up-front lectures and need explicit instruction on a need-to-know basis that shows knowledge as a tool for the task.
Move initial content delivery out of class to free the scarce and expensive resource of class time for rich learning experiences that cannot easily happen anywhere else.
Protect learner attention and practice time by selecting content for required performance and removing overload that makes instruction boring, frustrating, or wasteful.
Apply cognitive-load reduction most aggressively for novices, since load-reduction methods matter less as prior knowledge grows.
Apply the full guideline set to virtual classrooms, and apply the extraneous-load guidelines especially strictly there because the class runs at the instructor's pace, not the learner's.
Seed a research collection with a few false and disreputable sources to force skepticism and cross-checking of references.

Note that students asked what they learned most commonly name a fact or topic, with acquired intellectual power absent except in the arts, physical education, vocational education, and courses outside the mainstream where they name an acquired ability instead.

Copy the features that earn foreign-language courses strong ratings — every student contributing regularly, small-group work outside class, regular written assignments, and constant feedback enabling repeated midcourse corrections — since students are enthusiastic when classes maximize personal engagement and collegial interaction.

Diagnose reliance on global student ratings as a symptom of missing shared criteria: without a common vision and language for good teaching and good learning, the default becomes how much students liked the course, which diverts teachers from student learning to student approval.
Check for deficiencies in students' prior experience before concluding that what they need is more knowledge, a diagnosis teachers at secondary and college level routinely get wrong.

Have teachers map the overlap between their textbook and their standards as a diagnostic, since the imperfect correlation shows both that part of the text does not serve the standards and that other resources will be needed.
Continue seeking evidence for improvement even when current teaching is not visibly failing.

Diagnose a failing course as a design problem before treating it as a student problem or a delivery-skill problem: the recurring root cause is that the teacher wants higher-order learning but uses a form of teaching that cannot produce it.

Read the standard cluster of student symptoms — falling attendance, unread assignments, low discussion energy, grade focus, minimal out-of-class study — as evidence about the design rather than as evidence about the students, since students disengage from learning they see no reason for.

Make the first diagnostic question about a struggling learner which prerequisite skills that person failed to learn — not what genetic deficiency or general intelligence he has, since those questions lead to solutions that merely remove the learner from the learning environment — because responsible diagnosis seeks what the learner needs to learn, very likely a prerequisite skill for which instruction can readily be designed.

Do not use norm-referenced tests for diagnosis or for lesson outcomes: their items mix objectives that often cannot be identified singly, so they cannot readily serve diagnostic testing of prerequisites nor give direct unambiguous measures against defined objectives, and used on lesson objectives they are likely to miss the point entirely and neglect both mastery assessment and the diagnostic identification of missing prerequisites.

Define equipping as enabling the learner to eventually perform with understanding and increasing autonomy — very different from preparing them for a test of discrete items — and ask which knowledge, skill, and habits of mind are prerequisites for the final performance.
Tag each learning event with the WHERETO elements it serves so it is visible whether every element is actually covered by the plan.

Scaffold with tools for the mental processes the learner must internalize, using a fading sequence — teacher's completed example, partial examples, modelled use with think-aloud, guided practice with feedback, then independent application — until repeated use makes the process internal and the prompt unnecessary.

Integrate teaching of metacognitive skills across subject areas and make the processes explicit, because metacognition takes the form of an internal dialogue that many students never recognize as important.

Move constantly between whole-part-whole and learning-doing-reflecting, returning to earlier provisional facts rather than only moving forward, and immerse learners early in intriguing problems while postponing definitions, rules, and theories until they are needed to make sense of the experience.
Keep the cognitive work with learners: negotiate unfamiliar activity and provide targeted explanation or scaffolding only where it enables increasingly independent performance.

Give only the conceptual preparation needed for outcome-framed learner discussion, facilitate without supplying the required reasoning, observe the process holistically on authentic issues, and make the analysis visible through feedback.

Classify learner strategies by control function into rehearsal, elaboration, organising, comprehension-monitoring, and affective strategies, so that the strategy chosen matches the function the learner needs.

Realise the events concretely frame by frame in a mediated lesson: attention-getting instructions with visible change, a paired contrast example to state the objective, questions recalling prior concepts, a definition with worked instances and explicit noninstances, learner-typed responses, item-specific feedback, a fresh set of instances and noninstances for assessment with mastery guidance, and varied-form instances plus spaced review questions for retention.

Use group instruction for retention and transfer inside an individualised program: once several learners have been assessed at the same point, teacher-led discussion lets them hear each other's applications while progressing toward terminal objectives in attitudes or cognitive strategies.
Design and discuss interactive learning through mutually reinforcing context, challenge, activity, and feedback rather than through process labels or content descriptions alone.

Use presentation alone only for simple knowledge-enabled performance with highly motivated learners; teach complex tasks through context and practice, focusing core instruction on the few behaviors that matter.

Build thinking-skills training on the three features of successful programs: a few well- defined skills, contextualized in authentic tasks, with social learning through instructor modeling and learner collaboration.
Make the invisible thinking process explicit, because teaching solution procedures alone leaves learners knowing what to do but not when to do it or whether their approach is working.

Prompt each example with attention-focusing information linking its specific attributes to the labels the definition uses, then fade that prompting in the later stages, because constantly available help lets learners stop studying examples and gives them the illusion of understanding while fading is what produces the mental effort real understanding requires.

Use a synthesizer to interrelate and integrate ideas — which supplies a valuable kind of knowledge, deepens understanding of each idea, increases meaningfulness and motivational appeal, and increases retention — choosing the conceptual, procedural or theoretical type to match the content, and placing it contextually at the start of a lesson or as post-synthesis at the end.
Activate a learner's generic cognitive strategies either embedded, by supplying a mnemonic or analogy, or detached, by telling the learner to think one up.

Deliver a complete elaboration design as an elaborative lesson sequence, a within-lesson sequence including prerequisite sequences, a summarizer and synthesizer per lesson, analogies and cognitive-strategy activators as needed, and learner control to the extent appropriate.
Engineer rethinking by having students state an initial theory, confronting them with a case the theory cannot accommodate, then with conflicting maxims that force a third revision.

Treat design as unfinished until the particular students are factored in through diagnostic preassessment, and adjust mid-course for misunderstandings, unanticipated rough spots, and serendipitous opportunities.

When no available theory addresses an aspect of the situation, note that a researcher may delimit the inquiry and say so, but a designer must decide how — not whether — the aspect will be handled, treating the gap as an opportunity for new variables to study or for prior experience to fill.

Make the method itself visible and criticizable by separating observations into facts, near-facts, knowledge claims, and a final interpretation, withholding an artifact's established name so the label does not influence interpretation.

Treat built-in rethinking as a critical deliberate design element, since students must reconsider earlier understandings to get beyond simplistic thinking, and highlight the perspective, empathy, and self-understanding facets because shifts of perspective and required empathy are what demand rethinking.

Require warranted opinion rather than right answers when assessing explanation, and treat the facets as mutually reinforcing — the more a student can explain, apply, and offer multiple points of view on the same idea, the likelier that they understand it.

Design in cheap metacognitive moments — mid- and end-of-lesson pauses on what has been concluded and what remains unresolved, a self-assessment attached to every formal product, a one-minute closing essay, and an honest postscript on what is and is not understood — and guarantee that students will not be penalized for that honesty.

Build on the three findings of modern learning science — students arrive with preconceptions that must be engaged, competence requires a deep factual foundation understood within a conceptual framework and organized for retrieval, and a metacognitive approach helps students take control of their learning — since incorporating them improves achievement.
Do not use graded self-reports of preferred strategy use as primary evidence of metacognition, because learners can supply the normatively expected answer.
State and teach metacognitive objectives explicitly so every learner receives sustained support for self-monitoring rather than leaving regulation to an implicit curriculum.

Teach metacognition by modelling it aloud — including deliberately entering an unproductive path and then stopping to ask whether it is working — and by asking learners metacognitive questions about what they are doing, why, and what alternatives exist.

Design constant reflection in and expect it of all learners rather than only the naturally reflective, supported by a transparent system of performance goals and robust feedback, or the reflection will not be focused or helpful.

Do not let receiving information stand alone: it is real learning but very limited by itself, and treating the job as covering the material fills class time with teacher talk while leaving reflection as an optional act the design never guaranteed.
Reject opening with dozens of pages of definitions, rules, and drills including technical hair-splitting out of context, which confuses getting going with precision the learner has no use for yet.

Reject the basics-first objection as against common sense, since no complex performance in music, drama, athletics, or the professions is mastered by front-loading knowledge out of context in a linear scope and sequence.
Select foundational facts and terminology deliberately, require only the precision later reasoning needs, and guard against expert overestimation of novice vocabulary requirements.
Judge teaching by its results and use any method that works to cause understanding, with no ideological commitment to conventional or progressive approaches.
Judge and improve teaching by the cognitive and practical activity it elicits from most learners, especially the activity required by higher-order outcomes.

Treat the teacher's stance as load-bearing: good teachers love their subject, their students, and the teaching and learning process — omitting any one makes teaching tyrannical, directionless, or inept — and self-regard adds the confidence to lead, the humility to not know everything, and the trust to let some learning come from inside students and from each other.
Judge these ideas by usefulness rather than by truth or falsity — as a raft that can carry a teacher somewhere rather than a doctrine to be ruled right or wrong.
Judge a practice exercise by the psychological processing it demands rather than its format, and avoid regurgitative questions that only require recognizing lesson facts.

Recognize that teaching on its own never causes learning — only the learner's successful attempts to make sense of it do — so having taught well means having caused understanding through words, activities, tools, guided reflection, the learner's effort, and feedback.
Remember that we do not learn by doing unless we reflect on what we have done — it is the guided reflection on the meaning of the activity, not the activity, that causes the learning.

Disambiguate learning how to learn into its three meanings — becoming a better student, learning to inquire and construct knowledge in this domain, and becoming a self-directing learner — because each implies different teacher actions.

Build better students structurally rather than only by instruction in study skills: a course that requires students to learn substantial material on their own produces cohorts that downstream instructors observe organizing for effective learning faster than their peers.

Prepare students to fulfil their part, since learning is accomplished by students rather than teachers, with formal structures for reflecting on what constitutes good teaching and learning running throughout the college experience rather than only at its ends.

Hold better teaching to its dual meaning — helping students learn something significant about the subject and helping them build a strong proactive sense of themselves as learners — since without the second, schools keep producing graduates who can pass courses but remain second-rate learners.

Recognize that covering material makes everything appear of equal value to the learner — facts with no hierarchy, priority, or connected meaning — and that a breathless march through isolated facts cannot deliver in-depth understanding or even lasting recall.

Recognize that coverage actually makes learning harder, since levelling content into verbal material for recall is more difficult for the learner than a telling experience plus a conceptual framework for making sense of it.

Reject the brick-by-brick view that doing what one is told piece by piece builds the house of understanding: learning is more like solving a difficult crossword or sculpting with an idea in mind, and encyclopedic organization is useful only to a reader who already has questions or performance needs.

Teach a fact by presenting a cue that reminds the learner of the larger knowledge network, presenting the fact, suggesting the association to be acquired, optionally elaborating with related facts and imagery, and providing for rehearsal or spaced review — since acquisition requires accessing an organised network of declarative knowledge, which may differ for each learner, and relating the new fact to it.
Fix incoherent content before fixing presentation: material that is a collection of isolated facts makes the learner's model-building fruitless no matter how well it is displayed.
Gauge lesson complexity by counting the elements and the interactions among them, judged against the target audience's prior knowledge rather than in the abstract.
For fact learning, randomize the order each pass, chunk to no more than five to seven new items at once, require immediate recall with no delay, and require that all the facts be learned.

Note that textbooks obscure the most important ideas by focusing on technical terms and superfluous detail that translate easily into multiple-choice items, and that their illustrations are rarely helpful because they are too abstract, needlessly complicated, or inadequately explained.

Note that almost all textbooks open with definitions, rules, and algorithms or the most distant events, removed from any problem or performance context, and make the first order of business in a course establishing the questions and issues that make the content seem interesting, meaningful, and valuable.

Note the independent finding that textbooks fail to make important ideas comprehensible because a commercial market requires covering the entire range of facts at the cost of depth on the central concepts.

Locate the real problem not in the textbook but in the assumption that it is the course of study from which all design flows, since even the best text serves only some of the desired results and the designer must supply the rest, reading selectively and supplementing.

Diagnose a design by tracing each stated goal to the activity that practises it and the assessment that measures it, and naming the missing links; a lecture course with only a midterm and final cannot reach a thinking goal because students get no practice and no feedback on thinking.
Define teaching as the organization of learning for authentic results, which dissolves the futile argument over whether the teacher should guide or direct — the answer being both.

Do not teach only from textbooks without active inquiry into their claims, which misleads students into believing knowledge is there for the plucking rather than the result of trial and error, inquiry, and argument.

Reject the misconception that teaching for understanding condemns lecturing and prescribes discovery, since all coaches lecture and Socratic teachers still give explicit instruction and feedback; when lecturing is properly criticized it is because the goals call for more learner attempts to test and apply ideas than the lectures allow.

Reject the doctrine that students should first learn passively and only afterwards apply, since applications are part of the knowledge and unapplied knowledge is knowledge shorn of its meaning; because understanding is wise performance, teaching for it is closer to coaching than professing.
Treat deciding what to teach as potentially the most important focus of an instructional theory, not a preliminary to deciding how to teach it.

Guard against lending learners the adult's own ideas rather than entering into theirs, since the teacher's enthusiasm cannot be transmitted by directing attention to what moves the teacher — the learner perceives the objects but not the relations linking them, lacking the necessary experience.

Treat ideas as genuine only when they are tools for searching out material to solve a problem: a concept becomes real when it makes sense of experience or opens new intellectual power, and repetition can weld a statement into memory without the idea being acquired.

Require something before teaching — designed and artfully facilitated experiences that raise the right questions and make the ideas seem real and worthwhile — since teaching after a revealing experience is often more effective than teaching a good amount before any experience.

Include the teacher as a situational factor: prior experience with the subject, whether it is a first or last offering, and whether it sits at the edge of competence all bear on preparation time and on how much risk the chosen strategy can carry.

Treat course design as necessary but not sufficient: good teaching and learning also require good teacher-student interaction, which can be worked on through teacher credibility, leadership, and the spiritual dimension of teaching.

Treat a writing style suggesting that inquiry is over and the student's job is to apprehend what is known as needlessly closing off thought, and scour the text for passing statements that can be reframed as essential questions for investigation across units and courses.

Interrogate a text's confident claims with the facets — where is the evidence for this, what primary sources justify it, and how do the authors know — especially where it asserts with finality what a historical figure believed or felt.

Teach an axiomatic or foundational system by showing the assumptions as the needed underpinnings of the theorems one wanted to prove and by revealing that other assumptions yield other systems of practical value, since key assumptions come from inquiry over time rather than being intuited or found whole.

Treat teaching as three distinct roles — direct instruction, constructivist facilitation, and coaching of performance — plus three noncontact roles of designer, evaluator of student work, and researcher into one's own effectiveness.

Give faculty dual roles — teaching their subject and designing the assessments for cross-cutting competencies — which makes each instructor think about their role in relation to the mission and keeps those competencies from falling through the cracks of subject-focused design.

Consider the enlarged three-dimensional view of teaching — intellectual, emotional, and spiritual — in which education results from three interdependent influences, teacher, student, and subject, with the subject at the centre and teacher and students as fellow learners about it, and which asks of the teacher a strong personal identity, the ability to create community, and deep listening.

Prescribe no blanket ratio among the teaching roles without knowing the desired results and assessments, since some goals call unambiguously for direct instruction while others cannot be met by instruction at all, and the mix changes across units and among teachers teaching the same unit.

Read excess teacher talk as a symptom of unclear goals, since without an explicit performance goal teachers become excessively didactic, whereas good coaches teach in smaller and more timely doses because they stay focused on enabling the learner to perform.

Watch for the characteristic failure of over-teaching by restating the textbook in different words while under-coaching by withholding feedback against models and rubrics until after the student has presented, and let the question of the best use of limited class time reallocate effort from giving information toward assessing and coaching.

Hold every instructional communication to the sole aim of aiding learning rather than informing, since keeping firmly in mind that anything beyond facilitating learning is mere chatter is the best guard against talking too much — while recognising that much teacher communication is essential, sometimes in large amounts and on other occasions not at all.

Do not make the student guess what is in the instructor's mind: it is probably best not to assume he knows the lesson objective, since communicating it takes little time, prevents his getting off the track, is consistent with the frankness of a good teacher, and helps the teacher stay on target.

Distinguish just-in-time from just-in-case instruction, saving extended telling for after learners have applied the learning, because memory cannot hold much when key information arrives in large amounts before any opportunity for meaningful use.

Free time for other kinds of learning by moving initial exposure to content out of class without abandoning the foundational-knowledge goal; the key is an in-class activity that makes the prior reading absolutely necessary and is itself visibly valuable, and when that holds the majority of students do the out-of-class work.
Let models do the teaching, since comparing strong and weak models develops increasingly refined conceptual and procedural distinctions in the learner.
Repeat a valid pre-instruction representation task after teaching to measure change in the learner's conceptual model directly.

Face the parallel timing decisions in discussion — when to frame the talk versus let students launch it, when to challenge an inappropriate answer versus let a student do it, when to correct a wrong fact versus let it stand, and when to observe versus coparticipate.
Note that the case method — students deriving meaning from specific cases with Socratic facilitation — has spread from business to medicine, engineering, and secondary problem-based courses.

Follow the professional case-method pattern in which the basics are met in the context of meaningful application, structured as repeating loops of challenge, model, practice, feedback, practice, performance, and feedback with increasing complexity.

Where the goal is learning to analyze and solve problems, put the problem first — an open-ended, ill-defined case the student must scope, research, and resolve — rather than front-loading content and deferring application.

Give students in problem-based learning a realistic case-form problem first rather than a body of information, ideally one they might actually meet in later work, reversing the tradition of front-loading content before any practice problem.

Prefer anonymous or semi-anonymous response over a show of hands, since students do not want to answer against the person next to them, and note that interspersed response questions let even a large lecture see the distribution of answers in real time and backtrack accordingly.
Use classroom devices that immediately record students' answers for the teacher, which allow the lecture to be reprogrammed on the spot.

Revisit the basics with every new group no matter how expert a student is, treating that review not as time lost but as embedded in work toward excellent performance, and keep both kinds of learning by doing running — simplified drill and complex fluid performance.
Distinguish the logic of learning to do things with content from the logic of transmitting content, since the difference has consequences for which kinds of teaching are used and in what sequence.
Do not infer learning from subject matter alone; the same content can yield different knowledge types and outcomes depending on objectives, instruction, context, and assessment.
Distinguish the four levels at which the sequence problem arises — course, topic or unit, lesson, and lesson component — because quite different considerations apply to each.
Classify the content type — fact, concept, process, procedure, or principle — because it determines both the graphic type and whether the lesson should be procedural or principle-based.

Restructure a course to open and close on the same essential question with an authentic role for the student, moving backward and forward in time as needed — a sequence that is logical though not chronological — without sacrificing content.

Apply continuity, sequence, and integration to the learner's experience rather than to how the material looks to someone already in command of it — continuity as recurring emphasis, sequence as increasing breadth and depth of development, integration as increased unity of behaviour — noting that chronological marching does not pass the test of intelligent continuity.

Treat improvisation as no substitute for planning — the purpose of planning is predictable results and intelligent improvisation rests on a good blueprint — and reject the belief that good teaching comes through artful spontaneity, which minimizes planning and supports the folk belief that good teachers are born.

Plan instruction deliberately at nested levels — lesson inside topic inside course or curriculum — rather than leaving it to moment-to-moment improvisation, since the authors hold that unplanned and undirected learning is very likely to leave many individuals unable to derive personal satisfaction from living in society.

Read the template as a completed aligned design rather than an order of work, since all design is nonlinear: the product must obey the three-stage logic while the process unfolds unpredictably and differently for each designer.

Work the real-world entry point by clarifying what mastery enables one to do, identifying the core challenges and authentic tasks, then determining the understandings, knowledge, and skill needed plus the practice and feedback plan that develops them.

Work the skill entry point by asking what complex worthy performance the skill enables, locating the relevant standard and its implied assessments, identifying strategies for using the skill well, and surfacing the big ideas and essential questions that undergird it.
Align activities, prerequisite and enabling skills, assessments, and the use environment directly with the targeted capability.
Assess feasibility from content stability, staffing, time, budget, and representative-learner access; estimate learning time from a mastery-oriented strategy and refine it through tryouts.
Keep the popular culminating event while honing it to better support the goals, since revision by backward design need not discard what students love.
Expect framing a unit in the template to reveal a missing perspective the designers had not seen the need for, and add it with its own understandings, essential questions, and performance task.

Improve a textbook-only unit — which shows up as Stage 2 and 3 full of chapter reviews and homework with Stage 1 empty — by planning backward from standards, adding understandings and essential questions, and supplementing with performance tasks, keeping the same core knowledge but embedding it in real-world issues with the textbook problems subordinated.

Open a revised unit with K-W-L to assess prior knowledge and set goals, review the rubrics and product examples with students before they begin the tasks, and add nonfiction sources at varied reading levels to accommodate differing readers while keeping the same desired results.

Reject the assumption that everything in the textbook should be taught or learned by all students, since a course has priorities framed as performance goals and understandings, and reject the two unfounded assumptions behind the perceived need to cover — that whatever is taught will be adequately learned and that whatever is not taught didactically will not be learned.

Audit the existing account of the content before adopting its features: textbooks typically supply properties without teaching what to do cognitively with them, and the properties chosen can themselves create difficulty in understanding the class and in classifying instances.
Use the template as a self-assessment guide, which clarifies purposes, sharpens priorities, and makes them clear to learners, producing a more powerful and coherent approach with the same content.

Avoid over-reliance on a recipe, which closes off responsiveness by fostering the belief that a well-thought-out plan must work and that failure is the students' fault, and which would over-proceduralize decisions that depend on the designer's reasoning; slavish devotion to recipes also robs practitioners of the experiential knowledge that builds trust in their own judgment.

Weigh authentic application, which is difficult and time-consuming to implement and evaluate precisely, against traditional tests, which are easy to design and grade but often yield invalid results and unhelpful feedback about what learners understand.

Locate authenticity in the context — the messiness of the problem, the ability to seek feedback and revise, access to appropriate resources — rather than in the task being performance-based or hands-on, and expect authentic assessments to teach students and teachers what doing the subject looks like and which challenges the field considers most important.

Negotiate teacher control versus learner control and direct versus constructivist approaches as standing dilemmas — when the expert should frame the issues and when students should pursue their own questions, when explicit teaching is more efficient and when the messy construction of meaning is required — a dilemma that recurs in teacher training as creativity versus working from expert designs.
Reject the assumption that any expert can teach: teaching is complex and requires considerable training, so subject mastery is not a substitute for design capability.

Bring an outsider into a redesign — an instructional consultant, or failing that a colleague interested in innovative teaching — because someone who is neither student nor coteacher can ask probing questions about what terms mean, about the plan, and about likely problems.
Treat instructional design as professional work requiring knowledge and practice, and use contrasts between weak and strong instruction to align leaders who underestimate that expertise.

Negotiate depth versus breadth as a standing dilemma, including when interdisciplinary work around a few big ideas is wise pedagogy and when it unwittingly produces superficial learning by attempting too much in too little time.
Negotiate simplified versus simplistic — making big ideas accessible without dumbing them down and simplifying without cutting off future inquiry or rendering the work vapid.

Justify and scope interdisciplinary work by the problem: because most large problems are bigger than one discipline, graduates need to view a problem through two or more lenses and work with people who hold them, and this can be delivered at scales from one teacher to a whole curriculum.

Negotiate comfort versus challenge, since essential questions may provoke irritation and confusion and complex tasks may frustrate easily defeated learners, yet a low-stress context is what lets students take risks.

Adapt guidance to learner differences and release it incrementally: didactic instruction with low-level questions suits high-anxiety learners while low-anxiety learners respond to difficult questions, and frequent pictures and oral communication aid poor readers while being inefficient for skilled ones — so give guidance a little at a time and let the student take as much as needed, since too much condescends to the quick learner and too little frustrates the slow one.

Negotiate uniform versus personalized work — how to hold appropriately different expectations without lowering standards or treating some students as second-class, and when differentiation becomes counterproductive.

Negotiate plan versus flexibility, since goals are usually achieved only by deviating from the plan in response to feedback and teachable moments while the designer must avoid losing sight of the goals in response to every student reaction.

Act on the finding that faculty and students independently name the same two highest-value changes — enhancing awareness of the big picture rather than only topic details, and regular helpful student feedback enabling midcourse corrections.

Adopt scholars' own framing questions about a domain directly as the essential questions of a course, and note that a whole course can be governed by as few as three or four questions including the meta-question of how practitioners construct and evaluate their accounts.

Apply big-idea frameworks outside the humanities as well: an entire physical education curriculum can be framed with big ideas, enduring understandings, essential questions, and standards, each big idea pairing an understanding with a probing question.

Frame the macro curriculum via the assessments by asking which key performance types or genres a student must master, and operationalize progression with a genre-by-grade matrix naming the specific task type at each level.

Adopt a shared set of common assessments by genre judged by common rubrics with one common prompt per genre per grade, which brought greater programme coherence and improved student performance where it was tried.
Solve the generalization problem by using a wide variety of student work of a similar type or genre collected over the year as part of the summative assessment.

Lay out course and curriculum sequences in a scope-and-sequence matrix as a first step in defining levels of skill across content topics, and cross it with outcome types, which is especially useful for surfacing the affective outcomes that would otherwise be omitted.

Run assessment throughout an individualised programme for four purposes: initial placement at an approximate level, mastery of each module and completion of enrichment objectives, diagnosis of difficulties to identify needed assignments, and measurement of yearly progress across the curriculum.
Expect that once this way of thinking is internalized it becomes very difficult to go back to creating disconnected activities or covering facts without a broader context.

Distinguish rubric levels by whether errors interfere with fluency and whether the intended meaning can be discerned rather than by error count, and attribute low levels partly to an insufficiently thought-through meaning — treating unclear communication as partly a thinking problem.
Use longitudinal rubrics describing increasing attainment across many years to chart progress over time, as national standards-based curricula do.

Build a developmental inquiry rubric around growing epistemic sophistication — from describing observed features, to recognizing why data must be collected, to recognizing that ideas rest on evidence, to explaining how interpretation of evidence yields new accepted ideas.

Put self-scrutiny of evidence at the higher levels — identifying observations that do not fit the pattern, deciding when to repeat measurements, judging whether the data suffice for the conclusions — and awareness of uncertainty and alternative views plus the ability to explain how evidence modified accepted theories at the top.
Use the six-facet rubric as a framework for building other developmental rubrics alongside existing proficiency guidelines in foreign language and literacy.
For written or oral creation, interpret the full product demand, introduce purpose, audience, content, organization, and criteria early, and explicitly teach any rubric learners cannot yet use.

Follow four sequencing rules for a curriculum aimed at wise performance — backward design from explicit performance goals with constant adjustment on feedback, frequent movement between an element and the whole task that justifies it, regular alternation between being instructed and applying, and a sequence permitting learning from results without penalty before formal performance.

Derive curricular sequence independently of the textbook's content and pagination, redesigning scope and sequence itself against standards related to learning goals — backward design pushed to a new level.

Apply those lessons to academic areas by agreeing on the core performance tasks in each field and designing programmes and syllabi backward from them, letting learners play the real game in a scaffolded way, and recognize that sequence experimentation is rare partly because many teachers have never experienced another sequence.
Think sequence through first at a manageable level — the course or the year of work in a subject — rather than attempting whole multiyear sequencing at once.

Organize the sequence around performance mastery because that is how people learn most effectively, not because students will become professionals — the unpredictability of each learner's future performance needs being beside the point.

Make curriculum reform depend on putting textbooks in their proper place as resources and framing syllabi and programmes around the optimal flow of inherently iterative, nonlinear learning to use big ideas in performance.

Aim a teaching strategy at a sequence whose activities work synergistically and build student energy across the course, and lay it out on a castle-top template alternating class sessions with between-class intervals so the planned sequence can be inspected for that build.

Plan sequence by determining the capability type, inferring its necessary conditions, and tracing backward from the outcome to the subordinate prerequisite objectives, because whatever must be recalled for a task must itself have been learned earlier.

Specify performance objectives because that is what makes it possible to determine the conditions of learning each acquisition requires, to analyse the curriculum for sequence, completeness, and prerequisites, and to estimate and coordinate the development schedule across the design team, teachers, media producers, and trainers.
Use a fully worked-out hierarchy for two purposes — guiding the design of an instructional sequence and guiding student and teacher in planning instructional assignments.

Sequence from simple prerequisite skills to complex target skills, which take longer to accomplish, and remember that one very important determinant of what students learn and how fast is what they already know.

Plan lessons around the order in which the performance objectives are best learned rather than worrying about mixing outcome types in one lesson, since once objectives are grouped by functional relationship and available sitting time, integrating the necessary conditions of learning becomes straightforward.

Sequence strategy improvement as repeated opportunities to apply the strategy, interspersed with instruction having other outcomes and recurring over relatively long periods, since gradual improvement is what can be expected and observable metacognitive gains are unlikely within a single lesson or two.

Use a different sequencing rule at each level of a course or curriculum rather than applying one rule throughout, and design the sequence top-down: general goals first, then progressively more specific objectives.

Meet the four conditions of chain learning when teaching a procedure: each step performed in the proper order, the steps performed contiguously with minimal lapse, the sequence repeated by the learner, and completion producing immediate satisfaction — since delayed reinforcement makes a chain harder to learn and the conditions are rarely all met on a first pass.
Design within-lesson sequencing after all lessons in the course have been sequenced, because working the later parts of the overall sequence often forces revisions to the earlier parts.

Recognize that most academic courses have historically marched from basics to advanced material with a long delay in application, to the detriment of engagement and effectiveness, whereas a subject area is ultimately about doing the subject — which is why it is called a discipline.

Note that however modern the content, a march through what is known organized by the logic of the content is a premodern tradition predating printing, public disagreement about truth, and any aim of serving the learner as a user.

Recognize that improving how content is framed and delivered is insufficient — the structure of much curriculum is itself inadequate — and that adding content in the name of rigour makes the big ideas harder to grasp within a traditional sequence.

Reject the assumption that presenting subject matter in its perfected form is a royal road to learning, since starting the immature where competent inquirers left off has a disappointing outcome written large in the history of education.

Develop curriculum spirally around recurring ever-deepening inquiries into big ideas and important tasks, revisiting the same ideas and materials in more complex ways, and note that the spiral has been praised for a century while few curricula actually embody it.

Recognize that until a course is organized backward from big ideas and performance goals with content as the means, results will remain disappointing and understanding will fall through the cracks, since a curriculum that constantly postpones the meaning of content cannot yield understanding, maximal recall, or a passion for learning except in the few able to learn on their own.

Frame a redesign as seven concrete changes: more ambitious goals, a wider range of activity types, rich learning experiences, repeated in-depth reflection on the learning process, alternative ways to introduce content, a coherent course structure, and a dynamic instructional strategy — all of it amounting to as much significant learning, active learning, and educative assessment as possible inside an effective strategy and coherent structure.
Frame teaching change as changing some things rather than everything, which makes it tractable despite how hard ingrained patterns are to alter.

Use the curriculum map to find holes in the instruction and extraneous dead-wood objectives that relate to no target objective, and remember that supportive verbal-information objectives need not be prerequisites of each other yet may still be taught in a contextual sequence.
Supply explicit guidance on how to build the structure as well as coherent content; structured material presented without structural guidance can overwhelm the learner's model-building effort.

Manage essential processing by restructuring the presentation — segmenting, pre-training, and shifting words to narration — rather than by deleting essential content; essential load comes from the complexity of the material for that learner.

Settle on other grounds the order of two bodies of content with no elaborative relationship, and recognize that grade-level and module divisions are often arbitrary organizational choices driven by how the content interleaves with the rest of a curriculum rather than consequences of the sequencing theory — the same content re-sequences for a different audience.

Apply the sequence found in modern performance areas to traditional academic subjects if understanding and even recall are to improve, following the reference-manual versus tutorial split: a reference explains every feature one by one, while a tutorial's flow follows the logic of learning to use the content in increasingly complicated applications.

Provide the nine events of instruction — gain attention, inform of the objective, stimulate recall of prior content, present the material distinctively, guide learning, elicit performance, give feedback, assess, and arrange varied practice — each chosen because it supports a specific internal process, treating the order as approximate rather than fixed.

Build systematic review into the sequence by cycling back to substantially the same principles in a new and more complex application, which also walks learners through the same discovery of similarities that characterized the discipline's development and works in an expository as well as a discovery mode.

Recognize that in far too many courses the basic learner questions of why this, why now, and so what are postponed or ignored by the work itself regardless of any verbal rationale, and consider that those who persevere may simply be those most able to delay gratification or trust adults.

Recover the original meaning of scope and sequence — scope as the major functions of social life and sequence as the centres of interest in students' lives — so that syllabus order derives from what would seem most natural and interesting to the learner.

Recognize that the specialist's order — technical concepts and definitions at the outset, laws early with little indication of how they were arrived at — leaves the pupil learning symbols without the key to their meaning and often acquiring simply a vocabulary.

Vary the position and form of the objects studied, because learners often recognize instances only in a standard position or typical form and an atypical presentation prevents recognition; a prerequisite review can do this double duty, broadening the concept while refreshing it.

Watch for the anatomical phase in which understanding is thought to consist of multiplying distinctions and naming each element, and instead individualize a specific property only when it clears up a present difficulty.

Reject the claim that a sequential subject must be taught in the textbook's order as confusing the logic of the summary with the logic of learning — one does not teach English via the dictionary — since easy hierarchical organization does not entail that the summary is the best way to learn the ideas and the value of their relationships.

Understand why textbook-driven sequencing persists — it is logical and easy to apply, lets the least capable teacher assign pages and hear recitation, supplies an alibi for failure, and from the administrator's view makes the work easy to divide and appear to run smoothly.
Confront unfamiliar or radical forms after more familiar ones, which deepens understanding of the earlier lessons about form, mechanics, and impact.
Start from learners' current experience and conceptions, engage them in constructing new relationships, and confront incompatible misconceptions through purposeful variation and activity.

Develop durable understanding by connecting new learning to prior knowledge, organising cases under higher-order relations, balancing guidance with learner construction, and revisiting ideas through varied, spaced encounters.

Follow the fields that redefined themselves around performance and abandoned the piece-by-piece approach — writing taught by writing from the start, novice skiers introduced immediately to the holistic process — and note that medicine, engineering, and design revamped their curricula quickly to be transfer-focused.

Recognize that high-stakes external testing has unwittingly given teachers a rationalization for avoiding in-depth teaching, resting on an assumption for which research is rarely offered — that the only way to safeguard scores is to cover what is tested and mimic the test format locally.

Deny that an obligation to teach to standards entails mimicking the test format in all local testing or haphazardly covering all prescribed content, since restated plainly the argument asks us to believe the only way to raise scores is to teach worse.

Accept that a good test need not involve the core daily performance provided its indicators yield valid inferences to the standards, and assign responsibility accordingly: the state audits, local educators own the underlying rigor, and absent data showing invalid inferences the task is rigor rather than test prep.

Distrust face validity, since inauthentic-looking tests can yield valid inferences if properly designed while performance-based projects can yield poor results when unrelated to the standards, and note that inferring instructional practice from test format leads to a random superficial survey of content.

Concede that teaching to the test raises scores in the short run where attention to common standards was previously lacking, while noting that once the format and test-taking skills are learned there is rarely long-term progress and scores typically drop when the test is altered or re-normed.

Check the provenance of claimed external pressure to march through texts, since such claims were never traceable to an administrative source and typically reflect teachers interpreting a focus on scores as an implied request to stick to textbooks and test prep.

Manage external assessment as a high-stakes constraint by mapping its underlying knowledge and processes against local objectives, teaching the substantive learning, limiting format rehearsal, and retaining unit-specific criteria.

Read a state test as an audit like an annual physical — valid because a few quick indirect indicators suggest the state of health, not because they define it — and recognize that concentrating on the indicator to the exclusion of the underlying regimen makes long-run health less likely.

Hold system-level agencies partly responsible for the confusion — for not making local assessments part of a comprehensive accountability system and for not designing more transparent accountability such as releasing tests and results after administration.

Weigh the multi-school evidence that students in classrooms with high levels of authentic pedagogy and performance were substantially helped whether high- or low-achieving, and that inequalities between high and low performers were greatly decreased when low-performing students used authentic strategies and assessments.

Reject the assumption that low-achieving, economically disadvantaged students are best served by didactic methods and review; to elevate mastery of basic skills, increase interactive instruction and moderate didactic instruction and review.

Combine significant learning goals, active learning, and educative feedback rather than adopting them singly: a multi-programme study found each of four learning activities individually related positively to graduates' rated first-year performance, but the major impact appeared only in the high-exposure group that had all four.

Define authentic intellectual work as construction of knowledge through disciplined inquiry producing discourse, products, or performances with value beyond school, and note the three-year finding that assignments calling for it actually improve scores on conventional standardized tests — including in very disadvantaged classrooms, where all students benefited.

Note the field observation that higher-performing schools show more in-depth teaching and demanding assessment while lower-performing ones show drill-and-practice orientations, and conclude that the target is the standards and the complex assessments their language implies rather than the audit.

Align institutional structures and external review with the course teaching theory, and prevent late examiner changes from breaking the relationship between taught activity, expected performance, and assessment.

Audit quality-assurance procedures for their effects on aligned teaching and redesign controls that cause overload, risk aversion, narrow assessment, or perverse incentives unless their benefits cannot be achieved less distortively.

Recognize two-midterms-and-a-final as audit-ive assessment by definition — backward-looking, serving only to grade — and expand the view of feedback and assessment toward educative assessment as deliberately as the view of goals was expanded toward significant learning.
Audit alignment across all three pairs—objective and instruction, objective and assessment, and instruction and assessment—using underlying knowledge-process demands rather than surface wording.

Recognize that standards committees working in isolation produced overly ambitious lists so that the plethora of standards worsened the overload it was meant to solve, and that publishers covering the waterfront to appease many constituencies invariably produce superficial treatment of everything.

Recognize that few systems have performance-based job descriptions or ask what the job is when hiring and evaluating, so without clarification it is easy to fall into thinking the textbook is the job.

Weigh the specific comparative gaps — student presentation of alternative solutions at 42 percent versus 8 percent, 44 percent versus under 1 percent of class time spent inducing the idea from problems, 95 percent versus 40 percent spent practising a procedure, and 96 percent versus 40 percent of teachers linking to other lessons.

Alternate the problem-based cycle across class boundaries: groups receive the problem and decide what information is needed, individuals seek it between classes, groups apply it to the original problem, students review solutions, and groups present to teacher and class.
Teach problem solving as both constructing an adequate problem representation and devising and executing a solution plan, including structural analogy when appropriate.

Expect the same programme to produce markedly different operations — one teacher encouraging students to invent a way of finding the answer while another requires only what the exercise book describes — with equally marked effects in the outcome measures, reading such divergence as the need for additional teacher instruction or training in a formative study and treating the two groups' results separately in a summative one.

Replace superficial coverage of all topics with in-depth coverage of fewer topics that lets the discipline's key concepts be understood, since equal attention to each little fact simply does not maximize test scores.

Answer the coverage problem by identifying the fundamental knowledge of the subject, ensuring students master that, and teaching them how to keep learning afterwards, since no course covers everything and cramming more in does not produce learning that lasts.

Concede that the time objection is partly valid — the work is genuinely challenging and individual teachers do not have all the time — while identifying the four hidden assumptions that inflate it: that each unit must be climbed alone, that time must come from teaching time, that each standard needs its own from-scratch unit, and that hard and time-consuming is bad.
Treat educators as causes of and students of learning rather than merely teachers, and treat the time needed for that work as essential rather than extra.

Make professional development practise what it preaches — uncovering rather than covering the big ideas of learning through ongoing inquiry and discussion — with local research small in scope but deep: one unit a year designed collaboratively, tried and adjusted, with intensive analysis of the student work.

Redirect existing time — roughly twelve hours of professional development days and sixteen of staff and departmental meetings a year — toward required lesson study, and make action research an obligation of all teams with annual reports on targets tackled, research undertaken, results found, and new inquiry proposed.

Run the collaborative cycle of bringing one's best existing unit to a shared design workshop, pairing with peers on the same topic, working with a content expert, reviewing against design standards, revising on feedback, field-testing, jointly evaluating the resulting student work, and submitting for expert review.
Make professional development results-oriented rather than coverage of educational trends by outside speakers, given how limited the available time is.
Make teaching professionalism durable through rewards, accessible development funding, sustained learning, and recruitment criteria that value student-centred practice.
Require one thoroughly developed unit per year — collected, reviewed, and shared — as a job requirement backed by supervision, on the logic that nobody prepares a gourmet meal every evening.

Recognize that standardized tests sample standards one at a time through decontextualized items and that the look of those tests misleadingly suggests teaching one bit at a time as if each standard were equally important, whereas rich units culminating in complex performance address dozens of standards simultaneously in hierarchical order and with more coherence from the learner's perspective.

Recognize that raising content standards does not necessarily raise performance standards, since content is input and performance output, and that raising only the difficulty of what is taught will likely worsen performance in the short term if teaching and time remain constant.

Use standardized to mean only that administrative conditions are uniform — so a uniformly administered road test is standardized — and reject the three attached misconceptions that multiple-choice and standardized are synonyms, that standardized tests are always machine scored, and that only national norm- or criterion-referenced tests can be standardized.
Align assessments with the exact objective performance and choose formats suited to the learning outcome rather than defaulting to one test type.

Expect resistance because true learning is always difficult — it upends old learning and produces disequilibrium — and consider that redesigning schools around ongoing collaborative research may be the only way to overcome resistance to changing habits, timidity about experimentation, and fear of criticism, since a group generates courage and helpful peer pressure to learn.

Hold that regardless of what cannot be controlled about students, schools, and society, the things in the educator's control — design, instruction, and giving feedback — can still significantly affect achievement.

Expect the reported paradigm shift to come from teachers evaluating every assignment and assessment for validity and letting go of time-honoured favourite lessons not aligned to the desired results, since many educators report not fully understanding the framework until they applied it to a real design and received colleague feedback.

Design against the learning paradigm rather than the instruction paradigm: judge the course by quality of exiting students and specific learning results rather than by material covered, and treat the teacher's role as designer of learning methods and environments.
Do not read a call for active inquiry and application around a big idea as a blanket endorsement of discovery learning.
Do not use unguided discovery learning; use a structured lesson that provides guidance.

Keep the general preference against overreliance on indirect tests separate from the narrower validity point that indirect inauthentic tests can yield valid inferences while authentic tasks can yield invalid ones, and note that recent studies cast doubt on extravagant test-prep score-gain claims.
Accept that an indirect test can be valid despite being less authentic if its results correlate with results on direct tests.

Judge validity relative to purpose, since the same test can be valid for one purpose and invalid for another, an inauthentic test can be technically valid as an efficient predictor, and an authentic task may not be valid.
Read an audit test as a brief instrument using simpler indicators as proxies for important complex goals, so attending solely to the audit makes little sense.
Distinguish an authentic test that directly measures the valued performance from indirect measures such as multiple choice — the difference between a driving road test and the written test.

Recognize that a benchmark anchored by the best possible samples sets the highest rather than an average standard, so such an assessment should not be expected to yield a predictable curve — standards differ from reasonable expectations.

Disambiguate the word standard, which is used variously for high expectations, a best-possible benchmark, a minimal passing score, a general guideline, and the criteria for judging, and note that a rubric alone is insufficient without an articulated performance standard made real by anchors or exemplars.

Remember that Bloom's Taxonomy was written to solve a testing problem — how ill-defined objectives such as really understand should be measured — and that its narrow sense of application differs from the richer sense here, which better matches its synthesis category stressing the student's unique production.

Test criteria for validity — grading research only on source count and page length is invalid because excellent research could fail it — and make criteria correspond to the qualities of masterful performance, noting that impact criteria are commonly undervalued.

Ask the scoring system's own validity question — whether it targets the most important aspects of performance or merely what is easiest to count, that is, whether validity has been sacrificed for reliability.

Define an ill-structured task as lacking a recipe or obvious formula, often fuzzy and needing further definition before a solution, demanding judgment and imagination and constant self-assessment and revision — the form all good essay questions, science problems, and design challenges take.

Note that most school testing is not longitudinal because tests are one-time events with one-time scoring systems, whereas longitudinal assessment requires scales and tasks usable across many grade levels.
Hold that open-ended does not mean all answers are of equal value: many acceptable answers are possible and are judged justified, plausible, or well-defended rather than correct.

Use a portfolio for both documentation and evaluation — revealing control over the course's major areas and genres, letting students select and reflect on their best work, and showing how works evolved and were refined.
Scaffold reflective portfolios with explicit goals, an explanation of reflection's learning function, and structured meaning-making rather than mere accumulation of experiences.
In portfolio assessment, let learners select and justify authentic evidence within a bounded range, preserving originality and valid unanticipated achievement while holding standards comparable.
Use capstones and longitudinal portfolios for programme outcomes that emerge across courses, requiring cross-course integration, open evidence, explicit criteria, and curation over time.

Build a succinct teaching portfolio as an evidence-backed argument linking philosophy, decisions, student learning, evaluation, baseline, improvement, and next development, with detailed or confidential support handled appropriately.

Evaluate teaching with multiple course-sensitive standards and corroborating evidence, adapting instruments to the aligned activities and using portfolios to connect philosophy, practice, and student learning.

Add reflection on the learning process itself, not only on the subject, using journals, learning portfolios, or critical-incident writing in which students record what they are learning, how, what role it plays in their life, and how it makes them feel.

Scale reflective writing across three forms — one-minute papers, regular journals or learning logs, and end-of-course or end-of-program learning portfolios — since each does something the others do not.

Use a learning portfolio as the integrating device, since it simultaneously carries significant learning goals, active learning, and educative assessment, and give it two parts — a narrative statement of the meaning of the whole experience and an appendix of supporting material.

Precede a learning portfolio with frequent smaller reflective writing, because students become more capable of reflecting and arrive at the end with a substantial body of material to organize, and announce the portfolio in advance so students reflect along the way.
Grade a reflective portfolio or journal on the care with which the experience is documented, never on the quality of the experience reported, so students are not penalized for honest reflection.

Structure a reflective portfolio with explicit prompts — what was learned about the content, how the learning fits the student's individual, social, and work life, and what they learned about how they learn — or with one prompt per taxonomy category.

Expect a portfolio to serve three audiences at once — the student communicating what they learned, the student's own self-assessment, and institutional assessment — and to raise the credibility of the rest of the course as students hunt for connections and material.

Use a concrete self-direction sequence: have students survey the field's range of topics, pick the three most important to them and argue why, then close with a portfolio section stating the learning agenda and the plan of action they will pursue next.

Build reflective dialogue into technical courses too, as periodic short writing on the course and its activities shared with classmates, closing with an extended end-of-course essay in learning-portfolio form.

Run a reflective teaching or practice journal with entries after every session, opened with hopes, fears, and self-evaluations, so it serves both as a reflective tool across the whole programme and as a record of professional development that later feeds a portfolio.

Draw evidence of learning for an evaluation from both parties — teacher-supplied samples of student work showing the types and range of learning, and student reports through questionnaires and portfolios — and use the taxonomy as the language for asking whether the work shows evidence beyond foundational knowledge.

Set journal guidelines for course-description articles to require the situational factors, the types of learning promoted, the activities and how they were assembled into a strategy, the feedback and assessment procedures, and the criteria used to judge the quality of student learning.
Expect a learning portfolio to do two things at once — foster the author's self-awareness and communicate something about the author to others — and design the prompts so both are served.
Assess long-running authentic work across development, peer review, audience response, and longitudinal portfolios, letting learners refine defensible rubric criteria and use them for revision.

Recognize that school standards are set de facto by the choice of peer-based anchors, so ask where the samples should come from and what would be a valid choice — and routinely give students anchors from slightly more advanced students as a longer-range target guiding ongoing feedback.

Keep criteria fixed regardless of age or ability — every persuasive essay must use appropriate evidence and effective reasoning — while treating how sophisticated the argument must be as the question of standard.

For persuasive work, require evidence-backed reasons and supplement generic writing criteria with disciplinary accuracy and reasoning, rewarding independent inference only when relevant and defensible.

Do not rely on persuasive communication to establish or change an attitude: a great deal of evidence shows repeated maxims, emotional appeals, and carefully reasoned argument all often have equally poor effects, and the methods that do work differ considerably from those for intellectual skills and verbal information.
