Reject an arbitrary cutoff as a standard, since few tests are designed so that a qualitative difference distinguishes adjacent scores and treating a standard as a cutoff turns a criterion-referenced system into a norm-referenced one.
Treat teaching quality as a systemic responsibility: couple teacher development with programme work, enabling institutional policy, and the scholarship of teaching and learning.
Derive course and programme outcomes from graduate purposes, embedding both foundational and higher-order capabilities in authentic disciplinary or professional contexts.
Build a coherent outcome hierarchy in which graduate purposes guide contextual programme outcomes and component courses provide the concrete teaching and assessment.
Develop complex graduate capabilities through disciplinary practice, repeated programme experiences, institutional ethos, and integrated evidence—not through generic labels or one isolated course.
When benchmarking qualifications or transferring credit, make equivalence visible without sacrificing distinctive strengths or lowering defensible standards.
Treat deep and surface approaches as task-and-context dependent: diagnose whether the learner's activity matches the required performance and use course-level patterns as feedback on the environment.
Coordinate workload and deadlines across teachers and courses, reducing breadth where necessary so learners have time for deep, transferable understanding.

Screen learning activities for visible value, feasibility, connection to prior knowledge, relevant learner action, formative feedback, and reflection; select among methods using outcomes, resources, and context.
Design cases with outcome-relevant complexity and realistic noise, sequence them into a coherent knowledge structure, progress toward learner-managed performance, and monitor workload.
State a complete goal as observable learner performance with material limits, identifying the learners, performance context, and available tools.
When learners must progress from recall to application, integrate targeted content with realistic problems, guidance, embedded assessment, remediation, and enrichment.

Split broad goals where subperformances have different structures, teach prerequisites when demonstrated entry performance is weak despite prior exposure, and describe learners, learning context, performance context, and tools distinctly.
Build motivation by connecting intended learning to goals learners value and by making success credible, rather than manufacturing urgency through threatening assessment.
Develop motivation by addressing both perceived value and attainable success through authentic problems, visible disciplinary value, and repeated meaningful achievement.
Align incentives and grades with intended learning so competition, fear, or strategic mark-seeking cannot succeed through low-level activity.
Support motivation at both initiation and persistence with challenging attainable goals and restrained use of rewards, punishment, or competition.

Test a proposed learning outcome against the three value axes it must serve at least one of: enhancing the learner's own life, enabling contribution to their communities, or preparing them for the world of work.
Target the goal as significant learning, not merely learning, because the learning-paradigm framing alone does not specify the quality or durability of what is learned.

Make the integration, human-dimension, and caring goals specific decisions: which kind of connection matters here, whether students should see themselves in a new way and how they should interact with others around the subject, and which changes in feelings, interests, or values are wanted — writing the valuing goal down explicitly rather than leaving it as an unstated hope.

Treat more-is-better in goals as conditional on real support: extra kinds of learning improve each other only when backed by activities and assessment that make students aware of what they are learning and how it relates, not when merely listed.

Treat a strategy that starts by motivating the mind and ends by reflecting on what and how one learned as a usable but weakly evidenced option in higher education, since its track record so far is in schools and corporate training.

Once goals extend to the human dimension, caring, or self-direction, treat students as partners rather than objects: share the goals and strategy, let students add their own goals, help choose the feedback forms useful to them, and take part in rethinking which strategies work.

Read poor student motivation as a symptom whose usual root is poor course design — low-level goals, audit-ive assessment, passive learning — and expect better design to eliminate or diminish many common teaching problems.

Build every application goal on the same pattern: a doing activity giving repeated practice at the target ability followed by feedback that is prompt and criteria-based, with the activity shaped to the kind of thinking — critical assessment of real work, creating a realistic invented case, or diagnosing a problem with incomplete information.

Supply a shared vocabulary before asking teachers to raise their goals, since teachers need terms for learning that reaches beyond understand-and-remember and beyond application before they can formulate such goals — and note that each familiar curricular goal in the literature expresses one kind of significant learning while none captures the whole.
Build accurate metacognitive self-knowledge with evidence-based feedback about capability, motivation, strengths, weaknesses, and knowledge gaps rather than inflated praise.

Derive training needs from a documented discrepancy — a job analysis or productivity data in industry, achievement against expectation in schools — and treat perceived or felt needs as legitimate inputs to goal setting while recognising they rest on no documented gap.

Expect the learner's goal to govern which strategy he selects in an unstructured environment: a student studying for a test will probably use a different strategy than one preparing to teach the same skill, so the goal communicated shapes the processing that follows.

Let learners set their own goals, report their own progress, and periodically re-evaluate those goals, because affective behaviour passes through awareness, acceptance, and valuing, is relatively resistant to change, and self-set goals build confidence as learners move toward the desired behaviour.

Treat motivation as a construct explaining the initiation, direction, intensity, and persistence of goal-directed behaviour that cannot be measured directly and must be inferred from observed behaviour.

Organise motivational design under attention, relevance, confidence, and satisfaction — capturing interest, letting learners set their own goals, providing practice with a high degree of success, and rewarding good performance — with the object of getting students to give the time and intensity of effort the learning requires.

Expect a lesson to have one primary objective without which it would hardly be worthwhile, plus supporting objectives of other capability types that must be learned first — an intellectual-skill lesson typically supported by information, cognitive-strategy, and attitude objectives.

Begin provision for multiple objectives from the goals of the particular instruction being designed, since learners' differing goals for the same subject imply different lesson objectives and different combinations of them.

Activate the goal well toward the beginning of instruction within the objective-informing event, as a verbal statement of the goal and its relation to prerequisite skills, knowledge, and attitudes plus a scenario relating what is to be newly learned to the goal — communications that are relatively simple yet adequate and should be tied as far as possible to the individual learner's prior experience and motivation.

Expect an established goal schema to work metacognitively — monitoring new learning to keep it on track and free of distraction, rejecting attention to irrelevant events, aiding retrieval of prerequisite knowledge when performance is required, and supporting the mindful abstraction that enhances transfer.
Ground instructional goals in verified performance needs, then analyze goal performance, prerequisites, learners, and use contexts before choosing a strategy.
Validate goal clarity by asking colleagues and intended learners to interpret it and revising any material mismatch in meaning.
Classify the goal's learning domain before choosing its analysis method.
Decompose the performance from the learner's perspective into complete, nonredundant, learner-sized goal steps, excluding teaching activities and content that is not required for goal performance.

Ground a behaviorally expressed instructional goal in a demonstrated need, then analyze the goal, prerequisites, learners, and use environments before writing condition-and-criterion performance objectives.

Evaluate motivation through sustained attention, personal relevance, realistic confidence, and satisfaction proportionate to effort, including both credible external rewards and intrinsic accomplishment.
Design for motivation as a changeable influence on what learners attend to, think about, practice, retain, and apply.

Frame goals as target behavior linked to success measures, constraints, prior efforts, and delivery capability, then brainstorm events around what learners must do, what motivates them, and what surrounds the event.
Organize motivational analysis around four categories — Attention, Relevance, Confidence and Satisfaction — each with its own strategy subcategories.

Gain and sustain attention as the first step of motivation, keeping the motivational concern for getting attention distinct from the information-processing concern for directing it to what must be learned.

Build relevance three ways: familiarity through concrete language and examples tied to the learner's experience and values; goal orientation by presenting the objectives and the utility and by supplying or eliciting goals; and motive matching by using strategies that fit the learners' motive profiles.

Establish a positive expectancy for success, because people avoid an interesting and desired goal when they believe the chance of reaching it is too low, and adjust risk to the learners' confidence and the objective type — low psychological risk with no fear of losing face while acquiring a skill, a degree of challenge once mastery has begun.

Build confidence by making performance requirements and evaluative criteria explicit, by providing multiple achievement levels and success opportunities so learners can set personal standards, and by giving feedback that attributes success to the learner's own ability and effort.

Do not measure motivational success by achievement, which varies independently of motivation for other psychological and environmental reasons, nor by a global affect rating, which is too general; tie the measures to the motivational objectives as you would to learning objectives.

Skip expensive devices such as games, simulations and extensive motivational illustrations when the scope of the learning objectives is simple and limited, and judge every motivational enhancement by cost against benefit, omitting an illustration whose gain on a simple point is marginal.
Make goal-setting optional so it stays nonthreatening for learners who do not wish to exercise an achievement motive, while giving a salient scoring and feedback system to those who do.

Offer an optional high-interest problem-solving task so intrinsically motivated learners can use their new knowledge, and gauge the lesson's motivational level by informally polling learners on their reaction to it, since willingness to re-engage voluntarily is one of the best indicators of motivation.
Expect motivational and learning strategies to interact: the same edit that makes an example clearer also sustains the learner's expectancy for success.

Note that a motivational model asks continually why the student might want to learn this content, taking the student's perspective, whereas other theories consider how students interact with the subject matter.
Build systems and infrastructure that make effective practice normal for ordinary teachers instead of depending on exceptional individuals to overcome weak conditions.
Translate standards and curriculum materials into visible, precise operative objectives that teachers can understand and enact.
State outcomes clearly from the learner's perspective so teachers and students can orient activity toward the same visible performance.
Plan learning episodes from outcomes using a two-sided account of teacher and learner activity, treating timetable labels as flexible settings and including supported activity beyond the classroom.

Judge a learning experience on both dimensions at once — process (students engaged, class energy high) and outcome (significant lasting change that persists past the course, and learning with potential value in students' later lives) — never on one alone.
Expect clearer criteria and standards to pay off on both sides at once: students self-assess with more focus and clarity, and the teacher assesses performance with more confidence.
State outcomes precisely and align them with learner characteristics, prerequisite and enabling capabilities, activities, and assessments.
Give criterion-referenced feedback that shows the destination, current position, next improvement, and controllable practices that can produce future success.
Check the prospective outcomes of each planning stage against the goals adopted by those who manage the system as a whole, keeping technical knowledge consistent at every decision point.
Give explanatory feedback that states correctness and adds a succinct explanation; it beat corrective feedback with effect sizes of 1.16 and 1.87 and was also rated more helpful.
Aim feedback at the task or the strategy used, and avoid praise and normative or comparative feedback, which direct attention to the ego and carry little task information.

Choose the kind of feedback the objective needs: correct-answer information, helped feedback that adds attention-focusing information or works the problem, or feedback intrinsic to using the new generality — which is the best feedback for a find-level objective.
Combine autonomy and trust with clear goals, organised support, and fair safeguards; avoid intimidation, arbitrary control, or cynical busy-work that redirects attention toward compliance or escape.
Adapt teaching scholarship to local disciplinary conditions, investigate its effects on one's learners, and share findings that may improve practice beyond the course.
Improve teaching through repeated, systematic action-research cycles grounded in disciplinary knowledge, learning theory, local evidence, and triangulation across students and trusted colleagues.

Shift students' orientation to learning rather than only training study skills: developing their concept of learning, building metacognitive awareness and control, giving space to explore personal interests, making assessment demands explicit so only full understanding counts, and making teaching more active and interactive.

Use funder award criteria as a teaching-change lever: requiring proposals to name the kind of significant learning to be promoted and to incorporate situational analysis, clear goals, active learning, and educative assessment drives faculty to learn those concepts, as an assessment-plan requirement demonstrably did.

Work through disciplinary associations, since faculty seek recognition under their norms: a comprehensive effort sponsors research on effective teaching, provides forums, offers skill-building workshops, publishes synthesized good-practice materials, and addresses policy questions such as how teaching should be evaluated.

Retain what is good in disciplinary tradition — close reading with discussion and reflective essays, laboratory and field experience, case studies bringing social reality into the classroom — and combine it with stronger design and interaction rather than abandoning it, since the traditions are limited alone but far more powerful when integrated.
Choose pedagogy before technology: specify the intended learning and learner activity, then adopt a medium only when its access, timing, social format, tools, and assessment serve that outcome.
Teach strategic and selective use of large information sources rather than treating access to information as evidence of learning.
Prepare undergraduates for later just-in-time learning through information literacy, reflective self-direction, strategic search, contextual learning, and deliberate improvement from prior practice.

Reject the search for a universally best medium: research on media utilisation supports the conclusion that no one medium is superior for all outcomes and all learners, and media cannot be identified as particularly effective for a single subject at a single grade level — both design work and research suggest selecting media for specific purposes within a single lesson.
Narrow media beyond the learning situation using three categories of factor — physical attributes of the media, task characteristics, and learner characteristics.

Begin media selection by identifying the learning situation, because the most prominent differences among media relate to it, then let the type of learning outcome drive the choice — a multistep intellectual-skill procedure cannot be adequately taught by an instructor's lecture — and weigh the learning environment, the conditions for development, the culture, and practical factors after.
Treat "which medium teaches better?" as the wrong question. Media-comparison framing is the signature of technology-centred design; reframe to which design features support which cognitive processes.

Before abandoning an underperforming innovation, test whether its intended outcome, feasible learner activity, and assessment evidence are mutually aligned, and remove practices that conflict with the learning-centred design.
Take a learner-centered approach in which technology is adapted to how people learn; a technology-centered approach has failed repeatedly since the 1920s.

Replace long passive exposure with purposeful generative activity—such as explaining, teaching peers, or acting on accurate representations—and judge engagement by its service to the outcome, not its excitement.

Build perceived dynamism from genuine excitement about the subject, shown as high energy, interest, flexible deviation to hold attention, good presentation, varied techniques, some unpredictability, positive relating, and bringing one's own personality into the class.

Do not dismiss a behaviourally passive format as inherently ineffective: a well-designed narrated animation or explanation can drive active cognitive processing — selecting, organising, self-explaining — in a learner who is sitting still.

Treat generative processing as motivation-dependent: it is the learner's willingness to exert effort at making sense, so it can be invited by an engaging, conversational, polite presentation but cannot be forced by adding content.
Reject arousal theory as a design rationale: emotional adjuncts do not buy cognitive engagement, and interest cannot be added to a boring lesson like seasoning.
Keep formative error exposure safe and non-humiliating, treating misconceptions as shared inquiry while reserving summative judgement until learners have had a fair opportunity to improve.
Separate formative and summative purposes, label them unmistakably, and keep diagnostic practice safe enough for candid errors while using its evidence to change both learner and teacher action.

Prefer safe realistic consequences before evaluative judgments, support beginners more heavily, fade correction with proficiency, and provide guidance without making answers an escape from engagement.
In formative review, first decide whether the experience plausibly advances the stated performance goal; do not let incidental errors or implementation polish obscure instructional viability.
Show and clearly label the common incorrect ways of performing steps or making decisions, with a warning, because identifying them helps learners avoid the mistakes in their own practice.
Design online discussion for reflective, collaborative growth, manage sequencing effects deliberately, and judge the quality of ideas rather than participation counts.
Staff interactive online learning with enough facilitators who understand both subject and medium; meaningful responsiveness does not scale like one-way content delivery.

Evaluate a delivery mode by asking whether each of the three active-learning components can be satisfactorily fulfilled in it, and compare high-quality online against high-quality classroom rather than against poor classroom teaching.

Expect online delivery to be at least equal for access to information and adequate for reflection — with electronic dialogue letting reticent students contribute and giving everyone time to compose — while doing and observing experiences are the weak link that must be solved by assigning direct authentic experience outside class or by using case studies, simulations, and stories.
Identify transformative threshold concepts collaboratively, distinguish them from merely necessary core concepts, and support learners through the troublesome conceptual transition.
Build and assess conceptual understanding through integration with prior frameworks and complementary transformations such as interpreting, exemplifying, classifying, and summarizing.
Use an attention-grabbing opening to create affective interest and a conceptual organiser to supply cognitive structure, selecting either or both according to the learning need.

Teach affective strategies for focusing and maintaining attention, controlling anxiety, and managing time by making students aware of how the strategies operate and giving them ways to practise their use.

Choose attention-getting stimuli from objects already familiar to the learners, because a familiar stimulus simultaneously stimulates recall of the context into which the new information will be placed.
Prioritise the quality of teacher-learner and learner-learner interaction over allegiance to a named method when developing self-management.
Diagnose self-directed-learning needs as generic organisation, content-specific strategy, or reflective self-management; teach each explicitly in the contexts and assessments where it must operate.

Address self-learning as two distinct targets — a changed self-image of who the student is now, and a new self-ideal of who they want to become — either of which may arise intentionally or as a by-product of the course.
Teach self-regulation as both knowledge and action: learners need strategies, task conditions, likely effectiveness, accurate self-knowledge, and practice monitoring and adjusting performance.
State qualitative deepening explicitly with outcome verbs that match the intended structural level, then support and assess the required restructuring.
Keep the outcome set manageable by integrating compatible topics and removing redundant lower-level verbs, then review it for aim relevance, main purposes, level, context, and alignability.
When implementation changes the understood objective, reconcile, document, and recommunicate the revised target before final assessment.

Bridge academic theory and professional functioning before graduation through authentic or defensible simulated performance, using learner-selected evidence where practice cannot be rehearsed by the teacher.

Treat tertiary teaching as professional practice by connecting scholarly learning theory, alignment, assessment, reflection, and scholarship to educators' own work, and assess functioning capability rather than attendance.

Implement alignment as one agenda: specify activity, content, context, and standard; elicit the activity; assess it against transparent criteria; and convert the judgement through defensible grading rules.
Audit alignment bidirectionally: every intended performance must be practised and assessed, every major demand must trace to an outcome, and verbs, level, context, and criteria must agree.

Open a broad implementation by explaining its purpose, demands, and response to concerns; then prioritise supported outcome writing because all later activity and assessment alignment depends on workable outcomes.

Make evaluation part of the aligned course system: map every assessment criterion to course outcomes, audit course outcomes against programme specifications, verify elicitation in practice, and review strategies and resources against defensible outcomes.

Check alignment with a three-column worksheet — every primary goal, the assessment that will show it was achieved, and the activities students need to achieve it — because that is what catches the easy trap of giving lip service to a goal while teaching in a way that does not support it.
In unit review, compare intended wording, enacted activities, assessment content, and scoring criteria, using specific knowledge subtypes and processes to resolve conflicting signals.
Before labeling an unrepresented activity as misaligned, identify whether it briefly orients learners, supplies a prerequisite, or supports an explicit objective.

Treat objectives, instruction, and evaluation as three anchorpoints that must be checked for agreement with one another, and determine objectives first because they must guide instruction and evaluation rather than the reverse.
Use an activity as assessment evidence when performing it develops and demonstrates the same outcome, while protecting early formative attempts from harmful consequences.

Evaluate implementation through an action-research spiral that starts with formative evidence, tests targeted changes, responds constructively to learner resistance, and combines professional judgement with deliberately collected data.
Use the learning activity itself as assessment when it directly enacts the outcome and yields valid evidence, while preserving an ungraded phase where experimentation needs protection.

Use activity families deliberately for what each supplies — role-play, simulation, debate, and case studies for psychological and social as well as intellectual experience; writing as part of the learning process rather than only as after-the-fact assessment; service learning to pair a topic with firsthand observation of the problem in a community.
Keep an activity's learning purpose visible and combine discussions, observations, intermediate work, plans, and products as formative evidence against that purpose.
When an activity stands in for learning, state the intended result and success criteria, connect them repeatedly to the activity, and show representative evidence.
Prioritise content deliberately: identify threshold and core concepts, state why each topic is included, vary depth by purpose, and protect important outcomes from stakeholder-driven accretion.
Make alternatives visible and balance stakeholder influence so consensus does not become content accumulation or replace the goal of effective learning.
Calibrate outcomes to programme stage and context, interpreting each verb with its object, originality, working, and setting rather than treating the verb as a fixed level.
Calibrate goal-analysis step size to learner proficiency and task evidence, write each step as observable action plus product, and treat numerical step-count heuristics only as rough diagnostics.
Map graduate, programme, and course outcomes to verify complete but proportionate coverage, intentional progression, and the absence of needless duplication or capability gaps.
When explanation is an outcome, give every learner repeated opportunities to construct and communicate relationships; teacher explanation alone is not aligned practice.

Implement constructive alignment as an evidence-revisable cycle grounded in an explicit theory of teaching: derive needed support and action from that theory, identify blockers, evaluate operation, and revise.
Do not equate conceptual explanation with competent performance or definition recall with understanding; teach procedures for execution and assess concepts with justified novel cases.

Add instructional explanations to worked steps only when conceptual understanding is the goal, no self-explanation question is present, and the content is mathematical; otherwise they can depress learning.
During extended plenary teaching, interrupt passive listening with learner activity and end with learner-generated consolidation rather than a teacher-only recap.
Make pre-class preparation cognitively active with an explicit outcome, needed background, and a written thinking task; check genuine completion and synthesise it through group and plenary work.

Pretest only the assumed entering capabilities as a rule, but let any student who believes he has already mastered an objective take that test as a pretest and skip the corresponding instruction if he passes.
Use concept maps to expose and develop relational structure, requiring labelled links and evaluating conceptual organisation and correctness holistically.

Use short answers for bounded recall or interpretation and explained relational diagrams for concept relationships, without treating either as sufficient evidence of integrated themes they cannot reveal.

Match the encoding aid to the state of the learner's existing structure: concept maps are especially helpful where that structure is weak or nonexistent, whereas analogies work only by linking new information to a structure that already exists.
Model hidden expert processes with visible decisions, revisions, and mistakes, then require learners to perform the process rather than stopping at observation.

Exploit the distinctive contribution of e-learning: making invisible processes visible — reasoning maps against an expert's, hidden mechanisms, and the consequences of hypotheses tested in a simulation.

For complex tasks, teach the actual thought processes an expert uses while performing, not merely the task's outputs, and use objective methods to uncover them because experts are usually not consciously aware of what they do.

Recognize that leaving learners to discover expert processes independently, because the expert cannot articulate them, is what produces underachievement: discovery is complex and is not itself taught, so only some learners succeed.
Design peer-teaching programmes around explicit outcomes and roles, select and train suitable leaders, support them continuously, and use their feedback to improve the live course.
Keep supplementary peer-assisted study review-oriented and ordinarily voluntary, prioritising it where course scale, difficulty, failure risk, or learner diversity makes support most valuable.

Design formative peer review around explicit intended outcomes, broad staff access, voluntary participation, reviewee control, trained participants, agreed confidentiality, and practical support for acting on feedback.

Give high-quality teaching and teaching research visible workload, recognition, promotion, time, resources, and accessible seed funding, with proportionate peer review suited to authentic action research.
Retain tutorials only for a distinct aligned function; when learner-led, pre-check inputs, seed questions and confusion points, and reserve instructor time for unresolved issues.
Audit large sessions by outcomes, actual activities, and who performed them; establish interaction procedures early and use live time for value beyond accessible content.
Humanise large classes by making questions collective learning events, remaining visibly accessible, reducing anonymity with privacy care, and avoiding cultural assumptions in informal communication.
Make assessment private when public exposure would distort performance, and use context, challenge, activity, and feedback so each interaction can both teach and reveal what the learner needs next.
Educate professionals for informed action by combining a sound knowledge base with repeated authentic performance of the outcome before final assessment.
Use computer-assisted assessment for adaptive practice, repeated attempts, immediate guidance, and contextual multimedia decisions only where the system validly represents the outcome.
Structure group learning so members have relevant resources, responsibility, psychological room to test interpretations, and a cognitively demanding agenda tied to assessed outcomes.

In group projects, assess hands-on inquiry, collective product, individual contribution, group process, and each learner's understanding of the whole; assign roles for learning rather than convenience.

Answer the routinisation objection: a learning structure is a map showing starting points, destinations, and alternative routes, not a dictation of how the journey is made, and it describes accepted goals with their subordinate steps without prescribing how an individual must learn — the learning journey requires different internal events for each person.

Structure small-group testing as pretest, instruction, posttest, plus an attitude questionnaire and possibly discussion of the instruction and the tests, since comparing pretest and posttest begins to answer whether learning occurred and how much.

Match collaborative structure and modality to the intended interaction: pairs for close reciprocity, jigsaws for interdependent responsibility and reintegration, ambiguous evidence for judgement, and asynchronous modes for considered contribution.
Require three conditions for collaboration to work: social interdependence, an explicitly chosen outcome goal, and dialog in which everyone contributes substantively and no one is ignored.
Clarify legitimate collaboration in planning and resource discovery while preserving individual responsibility wherever assessment must certify individual achievement.

Align workplace learning through shared outcomes, a complete evidence-to-action practice cycle, trained supervisory teaching, structured reflection, and institution-workplace agreement on opportunities and rubrics.

Develop alignment capability through worked design practice, close professional learning with outcome-based self-assessment and next actions, and coordinate application at role-appropriate course, department, and institutional scales.
Teach creativity as generating and evaluating novelty, innovation as implementing worthwhile novelty, and convergent and divergent thinking as complementary advanced processes.

Teach creativity through sufficient disciplinary knowledge, open-ended creation, iterative performance and reflection, exploratory consequences, peer feedback, and a climate safe for unusual hypotheses.

Assess creative learning through purposeful experimentation, exploration, reflective transformation, and realised work, allowing a well-evidenced breakthrough to score highly even when a risk-bearing product remains partly unresolved.
Assess creativity under conditions that permit adventurous work, recognising that high anxiety and tight invigilation may suppress the very performance sought.

Assess creativity in the disciplinary work through grounded originality, ambition, experiment, critical inquiry, contextual appropriateness, and effective realisation while keeping criteria open to unanticipated forms.

Define lifelong learning within a field as handling unforeseen problems through just-in-time knowledge acquisition, responsive relationships, independent information use, reflection, and intellectual autonomy.
Assess embedded lifelong-learning capabilities through capstones or independent inquiry that elicit selective information use, self-monitoring, reflection, and strategies for unseen problems.

Name the full set of lifelong learning strategies for students — gaining new experiences, reflecting on the meaning of new and old experiences, acquiring new information and ideas, networking with others, observing people who have lessons to offer, and participating in formal programs — rather than equating learning with courses.

Treat knowledge as jointly constructed by students and faculty and the student as an active constructor and transformer rather than a passive vessel, with the mode of learning being relating rather than memorizing — and exercise practical thinking on hypothetical, simulated, or real problems, since the ability transfers to students' personal, social, and work lives.
Design for meaningful learning by combining retained relevant knowledge with opportunities to construct understanding, solve problems, and use learning in new situations.

Design PBL from its intended outcomes: use consequential authentic problems to build usable knowledge, reasoning, self-direction, motivation, and collaboration, calibrating ambiguity and guidance to learner readiness.

Build coherent PBL briefs by mapping cross-disciplinary concepts and skills, specifying authentic roles, data and deliverables, staging evolving information where appropriate, and equipping facilitators without scripting inquiry.

Run PBL as a recurring cycle of activating and verifying current knowledge, identifying gaps, seeking varied resources, reconvening to integrate, applying learning to the problem, receiving feedback, and reviewing self-management.
Evaluate PBL against its intended professional performances, learning strategies, implementation quality, and costs—not only against conventional recall examinations.

Align the whole PBL system: tutors facilitate rather than dominate, assessment rewards application, teachers integrate across specialties, and organisational boundaries permit authentic multidisciplinary problems.

Use peer recap to retrieve prerequisite learning, role play and lived experience to analyse complex interactions, and authentic field investigation when learners must diagnose and defend improvements to real settings.
Use norm comparison only for explicitly scarce selection after checking minimum standards; do not confuse relative rank with educational achievement.
Permit different task formats or working conditions to demonstrate the same standard when each route provides comparable, sufficient evidence and preserves necessary integrity.
Validate assessment by its alignment, interpretations, uses, target-domain coverage, and learning consequences; adverse backwash that contradicts the outcome undermines validity.
Gate expert judgment through congruence, content, design, and transfer analyses, stopping when a material mismatch or uncorrectable content defect makes downstream evaluation unjustified.
Integrate calibrated self- and peer review into examinations only with shared criteria, discrepancy review, integrity checks, and retained instructor authority.
Explain self- and peer assessment as practice in professional quality judgement, not as transfer of marking labour.

Design trustworthy high-order e-assessment by budgeting human review, using proportionate identity and authorship controls, and preferring authentic secure performances, staged work, or oral verification over an automatic retreat to closed examinations.
Select learning environments by the performance learners must practise, and use peer review or assessment when exchanging and applying professional critique is authentic to that practice.
Use shared quality criteria for instructor, peer, and self-review, collecting successive authentic products and adapting checklists as learners' judgment develops.

Make the correct end-state of a procedure visible throughout practice so learners can self-check, and give those who fail the self-check another attempt after reviewing the aid before instructor assessment.
Design and grade essays by the relational work demanded by the question—argument, explanation, comparison, interpretation, or reconceptualisation—not by fact volume.

Reflect the nature of the subject in the design: whether it is convergent toward one correct answer or divergent toward multiple valid interpretations, whether it is cognitive or also involves significant physical skill, and whether the field is stable, changing fast, or contested between paradigms.
Reduce irrelevant essay-judgement effects through feasible anonymity, controlled grading order, blind rechecks, broad-grade-first decisions, and targeted review near consequential boundaries.
Use automated essay scoring only after validating its outcome fit, reliability, feedback quality, and bias for the actual discipline, cohort, and task.

Treat objective tests as judgement-laden instruments: pilot consequential items, avoid inferring deep structure from recognition coverage, and use MCQs formatively with explanation when that better serves learning.
For ordered-outcome items, build and trial a cumulative progression from recognition to integration or transfer, then report the highest demonstrated level rather than averaging incompatible levels.
Make the qualitative judgement first—holistic for meaningful wholes or analytic for distinct components—and convert to administrative points only afterward, with substantively justified weights.
Define holistic grade levels as qualitatively different forms of understanding and publish the observable evidence that demonstrates each level, rather than unexplained score bands.

Distinguish task grades from outcome achievement: aggregate valid evidence by both task and outcome, retain task feedback, report outcome profiles, and use weak outcome patterns to improve activities and programme sequencing.
Report each learner's achievement by task and outcome so strengths and needs survive the overall grade, and use that feedback to inform rather than mechanically restrict later study choices.

Choose the grading model explicitly: use criterion-based holistic judgement for integrated qualitative performance, point accumulation only where it fits, and define whether grades represent whole tasks or outcomes inferred across tasks.

Use task classification to check coverage and choose conditions: classifying the objectives reveals whether any intended purpose was overlooked, identifies the conditions effective for each outcome type, and supports a curriculum map reviewed for the presence of the needed information, attitude, and skill objectives.

Use item analyses showing which items a majority passed or failed rather than total scores when evaluating instruction, since item scores are what tell where the instruction needs improvement — and apply the same measure-preparation principles whether the test covers one prerequisite skill, a topic, or a larger unit.

Interpret outcome differences only after the groups have been shown reasonably equivalent on aptitude and support variables, with statistical tests confirming the differences are significant at an acceptable probability level — and treat outcome evidence gathered during formative work as no more than initial indications, with further summative studies to follow.
Use random sampling of required repeated submissions to sustain practice while controlling assessor workload, checking all completions and ensuring the sample fairly represents performance.

Implement repeated practice as a full cycle — perform, capture the performance, receive immediate multi-source feedback, write a self-analysis, and be coached one-to-one before the next attempt — because that cycle is what moves learners from acting on correction to owning the whole activity and seeking their own improvement.
Use the practice exercises placed last in a section as test items when they exercise the full performance the objectives call for.

For professional cases, use authentic integrated performance, gate essential safety or correctness components non-compensably, diagnose components formatively, and control embedded-assessment workload.
Use confidential critical incidents as structured evidence of how learners interpreted knowledge in practice, diagnosed consequences, and proposed improvement.
Keep confidential teaching development institutionally separate from personnel investigation so educators can seek candid formative help.
Diagnose a critical teaching incident through the problem, observable evidence, plausible causes, prior response, and relevant theory before choosing a specific changed action.

Build learning contracts from starting attainment and needs within fixed outcomes, negotiate work and assessment routes, provide continuing consultation, and close with an explicit standards-based fulfilment decision.
Design portfolios around strategic evidence selection, early guidance, bounded workload, open but relevant artefacts, and holistic outcome-profile judgement rather than item averaging.

Let learners choose portfolio evidence only with outcome-based justification and complete coverage, judge integrated artefacts qualitatively, and convert to numbers afterward only when aggregation requires it.
Use portfolios for learner choice among valid evidence types while requiring complete coverage of every intended outcome.

Use presentations and posters where authentic professional communication is intended, with shared criteria, clear logistics, accessible formats, and relevant practitioner, peer, or student perspectives.
Assess reflective journals as selected outcome evidence of theory-informed self-evaluation and improvement, not as complete personal diaries or chronological event logs.

Make practica reproduce professional behaviours and standards, normalise observation and formative feedback before summative judgement, and combine trustworthy evidence sources under shared outcomes and rubrics.
Use structured peer assessment both to evidence individual contribution and team effectiveness and to develop objective collegial judgement as a professional capability.
Assess fuzzy and PBL problems as a profession-specific cycle of diagnosis, information learning, synthesis, action, monitoring, and feedback, using non-compensable gates for necessary stages.
Use shared digital portfolios for formative peer comment, self-assessment, and summative review only with appropriate access control, privacy, and attribution.
Separate confidential formative portfolios and peer review from consequential personnel review; for any summative use, declare purpose, evidence, procedure, criteria, and governance in advance.

Use separate portfolio, reflection, and client-facing products where creative process, professional communication, and artefact quality are distinct outcomes, with iterative peer judgement and only relevant real-world constraints.

Prevent and judge plagiarism by teaching reproducible scholarship, argument, attribution, and consequences explicitly, distinguishing copying and patching from synthesis, and using complementary evidence when writing proficiency could mask content understanding.

Teach research as distinct judgments and procedures: evaluate source relevance and accessibility, record usable sources, keep sortable notes atomic, and scaffold theme discovery only after meaningful effort.

Use a manageable portfolio, capstone, or other synoptic performance with explicit programme criteria when integrated functioning knowledge spans several outcomes and cannot be represented by one course task.

Use programme outcomes to replace disconnected subjects with integrated units, cases, placements, practical work, and e-learning, reducing transmission time when it crowds out the performances learners must develop.
Write course outcomes as observable uses of knowledge, and include responsible active learning only when activities and assessment validly elicit it.
Cap foundational-knowledge goals at what genuinely must survive in long-term memory one to three years later; a course may legitimately introduce far more than its retention goals name.

Recognise multiple aims: no single capability type suffices, since verbal information alone is an inadequate goal, intellectual skills alone do not produce independent learners, cognitive strategies need content to work on, and attitudes need a substrate of information and skills.
Do not infer learning outcomes from a course's topical title; identify them as the varieties of learned capability that make different types of performance possible.

Reject the claim that only one outcome type matters: with the exception of motor skills, every capability category is likely to be involved in planning any course, since no course exists without information, none leaves attitudes untouched, and none exists without intellectual skills.

Use the capability taxonomy for four jobs — evaluating the scope of objectives a course intends, grouping similar objectives to cut the strategy-design work, informing the sequence of segments, and planning the internal and external conditions each group requires — and assess coverage per category, exploiting the fact that the conditions of learning are the same for every objective within a category.

Design a unit to encompass several objectives of different capability classes and to achieve a suitable balance among them rather than pursuing one outcome type at a time, using the conditions of learning for each type to account for the prior learning presupposed and to plan the external conditions required.

Select and scope goals by importance, stability, learning difficulty, expertise, effort, materials, learner access, and available time; split oversized goals and expand undersized ones only with relevant adjacent capabilities.

Resource the first aligned implementation explicitly, realise it in concrete classroom practice, allow extra initial design time, and substitute feasible activities aimed at the same outcome when preferred resources are unavailable.
Coordinate course contributions and programme outcomes with colleagues while preserving local discretion over methods that remain aligned.

Reflect an outcome's programme importance in learning support and grade contribution, preserve non-compensable thresholds, and include graduate capabilities such as teamwork or communication only when the course authentically teaches and assesses them.

Triangulate implementation evidence across learner perceptions, performance samples, comparable criterion grades, learning processes, qualitative explanation, and reflective artefacts, respecting each source's causal, privacy, and comparability limits.
Triangulate impact evidence across learners and relevant workplace observers, time measurement to the work and skill, and sample the differences most likely to affect implementation.
Triangulate learner variation from direct evidence and multiple informants, adapting motivation and practice preferences only when they remain compatible with target performance.

Verify technology, access, reliability, context support, and instructor responsibilities from actual conditions, while triangulating learner characteristics and using authentic motivation suited to heterogeneous participation.

Use a context-aware critical friend to challenge interpretations and strengthen evidence, and assess implementation maturity by demonstrated practice and explicit next actions rather than by claims of familiarity.
Adapt an aligned course deliberately to institutional and collegial constraints, then collect teacher and learner evidence systematically and use a critical friend to challenge its interpretation.

Make leadership an enabling system for department-wide alignment: leaders must understand the design and resource implications, provide direction, engage staff, delegate responsibility, and cover process, educational, and political functions.

Judge mature departmental alignment by enacted programme mapping, support, collegial practice, evaluation, improvement, and learning gains; sustain it through coordinated governance, rewards, action research, and evidence-responsive change.

For department-wide alignment, combine committed leadership and explicit delegation with student representation, formative evaluation, learner induction, scholarship-informed development, and policies that visibly prioritise teaching.

Build durable local capability by selecting effective internal practitioners from evidence, recognising and workload-adjusting their facilitator role, and using external expertise to seed rather than permanently own routine problem solving.

Match rollout scale to commitment: use a supported pilot to build credible evidence when most participants are unconvinced, and coordinated broad implementation when leadership and a clear staff majority are ready.

Verify organisational implementation through changed classroom activity, learner communication, assessment, and grading—not completed paperwork—and address misalignment between manager and teacher commitment.
Support institution-wide reform with discipline-credible educational consultants, aligned assessment policy, local coordinators, and recognised implementation time.

Run quality as prospective enhancement supported by necessary assurance: predefine formative evaluation against the innovation's intended outcomes and explicit trade-offs, investigate unexpected effects, and convert findings into tried changes.

After an initial departmental implementation, produce a timely reflective report on teaching, learning, cross-course variation, enabling structures, unresolved concerns, and the next improvement plan.
Grade reflective learning on awareness of expectations and process, examination of progress, and organisation of future learning—not on personal disclosure.

Give department-level enhancement durable participatory governance, development expertise, privacy-respecting longitudinal evidence, collective problem solving, and a system-improvement response to weak outcomes.
Close formative peer review with the reviewee's own reflection, specific evidence tied to agreed outcomes, a practical improvement plan, and a confidentially retained record for later reflection.

Structure formative peer review with appropriate topic challenge, shared grade descriptors, and evidence-focused prompts; return it before revision, preserve the improvement trail, and close the loop by showing how advice affected the work.

Position teaching-development centres as embedded academic design partners, supplement one-off workshops with programme-linked development, and bring disciplinary precision and educational expertise into both local design and central policy.

Coordinate internal and external educational expertise across problem definition, proposal design, implementation, and dissemination, and require supported projects to share methods, results, limitations, and lessons ethically.
Use external experts and panels to assure essential programme outcomes and improve teaching and assessment, while preventing personal content preferences from creating curriculum overload.

Qualify trainers through demonstrated conceptual and practical alignment capability: combine foundations with redesign of a real course, then require an adapted local programme and a credible path to self-sufficiency.

Support a trainer cascade beyond initial instruction with context-appropriate resources, peer processes, portfolios, policy review, and reflective enhancement, keeping cohorts small enough for practice and feedback.

Scale alignment through context-designed trainer cascades and a systemic combination of enabling top-down policy and resources with bottom-up disciplinary ownership, while allowing local variation that preserves alignment.
Support realistic learner confidence with clear purposes, plausible prerequisites, learner-fit vocabulary and scope, manageable progression, and attainable challenge.
Audit capability at every trainer generation and judge scaled professional development by changed teaching, support systems, and student learning—not activity counts alone.
Audit which knowledge-process combinations are emphasized, mentioned, and omitted, interpreting gaps against retention or transfer goals without allowing the taxonomy to determine curricular values.

Exploit the audit trails technology-assisted learning leaves — the steps taken and progress attained by individuals and groups — to improve both the instructional plans and the theories behind them, which conventional classroom instruction cannot supply.

Evaluate constructive alignment separately as a design-and-review framework and as a possible cause of improved learning; adoption supports utility but does not prove impact, especially while institution-wide effects and costs remain under-tested.

Interpret alignment benefits contextually: connect outcomes to real practice, compare grades against stable standards and corroborating evidence, and monitor both learning gains and recurring staff and student workload.
Treat broad reported use of constructive alignment across countries and disciplines as evidence of adaptability, not proof of effectiveness in every context.
Use open qualitative outcome verbs to specify the process learners must enact while leaving room for unanticipated products or conclusions.

Accept that instruction often produces unintended outcomes judged desirable or undesirable only when later observed, so the planned objectives are the basis for evaluation without being the whole of what occurs.

Build stronger evidence for alignment with baseline-informed longitudinal comparison of multiple outcomes, implementation costs, and strategy-by-context effects, using causal language proportionate to practical and ethical design limits.

Use teaching recognition to strengthen the whole system: reward individual and team contributions across design, mentoring, delivery, and assessment, then support recipients to demonstrate practice and mentor others.

Rebuild recognition of teaching on two moves — clarify the criteria that define excellence, and expand who can receive it — because a few high-profile awards on haphazard criteria reach too few people to change practice.

Balance administration toward conditions for valid learning, retaining proportionate integrity and feasibility controls while rejecting psychometric assumptions, grade curves, or invigilation rules that cannot represent the intended achievement.
Design grading and assessment procedures that support learning rather than hinder it, so the procedure helps students learn better while still supplying a valid and fair basis for the grade.
Validate goals originating from content outlines, experts, or administrative mandates against current performance evidence and observable learner outcomes.
Staff foundational high-enrolment teaching with suitable experience and support, and align promotion, prestige, policies, and rewards with the institution's stated teaching mission.
Use transformative reflection at every organisational level as a feedback cycle in which theory frames a problem, informs a solution, and supports evidence-based testing and adjustment.
Structure group-process reflection around evidenced effective practices and improvement opportunities, avoiding unsupported individual blame.
Use supported volunteer courses and demonstrated success for gradual expansion when the existing organisation remains viable; use coordinated systemic change when the status quo is non-viable.
When practice change is required before full conceptual commitment, make the theory and rationale explicit and supply resources, collegial support, and an enabling climate.

Begin systemic faculty renewal with candid stakeholder diagnosis, establish a shared educational goal, distribute decision responsibility, and build cross-disciplinary teamwork where programme outcomes cross subject boundaries.

Create a trusted shared-responsibility climate and operate a continuous faculty evidence cycle using students, graduates, staff, institutional data, minimum standards, targeted support, committee governance, and staff-led action research.

Work all six faculty-support conditions together — awareness, encouragement, time, resources, cooperative students, and recognition and reward — because they are mutually reinforcing and no single organization can supply them all.

Rethink faculty work around two questions — what the institution really needs its faculty to be doing, and how to encourage that in a way that meets institutional and faculty needs at once — and add professional development as a fourth expected area alongside teaching, research, and service.

Hold the institution to five support steps: keep itself internally aligned, make professional development integral to faculty work and staff a center for it, have leaders — especially department chairs — who help faculty find the time, evaluate teaching so faculty attention lands on student learning, and build mechanisms to educate students so they cooperate with innovating faculty.

Interpret broad gains during a systemic reform as encouraging but not isolated causal evidence, and require major teaching decisions to remain consistent with the agreed educational culture and alignment framework.

Analyze realistic teaching cases as provisional evidence: classify intention, enactment, and assessment separately, reread as later evidence appears, and evaluate only after making sense of alignment.

Take whether the stated objectives were met as the essential formative evidence for revision, letting comparison with a supplanted unit and observations of unanticipated effects feed the decision when available — and use the observational records, questionnaires, and tests across all stages to decide whether a lesson should be kept, revised, reformulated, or discarded.
Place vocational projects in credible industry contexts, make online teamwork observable, and require research-backed proposals to withstand critique from peers, tutors, and relevant practitioners.

Design capstones as sequenced integrations of earlier learning, schedule formative feedback early enough for revision, and pair group performance with confidential individual reflection when personal development is also intended.
Formatively evaluate a usable draft in one-to-one, small-group, and field-trial stages, linking learner difficulties to design causes and revisiting underlying assumptions.
Formatively evaluate a usable draft through one-to-one, small-group, and field evidence, tracing learner difficulty back to any implicated design assumption or component and revising accordingly.

Compose the early design team from complementary decision, performance, learner, content, design, production, and constraint perspectives; choose collaborative subject experts and involve control functions without letting compliance dominate ideation.

Phase a complex authentic project so distinct capabilities build within one coherent professional task, and allocate projects, laboratories, or tests according to the performance each can validly elicit.

Build project-management learning from genuine multi-task complexity — a real proposal for a real client, or a research project the student must scope, source, analyze, and present — since it is the coordination demand, not the topic, that teaches it.

Structure an authentic project in phases — gather real information, work in teams to develop a proposal with a concrete artifact, then present it to the real decision-making body — and where a curriculum allows, make the project cumulative across courses so each addition must integrate with what came before.
Build authentic project environments with clear process scaffolds, examples, policies, job aids, purposeful teams, and the full specialist and administrative support ecosystem.

Design empirical inquiry as a connected progression from evidence retrieval and screening through contextual analysis, pattern formation, comparison with established accounts, supported generalisation, and practical application.

Make inquiry assessment reproduce the full evidence-to-conclusion process, rewarding relevant valid selection, rigorous screening, salient contextual patterns, logically supported generalisation, and qualified judgement of contested claims.

Use complementary written, oral, and extended inquiry formats when each reveals a different part of the outcomes, with format-specific criteria for issue selection, evidence-backed argument, viewpoint comparison, and independent analysis.

Trace each impact question to the evidence and instrument it requires, anchor measures in learned skills and job context, and prefer direct question-organized analysis unless the design requires stronger inference.

Integrate theory, research, professional action, and cultural context in practice disciplines, and make repeated metacognitive self-correction an explicit capability for consequential independent judgement.
Assess metacognitive knowledge through contextualized discussion, journals, observation, and longitudinal comparison with evidence, allowing legitimate individual differences.

Allow bounded topic choice in a critical review, integrate the several disciplinary and graduate capabilities the task can authentically evidence, and scaffold independence with worked analysis, guidance, models, and source-evaluation practice.

Grade scientific critique on both disciplinary analysis and effective expression, distinguishing description from integrated argument and reserving mastery for extended justification, transfer, original interpretation, and coherent evidence.
Use published course examples as prompts for context-sensitive reflection rather than templates, preserving explicit alignment while redesigning the details for the local setting.

Give the course one unifying theme, integrating question, or graphic so students can see its central focus and connect goals, activities, and assessment; the design question shifts from how much content is enough to how the content should be organized.

Distinguish a course outline, which shows only the organizing content and its sequence, from a blueprint, which adds the supporting content, prerequisites and objectives per lesson; work the supporting content out for every lesson, and mark which prerequisites are unmastered rather than listing them all.

Do not expect lecture alone to deliver retention, transfer to novel situations, thinking or problem-solving skill, or affective outcomes; a long research record shows even well-delivered lecture is limited on all four.

Use the lecture for what it does with the utmost economy — inspiring an audience with the lecturer's enthusiasm, relating the field to human purposes and student interests, and relating theory and research to practical problems — recognising these as instructional events: the lecturer functioning as a human model establishing positive attitudes, carrying motivational effect, and supplying a context of cues aiding retention and transfer.

Elicit a teacher's real goals with a forward-looking dreaming question — what should be true of these students one or two years after the course that is not true of others — rather than asking what the course will cover.

Derive application goals from the future situation: name the situations students will plausibly be in one to three years later where this learning is relevant, and what they should be able to do there.
Translate the teacher's own dreams for students into explicit course goals at goal-formulation time, using the language of significant learning to state them in a controlled and focused way.

Pose a real task at the very start as a diagnostic, because teachers can badly overestimate incoming knowledge and only a real task reveals it; then ask what the teacher hoped students would do, since that answer describes the intended end-of-course capability and is what allows the course to be refined.

Test a course-purpose statement by asking how one would know when the purpose has been achieved, since such statements may communicate general goals to fellow teachers yet fail to tell anyone how to observe what was accomplished without having been present at the lesson.

Expect a change effort to stall unless four conditions are met in sequence: the teacher sees that significantly different ways of teaching exist, is persuaded they produce good outcomes, receives guidance on how to do it, and has institutional recognition and support.

Expect substantial teaching change to be achievable both by teachers with a problem to solve and by already-good teachers who want to be better, and in both cases to raise student engagement and the teacher's own satisfaction.

Attribute weak teaching partly to structure rather than wholly to the individual: doctoral training targets research, new faculty are rarely taught to teach, and reward systems signal that publication comes first.

Ground any claim that instruction is adequate in evidence about what students actually learn and how much they grow, not in demand, enrolment, or satisfaction, because input-and-resource measures of excellence do not answer the question.

Treat instruction quality as the load-bearing ingredient of an educational experience: curriculum, instruction, and faculty-student interaction all matter, but an exciting curriculum and approachable faculty cannot compensate for instruction done badly.

Attend to the quality of learning a course produces, not only the amount, because students take either a deep approach seeking personal meaningful understanding or a surface approach content to reproduce what was presented, and teaching and assessment choices push them one way or the other.

Judge institutional quality evidence by level: testimonial and facilities imagery, then general outcomes such as retention, graduation rates, and accreditation, then whether graduates as a group actually demonstrate the specific learning outcomes and whether the programs produced that — and only the third level answers the question.

Judge an accreditation approach against its three options: inputs and process ignore whether resources are used effectively, taking the institution's own goals at face value gives no assurance the goals are significant, and only setting out general principles of quality learning asks whether students achieve them and whether programs support them.

Do not treat learner preference or satisfaction as evidence of learning: end-of-course ratings correlated only .12 and .15 with knowledge and skill, and matching learners to their preferred amount of practice did not help.

When weighing institutional strategy, note that a focus on process and outputs such as graduates, rather than on outcomes such as significant learning, is plausibly a competitive liability under the forces of information technology, new providers, globalization, and new kinds of students — but treat the market prediction itself as unproven.

Do not accept a teacher's claim to be teaching a competency as evidence that it is taught; require that they can define the competency and state the criteria and standards by which they judge student work against it.

Judge teaching excellence on three criteria — whether the teaching produced significant student learning, plus course design and teacher-student interaction — which first requires institution and faculty to agree what significant student learning means and faculty to document the degree it was achieved.

Work on both levels of credibility, since being competent, trustworthy, and dynamic and being perceived as such are independent: a genuinely competent teacher can lose credibility through behaviour that reads as incompetence.

Treat small-group work as conditionally effective: it can produce powerful learning about the subject, the problem-solving process, oneself, and working with others, but only given the right group structure and assignment design.

Separate the two halves of the group-size problem: diagnosing gaps in enabling skills can be done about as effectively with large groups as small, but designing and executing the instruction that diagnosis implies is greatly affected by group size — which is the basic rationale for individually prescribed instruction.
Use a team rather than individuals when the goal is a creative product or an ill-defined problem solution, where group products beat individual ones with a very large effect.

Use a taxonomy broader than the cognitive domain when setting goals, because learning how to learn, leadership and interpersonal skill, ethics, communication, character, tolerance, and adaptability do not emerge readily from a purely cognitive hierarchy.
Use the ordering of knowledge and cognitive-process categories as a broad complexity heuristic rather than an invariant task hierarchy.
Note the asymmetry honestly: cognitive strategies have not been broken into subcategories as intellectual skills have, and whether they can and should be remains open to future research.

Recognise that integrating objectives into learner goals requires more than an external map: the learner must acquire a higher-order cognitive structure — a goal schema — that represents the goal and relates it to its prerequisites in verbal knowledge, concepts and rules, cognitive strategies, and attitudes, together with a scenario relating learned knowledge to the enterprise.

Expect external requirements to have already moved beyond content: accreditation bodies require general professional skills and broad professional perspectives, national reports call for demonstrable gains in capabilities, skills, and attitudes, and employers name a consistent list of critical competencies.

Make the performance of graduates the paramount quality-assurance question — technical competence, the ability to gain and apply new knowledge, flexibility and adaptability, and the ability to address specific problems in complex real-world settings — since learning-centered accreditation is already demonstrably feasible in engineering and in a regional accreditor's principles.

Treat caring as the energy supply for a course rather than as a soft extra: when students care about something they gain the energy to learn more of it, and without that energy nothing significant happens.

Deliver feedback inside a caring relationship, because without empathy and personal understanding students filter it into instructions for getting a grade rather than information for building capability.

Build caring in two steps: first connect students with their own feelings about the topic — usually through stories delivered by film, novel, role-play, or a visitor, or through direct observation during service — then have them take an action informed by that connection, such as creating something, proposing an action, or reshaping ideas.

Design for several kinds of learning at once rather than trading one against another, because the kinds are relational and synergistic — achieving one raises the chance of achieving the others, so teaching is not a zero-sum game.

Write course-specific goals as concrete statements of what students will be able to do after the course, with at least one goal under each taxonomy category the course claims, rather than leaving goals in generic form.

Do not stop at stating better goals: defining goals in taxonomy terms does not by itself improve learning, and unless the course is designed properly the other components of effective teaching have only limited impact.

Generate goals by asking, for each kind of learning, what that kind would mean in this specific course, answering at least the most important prompt in each category, and using the category's characteristic verbs.
Start every goal with a verb and make the verb as concrete and specific as possible, because that is what tells both teacher and students what students should be able to do.
A single course can address all three forms of learning how to learn if the goals are kept selective and focused; without that selectivity, do not claim all three.

Decompose the course downward in named layers: end-of-course objectives, major units with terminal objectives, then performance objectives at a level appropriate for task analysis, one or more of which make up a lesson and which may span capability categories.

Make the kind of thinking explicit: treat thinking as the general concept with critical, creative, and practical as its three subcategories, and check which one an assignment actually asks for, since teachers who say they want students to think often mean quite different things.

Match the judging criterion to the kind of thinking: critical thinking is analyzing and evaluating and therefore turns on explicit criteria, creative thinking is judged by novelty together with fit to context, and practical thinking is judged by the effectiveness of the resulting solution or decision.

Operationalize critical thinking as identifying and challenging assumptions plus exploring and imagining alternatives, and promote it with three techniques: student writing and discussion, explicit emphasis on problem solving with varied examples, and verbalization of methods and strategies to encourage metacognition.

Supply students with both the conceptual understanding and the assessment criteria before expecting critical thinking, since judging the quality of an interpretation, explanation, or prediction requires a yardstick the student holds.

Supply or co-build the criteria rather than assuming students know them, since novices do not arrive knowing what separates high-quality from mediocre work; telling them works, and having them brainstorm and refine the criteria themselves is better where the situation allows.

Connect academic work to other realms of a student's life through concrete devices — oral-history interviews, internships alongside coursework, service learning, and journals linking course subject to personal events — rather than asserting relevance.
Design human-dimension learning around a real relationship, since learning about oneself or about others differs from learning about people in the abstract precisely in that a relationship exists.

Promote the human dimension by making students more self-aware and more other-aware in relation to the subject, using an imagined situation or simulated role plus a reflective log for the first and others' stories plus classmate discussion for the second, and combine both because the paired impact is especially strong.

Treat self-authorship as a legitimate and research-supported teaching goal: college teachers can do more than they currently do to help students internally define their own beliefs, identity, and relationships, which presupposes a strong sense of identity before students can take responsibility for constructing their own knowledge.
Expect learning about Self and learning about Others to be reciprocal, so a design aimed at one will likely deliver both — a claim held with hedging rather than as a guarantee.
Set the learner's expectancy of what he will be able to do, because expectancy and executive control modulate how a situation is perceived, encoded, and turned into performance.

Teach the inquiry method specific to the domain rather than a generic one, because the nature of knowledge differs by domain and so does how one adds to it; in practice this means teaching students to formulate questions and then seek the information that answers them.

Teach inquiry with two moves together — give students practice conducting inquiry as a doing experience, and give them constructive feedback on how well they conducted the process itself — with students formulating their own questions and then working to answer them.
