Teach inquiry as a dialectic between theoretical constructs and methodological procedures, and use concept maps to make visible how a student or an expert understands a topic.

Hold two goals at once in inquiry teaching: understanding deep enough that learners can make novel predictions in the domain, and the ability to construct and test general rules and theories on their own; teach facts and concepts only insofar as they fit the domain's general framework.
Aim inquiry teaching at getting learners to analyse problems like scientists — systematically considering different cases, forming and testing hypotheses, and looking for counterexamples.

Distinguish inquiry from discovery: inquiry opens instruction with a major question and directs everything that follows — expository or discovery — toward answering it, and is likely beneficial where motivation is a major concern, with discovery used occasionally but sparingly because of time limitations.

Do not count a pick-a-topic independent study as producing self-directed learners: without critical reflection on the learning process it builds only learner-controlled activity in the student role, and without asking what else to learn next and why it does not build autodidaxy or personal autonomy.

Do not stop at learning logs: self-awareness is a prerequisite but the next step is a forward-looking learning agenda naming what else the student needs to learn, plus a plan of specific actions such as reading, searching, consulting an expert, observing, or attempting it themselves.

Account for all three ways people learn — informal learning from everyday experience, self-organized adult learning projects, and formal structured programs — noting that a large majority of adults routinely run their own learning projects and that much of what people learn about themselves comes from their own, and sometimes mistaken, interpretation of events.
Set the self-direction target beyond mini-research projects: autodidaxy and self-directed learning in life, built on a learning agenda plus a learning strategy.

Distinguish the looser individualisation varieties by what is agreed and what is left free: independent study agrees only the most general objectives and places no restriction on preparation for a final examination, while self-directed study agrees specific objectives and supplies optional resources but still leaves the method entirely to the student.

In professional education, do not separate studying the principles of good practice from applying them; good professionals reflect on what they are doing while doing it, so the curriculum must support learning both simultaneously.

Recognize that a skills-based professional curriculum still needs all six kinds of learning to reach its application goals — foundational knowledge of the instruments, integration of parts into the whole, self-understanding and interaction with others, caring and professional attitude, and knowing how to keep improving.

Recognize the list-of-topics approach as a design failure mode: it is quick, but it organizes information while ignoring how that information will be learned, so it typically supports only foundational knowledge, which has a relatively short half-life.

Require the three primary components — goals, activities, and feedback and assessment — to reflect and support each other; presence of all three is not integration, and integration is the load-bearing proposition of the model.
Require integration at two scales as well: activities connect toward the conclusion of each topical unit, and each new unit connects with the preceding ones toward the conclusion of the whole course.

Do the situational analysis first and thoroughly, walking the whole checklist — specific context, external expectations, nature of the subject, learners, teacher, special pedagogical challenge — since only a systematic pass surfaces which factors matter, and a superficial pass yields a course that fails the students, the curriculum, or the teacher.

Close the situational analysis with one integrating question — what is the special pedagogical challenge of this course — recognizing that the answer is usually a student preconception rather than a content difficulty, and that meeting it makes success likely.

Collect situational information with real instruments — survey questionnaires, achievement tests, informal discussion — wherever the teacher's assumptions about the situation may conflict with the reality.

Judge a course design against five explicit criteria: in-depth situational analysis, learning goals spanning several kinds of significant learning, educative feedback and assessment, active teaching and learning activities, and integration and alignment of all components.
Separate specific from general context in the situational review, the general context covering the course's place in the curriculum and its professional-preparation role.

Write goals across all six categories regardless of how technical the subject is, since parallel goal sets have been produced for fields as different as microbiology, art history, and statistics under the same headings.

Phrase the readiness question operationally — having studied and learned X, is the student ready to do Y — and it can be run at programme scale, as with a portfolio judged by a faculty member and a practising professional against readiness to practise.

Run team-based learning as its full cycle — individual reading, then an individual and a group readiness test, then substantial class time on practice application exercises, then a test of both understanding and use, repeating per topic — since the Readiness Assurance Process is what quickly lifts nearly all students to moderate understanding and frees class time for application.

Mark entry skills — prerequisites the learner is expected to hold before the lesson and that will not be taught during it — distinctly on the hierarchy or map, so a readiness pretest can be constructed from them.
Budget time for motivation, readiness checks, instruction, practice, integration, and assessment, combining individualized delivery with prepared human support where learner readiness varies.

Expect missing criteria and standards to be the common failure rather than a solved problem: evidence shows faculty frequently omit them, and in a four-year collection of writing assignments the criteria were unclear even to the researcher.

Use comparative peer review — teams post solutions, all teams circulate and judge, mark the best and flag a written concern, and flagged teams answer — to make tacit criteria explicit and drive analysis of why one solution is better than another.

Design self-assessment so honesty is the winning strategy: grade the quality of the evidence and argument in the self-appraisal, not the flattery of its verdict, so a well-argued modest claim scores high and an unsupported strong claim scores low.

Supply both a scoreboard and applause: quick reliable feedback against clear criteria on whether this attempt succeeded, plus recognition of success by peers, the teacher, or an external assessor, since motivation needs both.

Sequence the feedback stance: when an authentic task sets the bar high, students initially do poorly, so start with encouragement and only gradually raise the bar toward honoring excellence while still providing a valid scoreboard.

Create the encouragement condition as a culture: make identifying as an effective teacher admirable, make it acceptable to be open about one's teaching problems and experiments, celebrate colleagues' successes informally, and hold departmental colloquia or college-wide conferences on teaching.

Expect fewer discipline problems under individualisation — personal attention motivates toward success, the method is designed to produce success which is itself rewarding, and less whole-class teaching leaves fewer opportunities to capture the group's attention — all of which lessen the traditional adversary relationship, discourage public confrontations in which neither side wishes to back down, and remove the temptation to use sarcasm or ridicule, quietly reminding the teacher that the goal is learning rather than platform performance.

Recognize that knowledge of results does two jobs at once — confirming correct responses and correcting wrong ones, and giving the achievement-motivated learner a measure of success — and that immediately available answers reward effort only when the items are moderately challenging and effortful learners get most of them right; self-evident answers make the feedback redundant.

Never insert esteem-building attributional comments unless learners who exert effort will in fact succeed, do not claim that effort leads to success unless the materials have been validated, and prefer citing an approximate measured figure from your own tests.

Avoid competition against a fixed criterion score during a learning exercise when some learners would be discouraged rather than challenged by failing it first time, tell learners explicitly that seeking help is acceptable, and where most learners are already confident leave attributional feedback out of the printed material for the teacher to give selectively.

Prefer more active methods over the lecture-discussion tradition, since the research literature questions that tradition's adequacy and indicates students learn more and retain longer with active methods; active learning means involving students in doing things and thinking about what they are doing.

Prefer direct forms of each active-learning component where possible, treating indirect or vicarious forms as a fallback rather than a default, and use the component-by-directness grid to see which cells a course leaves empty.

Combine solitary and shared reflection: some meaning-making must be done alone, but dialogue dramatically increases the chance of richer meanings and collaborative meaning-making creates the foundation for community.

Distinguish the indirect from the direct form of getting information: textbooks and lectures are pre-interpreted by an intermediary, while original sources and unanalyzed data are the direct form, and the more often students meet primary material the sooner they can use it themselves.

Use vicarious doing — case studies, gaming, simulations, role-play, in-class group problem solving — when a direct real action is not feasible, since it lets students practise the actual activity without the consequences a mistake would carry in the real setting.

Aim for rich learning experiences — single experiences in which students achieve several kinds of significant learning at once — drawing from the in-class family (debate, role-play, simulation, dramatization) and the out-of-class family (service learning, situational observation, authentic projects).

Use indirect observation through film, literature, and oral history to reach people, cultures, times, and places direct observation cannot, accepting that it is less full and authentic in exchange for far wider range.
Expand the experiential dimension first when improving a course, since that is probably the single most powerful change most teachers can make.
Aim at continual change rather than a single change, making small changes continually and major ones periodically, and treat teaching well as a journey rather than a destination.
Shift the criterion for good teaching from the teacher's own comfort level to the quality of student learning; award-winning lecturers have abandoned mature, student-approved styles after that shift.

Pitch the change effort at the teacher's level: experienced teachers can start from ambitious goals and innovations, while less experienced ones should first get clear about what their goals really are, even traditional ones, and about the relationships among situation, goals, feedback, and modification.

Treat the course as an occasion to exercise leadership, using the four transformational components: model your values so as to warrant admiration and trust, supply meaning and challenge with enthusiasm and a shared picture of what is possible, prompt innovation by questioning assumptions and reframing problems while never criticizing an individual publicly, and attend to each person's needs for achievement and growth with two-way exchange and effective listening.

Judge a candidate rich experience by whether it is complex, challenging, and context-rich enough to generate several kinds of learning simultaneously — real or simulated, on campus or at a distance, the format is secondary to that requirement.

Break the unread-assignment loop with all three moves together: stop lecturing on assigned reading, hold students visibly accountable for it such as with a quiz, and build an in-class activity that requires what they read — which supplies the intrinsic reason to do it.

Debug the design before running it, looking for correctable operational problems such as an assignment that allows too little time or too few copies of required reading for the number of students who need them at once.

Use a one-minute paper at the end of a session with a prompt such as the muddiest point, the most important idea, or what remains unanswered, since answering forces a mental review of the whole lesson; expect scattered answers at first and improvement as the practice and the responding feedback continue.
Allocate hybrid time by mode strength: use the online component for content access and discussion and reserve reduced live class time for experiential learning such as case studies and simulations.

Relocate and supplement lectures and secondary sources rather than eliminating them, since they retain value as a basis for study; the recommendation is about where and how they are used, not about their abolition.

Run integration as a check-and-change pass over each connection between components rather than as a step that generates new content, and check the decisions against the situational findings for invalid presumptions about student knowledge or attitude, a structure at odds with the teacher's own beliefs, and conflicts between student and teacher goals.

Run integration as two parts and do not skip the second: students first learn about each subject being connected, then give focused attention to the connection through thinking, writing, reflecting, and discussion — it is that second step, not the first, in which integration occurs.

Give each topic an introduction followed by opportunities to apply its concepts, allow unequal time across topics, and use the structure to make assignments progressively more complex and increasingly about interactions among topics.

Distinguish technique from strategy: a technique is a single discrete activity, a strategy is a particular combination of activities in a particular sequence, and inserting small groups into an otherwise unchanged course is using a technique, not adopting a strategy.

Situate a technique inside its instructional strategy and course design when writing about teaching, since technique-only articles show no awareness the technique exists elsewhere, do not note its cross-disciplinary use, and give little rationale or context — which limits transferability.
Develop strategy flexibility by having learners apply, explain, and compare multiple valid methods, and diagnose actual method use rather than inferring it from answers or speed alone.

Train higher-order strategies by direct instruction followed by spaced and varied practice: teach the strategy, then practise it across varied learning situations over an extended period using distinctive cues that remind the learner when it applies.

Prescribe methods together with the situations they fit: state which strategy components or model to use, and for which pairing of desired outcome with conditions. A recommendation that names a technique without naming its situation is incomplete.

Pair every strategy in a catalogue with an explicit account of when and why it is used, and interrogate any approach for the situations where it is not advisable and for its cost-effectiveness, not only for the situations it fits.
Add the missing reflective-dialogue component to team-based learning via periodic journals and learning portfolios, since the cycle natively covers information-and-ideas and doing but not reflection.
Produce the overall scheme by choosing an instructional strategy spanning one to three weeks and repeating it for each main topic, adjusted to the course's time structure.

Schedule the term by deciding how the course should begin, then how it should end, then filling the middle, and leave blank unscheduled time so overruns, cancellations, and mid-course additions can be absorbed without breaking the design.

Classify and choose an instructional strategy by its student-activity sequence — hear-read-test, read-write-talk, do-read-talk, hear-then-see-or-do, read then individual and group tests then practice with feedback, or a staged know, build know-how, do, then DO progression — with each activity building on the last and preparing the next.

Write the instructional strategy — a plan for assisting the learner's study effort for each objective — before developing the materials, so that instructional activities are tied to the objectives; the strategy takes the form of a lesson plan for teacher-led work or production specifications for mediated materials.

Spend an entire period on a single instructional event where it earns it — establishing motivation for a series of lessons, or clarifying the exact nature of the expected performance for a unit before instruction begins, which suits courses whose major outcomes are problem-solving skills.

Run a tutoring episode as a repeated cycle of stimulating recall of prerequisites, presenting the stimulus, providing guidance, eliciting and assessing performance, and giving feedback — confirming and moving on where the learner performs correctly at once, and where he errs telling him the correct response, having him repeat it, and running the same procedure for each successive component until the whole performance is correct.
Choose the strategy needed for mastery before fixing duration, then improve learning-time estimates from repeated tryouts.

State in the introduction what the learner will be able to do, how often the skill recurs in the course, and where it generalizes beyond the topic, and pose an intriguing everyday question the lesson will answer with a promise that they will know the answer by the end.

Require differentiation at two scales — variety in activity type from day to day within a topical block, and growing complexity and challenge across the units — since a course whose sessions all do the same thing is poorly differentiated.

Use the twelve design questions as the working checklist — where are you, where do you want to go, how would you know if you got there, how are you going to get there, who and what can help, what are the major topics, what will students need to do, what is the overall scheme, how will you grade, what could go wrong, how will students know the plan, and how will you know how it went.

Start design from what students will be doing after they have learned rather than what they will be studying, distinguishing target objectives to be attained at the end from enabling objectives that must be attained during the course because they are prerequisites, and working top-down from the targets to the enabling objectives.
Do not promise flow, since it happens to a person rather than being created at will; design instead for the activities that make it more likely.

Design for the three conditions that make flow likely — clear compatible goals, immediate feedback on how one is doing, and a right balance between high challenge and high skill — since the challenge-skill cycle is what makes flow a magnet for further learning.

Set the challenge from accurate information about what these students can and cannot do at the start, so it stretches them a bit but not too far, and always pair a challenging activity with activities that build the skills needed to meet it.
Challenge learners frequently in authentic situations, adjust difficulty to current progress, and offer assistance when requested or clearly needed.

Make an infeasible simulation feasible by relaxing an unrealistic constraint — for instance requiring students to work out everything that would have to be done rather than physically completing it — without losing the engagement the scenario creates.

Use structured devices that carry both awarenesses at once — a debate requiring students to argue views not their own alongside a log about their own experience, or readings from multiple cultural viewpoints alongside logs and discussion.

Embed human-dimension goals even in a skills or language course — by having students set goals about who they want to become and discuss progress, by having pairs create something the class will use, or by running each unit from the students' own experience of the theme out to the target culture's expression of it.

Use the published catalogues of goals as a prompt list when a category feels empty: the human dimension covers leadership, ethics and character, self-authorship, multicultural sensitivity, teamwork, citizenship, service, and environmental ethics; integration covers interdisciplinary connection, learning communities, and connecting learning with living and working; application covers critical and practical thinking, creativity, managing complex projects, and performance skills.

Take the human capabilities that make a goal's activities possible as the proximate goals of instruction, and in a complex society identify the capabilities that serve several different goals at once rather than planning instruction separately for each goal.

Require a complex-project assignment to be genuinely open-ended and multi-task if it is to teach project management, since it is the coordination of several unlike tasks — not the size of the topic — that produces the learning.
Adapt guidance in complex projects through worked models, coaching, purposeful questions, peer tutoring, and targeted instruction on diagnosed gaps.

Vary the form content takes — current periodicals, documentary film recording phenomena directly, dramatic film portraying them realistically, and field or lab work where students gather their own data — rather than assuming content means lecture and textbook.

Apply the short per-category recipes: inquiry needs practice with feedback plus analysis of how knowledge is created; caring needs connect-to-feelings then act; the human dimension needs a connection then reflection on its impact; integration needs learning the parts then thinking about the connection; application needs repeated practice plus feedback; foundational knowledge needs out-of-class time, varied content forms, and linkage to other activities.

Integrate business need, performance gap, learner need, treatments, scope, quality, milestones, roles, decisions, communication, and issue resolution in one project plan, with separate product- and process-success criteria.

Manage innovation risk deliberately rather than avoiding innovation: size up the political situation and personal tolerance, decide first how much risk is affordable, then pick the innovation that promises real learning gains within that limit — since avoiding innovation altogether condemns a teacher to stagnation.

Lower the risk of a new activity three ways: pick a lower-risk activity such as a brief paired task inside a lecture rather than a role-play, pick one taking less in-class time, and structure it carefully by anticipating where it could go and setting boundaries.

Begin where each student is: in a group, arrange other activities for students who do not need part of the planned instruction rather than defaulting to having them sit through it as review, which is not always the best solution.
Make the course emulate as closely as possible what students will actually be doing later, which is the argument for replacing cookbook exercises with the tools and projects practitioners really use.

Accept that lesson design partakes of art as well as science and cannot be reduced to a cookbook recipe, while using the events of instruction as the focus that aids both construction and revision after formative evaluation — since reference to the relevant conditions of learning sharpens instruction and prevents neglect of desirable functions that intuition and experience alone would miss.

Integrate the learned tool into the wider curriculum as a working instrument after initial practice, and give learners varied material rather than a single specimen type, since that is what supplies the variety and additional practice a dedicated exercise cannot.

In a laboratory or instrument-based science course, use a repeatable four-phase strategy — examine the concept and device, measure the device's properties, use the device to measure a physical property, then use that measurement to create knowledge about a further property — which walks students through the layers of inquiry by which knowledge is made in the field.

Ask students mid-semester what they think, explicitly request honesty, and visibly listen and respond, because that makes students see themselves as part of the experiment and become supportive of solving the course's problems.

Dispel students' prior expectations about course format as early as possible in a substantially redesigned course, because students perceive such a course as unlike an ordinary one and say so themselves.

Expect courses to differ enormously in definiteness — one may have consensus on objectives, mastery criteria, and teaching time with few objectives while another is broad with less agreement and far more of them — and treat the available time as a very important planning constraint when setting course and unit objectives.

Budget for translation work: even with good seminars and a design coach, the teacher must still turn general ideas into specific activities in a specific course, and the model does not remove that step.

Start from a draft design that is not fully worked out rather than waiting for completeness, provided the best available thinking is in place on goals, feedback and assessment, and activities — accepting the uncertainty of beginning with ideas still nebulous — and keep monitoring and refining through the term.
Count an iteration that clarifies needs or invalidates an idea as progress, and deliberately test a materially different alternative before accepting the first plausible design.

Once the basic components are in place, expect a significant improvement in one component to improve the others synergistically — in the documented case, clarifying the fundamental application purpose and then its criteria and standards was the breakthrough.
Escalate practice complexity across a performance curriculum — one-on-one, then small-group, then large-group — with the learner taking on more of the full responsibility as the programme progresses.
Expect large-group instruction to be carried out with only a moderate degree of control over the conditions of learning, because student responses are unpredictable and planning time is restricted.

Use small-group and individualised modes to gain precision through self-pacing and self-correction adapted to each learner's entering competencies and rate, supported by branching in programmed, computer-assisted, or computer-managed materials or by frequent self-tests.
Engage learners at the problem and task level across all four performance levels (problem, task, operation, action), not only at the isolated operation or action level.

Replace some practice with worked examples early in learning, then transition to practice to consolidate and automate; example-practice pairs cut training time roughly sixfold and reduced errors relative to all-practice.

Manage complexity by starting at a low challenge and escalating, either by learner-selected difficulty or by adapting to response accuracy, and by enabling only part of the interface at first on the training-wheels principle.
When whole-task practice is too difficult even with maximum cuing, practise each component skill or small group of them in isolation and then gradually link them into the complete performance.

When the target skill has too many elements to learn at once, teach each constituent set separately as part of an overall shaping approach, practising a portion of the performance before the whole and sequencing the part-practice problem immediately before the whole-performance one.

Target the faculty, because they are in charge of the courses and curricula that constitute the core of educational programmes and until the faculty changes nothing significant has happened to programme quality.
Pair ambitious curricular goals with a strong faculty development programme, so the faculty know how to implement what the curriculum promises.

Model a faculty development programme on what award-winning programmes actually do: improve teaching by applying knowledge about cognition and learning, targeting particular student or faculty groups, and developing a personal vision of teaching; redesign courses for new technologies and curricula; and change the environment by creating learning-centered colleges, focusing on student learning outcomes, and instituting incentives and rewards for teaching.

Name the concrete barriers faculty face before prescribing change: teaching from habit without time to examine it, colleagues who discuss teaching only to complain about students, no in-load time for development, an overwhelming literature with no framework for sorting it, students who resist changed rules, and a culture that reads success as pandering or as neglecting research.

Educate students as well as faculty about good teaching and learning through institution-wide mechanisms — freshman or ongoing learning courses and the student affairs office — because student resistance to changed rules discourages innovation and one teacher cannot shift attitudes alone.

Treat instructional development as dependent on organizational development, since how the institution is organized and operates is the single most significant factor in whether its faculty can change, and a change in one dimension alone will not last.

Start institutional goal-setting from the educational needs of individuals and society rather than from what the existing structure and resources make convenient, and hold the three enduring goals in view: enhancing individual lives, enabling contribution to communities, and preparing for work.

Expect the institution-level goal gap to be real: few institutions have a clear goal set, most faculty and students cannot state one, and where no coherent purpose exists at institutional level students experience their education as fragmented and unrelated.

Require institution-wide goals to be learning-centered, inclusive of a broad range of educational needs, and specific enough to be measurable, because programs that generate a good education cannot be designed until the institution knows what it means by one.

Run quality assurance for both audiences — the public that supports the institution and needs assurance, and the institution itself needing to know whether its own goals are met — via three moves: goals for all graduates stated in language meaningful to the public, institution-wide rather than per-department responsibility for assessing them, and procedures beyond current practice.

Align all five components of institutional effectiveness — significant measurable goals, programs able to implement them, a supporting organizational structure, supporting policies and procedures, and institution-wide assessment — because omitting any one greatly diminishes the institution's capacity, and start the sequence from the goals.

Translate needs and goals into performance objectives specific enough to show progress toward the goals, working from general goals to increasingly specific objectives so that goal-level audiences and teaching-level audiences are each served by the appropriate statement.

State an educational goal as a category of human activity rather than as an abstract noun — performing the activities that maintain health rather than health, carrying out the activities of a citizen rather than citizenship — since educational goals are the learnable human activities that let a society and its individuals function.

Check the delivery structure against the stated goals, since institutions commonly publish attractive general-education aims while delivering only distribution requirements plus a major; an across-the-curriculum goal needs a structure giving multiple connected opportunities, not one related course.

Expect to define course objectives without a complete goal-to-objective network, since a full mapping from the most general educational goals down to specific objectives has probably never been done for any curriculum.

Work backward at institutional scale: from the learning wanted in graduates, ask which experiences students need, where in the curriculum each will be acquired, and how curricular learning will be coordinated with extracurricular, co-curricular, housing, and student-organization experience.

Address the structural cause of weak institution-wide programmes: discipline-based departments as sole delivery unit control hiring, evaluation, tenure, and offerings, which yields strong departments and weak cross-institution coherence — counter it with cross-disciplinary field groups, dual membership in ability-based units, or an expanded teaching and learning center.

Audit policies and procedures for unintended barriers to faculty work on educational programmes, focusing on the two with the strongest impact: policies on faculty work and on the evaluation of teaching.

Confront the faculty-work dysfunction directly: institutions have more work than faculty to do it, ask for everything on the false assumption that faculty time is infinitely elastic, then evaluate on publication counts and a global student-rating average — which discourages the very improvement they say they want and reduces annual evaluation to modest pay adjustments.
Pair any addition of professional development to faculty expectations with realistic time estimates and joint expectation setting, since adding it alone simply worsens the overload.

Use a faculty-activity worksheet apportioning 100 percent of time across teaching, research and creative activity, service, and professional development, with development itself covering teaching, research, service, and professional self-management including time and stress management, work-life balance, negotiation, and prioritization.

Protect at least 10 percent of faculty time for professional development, rising to 15, 20, or even 25 percent during a major career change, and use an explicit time worksheet so both sides can see what is left for research and service and adjust when an unexpected opportunity arises.

Estimate teaching load with the 20 Percent Rule — an ordinary three-credit course taught well takes about 20 percent of a term, being three contact hours plus about six hours of preparation and grading against a forty-five-hour week — adjusted up for high enrolment or frequent writing and down for a graduate assistant or fewer credits, with separate allowance for supervision and advising.

Double the workload estimate for a course taught for the first time, since new preparations are almost always overlooked; two of them in one semester consume roughly 80 percent of a faculty member's time before advising, service, and research, which is why new faculty are overloaded and why that overload stifles creative teaching and pushes toward passive learning, easy grading, and lower-level goals.

Set expectations and assess faculty work as an explicit joint endeavour at the front of the year rather than leaving the trade-offs to the individual: the faculty member lists intended activities, the chair or committee weighs them against departmental needs, adjustments are negotiated with all parties present, and the revisable agreement becomes the basis for the year-end assessment.
Conduct faculty assessment so that it fosters growth of both the individual and the institution, with expectations set jointly.

Expect front-loaded joint expectation setting to change what evaluation conversations are about, shifting them from arguing over a rating decimal to asking which activities would be most valuable next year and what resources would support them, and letting development happen in-load.

Add process and context to a learning-centered evaluation, since the question is the relationship between learning quality and both the teacher's activities and the setting: ask whether the course was well designed and whether the teacher interacted well, and gauge context factors such as class size, room, and timing by asking teacher and students what helped or hindered.

Use the integrated-course-design criteria as the evaluation criteria for course materials — in-depth situational analysis, goals focused on significant learning, educative assessment, activities reflecting active learning, and an effective teaching strategy — read off the syllabus, sample activities, and exams.

Ground student questionnaire items in a conceptual framework of good teaching — did the teacher provide stimulating questions and ideas, seem to care whether you learned, make you feel included and comfortable — rather than asking for global liking.

Staff a campus office with professionals who know faculty's questions, the college-teaching literature, and how to work with faculty individually and collectively, since the vast majority of new faculty arrive with no formal preparation for their instructional responsibilities and the faculty is the institution's most costly and important resource.

Assign responsibility for faculty time to the institution: add professional development to the traditional expectations, then have each faculty member discuss allocation across the four areas with their chair or executive committee.

Develop a definition of good teaching nationally and adopt it locally, since a local committee working under a content-centered tradition will struggle to find a definition applying across disciplines, and national criteria in public education proved both producible and consequential.

Expect certification against teaching standards to require an evaluating body outside the institution, after which the percentage of faculty meeting the standards becomes a quality measure — and expect an internal-improvement instrument to become a public quality signal once high scorers publicize it.

Treat accreditors as the strongest available lever for change, while recognizing that their pressure so far produced assessment focused on student progress through the system rather than on higher-order learning, affective development, or professional skills.

Require a learning-centered quality framework to be broad, flexible, and intuitive enough for a wide range of constituents, and expect a requirement for evidence of significant learning to push institutions into re-examining goals, structure, programs, and policies.

Adapt every guideline to three considerations before applying it: the training goal, the learners' prior knowledge, and the delivery environment including platform, network, institutional culture, budget, and time.

Check a disciplinary teaching statement for what it omits, since leaders who ignore the general college-teaching literature end up refining and reifying their discipline's existing practice — one such statement covered content, disciplinary thinking, classroom environment, and student evaluation while omitting active learning, reflective writing, small-group work, classroom assessment techniques, authentic assessment, portfolios, and self-evaluation of teaching.
Classify the disciplinary knowledge learners must acquire, not the textbook, course, or medium used to represent it.

Rely on the translator pattern for disciplinary change: a leader inside the discipline who takes ideas from the general college-teaching field and renders them in terms and cases meaningful to that discipline's faculty, sustained at workshop scale over years.

Treat awareness as the hardest of the six faculty needs because it comes first: faculty must get the message from multiple sources multiple times that competence in teaching and course design is expected, and the institution's claim to take teaching seriously must be backed by changes to goals, programs, structure, policies, and assessment rather than by rhetoric.

Supply support in three complementary layers: campus centers for consulting, workshops, observation, discussion, and reading; disciplinary associations for the language and examples of a particular subject; and journals for a stream of emerging ideas and applications.
Note that almost all the needed supporting actions already exist somewhere; what is missing is the leadership and vision to connect the separate efforts into a coordinated one.

Distinguish cyclical learning challenges that recur for every generation across the life stages from linear ones that change with time, since for the latter one cannot learn what one's ancestors knew and must engage in entirely new learning.

Target the learner's sense of self as a learner, because passive learners let others dictate what and how they learn and their learning does not transform their life, whereas proactive learners derive what they need to learn from who they are and what they want to do and can develop strategies for it.

Reject the guide-on-the-side picture as too passive: good teachers are proactive and reactive at once and operate in an interdependent team, steering and coordinating while each student must understand both their own role and how to work with others toward a challenging shared destination.

Treat student attention as conditional on perceived credibility: an audience continuously judges the speaker and attends only if the judgment is favourable, and students decide whether to buy into a course according to whether they perceive the teacher as competent, trustworthy, and dynamic.

Build perceived trustworthiness by having students' best interest at heart and showing it: follow through on promises, give immediate feedback, explain grading rationally, teach from multiple perspectives without bias, treat all students the same, never embarrass a student, and stay flexible.

Offer principles rather than rules, since rules cannot cover every situation: the key design principles are that components incorporate active learning and educative assessment to achieve significant learning goals, and that structure and strategy show both differentiation and integration.

Debug a first-draft design against five criteria — in-depth situational analysis, higher-level learning goals, educative feedback and assessment, activities including active learning, and well-integrated components — plus mechanical checks on whether students have time for the out-of-class work and can actually obtain the resources, including enough copies for simultaneous demand.

Treat the five first principles as delivery-independent, prescriptive design rules: they are relationships that hold under appropriate conditions regardless of program or practice, learning gain rises in proportion to how fully they are implemented, and violating one produces a decrement in learning.

Apply a multimedia design principle inside its stated boundary conditions rather than as a universal rule; before recommending one, establish the learners' prior knowledge and age, the content type, the assessment type, and the medium.
Make structural analysis of the content the primary requisite of design: it defines the cognitive rules a learner must acquire, and those rules then become the content taught.

Make resource identification an explicit design decision, determining per activity which people, places, things, or media students will need and whether they can be obtained, using a four-column worksheet so resources are planned per goal rather than as an afterthought.

Diagram structure and strategy together and adjust them so the two reinforce each other, since diagramming makes the intended sequence inspectable and prevents the two from being designed independently.
Make decision questions, answer paths, loops, arrows, and continuation markers explicit so diagram position and numbering cannot obscure actual execution order.
Treat teaching values as both permissible and possible: help students become more sensitive to their own values, the values of others, and the ethical implications of personal and social decisions.

Read a purpose about taking responsibility as an attitude objective, since it concerns whether students act on all appropriate occasions without specific direction — a choice of personal action rather than a skill.
Examine one's own teaching through four lenses — one's own autobiography, students' eyes, colleagues' perceptions, and the theoretical literature — rather than relying on any single view.

Note what each named strategy is specifically for: problem-based learning is designed to promote learning how to keep learning after the course ends, and team-based learning differs from generic small-group work in being a strategy rather than a technique and in resting on teams rather than groups.

Recognise strategy planning as the point where learning and design theory are combined with experience of learners and objectives, and where creativity distinguishes the art of instructional design from its science; the work is most often done as part of a team.
Compose teams heterogeneously and size them to the goal: never an all-low-prior-knowledge team, pairs when individual learning is the aim, three to five members for creative problem solving.

Do not overstate problem-based learning: a 270-study meta-analysis found knowledge and diagnostic reasoning equivalent to traditional curricula, with advantages confined to the social dimension and to satisfaction ratings.
Use the same knowledge-process framework to plan instruction, design assessment, and inspect their alignment with intended learning.
Match instructional methods, materials, and learner roles to the objective's knowledge-process combination.

Pair the instructional designer with a subject-matter expert in new development to analyse the learning task, decide the delivery system, review existing materials for fit, and then determine how the remaining events and activities will be provided.
Design for knowledge construction — prompting the learner's own cognitive processing — rather than for information delivery or response strengthening alone.

Design instruction so knowledge and mental operations develop each other: teach knowledge in a way that builds the operations, and teach operations in a way that builds high-quality applicable knowledge.
Treat the designed algorithm as the program of processes to be formed in learners' minds, so the design artifact and the instructional target are the same object.

Go beyond clarifying objectives and evaluating progress: many design efforts stop there and leave the design of techniques, procedures and resources to intuition, whereas a developed theory makes systematic detailed provision for planning, presenting and evaluating instruction.
Treat empty taxonomy cells as prompts for deliberation, not commands to add content; curricular value judgments remain with educators and communities.
Word objectives in terms of intended cognition rather than observable response format, because verbs such as list, write, or state do not uniquely identify the learning process.
Distinguish intended learning from its means and evidence: an activity, test result, content label, or observed response is not itself the objective.
Classify intended, enacted, and assessed learning separately, using observations, tasks, and teacher explanation to resolve ambiguous wording.
Classify objectives from enacted learning demands and scoring criteria as well as wording, especially when standards or broad verbs conceal procedural application.

Vary the conditions of learning by what is being learned: the conditions that make learning occur depend on the outcome type, so no single uniform instructional method should be applied across objectives.
State objectives as observable, measurable performances rather than as content outlines or teacher activities, so that whether the objective has been reached can be measured.
Expect scores of objectives for a single course topic and several for each lesson, since precisely defined objectives reveal the fine-grained nature of instruction.

Tell the learner what performance will indicate that learning has been accomplished, unless the aim is genuinely obvious or already known, since many school objectives are not obvious — reciting a passage verbatim is a different objective from stating its major ideas.

Dismiss the worry that communicating an objective stops students pursuing objectives of their own: it has never been observed and is highly unlikely, since the communication's basic purpose is simply to answer how the learner will know when he has learned.
Orient learners by showing the actual whole task or problem they will be able to complete (for example a worked example as the first problem), rather than listing abstract objective statements.

Replace an abstract statement of objectives with a concrete demonstration of the terminal capability the learner will acquire, since research shows stated objectives are often of little value because they are too abstract to communicate meaningfully, and the demonstration also previews, motivates and synthesizes.
Articulate important shared outcomes while preserving room for tacit, personal, and unanticipated learning in deliberately open-ended experiences.
Classify an objective from the learner's complete cognitive demand, allowing multiple cells when it genuinely contains multiple knowledge types or processes.
Separate contextual constraints and named instructional artifacts from the target knowledge, retaining a modifier only when it changes the actual cognitive demand.

Read an objective's capability type from the performance its wording names — solving problems of a stated kind names intellectual skills, designing something in a novel situation with little guidance implies cognitive strategies, and valuing an activity names an attitude — because the categories cut across content, each makes a different performance possible, and each requires a different set of learning conditions.
Use the taxonomy map to surface higher-order and metacognitive possibilities, then adapt reusable patterns to the subject and learners rather than requiring every category.

Operationalize cognitive categories with definitions, examples, assessment tasks, and instructional activities, and use disputed classifications to improve design rather than to win a labeling contest.

Teach categories through their defining common structure and useful disciplinary applications; when a misconception is systematic, diagnose and repair the underlying categorization rather than adding another definition.
Teach category structure with examples and nonexamples, then require classification or exemplification of new cases; recalling the category label alone is insufficient.
Use taxonomy as an adaptable analytic heuristic, not a literal reality, source of educational aims, guaranteed solution, or unique teaching prescription.
Select a learning taxonomy for the analysis and strategy guidance it provides, and treat cross-taxonomy mappings as approximate rather than exact.
Respect learners' active meaning-making while guiding inaccurate conceptions toward the best current disciplinary account supported by evidence.
Ground principles in sufficient experience with the phenomena they summarize, then teach how principles interrelate within models and where competing models are strong or limited.
Teach and assess procedural knowledge at three distinct levels: knowing the method, knowing concrete conditions for choosing it, and successfully applying it.
Teach and check factual knowledge early when it is raw material for later reasoning, but weight that check according to its supporting rather than culminating role.

Ask what is to be learned first, because the answer places the objective in one of the capability classes and thereby fixes the conditions required — there is no better guide to applying learning principles to instruction.

Expect a lesson whose primary objective is a procedural rule to need verbal information about the varieties involved and attitudes such as carefulness, precision, and hazard avoidance, and trace those interrelationships on a curriculum map.
Require learners to apply new knowledge to solve problems, and keep the practice and posttest consistent with the objectives, with the practice type matched to the kind of knowledge or skill.

Teach intellectual skills through activated prerequisites, explicit prior-to-new links, diagnostic examples and nonexamples, application steps and quality criteria, progressive transfer cases, authentic application practice, and explanatory feedback.

When a lesson mixes outcome types, make the intellectual skills the organizing spine of the plan and attach verbal information, cognitive strategies, motor skills and attitudes at the points of most appropriate linkage.

Include the characteristics of a correct outcome alongside the steps of a procedural aid, structured so goal, action and success criterion are read across together, with the goal stated before the action because the goal is the condition under which the learner must later choose that action unaided.
Define which type of knowledge is at stake — an image, a concept, or a proposition — before choosing a teaching method, because each requires different instruction.

For a procedural course, identify the simplest version of the task and the simplifying assumptions defining it, then relax those assumptions in order of importance so progressively more complex paths are taught, recording per lesson which condition is relaxed and which steps that adds.
Choose rehearsal for straightforward retention and prefer elaboration or organization when the goal is deeper comprehension.

Keep the demands of words, sentences, diagrams, and intermediate results well inside working-memory capacity, since short-term storage decays in under about twenty seconds without rehearsal and holds only a few items, and tasks that force intermediate results to be held are markedly harder.

Vary the amount of learning guidance deliberately, since minimal guidance is what emphasising discovery means and extensive verbal communication de-emphasises it; small amounts of guidance appear to have advantages for retention and transfer, and discovery techniques use pointed questioning to lead the learner to the proper ordering of component concepts.
Scale the rehearsal strategy to task complexity: repeating names in an ordered list suffices for simple material, while complex material calls for underlining main ideas or copying portions of text.

Choose the strategy by the information-processing stage it supports: highlighting, underlining, advance organisers, adjunct questions, and outlining for selective perception; paraphrasing, note taking, imagery, outlining, and chunking for rehearsal; concept maps, taxonomies, analogies, and schemas for semantic encoding; mnemonics and imagery for retrieval; metacognitive strategies for executive control.
Do not mistake superficial substitutes for instruction: tell-and-ask presentation and a few multiple-choice questions labeled as practice are, by themselves, seldom effective.
When assessing inference, require learners to state the relation or principle that accounts for the examples rather than crediting only a mechanically correct continuation.

When learners know taught facts and procedures but cannot derive new support, check evidence sufficiency and then add explicit interpretation and inference instruction rather than reteaching everything.

Present a variety of examples differing in irrelevant properties when teaching concepts and rules — the importance of which can hardly be overemphasised for young children, since failing to vary examples produces the learner who recognises a property with one object but not another — and for rules require the learner to work a variety of examples, because knowing the formula and its component concepts is not enough.
Teach analogical transfer by mapping relational structure between cases and checking that the inferred structure genuinely fits the new problem.
Distinguish routine execution from adaptive implementation; for the latter, require recognition of the problem type, selection or construction of a fitting method, adaptation, and execution.

Assess adaptive application with unfamiliar problems and rubric components for classification, knowledge or procedure selection, execution, and result, weighting each according to its intended importance.
Use analysis to select relevant elements, organize their relation to the whole, and infer underlying purpose; represent the resulting structure explicitly when useful.
For complex analyze, evaluate, or create objectives, make the operative organizing principles, criteria, design constraints, and domain knowledge explicit rather than naming only the artifact.

Identify every attribute essential for using a concept, then split them into those used to identify instances and those used to solve other problems such as drawing inferences, forming hypotheses, or judging practical fitness.
Classify work as creation only when the learner reorganizes material into a coherent new whole relative to prior knowledge under task-relevant constraints.
Support creation as an iterative cycle of reframing, divergent generation, convergent planning, and production; assess alternatives and plans explicitly when they are important targets.
Budget orientation, prior-knowledge work, synthesis, and final integration from the outset, then govern delivery by objective progress rather than completion of every planned activity.
Embed authentic complex performance in a coherent context, coordinate its component knowledge and processes, and share functional product criteria before learners begin.
Demonstrate a capability's value through contrasting authentic products and show how component skills combine into the whole performance.
Choose focused assessment for deep evidence of one target and distributed assessment for broad diagnosis of contributing processes, making the depth-breadth trade-off explicit.
Validate component classifications before diagnosing misalignment, then repair a confirmed mismatch through whichever element is wrong: objective, instruction, task, or scoring criteria.
Classify a task for a specified learner group and prior-experience state, because repeated exposure can turn analysis or implementation into execution or recall.
Separate supported formative performance, completion, and effort from independent mastery evidence, choosing the degree of assistance according to the decision the evidence must support.

Use teacher characteristics — level of formal education, education in the subject's methods, and years of experience — as a stand-in for support variables on the inference that a typical range of teacher backgrounds produces a range of differential opportunities for learning, while recognising that the support measures more relevant to summative work, such as availability of reading materials and encouragement of independent reading, may go unmeasured and that partial evidence can reveal enormous individual variation.

Match prompts to their intended process: finding instances supports exemplification, explaining significance adds analysis, counterfactual alternatives support generation, and judgment requires explicit criteria.
Evaluate material or methods against purpose-relevant criteria, distinguishing internal consistency and accuracy from external standards or exemplars.
Match interventions to verified causes, prefer a coordinated mix when causes interact, compare costs, and evaluate lower-cost changes before escalation.

Match practice mechanics to the target action; for classification, reveal categories progressively when appropriate, require correction with scaffolding, and request justification only when reasoning is part of competent performance.
After a long interruption in a cumulative unit, restore prerequisite context before resuming advanced work.
Make the relative roles of factual tests, complex projects, and affective participation explicit; none should silently stand in for a different objective.
Prioritize conceptual use over technical labels when labels are unnecessary, but teach the terminology when later communication or reasoning depends on it.
Build fluency from conceptual relationships and progressively faded representations, prioritizing meaning before formal labels while preserving labels needed for later communication.

Do not mistake a label for a concept: knowing a label is supplying the name of a specific object and is simply a short verbal chain, whereas knowing the concept requires identifying examples and nonexamples that define and delimit the class.
Introduce class names only after learners have established the distinguishing features themselves, so the term labels a distinction they already hold.
Develop fluent access to frequently reused foundational facts without replacing conceptual understanding, and schedule recurring review when durable retention is needed.
Collect separate process, conceptual, metacognitive, and outcome evidence when the same incorrect or unused strategy can arise from different causes.

Select methods by knowledge target: rehearsal for factual retrieval, attributes and contrasting examples for categories, visible sequences for procedures, and sustained strategy practice for metacognition.

Expect most useful cognitive strategies to be domain specific and expect a general strategy such as induction to need experiences across widely different situations before it becomes dependably useful — and to be usable then only where the requisite intellectual skills and information are also present.

Treat a cognitive strategy as a control process by which the learner selects and modifies his own ways of attending, learning, remembering, and thinking — what differentiates it from other intellectual skills is that its object is the learner's own cognitive processes rather than environmental objects and events.

Distinguish metacognition — the internal processing that uses strategies to monitor and control other learning and memory processes — from metacognitive knowledge, which a learner possesses when he becomes aware of and can describe those strategies.

Expect metacognitive strategies to arise mainly by generalisation from many specific task-oriented strategies after varied problem-solving experience rather than from direct communication plus practice, since the weight of evidence appears to favour generalisation.

Treat a cognitive strategy as a production governing the selection and use of intellectual skills — usable only when those underlying skills are already known — and expect it to be structurally simple yet broadly general within its domain and irrelevant outside it.

Apply the per-outcome pattern for events three to five: intellectual skill — retrieve prerequisite rules and concepts, state the rule with examples emphasising component concepts, then present varied examples in varied contexts with elaborations furnishing retrieval cues; cognitive strategy — recall task strategies and relevant skills, describe the task and strategy and show what it accomplishes, then give application examples; verbal information — recall a familiar organised body of knowledge, display statements emphasising distinctive features, then elaborate by relating to larger bodies using mnemonics and images; attitude — recall the situation and actions of the choice and remind of the model, then have the model describe the choice; motor skill — recall the executive subroutine and part skills, display the starting situation and demonstrate the subroutine, then practise with informative feedback.

Treat teaching a new cognitive strategy as getting learners to modify an existing strategy or drop it and adopt the new one, since one usually cannot specify a particular sequence of prior learning leading to a strategy and students already possess strategies as automatized rules for processing information.
Arrange a cognitive-strategy lesson as recall of the relevant rules and concepts, a verbal statement or demonstration of the strategy, and practice of the strategy in novel situations.
Separate development evidence of reaction and learning from field evidence of behavior and organizational results, then use post-course outcomes as an outer improvement loop.

Protect access to a common higher-order product with trustworthy sources at suitable reading levels, equitable peer support, constrained choice, early checkpoints, targeted questions, and a revisable production cycle.
Design cross-disciplinary units with explicit objectives, sequence, support, and grading for each domain, justifying rubric weights so generic criteria do not dominate disciplinary learning.
Launch conceptual change by eliciting explanatory models in multiple representations, surfacing their diversity and causal structure, and discussing alternatives without premature consensus.
After extended procedural or data work, deliberately reconnect decisive facts to the explanatory theory and primary conceptual objective.
Frame authentic inquiry with a specific reusable objective, consequential decision, audience, quality criteria, and an initial analysis of what evidence and knowledge the decision requires.
Map diagnostic questions to factual, conceptual, procedural, and inferential components, then use evidence-based discussion to localize and correct the actual source of error.

Preserve warranted uncertainty in evidence-based judgment: teach or standardize irrelevant data-format complexity, reserve time to evaluate sufficiency and limitations, and examine competing warrants rather than forcing consensus.
State plainly where a set of prescriptions lacks empirical support, so confidence in their validity is scaled to the evidence rather than to their coherence.
Establish collaboration routines and foundational production criteria before a unit that depends on them, unless those prerequisites are themselves the unit's targets.
Scaffold a complex procedure from reduced common material to independent projects, modeling both actions and decisions, monitoring guided practice, and remediating before release.

Scaffold problem solving through distinct levers (adjust task difficulty, restructure the task to supplant missing prior knowledge, or provide alternative assessments), starting from tasks the learner can already perform and adding difficulty until they cannot perform alone.
Keep worthwhile collaboration, perspective-taking, and civic-process activities visible as broader course outcomes rather than forcing them into an unrelated unit objective map.
Monitor and coach each high-leverage stage of a long production process, triangulate observations when possible, and use final shortfalls to target reteaching while opportunities remain.
Maximize work deliberately left undone, let capable teams organize execution, and use regular reflection and project-close debriefs to improve the next cycle.
Gate drafting and creation on verified adequate, relevant, and accessible source material, then deliberately shift from enabling research procedures to the culminating product.
Supplement generic product scales with objective-specific content and organization criteria, and classify the learner demand rather than the teacher's act of scoring.
When a complex procedure fails, inspect each embedded selection, differentiation, organization, or evaluation step and assess the quality of the resulting structure directly.

Structure adult materials and procedures more loosely: performance checks come after a rather long period of study whether the module carries one broad objective or many, directions may be greatly abbreviated with the objective itself serving as the main direction, and materials may be highly structured, semistructured, or unstructured as the task requires.

Use analyze, evaluate, and create either as explicit transfer objectives or as means to simpler learning, and allow them to initiate or iterate with other processes rather than imposing a fixed sequence.
Treat instructional analysis and learner analysis as parallel rather than strictly sequential steps; either may be done first or both simultaneously.

Do not assume learners run the five processes in a fixed order or that they will coordinate them unaided; sequencing and monitoring across the processes is learner- driven and is not yet well characterised by research.
Inspect apparently unaligned activities by their supporting function before removal, and scale the depth of formal taxonomy analysis to its likely reuse and impact.
Plan cognitive, affective, and psychomotor aspects together when an objective combines competence, disposition, and performance, even if each domain is analyzed separately.

Classify every objective into one of the five categories of learned capability — intellectual skills, cognitive strategies, verbal information, attitudes, motor skills — using the same taxonomy for prerequisites as for outcomes.
State planned outcomes as performance objectives — instances of human performance that can be reliably observed and assessed — and classify each into its capability category.

Simplify planning by assigning objectives to the five capability categories, since each leads to a different class of performance and requires a different set of instructional conditions, while within a category the same qualities of performance apply regardless of subject matter.
Classify a goal as psychomotor only when mastery depends on learning and practicing a nontrivial physical execution.
Interpret process categories by qualitative cognitive function and broad central complexity, allowing overlap rather than requiring a cumulative hierarchy.
Decompose critical thinking and problem solving into the knowledge types and ordered or iterative processes required by the specific domain and problem.
Assess creation against the kind of new whole intended: an effective organized communication, a constraint-satisfying plan, or a revisable explanatory relation.

Arrange both the external and the internal conditions of learning: verify that the internal capabilities the task presupposes are present, because a learner given the external presentation without them will not learn what is presented.

Plan a lesson from its performance objectives first, then arrange the external conditions most effective for that learning, taking learner characteristics into account because they determine many of the internal conditions, and select media accordingly.

Define a problem-solving episode by the absence of external learning guidance — the guidance is supplied by the solver alone — and set it up as a real or represented problem situation not previously encountered with verbal cues minimal or absent.

Establish the internal conditions before modelling: respect for or identification with the model must already exist or be established first, and the intellectual skills and knowledge related to the modelled behaviour must have been acquired — while remembering that this prerequisite knowledge does not itself engender the attitude.
Treat the learner's learned characteristics as the internal conditions of learning for each capability type, since these are what exert critical effects on new learning.

Require of any objective that it state a capability which, if possessed, can be observed as a performance, and answer before developing anything what the learners will be able to do afterward that they could not do before.

Establish the conditions — nature of the content or learning task, of the learners, and of the institutional setting — before judging a method, because the same method produces different effects under different conditions and observed outcomes alone cannot establish when to use it.
Treat knowing which operations to perform as necessary but not sufficient for a cognitive skill: internalization, including automatization, is the second necessary condition.

Practise against the stimulus named in the objective: where a model or prompt stands between the intended cue and the response, fade it in stages so contiguity is established with the intended cue rather than the prompt.
Present as stimulus material only the information that must be learned; topically adjacent content that does not serve the objective is an incorrect stimulus even though it is information.
Aim every design at transferring stimulus control from cues to the discriminative stimuli, so that at the end the stimulus alone elicits the response with no cues available.

Treat repetition as a practical procedure that helps ensure the other conditions of learning are present rather than as a fundamental condition in itself, since repeating newly learned ideas does not always improve learning or retention.
For instructional purposes use the contingency form of reinforcement — make an already-preferred activity contingent on the new performance — rather than assuming any reward will strengthen learning.

Do not treat contiguity, repetition, and reinforcement as sufficient: applying all three still does not guarantee an efficient learning situation, so the wider set of conditions of learning must also be accounted for.
Build deliberate recall of previously learned content into the lesson, because the memory contents present in working memory at the moment of learning are themselves conditions of learning.

Plan cognitive strategies over long spans rather than single lessons, because these capabilities govern the learner's own learning, remembering, and thinking and improve gradually as the individual engages in more studying, learning, and thinking.

Employ repetition as spaced occasions for the learner to recall what was learned rather than as mere re-presentation, since retrieval processes are apparently the most important factor in remembering both isolated facts and larger bodies of information.

Plan systematic reviews spaced across weeks and months, each requiring the skill to be retrieved and used, since spaced repetition contrasts sharply with the relative ineffectiveness of repeated examples given directly after the initial learning.
Make retention exercises require applying the learned content to a new question rather than recalling it again, since verbal information is remembered best when it is practised — used.

Use a review of previous lessons' skills to serve two events at once — enhancing retention and transfer for the earlier skills and stimulating recall of prerequisites for the current targets — and treat consecutive events for one objective, such as guidance, performance, and feedback, as a single activity where that is helpful.

Establish reliability in both its senses — consistency across items aimed at the same objective, and dependability on temporally separated occasions — using additional items of the same class because the purpose is to discover whether the learner can perform a class of operations rather than one particular instance.

Rely on careful sequencing to make recall of immediately prior learning highly probable and on structured materials to make initial mastery of prerequisites more probable, with frequent progress checks after each objective preventing the cumulative forgetting that would slow further learning.
Use distributed practice for durable retention and add mnemonic or novel elements only when they reinforce attention to the target performance.

Make every practice and test instance new — different from those used in teaching — or the item measures recall rather than the intended performance, and require a paraphrase rather than a verbatim restatement when the learner must state a generality.
Repeat within the display the prerequisite information the learner acquired earlier, because repeating it facilitates recall of what the current display depends on.

Design each external event against a named internal process of the information-processing model — reception, selective perception, rehearsal, semantic encoding, retrieval, response generation, and performance — rather than against the content alone.

Exploit the fact that internal processes, though largely self-activating, can be influenced by external events — selective perception by highlighting, underlining, or bold printing, and semantic encoding by externally supplied meaningful information — since that influence is what makes instruction possible at all.

Map each event to the process it serves: gaining attention to reception; informing of the objective to activating executive control; stimulating recall to retrieval into working memory; presenting the stimulus to selective perception; providing guidance to semantic encoding and retrieval cues; eliciting performance to response organisation; providing feedback to reinforcement; assessing to retrieval plus reinforcement; and enhancing retention and transfer to retrieval cues and strategies.

Define the learning purpose of each design step as far as possible, and recognise that beyond that point the craft of print, pictures, and sound is a separate technology governed by other considerations.

Analyse a multimedia message by how the learner processes it (presentation mode: verbal versus pictorial; sensory modality: auditory versus visual), not by how many delivery devices it uses. Reject delivery-device counting as a design frame.

Treat multimedia as any words-plus-pictures instruction regardless of technology, and apply the same design principles to printed pages, chalk-and-talk, slideshows, video, games, and virtual reality alike.
Start a multimedia design from how the human mind works and ask how to adapt the technology to aid cognition; do not start from the technology's capabilities and ask what can be done with them.

Select the analysis type that fits the objective — procedural analysis for the steps of a task, information-processing analysis for the mental operations of a learned complex skill, task classification for the outcome type, and learning-task analysis for the subordinate skills of an intellectual-skill objective — and expect to apply several of them to one unit.
For every decision and action an information-processing analysis exposes, estimate explicitly whether the intended learners enter with that capability or must be taught it.

Write performance objectives during task analysis rather than strictly after it, because writing them clarifies the target objectives and classifies the skills to be learned so that further analysis becomes possible.

Begin writing any objective by deciding what type of learning outcome the instruction aims to produce, since writing a five-component objective is itself a problem-solving task and this is its first sub-problem.
Use the same task-analysis process for a course as for a lesson, varying only the scope of the analysis and the number of steps.
