Distinguish the two classes of task analysis — procedural or information-processing analysis of the steps in performing a task, and learning-task analysis of the prerequisites — and use both where the unit calls for them.

Include the mental steps — recalling an item, deciding between forms — as well as the observable ones in a procedural analysis, since that is what makes the analysis account for the intellectual skills that are components of the total task, and distinguish kinds of step in the diagram because choices differ from actions.

Use information-processing analysis for two returns: a clear description of the target objective including its procedural steps, which fixes the sequence for presentation, and the revelation of individual steps — especially internal decision steps — that would not otherwise be obvious.

Treat each decision step the analysis exposes as a specific skill that must be acquired if not already known, making it one of the target objectives of the total task, and then write the component skills as five-component objectives — which requires classifying them by outcome type and thereby makes the learning-task analysis possible.

Start sequencing from the intellectual-skill objectives, because of their importance as curriculum components and because more is known about sequencing relationships among them, then weave in objectives from other domains insofar as they support those skills — unless the terminal objective is an attitude, in which case identify the intellectual skills supportive of it instead.
Analyze procedural intellectual and psychomotor goals as efficiently ordered major steps containing both observable action and relevant content, with enabling subordinate skills.
Analyze intellectual skills at the actual performance level—discrimination, concept classification, rule application, or problem solving—and derive prerequisites accordingly.
Classify the goal as intellectual skill, psychomotor skill, attitude, or verbal information before selecting its analysis and instructional methods.

Identify which kinds of knowledge an objective targets — facts, concepts, procedures, strategies, or beliefs — since complex performance requires a combination and each kind needs different instructional treatment and assessment.

Choose an objective set that spans the learning types of real tasks — remembering information as well as applying skills, and within skills at least concept classification, rule using and procedure using — rather than sampling one type.

Perform hierarchical task analysis on each performance objective, decomposing it into enabling objectives that are either essential prerequisites or facilitating skills, and teach the resulting components parts-to-whole from the bottom of the hierarchy upward.

Identify the type of objective — recalling or applying facts, defining and explaining or applying definitions to examples, following procedural rules, or solving problems — and note which one or two component skills predominate in it, since every category involves all four but is distinguished by its predominant ones.

Follow the full pipeline when engineering instruction on a cognitive skill: penetrate the unobservable expert process, break it into relatively elementary component operations, describe those operations explicitly as a descriptive model, compose a prescriptive algorithmic or heuristic model of what a nonexpert should do mentally, and build the instruction from that prescription.

Build an algorithm from operations that psychological analysis of the target population shows are elementary for them, since elementariness is relative to the audience, and develop down to that level, which corresponds to the entry level of a learning hierarchy.
Perform task analysis first when handed only objectives, test items, generalities and text, expecting it to yield additional objectives and modifications to the ones supplied.

Determine the audience's entry skills by interviewing and testing the target population rather than guessing, then choose a starting point knowing the instruction will be redundant for some and necessary for others, and identify learners who need remediation instead.

Build a lesson map by asking both what the learner must know to learn the new skills and what these learners already know that matters — the second question defining the entry skills — beginning from information about the audience and making explicit assumptions about what they bring, which usually requires a fairly detailed analysis of the intellectual skills involved since that analysis is the organising factor for sequencing.

Use performance measures for three distinct jobs — diagnosis and placement that confirm prerequisites and avoid unnecessary instruction, in-lesson checks that detect and remediate misunderstanding before continuing, and end-of-unit documentation of progress.
Conduct front-end performance analysis without presuming training; commit to needs assessment and instructional design only for verified skill gaps.
Build and validate a job-task inventory from observation and performer accounts, then prioritize tasks by occurrence, frequency, time, criticality, and difficulty.
Verify digital reliability, access, support, and instructor readiness alongside managerial, physical, social, and performance-tool readiness before depending on a context for instruction or transfer.

Review every goal step and subordinate skill separately for accuracy, completeness, job alignment, and assessment coverage, stopping at material inaccuracy and preserving both coverage rates and item-level interpretation.

Assess the operating learning environment and prior performance-improvement system—including motivation, equipment, work conditions, instructors, infrastructure, incentives, mentoring, job aids, and field support—before finalizing delivery.

Distinguish formative from summative evaluation by the state of the product: formative supplies data for improvement while the materials are still being formed, summative determines success and worth of the course in its final form when no further changes are planned.

Conduct summative evaluation only after the system has left its formative stage and is no longer under point-by-point revision, and conduct it across an equally varied range of conditions when wide use is expected.

Distinguish the two roles by what they decide: formative evaluation collects evidence during development and uses it to form the programme itself, leading to revision decisions, whereas summative evaluation leads to decisions about programme adoption and continuation.

Measure all four classes of variable — aptitude, support, process, and outcome — in any evaluation study whether formative or summative, since what differs between the two roles is the interpretation of those measures rather than which are collected, and a single study can serve both roles at once.

Read the same aptitude data differently by role: formative evaluation needs to know the classes span a range of aptitudes representative of the system's intended usage, whereas summative evaluation needs equivalence of that variable between experimental and control groups.

Judge an event of instruction by whether it is successfully performed, not by who performs it: the events apply across all outcome domains, though the details of implementing each imply somewhat different conditions of learning by domain.
Classify the task in order to design the conditions necessary for effective instruction, since each of the five outcome categories carries different implications for the conditions of learning.
Do not treat the events of instruction as invariably required for every lesson and every learner: make a judgment about how much self-instruction the learner can undertake.

Take process variables into account in any well-planned evaluation regardless of how far the design prescribes them, since instructional entities vary greatly — a textbook may imply a sequence through its chapters while leaving the events entirely to teacher or learner, whereas a designed topic may specify both sequence and events — and the outcomes observed may be substantially affected by how the programme was actually operated.
Define attitudinal outcomes by the discretionary choice instruction should influence and evaluate the observable action selected in relevant circumstances, not knowledge alone.

Assign media event by event and objective by objective within the chosen delivery system, because media differ in which events they can provide — teachers excel at learning guidance and feedback while recorded media can present stimulus situations a teacher could not otherwise supply.

Design the events to move learners from where they are to the capability named in the target objective, deliberately arranging them rather than relying on their arising naturally from interaction with the materials.

Decide the exact form of the instructional events for each learning objective rather than specifying it in general for all lessons, choosing communications designed to have the desired effect in supporting the learning processes.

Elaborate the objective-informing event into a goal schema when multiple objectives serve an enterprise: tell the learner what purposeful activity the new learning is aimed at — passing a test, teaching others, applying it practically, solving a problem — and give a scenario relating the single objectives to that goal.

Use media in the broad sense — a teacher's speech or a printed text as much as sound and video recordings — defining an instructional medium as the physical means by which an instructional message is communicated.

Decide media during lesson planning by asking what medium is wanted for each intended outcome and where the specific materials will be found, because available materials are not indexed or catalogued by intended instructional objective.

Narrow media first by four decisive features of the learning situation — teacher-delivered versus self-instructional communication, learners with versus without sufficient verbal comprehension for print, direct versus centrally broadcast delivery, and whether errors in the performance are serious — which yield six decision types each setting certain media aside while leaving several options.

Never let available materials redefine the objectives: because commercial materials are referenced by content rather than by objective and rarely address the events they provide, check existing materials against the objectives and supplement the ones they miss, rather than choosing materials for convenience and letting students learn content unrelated to the goals.
Make objectives specific enough to determine which conditions of learning must be built into the materials, which is the reason for using a form more specific than a bare behavioural statement.

Infer the objectives when materials do not state them and design the lesson so the textbook's objectives are supplemented by others, since determining the categories of expected outcomes matters as much for the teacher as for a design team.

Preview the actual materials before final selection rather than choosing from catalogues, because materials are usually not designed for the exact objectives adopted and rarely provide all the desired events, and state in the lesson plan how they will be used and how the missing events will be accomplished.

Do not assume materials sold as objective-keyed have been validated: few publishers have validated their effectiveness and usually have simply added objectives and test items onto existing materials, a deficiency one state addressed by requiring validation as a textbook-selection criterion.

Let materials carry encoding-level guidance as prompts, cues, and suggestions blended with the stimulus more precisely than a teacher can outside tutoring, while the teacher gives the more general guidance about which alternative materials and which enrichment objectives to choose.
Choose between original and existing materials from outcome requirements, relevance of available materials, and development resources.

Weigh develop-versus-select by four rules: the more innovative the objectives the more must be developed; developing for a particular delivery system is almost always dearer than selecting; integrating available materials into a module covering all the objectives saves expense; and the teacher's role shifts with the delivery system because the teacher supplies whatever events the materials omit.
Select medium, instructor involvement, and grouping as contextual design decisions; prioritize the quality of analysis and strategy over delivery fashion.

Do not treat formative evaluation as optional: it is one of the most frequently overlooked stages because it comes late and takes real effort, yet using systems feedback to correct the system is the essence of the systems philosophy, and design without it is incomplete.
State explicitly when a design has not been taught and formatively evaluated, giving the reasons, rather than presenting it as validated.
Let formative evaluation data reopen products from any earlier design stage, not only the materials stage.

Hold an exemplary-product claim to three tests: the evidence of effectiveness must be valid and reliable, the effects must be large enough to have educational importance, and it must be possible to reproduce the intervention and its effects at other sites.

Add the system-level stages when designing for a whole educational system: analysis of resources, constraints, and alternate delivery systems; curriculum scope and sequence; teacher preparation; field testing and revision; and installation and diffusion.

Design the teacher training as part of the instructional systems design whenever the new system demands skills in-service teachers lack, prepare teachers before the materials are distributed, and take their input along the way, because the more input they have the more likely the materials fit the existing system and are adopted.

Check the administrative practicality of a medium — school budget, class size, capability to develop materials, equipment availability, teacher capability and availability for design work, availability of modular individualised materials, attitudes of principal and teachers toward innovation, and school architecture.

Treat the delivery decision as a constraint on everything downstream, since the delivery system includes all that is needed for the instruction to operate as and where intended and directly limits the available personnel, media, materials, and activities.

Stop planning when the goals exceed every available delivery system and resolve the conflict first — change the goals, change the resources or constraints, or conceive another delivery system — because proceeding produces piecemeal planning and waste such as unused equipment, unusable laboratories, disrupted activities, and goals missed for want of prerequisite experiences.

Let teachers see the system working in an environment like their own — a pilot-school visit alongside or instead of a workshop — and expect adoption to take time, since most teachers report needing about a year of experience beyond initial training before preferring the new system to their prior practice.
Require an acceptable degree of merit shown in one or more summative evaluations before a system is offered for widespread adoption.

Plan installation as real work: adjust storage, schedules, and duplication of expendable materials to each site, and above all attend to the nature of the system the innovation enters, because new technology is often perceived as a threat and blocked by the very people who should use it.

Consider diffusion early if it is a project goal, and budget for maintenance: a publisher's operating procedures can constrain the final product or delivery system and force the goals and system objectives to be rethought, and securing enough adoptions to amortise development, marketing, and the often-overlooked maintenance cost is a frequent problem.

Treat the instructional systems approach as a process that draws on research and learning theory and uses empirical testing as the means of improving the instruction, focusing on the same three anchor points every model shares — performance objectives, materials, and evaluation instruments.
State desired outcomes clearly and unambiguously, because instructional design technology corrects and revises instruction on the basis of empirical testing and cannot do so against a vague target.

Look for published modules that direct both teachers and learners on how the materials and exercises reach the objectives and how to know they have been reached, since these are usually designed to implement a systematic instructional strategy even when not built on this specific event list.

Make the field trial the critical test of feasibility and effectiveness: give the revised pretest and posttest around the instruction with an appropriate sample of the intended audience, survey the attitudes of learners and participating instructors, and observe the adequacy of the materials, their directions, and the instructors' performance — with achievement gains under near-typical conditions of crucial importance for the near-final revision.
Derive the instructional strategy from prior analyses and include motivation, observable presentation, active practice with feedback, assessment, and support for real-world use.
Reevaluate the instructional goal whenever front-end, learner, or context analysis changes the evidence supporting it.

Derive instructional strategy from the goal, analyses, objectives, and assessments, covering motivation, presentation, examples, active practice, feedback, assessment, transfer, and delivery constraints.
Define and refine an instructional goal as a demonstrable learner capability grounded in a verified need, context, resources, and a clear problem statement.
Derive instructional goals through a narrowing evidence chain from organizational performance to learning needs and, where required, curriculum, job, and task analyses.
Evaluate instructional strategy across preinstruction, presentation, participation, assessment, follow-through, motivation, and operational management, adapting criteria to outcomes and learners.
Define the desired instructional product, performance outcomes, and product characteristics before selecting or tailoring the process and tools.
Test instructional effectiveness by tracing relevant context, target behavior, sufficient durable practice, authentic activity, and consequence-based feedback through the learner experience.

Require of any instructional theory that it identify conditions and treatments and match them systematically, covering both the objective type and the mix of component skills and stimulus/response characteristics that make the objective difficult.

Accept that an instructional theory can be built purely inductively by observing expert practitioners, cataloguing their strategies, and formulating prescriptions for when to use each, without deriving it from a learning theory.

Classify every instructional outcome — whether written as an objective or as a test item — on both the performance required (remember an instance, remember a generality, use, or find) and the content type (fact, concept, procedure, or principle).

Recognize what made instructional theory distinct at its emergence — systematically clarifying objectives, detailing the techniques and conditions that facilitate them, and using empirical methods to assess merit and plan revision — and that its progress has been uneven, with much of the work done when the enterprise was unpopular.

Treat producing relevant, effective and affordable technology-assisted instruction as much harder than most instructors and administrators realize, and use instructional theory to identify both the characteristics that facilitate learning and the design-development steps needed to produce the resources.

Plan computer-based instruction at least as carefully as any other resource, since someone must still decide the instructional relevance of each use, and use instructional theory to decide why and how to use a resource rather than adopting it and inferring its value afterwards.
State each design objective in testable form so that the success of the design itself can be evaluated.

Use one precise definition of each objective to serve both communication and evaluation, so that what is evaluated and what is communicated as the intended outcome carry a common meaning and the definition specifies the domain from which achievement-test items are drawn.
Write each performance objective with an observable skill, demonstration conditions, and a success criterion.
Use current motivation, outcome-type, and strategy principles as explicit design-analysis criteria, recording both strengths and weaknesses for defensible synthesis.

Validate the learning goal with the full design group, test every creative decision against it, allow evidence-based reconsideration during early iteration, and stabilize the goal before detailed design.
Set goals through early design-prototype-evaluation cycles, then stabilize behavioral objectives that specify observable performance, its conditions, and success criteria before detailed design.
Hold the objectives and the test items constant when comparing rival designs, because a shared target is what lets differences in terminology be seen through and the designs compared directly.
Treat subject-matter labels as gross simplifications of educational goals that lose information at each stage of condensation, since a subject name stands in for many different human activities.

Describe a course by its objectives rather than by its title or topic list, because titles and topic designations are ambiguous — the same title can mean different content at different grades — and that ambiguity really impedes students planning programs of study.

Keep capability and performance distinct: the capability is an internally stored state that is inferred, and the performance is what is observed, so evidence statements must name the performance while objectives name the capability.

Write objectives in five components — situation, learned capability, object of the performance, specific action, and tools, constraints, or special conditions — carrying two verbs, one defining the capability and one the observable action, because a capability can only be inferred from performance and the action exhibited is often confused with the capability itself.

Include a learned-capability verb in every objective, because a statement phrased only as observable behaviour leaves the intended capability ambiguous — the same visible act may be copying or composing.

Use the nine standard learned-capability verbs — discriminates, identifies, classifies, demonstrates, generates, adopts, states, executes, chooses — to name the outcome type, since including the capability verb both communicates the intended behaviour and makes the conditions of learning for that type readily applicable.

Keep the object and the action distinct — the object names the content of the performance and the action verb describes how it is completed and hence what would be observed — and never use one of the nine capability verbs as the action verb, because that creates confusion when the objectives are later sequenced.

Leave the criterion of performance out of the objective statement, because criteria are likely to differ by capability type so a uniform one would be an error and criterion setting is a measurement question best handled with the assessment procedures — including it under tools and constraints only where the criteria are already known.

Take a second and third differing example before concluding a capability is present, since a single observed performance may be due to chance or guessing and each further instance raises the reliability of the inference.
Treat each learned intellectual skill as a component of further learning, since acquiring one rule contributes to the more complex skills that build on it.
Verify an intellectual skill by observing a category of performance — several specific instances of applying the rule — never a single instance.

Provide both halves of problem-solving capability: intellectual skills are essential but not sufficient for a novel problem, since the learner must also apply a previously practised cognitive strategy as the mode of seeking a solution.

Order intellectual skills by the complexity of the mental process inferred to account for the performance — discriminations under concrete concepts, concepts under rules, rules under problem solving — treating these complexity categories as independent of subject matter.

Do not require a learner to state a rule as evidence of possessing it: rule-governed performance implies an internal capability that makes behaviour regular, and a learner may apply a rule he cannot verbalise while another can recite one he cannot apply.

Describe every intellectual-skill objective by three components of the learning situation: the performance to be acquired, the internal conditions (the capabilities recalled and integrated into the new one), and the external conditions supplying stimulation.

Distinguish the varieties of intellectual skill by the class of performance they make possible, the internal and external conditions they require, and the complexity of the internal process they establish in memory.

Model an intellectual skill as a production of the form IF condition THEN action, and expect a complex rule to activate its simpler prerequisite skills on retrieval because those skills are actual components of it.

Separate the two channels by which prior learning acts: learned capabilities and schemas exert direct, specific effects that are retrieved into the new learning, whereas abilities and traits do not enter it directly but influence how easily the learning processes are carried out — and which channel dominates depends primarily on the objective, so organise the analysis of prior learning by the expected outcome type.

Express the prerequisite analysis for a new intellectual skill as a learning hierarchy, since the absence of any subordinate skill markedly decreases the ease of learning the superior skill connected to it.
Describe the situation carefully for rule-using skills such as interpreting charts, because more complex instances may require several intellectual skills or a combination of them.

Expect an intellectual-skill target to be composed of two or more simpler subordinate skills learned before the target is put together, and look for the distinct rules that superficially similar problems conceal — as subtraction by borrowing decomposes into no-borrowing, nonadjacent borrowing, successive adjacent borrowing, and borrowing across zero.
Derive subordinate skills by asking of any intellectual skill what simpler skills a learner would have to possess to learn it, then repeating that question of each skill identified.

Ensure the learner can recall the subordinate skills that compose a new skill, since that is when it is learned most readily, and interject the learning of other capabilities at appropriate points before, during, or after the intellectual-skill sequence.
Raise an intellectual-skill goal toward more transferable concept, rule, or problem-solving performance when learner capability and the use case justify it.

Analyze intellectual performance at its actual transfer level—from discrimination through concepts and rules to structured or ill-structured problem solving—and raise the target only when learner needs and application justify it.

Distinguish attainment evidence for the higher categories: problem solving requires combining two or more previously learned rules in an unfamiliar situation and choosing which rules apply; a cognitive strategy is a learned way of improving one's own learning; an attitude is inferred only from consistent choices across repeated similar situations; and motor-skill mastery says nothing about knowing when to apply the procedure.

Restrict hierarchical analysis and sequencing to intellectual skills, because learning any one intellectual skill depends on prior learning of simpler ones along the chain from discriminations to concrete concepts to defined concepts to rules to problem solving.

Design and assess verbal information for gist rather than verbatim recall, since connected prose is stored and recalled as the gist of paragraph-length passages, and recognise that much information is also acquired incidentally outside formal instruction.

Expect connected prose to be retained as meaning rather than detail, with general ideas recalled better than specific ones and details reconstructed from a schema representing the gist — so assess and design for gist rather than for component facts.

Make retrieval cues as distinctive as possible to avoid interference among stored propositions — using memorable stimuli such as rhymes, reducing confusion with similar ideas, and arranging component ideas into tables or spatial arrays — and elaborate new ideas with related information, since each addition supplies further retrieval cues.

Guard against verbal chains masquerading as verbal information: individuals can recall extremely long chains verbatim without comprehending the words, so require the learner to state the information in his own words or use it in a different question — though verbatim recall does not by itself prove the information is not meaningfully stored.

Recognize that a recall objective can have distinct paths — verbatim recall and paraphrase — whose equivalence classes differ, one containing essentially the given wording and the other any reply carrying the critical elements.

Include the facts a rule's application requires even where a large stock of facts is not a defensible primary goal, because a rule cannot be applied to a specific case unless the relevant information is recalled at that moment and information also supplies the directions for how to proceed in further learning.

Decide for every fact in a course whether it is of such infrequent use that it should be looked up, referenced often enough that learning it is efficient, or fundamental enough to be remembered for a lifetime — since facts matter both for everyday living and as the information a rule's application requires.

Measure an attitude as the frequency with which the person chooses the item across a variety of circumstances, not by whether the choice was made on any single occasion, since an attitude is a persisting internal state that modifies choices of action toward a class of objects, persons, or events.

Assess an attitude as a shift in the probability of choosing a course of action over time rather than as a single measured state, and where direct observation of choices is impractical use self-reports only with precautions against transparent-intent responding.

Define an attitude operationally as an internal state affecting the choice of personal action, inferred from behaviour rather than being the behaviour, and never infer one from a single instance — the inference requires a number of instances of the same class across different situations, each of which is a choice.

Phrase attitude questions about a specific personal action — working with, living near, sitting beside — rather than at a broad group level, which is too general to be answered sensibly, because it is the choice of action that the attitude affects.

Measure attitudes as proportions of chosen personal action — by direct observation over repeated periods where the choices occur in the observable environment, and otherwise by questionnaire self-report of choices in described situations, since many relevant choices occur outside it.

Connect the desired behaviour to a larger framework of values where one exists, because attitudes reflect values and people who see themselves as important members of an organisation or class make different choices than those who feel unimportant.

Expect an attitude's memory to include the model's choice of personal action, a self-standard reflecting the model's standard, and a feeling of satisfaction from direct or vicarious reinforcement — and to be stored within propositional networks organised by situation, so an attitude may apply to one situation and not another and is revived when the situation is.

Supply the intellectual skills that make an attitude's choice actionable — estimating concentrations for a safety attitude, calculating intake for a dietary one — since the learner must be able to carry out the action the attitude selects.

Build and activate the situational schemas that represent where the attitude will be displayed, because the attitude is most effective when those schemas can be readily recalled at the time of learning.

Do not build an attitude design around traits such as sociability or external locus of control, since little evidence is available on their effect on modelled attitude learning and the relationships are judged not to be of great significance.

Write attitude objectives with choose and state the situation precisely, because situational factors determine the choice — choosing an action when convenient is a different objective from choosing it when inconvenient.

Take attitudes toward a subject as a strong influence on the ease with which it is learned, retained, and used, since a review of the literature shows attitude learning strongly related to the learning of cognitive skills.

Recognise that acquiring an attitude may essentially require prior intellectual skills and specific verbal information — comprehending a label plus knowing about ingredients before an attitude about labelling can be acquired.

Begin an attitude sequence with the intellectual skills and verbal information relevant to the attitude and only then introduce the procedure that establishes the tendency itself, since an attitude cannot be established without the skills and knowledge that make up the personal action the learner is expected to choose.

Abandon mastery for attitude objectives and measure strength instead as the proportion of times the person behaves in a given way across a sample of defined situations, framing the objective as improvement — more instances of the target behaviour in a later period than an earlier one — with anecdotal records quantified as a count of positive actions or as a proportion of positive to total, and occasions offering no opportunity for the behaviour simply not recorded.
Scope attitude objectives deliberately rather than assuming them universal, since many attitudes are acquired outside the institution and many are not appropriately within its instructional function.
Withhold the objective when teaching an attitude and inform the learner only after they have chosen to behave in the target manner, because stating it in advance defeats the instruction.

Design instruction to meet accepted educational goals, recognising that the capabilities derived from analysing societal activities would probably not correspond simply to the traditional subject-matter categories of the curriculum.
Design a catch-up path for the simpler prerequisite skills whenever the assumption that lower-level skills are already held turns out to be wrong.

When something obvious to most students makes no sense to one, analyse that individual's schema for missing prerequisite skills or knowledge and teach those prerequisites before the primary intervention.
Set a higher mastery level for a skill that is prerequisite to further learning than for one that leads nowhere else.
Classify the task before identifying its prerequisites, because essential and supportive prerequisites differ considerably in character for each task category.

Identify a prerequisite by asking what skill the learner must have to learn this new skill, the absence of which would make that learning impossible — being simpler is not enough, the prerequisite must be integrally related such that the superior skill cannot be performed without it — then check the list by examining the demands the new skill makes and where the learner could go wrong.
Align prerequisite checks and authentic whole-goal pretests to explicit skills and realistic conditions, then use results to bypass, group, or route learners without scoring untaught capabilities.
Add prerequisite instruction for demonstrated deficits, move broadly mastered capabilities into entry checks, and branch learners to only the teaching or review their profiles warrant.
Teach unfamiliar participants that early work advances in small disposable steps and needs learner checks, while explaining only the process detail required for each participant's current role.

For a terminal objective in the intellectual-skills category, identify the learning prerequisites the learners have not yet mastered and teach them first, sequencing simpler component skills before the more complex skills of which they are part.

Check rather than presume the elementary discriminations a task requires: relevant discriminations are usually assumed learned early in life, but the assumption fails for adults and specialists facing a foreign-language contrast, a microscopic boundary, or a material grain.
Teach a discrimination with contiguity, differential reinforcement for right versus wrong responses, and repetition, adding repetitions when several discriminations must be learned at once.

Teach a concrete concept by presenting instances that vary widely in their non-relevant characteristics together with negative instances, so correct performance is shown by both selecting members and rejecting non-members, and ensure first that the underlying discriminations are recallable.

Arrange a discrimination lesson as recall of the responses, presentation of same and different stimuli with emphasis on distinctive features, and repetition of same and different stimuli with feedback.

Train every teacher specially to conduct and manage individualised instruction, since they cannot be expected to function adequately let alone enthusiastically without it and may at first feel their most cherished functions are being usurped — and expect that not all will like it, some refusing to relinquish the familiar role while others tired of repeating the same lesson welcome the change, though once trained and experienced most come to prefer it, usually after a year.
Teach concepts with definitions, varied examples, contrasting nonexamples, guided discrimination, and immediate explanation, using fresh parallel instances across assessment occasions.

Test a concrete concept by having the learner identify two or more members of the object-property class, accepting any pointing response — choosing, checking, circling, grasping, or naming — provided the learner can already perform it, and remember that positions such as above or beside qualify as concrete concepts because they can be pointed to.

Write a concrete-concept objective with identify and accept any of several actions — describing, pointing to, touching, selecting, or recognising pictures — since a learner may know the concept without being able to describe it, while remembering the objective presupposes the underlying discriminations in whichever sensory modality is available.

Require visual display for teaching identification of concrete concepts such as shapes and objects and for spatial relationships such as locations and distances, and use pictures rather than verbal descriptions whenever the content is spatial or spatiotemporal.

Arrange a concrete-concept lesson as recall of the discriminations of the relevant object features, presentation of several instances and noninstances varying in irrelevant qualities, and identification of instances by the student with feedback.

Realise a concrete-concept lesson concretely: varied figures for attention; paired examples and nonexamples with this-is and this-is-not statements plus a pick-out question for the objective; the critical attribute contrasts for prerequisite recall; example-nonexample pairs with feature naming for guidance; a mixed worksheet for performance; item-by-item review naming the present or absent critical feature for feedback; a similar test for assessment; and producing the figure from varied starting points plus finding it in real objects for transfer.

Choose example objects that are concrete, familiar, and verifiable by the learner from the accompanying illustration, and avoid introducing an unexplained technical term where a plain word suffices, since clear confirmation keeps learners from running aground on incidental impediments.

Do not accept a discrimination as evidence of a concept: telling two particular figures apart shows only that, whereas concept attainment requires identifying several instances that differ widely in irrelevant qualities such as size, colour, and border thickness.

Establish discriminations by enlarging the differences between the objects first and reducing them later — large shape differences before small ones, distorted forms before the true smaller contrasts.
Keep discrimination items purely perceptual: they require only an indication of same or different, not naming the stimulus or identifying its attributes.

Establish the concrete concepts a definition's words refer to before teaching the defined concept, since a learner who cannot concretely identify those referents cannot in any complete sense know the defined concept's meaning.

Require a defined concept to be demonstrated rather than stated: classifying an instance in accordance with the definition is a different mental process from reciting the definition, and asking what a term means is always open to the learner repeating a verbalisation without knowing the meaning.
Accept a verbally stated definition as sufficient to induce a defined concept only when the learner can retrieve the component concepts rather than merely the words.

Treat a defined concept as a classifying rule, formally no different from other rules and learned in much the same way, while recognising that rules in general also cover relations such as equal to, greater than, before, and after.

Write a defined-concept objective with classify — the learner classifying an instance by reference to the definition — and accept observation by describing or illustrating the concept from its definition, by selecting conforming instances from descriptions that do and do not, or by applying the concept properly in a sentence.
Arrange a defined-concept lesson as recall of the component concepts, demonstration of the concept using its definition, and demonstration of a concept example by the student.
Guide a defined concept by contrasting the general case against the particular in matched pairs to show the definition being applied, before the learner produces instances.
Establish meaning from the sentences before presenting a text passage as verbal information: define the specific unfamiliar words and ensure the syntactic structures are recognised.

Prefer a constructed diagram to a spoken definition for a defined-concept item, since the former is less dependent on verbal ability while the latter is open to distortion — a stated definition counting only where the subordinate concepts are known to be mastered, though verbal statements in the learner's own words are nevertheless often used.

Define mastery by the evidence the category requires: recall for verbal information, instant recognition of unencountered instances for a concrete concept, definition-based classification of an unencountered case for a defined concept, and application to unencountered instances for a rule.

Treat knowing and applying as different psychological phenomena: applying a definition requires converting it into an algorithm, which learners do spontaneously for simple definitions but often cannot for complex ones, so accurate recall of a definition is no evidence that it can be applied.
Define a composite term by first defining each component term it depends on, so the target definition is assembled from already-defined parts rather than introducing several unknowns at once.

Recognise that many concepts — family, city, justice — can only be acquired as defined concepts, and that where a defined concept shares a name with a concrete one their meanings overlap without being identical.

Require relational regularity across varied situations as evidence of a rule: sorting items by a fixed label may show only concrete concepts, so a rule is demonstrated by applying it to one or more concrete instances rather than restating it.

Use the verbal communication that teaches a rule to remind the learner which component concepts to recall and to cue their correct ordering — not to teach a formal verbal proposition — so it need not be precisely phrased.

Treat higher-order rules as combinations of simpler previously learned rules invented to solve a problem class: the rules combined must be recallable though the solver cannot necessarily verbalise them or have met them in a formal course, and the new rule generalises to problems with similar formal characteristics.
Confirm a higher-order rule by having the learner demonstrate it in other physically different but formally similar situations — that is, by showing transfer.

Recognise that large amounts of information are learned outside instruction from books, press, and broadcast without special teaching, provided the audience holds the intellectual skills to interpret those communications — and that verbal information is stored as networks of propositions conforming to the rules of language.

Recognise that new verbal information rests on language skills — synonyms and metaphors, rules of syntax, and logical sequencing of ideas — which strongly affect how readily declarative knowledge is acquired and how much is ultimately available, and that the more elaborated the prior knowledge the more readily new information is learned and remembered.

Write a rule objective with demonstrate and make the object specific enough that the class of stimulus situations is unambiguous, since most rules are complex and require previously learned concepts and rules, and only a precise object lets the components be described and the right instruction designed.

Expect verbal information to support intellectual-skill learning by aiding the verbal communications of instruction — often as labels for the concepts in a rule — and by providing a context of retrieval cues for the skill.

Assume the language skills of forming propositions in accordance with rules of syntax as a prerequisite for storing verbal information, and classify the larger context of meaningful information — learned immediately before or long previously — as a supportive prerequisite, since information is most readily learned and retained within it.

Give learning guidance as hints and questions that suggest the line of thought leading to the combining of subordinate concepts and rules rather than telling the answer, since what matters is not what the teacher literally says but that the communication stimulates a direction of thought and keeps the learner on track.

Recognise that in attitude learning the human model and the communications it delivers constitute the learning guidance, giving the event a more complex form than for verbal information or intellectual skills while still serving semantic encoding.

Arrange a rule lesson as recall of the subordinate concepts and rules, demonstration of the rule using a verbal statement, and demonstration of rule application by the student — and a higher-order rule lesson as recall of the relevant subordinate rules, presentation of a novel task or problem, and demonstration of the new rule in the student's solution.

Reject the view that good communication is the teacher's job and profiting from it the student's — leaving students to infer the objective, remind themselves of prerequisites, and choose an encoding — since it runs contrary to mastery learning, which relates instructional quality to cues, participation, reinforcement, and feedback with correctives and so requires managing events beyond the giving of information.
Teach verbal information in a relevant, prior-knowledge-linked organization and rehearse meaningful recall cues, using logical mnemonics only when meaningful elaboration is insufficient.

Provide learning guidance by making the stimulus meaningful: use concrete examples of abstract terms and elaborate each idea by relating it to ideas already in memory, giving divergent instances and noninstances plus cues to the proper combining sequence for intellectual skills, a reinforced human model for attitudes, and direct continued practice with performance feedback for motor skills.

Verify before teaching a rule that every concept forming part of it has been previously learned, and stage recall of those component concepts, because that is the necessary internal condition for rule learning.

Use elaboration to associate the item with other readily accessible material — an acoustic-link image for foreign vocabulary, or paraphrasing, summarising, note taking, and generating questions with answers for prose.
Use chunking to organise separate items into more general categories and so reduce the number held in short-term memory, whose capacity is limited to about seven separate items.

Design for a small working memory: only a few items are held per channel at one time, memory span averages about five to seven chunks, and what is held is a selection of portions rather than a copy of the presentation.

Do not mistake embedding a strategy in the materials for teaching it: an embedded strategy performs the function for the learner, whereas a learned strategy lets the student perform that function himself, so where strategies are themselves an intended outcome the conditions for learning them must be designed like those of any other outcome.

Write cognitive-strategy objectives with adopt and do not hand the learner the strategy: adopt implies selecting an already known technique, whereas a learner who truly originates a strategy is doing problem solving.

Treat as open the question of what learners who construct their own outline acquire that learners studying a prepared outline do not, and what test would reveal the difference — it awaits empirical research.

Temper claims about teaching students how to think: genetic factors not amenable to education play an important part in creative thought, and the internally organised nature of cognitive strategies means instruction can affect their acquisition only indirectly.
Design for cognitive strategies by arranging favourable conditions — opportunities for their development and use — since to learn to think the student must be given opportunities to think.

Expect the essential prerequisites of cognitive strategies to be very basic mental abilities such as forming visual images or dividing a verbally described situation into parts, and accept that whether these depend on innate maturation or on learning is disputed — on either account they develop over a considerable period.
Distinguish creative thinking, critical thinking, and metacognition, and expect thinking- skills programs to produce moderate rather than large gains with transfer only to similar tasks.

Expect the strategy itself to be structurally simple — underline main ideas, divide the problem into parts — even though the prior knowledge it operates on must be retrievable, and expect even young children to respond to a suggested strategy.

Expect a cognitive strategy's own prerequisites to be simple and well known — the more general the strategy the simpler they are — and expect a schema to supply the retrieval cues for a strategy, since recalling a previously encountered problem's whole schema is what reveals the analogy.
Build a theory by analysing the differences among existing strategies, identifying the situation each fits best, then extending and operationalizing the optimal strategy for each situation.

Draw on the documented adult strategies for verbally stated problems — inferring transformed conceptions of the givens, classifying rather than randomly choosing action sequences, hill climbing toward the goal, identifying contradictions showing the goal unattainable, breaking the problem into parts, and working backward from the goal — while noting they are most obviously applicable to algebraic or geometric brain-teaser problems.

Emphasise intellectual skills and problem-solving strategies over presently known facts, because the capabilities a child will need to reach his goals and solve problems not yet foreseen by today's adults cannot be determined exactly.

Sequence a progression of increasingly complex problems that are explicitly compared to one another; a single problem or a no-guidance sink-or-swim approach is insufficient for mastering a complex skill.

Pose problems that are interesting, relevant, and engaging, and (for problem-solving learning) ill-defined enough that some aspects are emergent and definable by the learner rather than fully specified in advance.

Analyse down to the skill types the learners genuinely lack rather than to every type: a grade-level presentation may legitimately assume the simpler learning is done, but where the discriminations are genuinely new — using an instrument, judging a material — they must be learned before the concepts, rules, and problem solving that are the course's main aims.

After classifying a lesson's objectives by capability type, check whether an original intention was overlooked or under-represented, whether the balance of expected outcomes is suitable, and whether the instructional approach matches each objective's type — applying the same checks at topic and course level.

Stop the analysis at a pragmatically determined point where, given knowledge of the student characteristics, the lowest-level skills are judged already known — and expect that point to vary with the learners' educational background, so the same target skill yields a deeper hierarchy for less prepared students.

Assess the quality of thought as a learning outcome rather than as a trait, requiring two things: that the problem call on knowledge, concepts, and rules recently learned rather than acquired years earlier, and that all students be assumed or preferably shown to hold the prerequisite information and skills, so no one's solution is handicapped by missing knowledge.
Analyze actual learners and both learning and performance contexts instead of relying on assumed characteristics or idealized conditions.
Teach classification with coherent learner-relevant examples, diagnostic nonexamples, removal of irrelevant shortcut cues, and rule-based explanations for every judgment.
Interleave problem types during practice when learners must discriminate among them, accepting poorer in-lesson scores for better delayed learning.
Refresh prerequisite discriminations with additional practice at the point of use, even when learners are assumed to possess them already.

Plan instruction in a body of information where certainty of learning matters, because incidental exposure yields learning that varies greatly across individuals whereas a planned course aims at all students learning what is deemed essential — justified when the information must be recalled repeatedly for further study or is continually useful throughout life.

Recognise knowledge as information organised into meaningfully interconnected facts and generalisations, the form in which specialists store their information, and treat general cultural knowledge as serving communication for citizenship and possibly identity — while noting that the stronger claim that knowledge is the vehicle for thought and problem solving rests on incomplete evidence.

Expect name-learning difficulty to rise sharply when many names must be acquired at once, accept label learning as useful even when it amounts to memorising because it establishes the basis for communication between learner and teacher or textbook, and support it with mnemonic techniques such as embedding a word pair in a made-up sentence or the keyword image method.

Recognise that classical conditioning can establish approach or avoidance toward a class of objects, events, or persons, so some attitudes learners bring with them originate in earlier conditioning experiences rather than in anything the instruction did.

Use reinforcement contingencies as a direct attitude method — making an already-preferred activity contingent on the new performance so the learner acquires a liking for the new task as well as learning it — and expect success in a learning accomplishment itself to produce a positive attitude toward that activity.

Recognise and reward the choice behaviour when it appears and take care not to punish it inadvertently — rewarding work with more work breeds resentment, so arrange the reinforcement schedule to make the learner want to do more.

Attend to the affective components many cognitive objectives carry by shaping the context in which the skill is presented — making the new skill meaningful to the learner and building in as much reinforcement as possible.

Arrange an attitude lesson as recall of the verbal information and intellectual skills relevant to the chosen personal actions, establishment or recall of respect for the source, and reward for the personal action either directly or vicariously through the model; and a motor-skill lesson as recall of the responses and part skills, establishment or recall of the executive subroutine, and practice of the total skill.

Use contingency management with contracts where motivation must be built in: the student spends starting points to negotiate time for a module and earns points for completing it within the period, which can then be spent on free time or a preferred activity — the general form being to follow an initially nonpreferred activity with a preferred one, which reinforces the former.

Apply contingency management properly to establish and maintain orderly behaviour aimed at productive learning, instil a positive liking for learning and its accomplishments, and capture interest in problem-solving activities as sources of satisfaction — which requires the teacher to identify differences in individual students' interests, likes, and dislikes and use these in selecting the specific contingencies.
Give learners early activities that resemble the target task and avoid multiple-choice substitutes unless recognition among supplied alternatives is itself the authentic performance.

Have learners practise the very performance they are expected to produce, in the presence of the discriminative stimuli that will have to elicit it later, and follow practice with reinforcement in the form of confirmation, reward, or both.

Use human modeling as the principal indirect method for attitudes, delivered in person, on television, in film, or through printed literature, choosing a model the learners respect or identify with and who is perceived as credible and powerful.

Treat role playing and led class discussion as forms of human modeling — the actor models the choices of an imagined person and the discussion leader acts as a model — and recognise that a teacher's modelling role is load-bearing given the time students spend in his presence.
Ensure the learner holds the information that identifies a human model as a familiar, respected person and attests to his credibility before relying on that model.

Add a prerequisite step to establish or build up respect for the model when human modeling is used and that respect is not already in place, since a pictured figure is more likely to be respected if the learner knows of that person's accomplishments.
When modeling, use both behavioral modeling (showing how to perform the activity) and cognitive modeling (articulating the reasoning the learner should use).

Show both halves of the modelled episode: the learner must observe the model making the desired choice of personal action and see that the action leads to satisfaction or pleasure for the model — the vicarious reinforcement step — or the modeling does not establish the attitude.

Arrange the external conditions for modelling as a four-step sequence: present the model and establish its appeal and credibility; have the learner recall knowledge of the situations the attitude applies to; have the model communicate or demonstrate the desired choices; and show the model obtaining pleasure or satisfaction from the outcome.

Make the costs and long-term benefits of the desired choice explicit, because current behaviour persists through its positive consequences or habituation and competing behaviours often carry stronger short-term benefits.
Provide relevant models rather than exhortation, since do as I do outperforms do as I say and the more salient the model is to the learner the more likely the choice behaviour is adopted.

Ensure the environment actually affords the desired choice — the opportunity to perform it must exist — and treat an unmodifiable environmental conflict as evidence that the desired behaviour is not a viable objective.

Confirm desired choices or movement toward them with praise or support while assessing by unobtrusive measures observed over weeks, since self-reports of choice behaviour are imperfect indicators — and arrange environmental support such as a regular support group, because attitudes are reinforced by the environment.

Complement modelling with simulations, role playing, collaborative processes, or other involving experiences in which the benefits of the desired behaviour become obvious, rather than substituting them for modelling.

Do not pair an unrelated behaviour with the one being changed: habituation and attitudes form behaviour complexes, so the most important behaviours must be identified and prioritised for intervention.
Judge a motor skill by the rapidity, accuracy, force, or smoothness of bodily movement, and drop the terms perceptual-motor and psychomotor, which carry no useful added meaning.

Supply external knowledge of results early and expect its role to diminish: smoothness and timing depend on both internal feedback from muscles and joints, used as an error reference, and external knowledge of results, but as practice proceeds improvement comes to depend increasingly on the internal kind.
Provide repeated practice for motor skills, since there is no way to avoid it if accuracy, speed, and smoothness are to improve, and practice continues to yield improvement over very long periods.

Teach both the part skills and their integration, recognising that the executive subroutine organising a motor skill is not itself motor but a procedural rule controlling which movement is executed first, second, and so on.

Do not settle the part-versus-whole practice question in general — many studies give no clear answer and it depends on the skill — but do ensure both the executive subroutine and the part skills are learned, since practice on either without the other has repeatedly proved ineffective for the total skill.

Arrange motor-skill instruction by first communicating the executive subroutine — by verbal instruction, a checklist of the movement sequence, or pictures and diagrams — and then having the learner practise the movements with accompanying informative feedback.

Match the key condition to the outcome type: for verbal information, external cues relating the new material to an organised prior network; for attitudes, direct reinforcement of action choices or vicarious reinforcement through modelling; for motor skills, practice with frequent informative feedback once the executive subroutine is learned and the parts integrated — because each type makes a different performance possible.

Expect the core of a motor skill to be a centrally located motor program established by practice that attains automaticity, and expect the executive subroutine to survive years of disuse even when the performance itself becomes hesitant and rough.

Account for two kinds of prior learning in a new motor skill — the previously learned part skills that compose it and the procedural rule that constitutes the early cognitive stage — and remember that the procedure must always be followed for improvement to occur, whatever practice yields.
Treat part skills and a separately learned executive subroutine as essential prerequisites for a motor skill only where separate part practice is in fact the more efficient route for that skill.

Teach a strategy as a sequence of steps whose list and explanation serve as an executive subroutine, just as the movement sequence does for a motor skill, and make practising that subroutine the instructional activity.

Let the skill's complexity decide whether part skills or the executive subroutine dominates the motor-skill sequence — identifying part skills for a simple throw yields no useful plan while for a complex skill such as swimming part practice is often valuable — and place the executive subroutine early, before the part skills are fully mastered.
Classify an objective built from motor actions as a rule when the learner already possesses the component motor skills and what must be learned is the procedure for combining them.

State the instructional content of a step as the discriminations and manipulations that underlie it — telling parts apart, reading the physical cue, operating each control — rather than as the step's imperative alone.

Do not rank the outcome categories by importance: verbal information, attitudes, and motor skills are not less important than intellectual skills, and the categories differ in the internal conditions that must be assumed and the external conditions that must be arranged.

Do not assume information-type capabilities are essential prerequisites: empirical hierarchy validation showed that stating a fact about the target skill was helpful but not essential, contrasting markedly with the genuinely essential intellectual-skill components.

Apply the prerequisite map by outcome type: intellectual skills need simpler component skills as essential prerequisites plus attitudes, cognitive strategies, and verbal information as supportive; cognitive strategies need specific intellectual skills; verbal information needs meaningfully organised sets of information plus language skills; attitudes sometimes need intellectual skills and verbal information; motor skills sometimes need part skills and procedural rules.

Span all five capability types in the outcome measures — mastery tests for intellectual skills, novel-situation exercises for the quality or efficiency of problem-solving thought, tests of specified facts or breadth of knowledge for information, observations against a performance standard for motor skills, and probability-of-choice self-reports for attitudes — developing them specially for the study where commercially available or adaptable instruments do not exist.

Sequence on the enabling-prerequisite relations that hold among intellectual skills, and treat prior learning for verbal information, attitudes, and motor skills as merely supportive — a distinction with particular implications for determining instructional sequence.

Give first priority to intellectual skills as the central planning components — identify them, analyse their prerequisites, then add at appropriate points the cognitive strategies those skills make possible — except where the primary objective is verbal information, an attitude, or a motor skill, in which case the analysis instead reveals the supportive effects of prior learning.

Follow the design procedure appropriate to each learner characteristic: stimulate retrieval of prerequisite intellectual skills; provide for retrieval of cognitive strategies where available; stimulate recall of propositions and of the meaningful context or situational schema; activate previously acquired positive attitudes for motivation; and recall the essential part skills for motor learning.

Define a prerequisite as a task learned before a target objective that aids or enables its learning, recognising that the same task may be a target objective for one lesson and an enabling objective for a later one, and that prerequisites may have been learned years earlier, immediately before, or within the same lesson.

Classify every prerequisite as essential — an actual component of the total skill without which the target cannot be learned or performed correctly — or supportive, merely making the new learning easier or faster, and require essential prerequisites to be acquired before the target objective regardless of whether they were learned formally or incidentally.

Carry the analysis down through successively simpler components to produce a learning hierarchy of progressively simpler enabling skills, while recognising that the most important questions come from any two adjacent levels because the enabling skills of primary relevance to one objective are its immediate prerequisites.

Do not build learning hierarchies for information and attitudes: they are not learned by putting together subordinate parts as intellectual skills are, so their prerequisites tend to be supportive rather than essential.

Sequence lessons within a unit on the prerequisite relationships, requiring that new learning is supported by previous learning, that a learning analysis confirms the sequential order, that the sequences are complete, and that objectives irrelevant to the learning task are eliminated or taught at a different time.

Apply the sequencing principle proper to each outcome type: precede each new intellectual skill by prior mastery of its subordinate skills; involve recall of relevant intellectual skills in problem-solving situations; treat the order of major verbal-information subtopics as unimportant while preceding new facts with a meaningful context; establish respect for the source and mastery of the involved intellectual skills before an attitude's choice situation; and for motor skills practise the critical part skills intensively and the total skill too, with the executive subroutine learned first.
Ensure the verbal information relevant to a new intellectual skill, or to the choices in an attitude objective, has either been previously learned or is presented in the instructions.

Expect a proper prerequisite sequence to make intellectual-skill learning easy for the teacher to manage and highly reinforcing for learners, who repeatedly find they can suddenly do something they could not before — the opposite of drill and rote recitation.
State what a concept lesson presupposes in the longer sequence and begin with the simpler prerequisite concepts where the learners lack them.

Take mastery with complete seriousness for intellectual skills — each prerequisite performable with perfect confidence before more complex skills are attempted — since any lesser degree of prerequisite learning yields puzzlement, delay, and inefficient trial and error at best and failure, frustration, or abandonment at worst, which is also why letting the student choose the sequence is unlikely to be the most efficient procedure.
Go from prerequisite skills to higher-order skills and present the events through the activities in a sequence that facilitates information processing.

Teach verbal-information objectives first where they supply a supportive context aiding transfer to the main intellectual-skill objectives, even though they are not prerequisites, since prerequisite-sequencing considerations favour presenting the supportive content before the target objectives.

Weigh the measured gains: against conventional instruction in groups of thirty, mastery learning raised achievement from the fiftieth to the eighty-fourth percentile and tutoring from the fiftieth to the ninety-eighth, enhanced prerequisites alone reached the seventy-sixth and with mastery learning the ninety-fifth, and enhanced cues with participation exceeded the ninety-sixth when added to mastery learning.
Distinguish the three domains of learner control — content sequencing, pacing, and access to learning support — before accepting or rejecting a claim that a course is learner-controlled.

Stimulate recall of prior learning naturally related to the new learning, choosing what is recalled by outcome type: organized bodies of knowledge for verbal information, prerequisite rules and concepts for intellectual skills, similar task strategies for cognitive strategies, and the executive routine and part skills for motor skills.

Set the entry requirement each outcome type imposes before teaching it: a meaningful context for verbal information whose presentation order does not matter; the relevant intellectual skills and verbal information already in place for a cognitive strategy; established respect for the human model and the relevant information for an attitude; and the executive routine plus part skills followed by intensive whole-skill practice for a motor skill.

Revisit an objective's capability classification against the prerequisite structure rather than fixing it once: an apparently verbal-information objective must be treated as an intellectual skill when a later objective depends on it as a concept, and such a term is then taught twice over, as information and as a concept.

Review prerequisite concepts that were practised only minimally earlier, inside the presentation of the material that depends on them, because weakly learned prerequisites need the extra cuing before the dependent content.

Teach non-prerequisite supporting content immediately after the organizing content it relates to, with the exception that highly related coordinate concepts are always taught together — including a concept's sole coordinate even when it is not a prerequisite, since learning one exhaustive alternative entails learning the other.

Design around innate capacity rather than trying to change it: for genetically determined qualities the aim is to avoid exceeding human capacities — keeping words, sentences, diagrams, and other communications well inside working-memory limits rather than testing them — while sensory qualities such as visual acuity need attention only under extreme conditions such as fine print or fuzzy projection.
Design technology to complement human abilities — aiding what people are poorly suited to and enhancing what they are well suited to — rather than requiring the learner to accommodate the machine.

Expect retrieval to work by spread of activation through a propositional network whose elements connect at points with productions, which accounts both for apparently random association and for the flexibility of reflective thinking.

Expect a learner working toward an integrated goal to have to retrieve prior information and prerequisite skills, apply the encoding procedures suited to each objective type, associate retrieval cues with what is acquired, and keep in mind how the material will be displayed or used — and treat that mental set as crucial for transfer.

Conceive what is stored in long-term memory as propositions both declarative and procedural, images, and motor programs, organised into interconnected networks that can be searched and retrieved to serve an activity or further learning.

Work from the internal processes of a single act of learning — attention, selective perception, rehearsal, semantic encoding, retrieval including search, response organisation, feedback that sets reinforcement in motion, and executive control processes that modify any of the others — remembering that retrieved information may go directly to action or return to working memory to combine with incoming information and form new capabilities.
Expect a learner's schema to carry an attitude as well as knowledge, so content touching such a schema may affect personal choices as well as understanding.

Take seriously that schemas control perception — the learner sees a stimulus only in reference to a schema that directs attention and gives the event meaning — which makes learning highly personal, though learners raised in a fairly homogeneous society may activate similar process schemas, and process schemas can differ by culture where different algorithms were taught.

Determine what schemas the prospective student already holds before designing verbal-information instruction, because new information is best learned with a readily accessible schema whose slots the content can fill.

Do not design instruction to change abilities or personality traits: both tend to be stable characteristics persisting over long periods and are not readily altered by instruction or practice aimed at them.
Avoid the real design error, which is not mixing intellectual skills and information during instruction — that is normal — but confusing the two types of learning as target objectives.

Treat differential abilities as overlapping rather than distinct — their scores correlate positively with each other and low-to-moderately with general intelligence, and whether general or differential measurement is more useful remains unanswered — while knowing the standard set: reasoning, verbal comprehension, number facility, spatial orientation, associative memory, and memory span.

Expect real aptitude treatment interactions: high achievement motivation achieves better where instruction permits considerable learner control, anxious students learn more when allowed to review recorded instruction than when viewing it in groups without review, and internal locus of control may explain further findings.

Adapt to traits through the instructional arrangement rather than the content: very anxious learners may be reassured by frequent feedback during practice, while learners with high achievement motivation may thrive on discovery learning where low-motivation learners perform poorly.

Choose between the two ways of handling aptitude: circumvent a lack of it — easily read text plus elaborate guidance for learners low in verbal comprehension — or develop it through instruction and practice in cognitive strategies, remembering conservatively that domain-specific strategies are readily learnable while generalisable ones may take many years.

Treat the student's aptitude for learning as probably the most influential variable of all — no combination of improved methods, process arrangements, and best possible support influences outcomes as much — with intelligence-test measures accounting for as much as half the variation in outcomes across verbal information, intellectual skills, and cognitive strategies, and with aptitude entering the study as an input variable that can only be measured, not manipulated, despite having multiple determinants in inheritance, prenatal environment, prior learning, and opportunity.

Institute controls that separate the influence of entering aptitude from the effect of the instruction, and where the question concerns effectiveness independent of entering skills treat the prerequisite learner characteristics rather than general aptitude as the input variable.

Prefer measures that assess learning aptitude as directly as possible over correlated proxies such as previous school grades or family socioeconomic status, which are sometimes useful but not to be preferred.
