Partial out aptitude statistically by asking what the effect of instruction alone would be if aptitude were held constant, and accept that no study evaluating learning outcomes can provide valid evidence of instructional effectiveness without some way of controlling the aptitude variable — by measurement, random assignment, comparison of aptitudes, or statistical means.

Expect the outcome measures to reflect the instructional change in an unbiased manner once aptitude, support, and process variables have been shown or reasonably assumed to affect both groups equally.

Guard satisfaction against expectation mismatch — arbitrary-seeming grading, an intrinsically motivated learner locked into an external contingency system, or an experience unlike what was promised — and manage the balance between fostering intrinsic motivation and the sometimes unavoidable use of extrinsic reinforcement.

Choose verbal comprehension if only one ability score can be obtained for a group about to learn verbal information, since many studies show it predicts the ease with which new verbal knowledge is acquired.

Adapt instruction to differences in abilities and traits only as far as feasibility permits — easily read text for learners low in verbal comprehension, detailed guidance with frequent feedback for highly anxious learners — and pay particular attention to ease of verbal comprehension wherever the instruction is verbal in nature.

Expect only low-to-moderate correlations between abilities such as speed of movement, motor coordination, and spatial visualisation and motor-skill learning, so do not use them to predict or select strongly.
Expect contiguity to matter most for low-knowledge learners, complex material, long segments, and system-controlled pacing.

Design for intrinsic as well as extrinsic causes — building in questions that arouse curiosity or opportunities for social interaction and approval — while accepting that not all individuals are motivated by the same things because of differing prior learning, experience, and expectations, and that motivation research nonetheless yields principles generalisable enough to use in designing materials.

Present motivational design levers — emotional design, self-efficacy support, interest, and social cues — as preliminary and separately evidenced rather than as settled principles on a par with the established cognitive ones.

Treat a motivational design model as a supplement to an instructional-design model rather than a replacement, prescribing its strategies smorgasbord-fashion because any module could require anywhere from none to all of them.

State the audience assumptions motivational design rests on — responsiveness to curiosity arousal, sense of the subject's relevance, confidence built from prior experience in the domain, and responsiveness to feedback — recognizing that little prior success in a subject predicts low to moderate confidence, and that learners low in perceived relevance still respond to immediate utility or to the methods themselves.
Include provisions for detecting the presence of relevant schemas and activating them by questions, advance organisers, or other devices.

Define required interaction data, application evidence, reports, privacy, security, accessibility, certification, liability, interoperability, and standards early, then verify the platform can collect, connect, protect, and report accordingly.

Specify the stimulus situation the learner faces, because what the student actually does depends heavily on it — working from longhand copy, from an auditory message, or from notes are different tasks.

Present the stimuli actually involved in the performance that reflects the learning — oral questions for answering oral questions, verbally stated problems for solving verbally stated problems — because using the wrong stimuli can leave the learner having acquired the wrong skill, though a differently-stimulated task may legitimately serve earlier as a subordinate skill.

Expect learners to compensate differently for what a lecture leaves undone — one recovering it later by applying his own encoding strategies to his notes, another finding that ineffective and preferring the original oral form.
Describe the environmental conditions of on-the-job performance where they materially change the task — unimportant for many behaviours but critical for others such as donning a gas mask.

Treat named tools and constraints as conditions on the performance rather than as the skill being acquired, and check whether they, like the situation, imply further prerequisite skills that must be learned before the target skill can be adequately evaluated.

Write a discrimination objective around a sensory sameness-or-difference judgment with an action such as pointing or circling, and specify the performance environment where competing stimuli in the real setting would make the discrimination harder than in isolation.

Separate rule-using from problem-solving objectives by asking demonstrate what rule versus generate what rule: given the rule and asked to apply it, the outcome is rule learning; required to generate a new rule or synthesise existing ones, it is problem solving.

Focus a problem-solving objective on what the learner is constructing — the higher-order rule expressing relationships among other rules and concepts — rather than on the process of problem solving, which is hard to write about mainly because problem-solving skills are usually not formally taught.

Give guidance during problem solving only when rules appear to be misapplied or the learner sees no possible solution, in the form of options and questions about the learner's own rule, confirming good moves rather than supplying the solution — then assess with a different problem of the same type and test transfer by varying the situation along several dimensions at once.

Establish through analysis whether an objective needs only a single rule or higher-order rules acting on other rules, build one rule hierarchy across objectives so shared components are captured, and base the detailed design on the objective with the most paths when several share the same decision-operation structure.
Write only the components needed for unambiguous communication of intent, recognising that any component left implicit is left open to interpretation.

Classify seemingly content-bound objectives by the capability they demand: identifying the characters in a play is classification by relationship to the plot, paraphrasing a difficult passage is problem solving whose higher-order rules cannot be specified in advance, and recognising a concept that cannot be pointed to is a defined-concept classification.

Choose action verbs that both suit the capability inferred from the performance and describe the nature of the performance itself, and derive the different communications of an objective — for teachers, students, and parents — from one precisely formulated definition that also ties those meanings to the tests.

Build tests that directly measure the human performances described in the course objectives, so that the intended capability can be inferred to have developed as a result of the instruction — a direct rather than indirect measure, which removes the need to relate the measure to a criterion by a correlation coefficient.

Take the performance objective as the keystone of assessment planning: its verbs tell what the student should be asked to do, with the capability verb naming the intent and the action verb serving as the indicator that the intent has been achieved.

Do not substitute verbs that change the meaning of the capability or the action, taking particular care not to shift from an answer the student must construct to one he merely chooses, selects, or recalls — an objective to generate a position and its defence cannot be tested by multiple choice — and avoid vague verbs by using the standard capability verbs, fixing unambiguous meanings for words such as summarize, describe, list, analyze, and complete.
For attitudinal goals, identify the choice instruction should influence and analyze and assess the observable behavior that expresses it; do not equate knowing how with choosing to act.

State a course purpose as what the student will be like after the instruction rather than what he does during it — providing experience with apparatus describes activity, whereas stating the apparatus names or assembling apparatus for experiments describes learning.

Treat instruction as the set of events that acts upon and involves the student during a lesson — in a basic sense a set of communications, most typically verbal but gestures or pictures for young children.

State course purposes as expected current outcomes rather than distant ones, since acquiring a lifelong respect for a subject is not a realistic outcome of a single course even though nothing is wrong with the lifelong goal itself; at this stage specific five-component objectives are not yet necessary though the same guidelines apply.

Describe a course at five levels of outcome — lifelong objectives, end-of-course objectives, unit objectives, specific performance objectives at the level appropriate for task analysis, and enabling objectives — keeping the lifelong objective, which states what learners will continue to do afterward, distinct from the end-of-course objective, which states the performance expected immediately after instruction.

Keep sequential steps distinct from subordinate skills: the steps are what a person does in sequence when exhibiting the learned performance, whereas the subordinate skills are what the person must learn, in a sequence beginning with the simplest.

Let the learning sequence differ from the performance sequence where a skill used early in performance is more easily learned after skills used later, as when writing good test items becomes easier once objectives can be written even though on the job the item comes first.

For sequential intellectual, psychomotor, and most attitudinal performances, draft the competent performer's visible and mental steps, sequence them efficiently, identify enabling capabilities, and revise step size and placement.

Treat the claim that cognitive strategies speed skill learning, ease recall, or aid transfer as broadly accepted but weakly evidenced, since empirical evidence of the effectiveness of that support is as yet scanty and still needed.

Review earlier skills at the start of a lesson where ready recall is needed for the new learning, while remembering that intellectual skills once learned are recalled well compared with facts or labels.
Accept that the learner must allocate limited resources — what to attend to, how far to connect — and support that allocation with metacognitive guidance rather than leaving it to chance.
Treat cost and time savings from e-learning as illusory until the training demonstrably improves job performance, and require that outcome to be the justification.
Name the open questions about control honestly: whether metacognitive skill compensates for low prior knowledge, which navigational support suits which profile, and where dynamic adaptation pays off.
Do not use time-pressured fast-response game formats for cognitive outcomes, since speed displaces reflection; reserve them for skills that must become automatic.
Exploit shared components across independent path sequences deliberately, generalizing skills learned in one to another to improve learning efficiency.

Link the learner's outcome to controllable effort by telling them that effort applied to the examples predicts success on the problems, and attribute success explicitly to their ability and effort — stating there is no luck or magic — immediately before the graded assessment.

Exploit the mutual support among attitudes — a related attitude eases adoption of another and the degree to which a model is respected affects how readily his attitude is adopted — and supply knowledge of the specific situations where the choice will arise, since that contributes to the ease of acquisition.

Influence attitudes by making desired and undesired choices and consequences explicit, using relatable credible models, and ensuring feedback delivers the promised consequence directly or vicariously.

Consider macrolevel elaboration sequencing: present an epitome of a few general, simple, fundamental ideas first, then successively more detailed elaborations organised simple to complex and general to specific, repeating the overview-elaboration-summary-synthesis cycle until the desired coverage is reached.
Recognize presenting major steps first and elaborating their detail afterwards as elaboration sequencing operating inside a single procedural demonstration.

Recognize that macro-level prescriptions for selecting, sequencing, synthesizing and summarizing content are a separate layer from micro-level presentation prescriptions, and that explicitly teaching the interrelationships within content is its own strategy component rather than a by-product of teaching the parts.

Sequence like a zoom lens: open with a wide-angle epitome showing the major parts and their relationships without detail, zoom in on one part, then zoom back out to review the whole and that part's context before zooming in again, repeating the elaborate-summarize-synthesize cycle until the desired complexity is reached.

Epitomize rather than summarize when building the opening overview: present a few of the most fundamental and representative ideas at a concrete application or skill level, not a compressed account of everything to come.

Choose one content orientation for the elaborative sequence — what (concepts), how (procedures), or why (principles) — because virtually every course holds one of the three more important than the others, and those three are the only elaboration bases the sequencing literature offers.

Recognize five nested levels of simple-to-complex sequencing — ideas within a lesson, lessons within a unit, units within a module, modules within a course, courses within a curriculum — and expect different content types to organize different levels of the same design.
Scale how complete the designed instructional events must be to the sophistication of the learners, since completeness depends on which events the learners are expected to provide for themselves.

Expect any or all of the events to be supplied by the learner when self-instructing — not only with programmed materials but when studying textbooks, doing laboratory exercises, or completing projects — and expect this skill to increase with age and experience, so lesson events require far more teacher activity in the early grades than later.

Derive the desirable characteristics of instructional events from what is known about the learner's internal processes rather than inventing them, because that is what makes design at the level of the individual learning episode possible.
Recognise that the framework of instructional events constrains the functions rather than the creative form of the lesson, leaving considerable opportunity for the designer's art.

Vary the form of every instructional event by the category of learned capability targeted; designing events for an intellectual skill as though it were verbal information or a motor skill is a design error.

Ensure at course level that the prerequisite information and intellectual skills for any topic have been learned earlier — adding fractions after multiplying and dividing whole numbers, graphing relations after measuring variables, the concept of culture before comparing family structures across cultures.

Distinguish ordered from unordered units in the course map: where two units' intellectual-skill objectives are fairly independent their teaching order is not critical, whereas units whose skills are prerequisite to the next must be sequenced accordingly.

State topic-level objectives in performance terms, since wordings such as understand the procedure or appreciate the equipment are too ambiguous and may imply different performance objectives to different people.
Expect course, unit, and lesson maps to trade scope for detail as the level descends, in the relation of a globe to a country map to a state map.

Treat a course or site map as an orientation device for novices rather than a navigation tool, use a simple hierarchical structure, and organize it around the learners' goals since the map's scheme shapes what is learned.
Split the lesson map into two maps, each representing one period, when the mapped skills prove to exceed a single instructional period.

Expect multiple objectives because a lesson is most often only part of a larger unit, and engage the student in a comprehensive purpose that may require integrating verbal information, attitudes, concepts, and rules — using an instructional curriculum map to analyse that integrative goal into its component objectives across domains and to show each objective's role in supporting the larger goal.
Show the lesson's parts as a labelled diagram of the target object, so the structure of the instruction maps visibly onto the structure of the thing being learned.

Name the purposive external activity the learner is aiming at as an enterprise and the goal as its internal representation, treating each pursuit as an activity with a purpose rather than simply an activity — with common enterprise types being denoting, manifesting, and discovering.

Sequence course topics by common-sense logic where no hierarchy applies: one topic precedes another because it describes earlier events, because it is a component part, or because it provides a meaningful context for what follows.
Sequence verbal information by subtype — names, isolated facts, or the sense of a logically organised passage — with the meaningful context as the most important prerequisite throughout.
Sequence a purely factual or historical section after the practical and explanatory sections, so learners can recognize the relevance of the facts from experience already gained.
Treat the listed order as the most probable rather than an invariant one and do not provide every event for every lesson, since their role is to stimulate internal processes rather than replace them.

Treat the instructional functions as the invariant features of a lesson rather than any standard routine of communications and actions, adapting even those functions to the situation, the task, the type of learning, and the students' prior learning — while specifically considering every function in planning even where it is ultimately not provided, and organising the events flexibly with primary attention to the objectives.

Present the events in order because they follow the hypothesised sequence of internal processing, but treat them as guidelines: not all need be included, strict linear order is not required, and the plan must reflect both the learners' sophistication as self-directed learners and the nature of the objectives.

Order the cases within a lesson from fewest interacting effects to most, so each case adds a single new behaviour to the previous, and order sibling topics so the one whose relationship is precise and single-factored precedes the one governed by several interacting factors.

Use the list of events as a checklist in design practice, asking of each whether these learners need support at this stage for this task, and omit an event already obvious to the learner or one that experienced self-learners supply themselves.

Treat the nine events of instruction as a design checklist to be considered for any desired learning, not a mandatory script: each event is a candidate to weigh, the order may vary, some may be omitted, and the form each takes depends on the learning task and the learners.

Use partially or wholly nonverbal communications to gain attention — a demonstration of a novel physical event or an unusual filmed scene — and give the teacher one or more options in a preplanned lesson, since individualised instruction allows their content and form to be varied to match individual interests.
Place demonstrations and audiovisual media to gain attention at the moments when other critical instructional events are about to follow, rather than at arbitrary points.

Emphasise the features that determine selective perception when presenting the stimulus — italics, bold print, underlining, heavy outlining, circling, or arrows on the essential features of a picture or diagram.

Route words away from the visual channel when a graphic is present: pictures load the visual/pictorial channel and spoken words the auditory/verbal channel, but printed and onscreen text enters through the eyes first and competes with the graphic for the same limited channel. Prefer narration over concurrent onscreen text in a system-paced presentation.
Signal the important elements — circles, colour, arrows, headings, or emphasis — to direct attention, because too many information sources compete for limited capacity.
Use signalling — headings, bold, colour, white space, arrows, and narration emphasis — to highlight relevant material, treating the evidence as preliminary rather than settled.

Delineate the distinctive features of every stimulus presented — highlighting features of diagrams, using headings and emphasis in text, varying tone and volume in speech — and for intellectual skills present varied examples of the concept, rule or problem.
Present problems in words, in diagrams, and in combinations of the two over a period of time, since this is likely to enhance retention and transfer.
Place a few short printed key words next to the part of the graphic they label as signalling; this improves retention without hurting transfer and is the sanctioned exception to the redundancy rule.

Elicit the performance first with the example the learner has been working on, then follow with a second new example to make sure the rule applies to a fresh instance — the event serving to convince the learner as well as the instructor.

Do not treat learning as complete once the correct performance appears: the after-effects of the learning event importantly influence exactly what is learned, so at minimum give feedback about the correctness or degree of correctness of the performance.
Fade from a fully worked example through partially worked examples to a full practice problem, so the learner progressively assumes more of the work.

Test whether a newly correct understanding is general rather than case-bound by immediately reintroducing a systematically varied case phrased so it slightly entraps, and by pushing the learner's new rule beyond the class it was induced from to the contrasting class.
When a learner lacks the concept needed to extend a rule to a new class, supply it by analogy to a case they can already reason about and let them make the generalization themselves.

Recognize that most principles in an elaboration lesson are the same principle applied to a special case producing different effects within one behaviour category, and elaborate an already-taught principle by stating explicitly what learners may already have realized but never had stated or demonstrated as such.

Supply feedback from an outside source where the task does not provide it automatically, and phrase it however works — a printed answer, a nod, a smile, a spoken word — because the important characteristic is not its content but its function of informing the learner about correctness.
Rely on the meaningful context in which material was learned as the best assurance of its reinstatement, because the network of relationships it was embedded in supplies multiple retrieval cues.

Vary events three, four, and five sharply by capability type while leaving events such as gaining attention undifferentiated, since it is stimulating recall, presenting the stimulus, and providing guidance whose specific form differs by outcome.

Understand the general purpose of the events as arranging the external conditions of learning so that learning will occur, and concentrate the outcome-specific conditions on events three to six — stimulating recall, presenting the stimulus, providing guidance, and eliciting performance — handling the remaining events generically.

Value the two-person group for the flexible adjustment of events it permits — stimulation can be increased when a first attempt fails, alternative encoding schemes tried in turn, and comprehension checked immediately and again after a lapse of time.

Expect available materials to deliver content but not the other events — a film may not present the objective, guide encoding, or pause for response and feedback — so create those events separately or interrupt the material so questions and feedback can occur.
Accept that central-broadcast delivery limits media to those transmitting sound, pictures, or both with no interactive responding by the learner.
Expect broadcast to transmit verbal knowledge of all kinds readily and to teach intellectual skills successfully only where provisions are made for student response.

Apply the six-situation exclusion table: serious-error job competence allows only large equipment, portable equipment, or a simulator; central broadcast allows only TV and radio; self-instruction and instructor-led situations with readers leave all media potentially effective; self-instruction with nonreaders excludes discursive printed passages and complex audio; and instructor with nonreaders excludes printed texts and complex lectures.

Address appropriateness for learning before availability, feasibility, and cost so that critical errors are avoided — no printed discourse for nonreaders, no radio broadcast alone for intellectual skills, no instructor lecture for training vehicle driving — then let cost and availability decide among the remaining learning-appropriate options, since as a general rule most instructional functions can be performed by most media.

Apply the exclusion-and-selection table by outcome: intellectual skills and cognitive strategies exclude non-interactive media and printed discourse for nonreaders while selecting feedback-capable media plus audio and visual features; verbal information excludes only real equipment or simulators without verbal accompaniment and complex prose for nonreaders while selecting media able to present verbal messages and elaborations; attitudes take the same exclusions while selecting media able to present realistic pictures of a human model and his message; motor skills exclude media with no provision for learner response and feedback while selecting media permitting direct practice with informative feedback.

Distinguish simulator, training device, and training aid: a simulator reproduces the operating characteristics of real equipment, a training device permits practice of skills or part skills without necessarily resembling the real equipment, and a training aid merely exhibits a process the learner observes without interacting.
Use simple training devices for parts of the total task and reserve the more expensive complex simulator for consolidating skills and practising emergency procedures in a safe environment.

Use computer-based instruction where intellectual skills are the outcome, since when suitably designed it is truly interactive and provides adaptive informative feedback according to whether responses are correct or incorrect; television is normally not learner-interactive but can be made so by combining a recording with a computer.
Make interactivity the deciding media property for intellectual skills, since precise feedback about correctness matters greatly to learning effectiveness for that outcome.

For an intellectual skill keep only media that interact with learner responses — computer instruction and interactive TV — excluding motion picture, slide or videotape, and TV cassette, which do not permit the response interaction essential to effective intellectual-skill learning.

Make the effectiveness of instruction depend on whether the media employed can provide the events in the manner the outcome type and the learner characteristics require, and read the general finding of no significant media differences as possibly reflecting research that failed to consider when media differences matter rather than as showing they do not exist.

Treat the instructor's media functions as the voice delivering speech, the action demonstrating procedures, and the delivery of informative feedback adapted to learner responding — over and above the executive functions of planning and managing instruction.

Drive the selection model from logistic factors (group size), learner variables (readers versus nonreaders), and task variables (task importance and outcome type), suggesting the media able to deliver the events of instruction that provide the conditions of learning for that outcome.

Have the tutor act as manager of instruction — deciding which events to employ, which to emphasise, and which to assign to the learner's own control, with timing chosen to make each act of learning optimally efficient.

Improve one-way media by building in explicit provisions for learner response and feedback, which also signal when diagnostic testing, remedial instruction, or restudy is needed — a lecturer, televised or live, posing a question after a brief segment, pausing for the viewer to write or think of an answer, then giving feedback, since questions used with live lectures have been found to benefit learning and usually retention.

Use media that play a genuine instructional role and do not compete for attention: avoid gratuitous illustrations and attention-competing combinations (e.g. text plus a graphic), and prefer complementary combinations (e.g. audio plus graphics).

Read a medium's shortfall as a property of the available material rather than of the medium: most available films leave the teacher to inform the objective, guide learning, and give feedback not because film could not carry those events but because those films do not.
Use film for what only film does — portraying theoretical events such as particles in motion, and enlarging, condensing, speeding up, or slowing down observable activities in nature or manufacturing.
Prefer print on paper where printed text is otherwise appropriate for the outcome and the learners, since it is one of the least expensive media.

Write the prescriptions before choosing media to keep the media decision open, since a preselected medium forces the prescriptions to accommodate its limits — and note that substituting recorded for live delivery leaves prescriptions largely unchanged whereas mediating the same lesson as printed text changes them substantially, media decisions mattering most around whether learners are readers and the consequent requirements for visual display, practice, and feedback.
Do not add colour for its own sake: research findings indicate colour does not increase the effectiveness of instruction except where it is an essential feature of what must be learned.
Consider real objects as sometimes the most effective medium, notably for learning motor skills and complex procedures.

Require pictorial motion when the dynamic features of objects are part of the essential content, and value its capacity to display the actions of living beings — particularly humans — realistically, which is of hard-to-overstate importance in motion pictures and television.
Select media able to display a human model and the model's message about personal choices when the outcome is an attitude, which makes pictorial motion of human activity a major consideration.
Use animation or video for complicated manual and motor skills, and for interpretive effects such as slowing, speeding, re-angling, or tracing motion that reveal what is otherwise invisible.

Do not design around learning styles: whether such differences exist and interact with media has not been definitely established, and even if the styles were known it might not be feasible or economical to provide enough parallel media packages per lesson to accommodate them.

Run the practical media checklist — group size, viewing and hearing distance, ease of interruption for responding and feedback, adaptivity to responses, whether the stimulus needs motion, colour, still pictures, or spoken or written words, fixed versus flexible sequence and repeatability, which media carry most of the conditions of learning and instructional events, probable affective impact, obtainability and storability, disruption caused, backup availability, teacher training needs, budget for repairs, and cost against probable effectiveness — and keep a backup plan or alternative lesson, which minimises the damage when equipment fails or a medium proves unsuitable for the group size.

Treat the appeal to individual learning styles as resting on a phrase whose specific meaning is not entirely clear, since research has identified few intellectual and personality characteristics relatable to success with specific forms or media — while allowing that a material may work better for a learner because of matching entering capabilities, fuller provision of the events that individual needs, or design features such as small versus large steps, inductive versus deductive, and concrete versus abstract.
Engage learners in the whole cycle of learning phases even when they have learning-style preferences; do not restrict instruction to a learner's preferred activities.
Reject learning styles wherever it reappears — as a rationale for dual-format presentation, for style-matched paths, or for agent selection — because little evidence supports it.

Apply two remedies for low reading comprehension: write the printed or oral passage low in reading difficulty with familiar words and short sentences, and use pictures and diagrams as far as possible for novel concepts, rules, and procedures, which convey such content to these learners more rapidly and efficiently than verbal expression.

Use the experience-to-symbol scale — from direct purposeful experience through contrived and dramatised experience, demonstrations, study trips, exhibits, television, motion pictures, still pictures, radio and recordings, and visual symbols up to verbal symbols — going as low as needed to ensure learning for the group but as high as possible for efficiency, trading slow-but-sure direct experience against fast-but-risky verbal symbols for weak readers.

Invert the age-media relationship for attitude objectives: a young child who needs direct experience for cognitive learning may acquire an attitude by hearing verbal statements from respected people, while changing an already established attitude may require real-life experiences for children and adults alike — and since attitudes form by conditioning, persuasive communication, and human modeling, different media serve each method.

For an attitude choose motion pictures, slide or videotape presentations, or TV cassettes, because they can picture the situations the attitude applies to and realistically display a human model delivering the message; for verbal information with nonreaders choose audio alone unless visuals would help recall, in which case choose a pictorial medium, since visuals often aid recall by elaborating the information and adding cues.

Analyse cross-domain interactions in attitude learning with audit trails relating the target attitude to the other attitudes, verbal information, and intellectual skills that facilitate it, using the trail as a guide for sequencing the experiences leading to change.

Scope an attitude lesson to an appropriate audience and run it over time with performance, feedback, and assessment recurring weekly rather than concluding in one session, delivering the content through a person who has actually made the choice, is admirable and believable, and describes the shift made, the difference it produced, and the satisfaction obtained.

Do not lean on family-background data for media choice: it is unclear whether such data serve better for checking entering competencies or for selecting media, though indirect implications are likely, such as children of parents who do not or cannot read being less likely to have acquired a love of and skill in reading.

Do not plan a delivery system whose design and development resources are inadequate, since available time, budget, and personnel determine both which media can be developed successfully and which design model and team management system are feasible — and adapt the design model to the project's budget, time, personnel, facilities, equipment, supplies, and the institutional characteristics of both developing and using agencies, with the team leader setting task periods, assigning personnel, and monitoring the plan.

Require media to be acceptable to the users as well as affordable, since attitudes toward media differ between urban and rural populations and among ethnic, socioeconomic, religious, and cultural groups, and some regions lack the technical skills or electric power for broadcast media.

Decide the cost-effectiveness order deliberately: cost may be the overriding factor in one circumstance while in another a required level of effectiveness is fixed first and costs considered after, as when military designers separate the objectives that must be completely mastered at any cost from the less critical ones.

Establish the intended users' status and intentions before selecting media — by visits or questionnaires and perhaps best by making some users members of the design team, which also enhances the effectiveness of the whole design.
Expect experienced designers to perform much of the media analysis in their heads because the steps in the problem solution have become familiar.

Decide assessment, tracking, reporting, compliance, accessibility, access, and security needs early, and compare media alternatives by their fit, constraints, and consequences before fixing a look and feel.

Select media for its contribution to comprehension, emotion, motivation, retention, and quality signaling, then check it against culture, style, cost, equipment, printing, bandwidth, and interaction constraints.

Avoid transplanting a solution from one's own country where it is ill-suited — in the total instructional approach as well as the media — and review translations of materials and even straightforward teacher-guide directions carefully for clarity, since what is perfectly clear to the writer may confuse the reader.

For a motor skill in self-instruction with nonreaders, keep only portable equipment and a training device, since these alone permit the direct practice motor-skill learning requires — and route to the instructor-based situation if neither can supply adequate feedback during practice.

Write modules for affective and motor objectives as readily as for cognitive ones, and in shop or laboratory courses complete all the needed cognitive learning before the skill is practised on the equipment — saving the cost of duplicate machines and avoiding injury and damage by ensuring the trainee knows the safety precautions and correct procedures before gaining access.

Distinguish the three adaptive modes: individualised instruction begins from an analysis of entry skills and prescribes on that basis; self-paced instruction lets the learner take as much time as needed and is generally associated with mastery learning, where achievement rather than time dictates the rate; and adaptive instruction constantly monitors progress and changes the content accordingly, entailing complex record keeping usually facilitated by computers though workable manually for individuals or small groups.

Plan and develop individualised or self-paced instruction more carefully than teacher-based instruction, since immediate teacher help is often unavailable whereas a teacher can fill the gaps in an incomplete lesson plan.

Be precise about what is individualised: self-pacing varies only the rate, with all students using the same materials toward the same teacher-set objectives, whereas student-determined instruction may hand the learner control of objective selection, materials, scheduling, pacing, self-evaluation, and abandonment of an objective.

Understand computer-adaptive instruction as pacing the learner by pretest scores, performance history, and progress through the lesson, customising via learner analysis, alternative presentation strategies, and a knowledge database, typically on expert-system technology — while recognising that expert systems structure knowledge as rules and can learn by asking an expert for a new rule, yet face many barriers to use, not least the complexity of even a relatively simple system.

Expect individualised instruction to provide more frequent feedback and more frequent progress checks than conventional instruction, with the learner setting his own pace as a minimum even where the objectives are required.

Account for the variables besides instructional quality that determine learning — learner perseverance, time allowed as opportunity, subject-specific aptitude, and general ability to understand — each affecting the time a learner needs or actually spends, so that evaluating instruction requires considering motivation and environmental variables such as the opportunity to spend the time needed rather than instructional quality alone.

Distinguish static adaptive control, which branches once from a pretest, from dynamic adaptive control, which assesses continuously and branches immediately, and pick by how much within-lesson variation you expect.

Teach the bottom row of a hierarchy first and then each higher row, allowing options among boxes within a horizontal row but none in proceeding upward when one sequence must serve a whole group — while recognising that a particular student may succeed out of order because she already held some skills or had enough cognitive strategy to discover some rules unaided.
Build the within-lesson elaborative sequence by naming the simplifying and elaborating conditions that generate each successive case of the organizing content.

Treat a hierarchy as implying several possible effective sequences: only the essential-prerequisite relationships must be maintained, and otherwise no particular order is implied, which leaves room to insert instruction from other outcome domains.

Use the hierarchy for diagnosis as well as sequence: any lesson requiring prerequisite skills to be recalled yields diagnostic information, and where mastery is not achieved follow the assessment with assessment of the prerequisites and a relearning loop before the student proceeds.
Sequence major steps by tracing when one step's product becomes another's input, then use the validated sequence as the framework for subordinate-capability analysis.

Map complex target behavior to prerequisites the audience already has, use the hierarchy to expose scope and shared dependencies, cluster reusable prerequisites, and avoid dull bottom-up sequencing unless mastery is genuinely required first.
State explicitly the assumption a hierarchical sequence rests on — that all learners have mastered the entry-level behaviours and start at the same level — rather than letting it stay implicit.

Distinguish a facilitating order, which improves the overall progress of instruction but is optional, from a prerequisite order, which is required; label every sequencing decision as one or the other, and sequence any concept a later explanation depends on before that explanation.

Test selectively by sequencing items along the path hierarchy and probing until the learner fails, then begin instruction at the most subordinate path they cannot perform; hierarchical containment — the longer path holding all steps of the shorter plus more — is what licenses that inference.

Sequence simple-to-complex within a hierarchy, teaching subordinate paths before the superordinate ones that contain them, while recognizing that the order between independent hierarchies is not prescribed and several sequences are equally acceptable.
Recognize that a top-down conceptual sequence and a bottom-up prerequisite hierarchy both run simple-to-complex, so an elaborative sequence does not violate the hierarchical sequence's principles.
Identify a principle's unmastered prerequisites by hierarchical analysis of that principle and teach them immediately before it.

Let learners use their own encoding system rather than prescribing particular codes, since prescription is generally found less successful and what the learner mainly needs beforehand is how to encode — a metacognitive strategy — which is also why no specific prior content implying a sequence can reasonably be recommended for label learning, and why the imagery used may be entirely arbitrary.

Sequence organised knowledge by the existing schemas it can be subsumed under, structuring new information so it builds on what the student already knows — as in correlative subsumption, where material similar to an existing schema is absorbed into it and the schema broadens.
Sequence the individual part skills too where they have prerequisites of their own, as the concrete concept of a correct sighting picture is a valuable subordinate for target shooting.

Attend to every event and how it will be operationalised when designing mediated instruction, since the teacher-led model can be less exact because the teacher fills the gaps — while asking the same planning question in both cases, how will I accomplish this event with these students, and devising another way when the wanted material cannot be found.
Study existing mediated materials for the learning activities they apply to and particularly note the events they do not address, so those events can be planned into the lesson.
Gain attention by presenting an anomaly the learners notice for themselves and then asking what is unusual, rather than by announcing the topic.

Expect learners to question relevance once curiosity is aroused, and recognize that establishing relevance is generally harder than gaining attention: unless job or admission requirements settle it externally, the instructor must connect the objectives to the learners' own interests and motives.

Where attention and relevance are already present, aim only to avoid boredom and preserve the sense of relevance learners arrived with, rather than adding further strategies; for extrinsically motivated learners, produce the expected reward or evidence that this achievement is a step toward it.

Span the hard conditions when eliciting performance on a defined concept — items with no instance, one instance at the start, one embedded, multiple instances, and near-miss forms — rather than only easy positive cases.

Supply in prerequisite recall the specific quantities and conventions the rule operates on — not merely the abstract formula — then push guidance from a single application to a compound case that requires combining results and asking how the answer could be proved, and watch feedback for the specific predictable error rather than only marking answers right or wrong.

State the criterion of an acceptable problem solution in performance terms so competing solutions can be compared, enumerate in prerequisite recall the specific subordinate rules the solution must combine, and restate the problem first in general terms and then with the specific constraining details.

Group objectives and events into instructional activities when planning a multiple-objective lesson, an activity being something the teacher does or has the student do that represents one or more events for one or more objectives — showing a film may both motivate and present content, a team game may both motivate and elicit performance — with a lesson consisting of one or more such activities inside a predetermined framework, usually a fixed period of time.

Build an objectives/time-line matrix listing the objectives vertically in teaching order against a time line, with cells holding the event numbers, then group events across or within objectives into activities — completing the matrix and the lesson-planning sheet simultaneously, with the sheet listing activities rather than bare events.

In tutoring, restate the objective in different terms or demonstrate an instance of the expected performance for flexibility, and omit the event entirely only when the student already knows the objective.

Choose problems with multiple solutions and attitudinal components for discussion groups, presenting ones that capture student interest and emotional involvement to enlist motivation — and expect such a group to depend very largely on students managing the events for themselves, supplying their own recall and their own encoding and problem-solving strategies, with attitude change as a secondary though not less important outcome.

Treat instructional events as analytic categories rather than disjoint blocks of lesson time: one portion of instruction may implement several events at once, and whether a reapplication counts as transfer enhancement or as another elicitation turns on its scale and novelty.

Write motivational objectives naming the student behaviours to be observed, whether cognitive such as a higher expectancy for success midway through, affective such as rating the instruction at least moderately interesting, or psychomotor such as duration of attention, time on task, or participation.

Use placement tests to reveal each student's pattern of mastery and nonmastery in the sequence and so fix the starting point, because even a group that left the previous term with similar capabilities will not all start at the same place — skills are forgotten and new information, skills, and attitudes acquired in between — and the more suitable the provisions made for each learner, the more precise the instruction and the more likely their success.

Build diagnostic tests from the prerequisite skills a learning hierarchy reveals, since a probable reason for falling behind in group instruction is that earlier skills in the sequence were not mastered, and use different methods and materials for the remedial instruction where the original ones already failed that learner.

Adopt the mastery stance: under proper conditions perhaps ninety to ninety-five percent of students can master most objectives to the degree now reached only by good students, so abandon the idea that students merely learn more or less well in favour of finding out why a student fails and remedying it — usually by more time for learning, different media or materials, or diagnosis of the missing prerequisite knowledge or skills.

Make the remedial decision for an intellectual-skill failure by administering a diagnostic test over the subordinate capabilities or by oral testing to find where in the teaching sequence the failure first began — and for a known slow learner use diagnostic tests of subordinate competencies as the performance assessments themselves, so small failures are caught before they accumulate into failures of whole lessons, topics, or courses.

Define mastery for the test and thereby fix the criterion of success for the objective, recording how many students reach it to show whether the instruction met its design objective — a frequently used course criterion being ninety percent of students achieving mastery of ninety percent of the objectives, with other percentages usable and sometimes three criteria set from minimal acceptable success upward.
Keep in mind constantly that learning occurs within individuals even when instruction is delivered to a group, and aim to make each instructional event as effective as possible for every member.

Base diagnosis of entry capabilities on learning hierarchies, using simple tests or probes to reveal specific gaps in enabling skills — a procedure that is not itself an instructional event but makes the design of certain events possible.

Supplement large-group teaching with mastery learning: divide the course into roughly two-week units with clearly defined objectives, test after each unit to diagnose which objectives were and were not acquired, send masters to self-instructional enrichment, and give non-masters small-group study, tutoring, or extra materials with retesting when they feel prepared.

Use start-of-year diagnostic and placement tests to determine which objectives in the ordered sequence each student has already mastered and can recall, fixing the starting point, and update the record of prerequisite mastery by frequent subsequent testing.

Make a module contain or point to everything needed to pass its test — including practice tests by which the student judges readiness and directions for locating and using external materials — so the learner can proceed without another person's direction except when difficulties arise.

Sequence lessons by prerequisites and manageable progression, then use focused entry checks, authentic whole-task and lesson pretests, embedded feedback assessments, and component-plus-integrated posttests to route instruction and verify mastery.

Open a diagnostically designed lesson with an individualized test of key paths, accepting that two learners starting from the same item diverge onto different tests as soon as their performances differ.

Vary the frequency of progress checks with need — less often when a whole group is consistently progressing well and more often when several learners are struggling — since brief checks both assure learners they are progressing and give the teacher dependable information for planning the next steps.

Monitor progress by knowing both what each student is undertaking to learn and how fast and how well he is progressing, counting a module finished only when he has met a minimum standard on a test or other evaluation of its objective.

Settle validity by asking whether the performance required during assessment is the same performance the objective describes, having more than one judge make that judgment and reach consistency — while recognising that this assumes the objective statement itself validly reflects the lesson's purpose, so the consistency of specific objectives with the broader purposes may need rechecking, inconsistencies often surfacing when objectives are turned into tests.

Use the same objective-referenced results to promote students, to drive formative evaluation showing where the course needs revision, and — where the school requires it — to assign grades, since objective-referenced testing serves showing mastery, permitting early diagnosis of failure, supplying data for improving the instruction, and being fair because it measures the very objective the student was told to learn, which is consistent with the honesty of the teacher-learner relation.

Decide feasibility from reports of the difficulties instructors or students had conducting the lesson, but judge effectiveness on a more complex basis — whether materials were used and procedures carried out as intended, what attitudes were incidentally established, and most importantly the extent to which student test performance succeeded.

Use test generically for any procedure that assesses the performance an objective describes — written and oral testing as well as evaluation of student products such as essays, musical productions, models, or works of art.

Use norm-referenced tests only where their properties fit: they compare a student with a group and measure a mixture of objectives over large segments of content, which suits summative assessment over reasonably long periods such as midcourse or end-of-course examinations and gives global assessments across a set of topics.
Follow oral questioning with a test covering the whole lesson or topic, since questioning assesses only a sample of each student's performances rather than the whole repertoire.

Watch for objectives that share a surface performance but belong to different domains — composing and typing a letter requires the problem-solving capability of generating it, whereas typing a letter someone else composed requires only the motor skill — and remember that performances useful in themselves, such as copying, spelling the concept name, or explaining how a concept may be used, need not reflect the objective's intent.

Derive the test situation from the objective's five components, since for many objectives and older learners changing only a few words converts the objective into directions for taking the test — the more closely objectives follow the outline the fewer decisions and directions remain, though objectives and derived items must be restated in simpler terms for young children, and the more incomplete the objective the more must be filled in and the more the construction cautions are needed.
Change the objective itself — before planning instruction and before using it as a lesson objective or as test directions — when writing its test reveals that it needs changing.

Keep the situation, object, tools, constraints, and both verbs congruent between objective and test unless a change is deliberate, since large changes may make the test call for capabilities not yet taught — the worst mismatch being objectives calling for appreciation, teaching delivering facts, and an examination requiring use of concepts and rules, giving maximum incongruence among the three anchor points.

When one objective's solution path is the first step of another's, teach the shorter objective first and use correct performance on its test as the input to testing the longer objective's remaining steps.

Make the test neither easier nor harder than the objective, since the aim is accurately representing it rather than estimating how to make the test sufficiently difficult, and do not seek a wide score range or normal distribution, because the purpose is to discover which objectives each student has learned rather than to discriminate one student from another.

Recognise that grading on a normal curve fixes the academic goals of teachers and students at inappropriately low levels and reduces the motivation of both, and that the practice producing this is group-paced instruction — when pace and mode are both fixed, each student's achievement becomes primarily a function of aptitude, whereas letting mode and rate vary makes it likely more students succeed.

Vary the rate before trying to vary the mode, since it is easier to let learning rate vary than to predict which mode benefits each student and economics forbid a different mode for everyone — modularised individualised instruction largely solving the rate problem and partly the mode problem.

Draw test items from the class of situations the objective's situation component defines, since an objective saying given a verbal statement implies a different item form from one saying given a diagram.

Use multiple items to avoid measurement error from idiosyncratic features of a single one — convention suggesting ten or twenty for an arithmetic rule, while sequential-analysis assumptions permit mastery decisions on as few as three correct items.

Reject a single item as evidence of mastery, since a student may respond correctly from a memorised answer or incorrectly because a particular feature misled him; ask not how many items are correct but whether the number correct dependably indicates mastery, and take three items as a reasonable minimum with two of three correct giving confidence, because two items can yield an uninterpretable half-right result.

Watch what the response mode assumes: pointing and naming assumes only that the oral responses can be made whereas placing printed labels additionally requires that those words can be read — and count a concrete-concept item attained only when the student responds to every instance and to none of the non-instances.

Keep information assessment objective-referenced rather than content-referenced: the aim is to determine whether certain objectives were attained, not whether some content was covered, which requires stating clearly which names, facts, and generalisations must be learned so the core content is distinguished from the incidental information some students may also recall.

Do not make information objectives so exhaustive that no time remains for other domains: deliberately identify the informational outcomes most likely to contribute to attaining objectives in other domains, and do not let the lifelong goal of acquiring masses of information interfere with intellectual skills and problem-solving strategies.

Treat approval-seeking bias as the most serious limitation of attitude questionnaires, for which there appears to be no simple solution despite many investigations — obtaining the best results by first assuring students the assessment is not an adversary process and that they need not report what they think will be approved, with anonymous recording as an additional precaution in group administration, and by specifying the item domain along several dimensions of the situation so the set of personal-action choices is defined.

Set a standard of performance for motor skills rather than a mastery threshold, since standards refer to precision and often speed and both improve with extended practice — raising the standard progressively as practice extends over longer periods.
Define mastery as error-free performance for intellectual skills, motor skills, and information, but not for cognitive strategies and attitudes, where assessment deals with how well or how much.

Test temporal dependability by test-retest separated by days or weeks, asking whether the demonstrated mastery would be the same on another day or was determined by how the student felt, a temporary illness, or an adventitious feature of the testing situation.

Confine standardised tests to summative evaluation of total courses over several years, where they give valuable information about long-term effects, since their items are not derived from particular objectives, are selected to produce the largest possible score variation, correlate rather highly with intelligence, and rarely identify missing subordinate capabilities.

Design around three group sizes — the two-person group enabling tutoring, the small group of roughly three to eight favouring discussion and interactive recitation in which members affirm or correct each other, and the large group of fifteen or more where lecture and individual recitation predominate — while treating the boundaries as soft, since a group of eight to fifteen may be handled by discussion, lecture, or subdivision, and very large groups differ mainly in logistics such as seating and acoustics.

Analyse group instruction by asking what arrangements are possible and most effective for each group size rather than by mode label, since what matters for the effect on learning is the variation in what is actually done within a lecture, discussion, or recitation.

Treat group size as an important determinant of the learning environment because it fixes which interaction patterns are attainable — two-way between teacher and student in a two-person group, mutual with one student at a time while others merely receive in recitation, among students as well as with the teacher in interactive recitation and discussion, and one-way in the lecture — and those patterns may influence outcomes through how students perceive them.

Form small groups by dividing a class so that students at approximately the same point in learning a subject are taught together, since presenting print to pupils still struggling with oral language accomplishes nothing and forcing fluent readers through readiness exercises wastes their time.

Understand small-group instruction as multistudent tutoring — tutorial methods applied to single students by taking turns, managing the events for each individual but with evident loss of flexibility and precision.

Alternate small-group learning guidance between whole-group address and student-by-student tutoring as judgment dictates, the tutorial mode costing more time the larger the group while the event's function stays the same.

Judge varied examples and spaced reviews in a small group by averaging the group's performance rather than with tutorial precision, using the varied examples given to different students to serve retention and transfer on the assumption that uncalled students respond covertly — and for older students and adults treat the conduct of discussion itself as a major means of enhancing retention and transfer.
Divide a large group into small groups for part of its meeting time, or into smaller classes following a lecture, as a simple scheme for regaining precision in controlling the instructional events.

Expect group size to limit the effectiveness of the events: attention can be precisely managed in a two-person group but only loosely in a large one, the semantic encoding a lecturer suggests will be modified by each learner's own strategies, and while correct-or-incorrect feedback reaches a large group about as precisely as one student, feedback explaining the causes of error necessarily varies with the individual.
Expect stimulus presentation to lose almost nothing in a small group compared with tutoring, since emphasis by voice change or by making features prominent in pictures serves the whole group at once.

Accept that a small-group teacher trades a precise determination of outcomes for a probabilistic estimate — calling on one or two students and assuming the learning was equally effective for the rest, with feedback precise only for the student called upon and merely probable for those who responded covertly.

Accept that large-group instruction is a probabilistic strategy — effective on the average but not ensurable for each individual — because the teacher's cues for timing and emphasis come from many sources rather than one student and because readiness, motivation, the appropriateness of the suggested encoding, and access to relevant strategies all vary across the group.

Give prerequisite recall in large groups a great deal of design attention and use devices such as spot quizzes for the whole group, because calling on one or two students leaves the rest — many hoping to avoid being called — without the necessary retrieval, those students will probably not learn the objective, and the cumulative effects are quite serious.

Treat student response as a low-precision event in a large group — a tutor expects several performances per lesson while the class teacher calls on one or two and covert responding by the rest is not highly likely — and use frequent quizzes to compensate, knowing even daily quizzes cannot approximate the tutor's frequency, and that because feedback is tied to performance it occurs rarely and tends to be confined to tests covering many objectives at once.

Expect the effects of the necessary events on individual learners to fall from near certainty to lower probabilities as group size grows, so that outcomes come to depend increasingly on the learner's own self-instructional strategies — and expect diagnosis of entering capabilities to be the hardest thing to manage at scale, mattering most for prerequisite recall since students cannot recall what they never learned, with weak control producing a cumulative deficit.

Expect attention to be less of a problem in an individualised program, since each student is eager to begin a new objective after succeeding on the previous one and it is rare that more than one at a time is not actually working — and maintain it by the built-in cycle of presenting a problem, requiring a response, and providing feedback, allowing children who tire to switch activity, from which they usually return without prompting.

Expect a teacher to know more about each student's progress under a well-designed individual plan than under group instruction, one reason being that in individualised instruction every student responds to every question.

Expect a different individual pattern of prerequisite capabilities for each student — twenty different patterns among twenty students — which a tutorial handles easily and a class teacher finds a considerable challenge, making group size matter most for diagnosis of immediate prerequisites.

Exploit tutoring's decisive advantage on prerequisite recall: having diagnosed what is missing, fill the gaps first and only then require recall, which does much to ensure learning proceeds smoothly — and choose the number and varied features of concept instances to fit the student's need as shown by his immediately preceding performance.

Use questioning of each student in turn to diagnose attainment of the immediate prerequisites, which approaches the precision of the two-person group and is an important feature distinguishing small-group from large-group instruction — and note that a recall question put to one student also reminds the others of material already available to them.

Import the three tutoring-derived events into groups of about thirty to accomplish much of what tutoring gives — ensuring review of prerequisites, employing student participation as part of learning guidance, and enhancing retrieval cues by elaborating concepts and rules through explanations — with the underlying confirmation being that mastery procedures work particularly where they inform students of correct and incorrect performances and permit restudy until success.

Use peer and older-student tutoring where a teacher cannot be the second person, since such arrangements succeed and learning gains are reported about as often for the tutors as for the students — and recognise that in individualised systems teachers act as tutors when they follow a diagnostic prescription with oral instruction, so individualised instruction frequently combines self-instruction with two-person tutoring.

Do not credit tutoring's advantage to individual attention itself: the evidence indicates tutoring works best when the instruction it makes possible is highly systematic and that the freedom of the two-person setting produces poor results if it leads to sloppiness — and the advantages yield favourable achievement often but not always, so the mode alone guarantees nothing.

Shift the tutoring balance with maturity: the same steps apply to older students and adults except that greater dependence is placed on the student instituting the events himself, and university-level tutoring is usually almost entirely self-instruction with the tutor confined to assessing performance and suggesting retention and transfer means.

Give teachers a delivery system designed to adjust instruction to individual needs rather than merely asserting the determination to do so, since dividing time between individuals and groups leaves some pupils unoccupied and unable to progress — and recognise the second solution to the two-sigma problem alongside tutoring: materials that address the student directly without depending on a teacher and are tailored to individual needs.

Recognise that discussion depends heavily on the students' own self-instructional strategies, since adult members largely decide for themselves what they want to learn and select it from what they hear or say.

Recognise discussion as interactive communication in which one student speaks at a time to the whole group, the order of speaking is not predetermined, and students often respond to each other rather than to the teacher.
Set discussion objectives from the three kinds it suits — subject-matter mastery, attitude formation, and problem solving — expecting a class discussion to pursue more than one of them.

Do not conclude that individualised instruction suits only mature learners: because each lesson's appropriateness is assured and the instruction precise, it may be needed more by less mature learners, while adults and college students are expected to discern appropriate materials and supply many events themselves.

Run an issue-oriented discussion by opening with an incident illustrating the issue, soliciting and commenting on opinions, and progressively sharpening and clarifying the issue with different examples and statements from various members, often aiming at a consensus no member majorly disagrees with.

Read an attitude-forming discussion as learning guidance in which members and leader act as multiple human models, followed by the individual's choice of action as performance and by group consensus as feedback.

Accept that a suggested encoding in a large group can be made generally effective for the group as a whole but cannot be adapted to individual members as it can in smaller groups, and likewise that varied examples and spaced reviews can only follow what works best on average.

Do not ask a lecture to secure prerequisite recall or elicit performance with corrective feedback, since the lecturer can remind and encourage but cannot ensure recall or require performance — and when the lecture is the sole mode the student must institute those events himself, with quizzes and tests overcoming this only slightly because they are typically infrequent and coarse-grained.

Use a recitation question deliberately for the event it is meant to serve at that moment — stimulating recall of a prerequisite, eliciting performance, guiding encoding in the manner of guided discovery, or asking for application examples that supply cues for recall and transfer.

Face the unresolvable choice in large-class recitation honestly — calling on the well-prepared neglects those less able to guide their own learning while calling on the less able bores those who have already learned — since in practice the events reach only a few students on any occasion and students all too frequently learn to play the game of avoiding being called upon, which is the wrong game for learning the objectives.

Provide the total support system individualisation needs, since early experiments failed largely for want of it — no design technology and no agency developing and diffusing the special materials — which left too great a burden on the teacher.

Build an individualised delivery system that assesses entry skills, finds each student's starting point in a carefully sequenced series of objectives, provides alternative materials and media including print and nonprint choices, lets students learn at their own rates, and provides frequent convenient progress checks so no one becomes bogged down with cumulative failures — accomplished in part by designing materials that carry more of the support for more of the events, so every pupil can work each day within his own needs, capacities, prerequisites, and rate.

Locate an individualised program's strongest feature in the materials rather than the teacher — the appropriate and precise management of presenting the stimulus, eliciting the response, and providing feedback — while locating the teacher's primary strengths in managing and monitoring the whole system and ensuring personal guidance is available when the materials and tests fail for an individual learner.

Name the standing problems of individualised instruction as the development of materials and the maintenance of the system, recognising that new technologies may demand an entirely new teacher role — instructional designer-developer — for which conventional lecture-and-discussion training does not prepare teachers, and that ease of operating the equipment is not the bottleneck since the difficulty lies in training teachers how best to use it.
Expect proved effectiveness not to be enough to sustain an instructional system: three nationally diffused individualised systems declined or were discontinued when their funding ceased.
Expect formative evaluation to expose practical infeasibility as well as ineffectiveness, and let the specific difficulty decide the remedy — a simple substitution, a rewrite, or abandonment.

Expect an innovation to persist only when it has an identifiable support group and constituency and can be monitored cost-effectively; several prominent instructional innovations failed to persist for want of these.

Adopt rather than rebuild where a school's objectives coincide closely with an available system, since repeating an instructional design already carefully done is wasteful — the options being adoption with few modifications, heavy modification, purchasing some components and developing others, or building from scratch.
Design instruction as a problem-centered cycle of four phases (activation, demonstration, application, integration) rather than over-investing in the demonstration phase alone.
Adapt generic design practices coherently to the chosen learning theory, goals, learners, and environment.
Use an instructional-design model as a learning scaffold, while allowing evidence-informed iteration, concurrency, and contextual adaptation as design expertise grows.

Clarify what you expect a theory to provide before adopting it, because education and training have repeatedly adopted allegedly good innovations without evaluating their contribution to teaching and learning processes and outcomes.
Expect great variation in the specific classroom application of the same individualised system across schools even where all are directed toward the same purposes.

Arrange the individualised classroom so learners at very different points work simultaneously on their own objectives — some on perceptual discriminations with programmed material, some on naming by machine, some in a small teacher-led group, some with recorded support, some testing or self-checking — so that slow learners experience success rather than failure during the hour.

Individualise selectively rather than wholesale: a school may individualise only some subjects while teaching others conventionally, and schedule common activities where all pupils can participate at a shared level.
Expect the composition of small groups to shift constantly under individually paced programs, since five students at the same point one day may not be at a common point on another.

Expect an individualised system to start rough and improve with experience — slack time while pupils wait and a teacher harassed by too much to track at first, then a more skilled independent learner and a calm, easy pacing — and use flexible scheduling across a whole school so a student may concentrate heavily on one subject one day and range across many the next, relieving schooling of much of the boredom of an identical daily schedule.

Make definite administrative arrangements to ensure randomness when assigning students to classrooms, since it cannot be assumed, and treat matching schools on student aptitude as the alternative — with all such designs needing careful management for a valid comparison.
Ask each participating district to supply comparison groups as equivalent as possible in the characteristics of both teachers and pupils.

Differentiate by subject how the objectives are individualised: reading and mathematics often adopt a single sequence for all with materials and pace varying, whereas science and social studies often set core objectives for all plus enrichment objectives chosen by student interest.

Scale the objective-informing event to the structure of the material: it matters less for highly structured material where the objective is often evident, and more for loosely structured material where the student needs the objective to decide which portions are most relevant for selective reading and review.
Permit learner choice of objectives in schools mainly for enrichment exercises and only after the required core skills are mastered, often offering that choice as an incentive to learn the core.
