Expect an individualised system to free teacher time for individual pupils once they have learned the pretest-learn-posttest procedures and how to find materials, while recognising the teacher is not idle and students may have to wait, turning to enrichment activities meanwhile.

Use individualisation to protect slow learners from inappropriate tasks and hence from failure and to free fast learners from the boredom of unnecessary instruction — but hold the teacher responsible for seeing that the arrangements are suitable for each learner.

Let learners self-test with an answer key for some objectives, but have the teacher make the assessment at least periodically — and more often than in large-group instruction — using the time freed from other instructional events.

Spend the teacher's day in an individualised system on advance planning sessions with one to six students, reviewing progress and test results, giving next assignments, individual diagnosis and remedial instruction, schedule changes, and small-group sessions for students at approximately the same point — with students and aides maintaining the materials files once taught the system and aides administering and scoring tests, keeping records, helping students find materials, tutoring, and backing up the teacher to implement the plans agreed between teacher and student.
Reserve the looser individualisation varieties for selected groups, since they place greater responsibility on students to provide the instructional events and permit greater freedom over objectives.

Scale the unit of management to learner age — single objectives for young children, since one may be masterable in an hour or less, and week-or-two modules with evaluation over a cluster of objectives for older students — decreasing the frequency of formal progress checks and of responding with feedback as learners mature, by design of the materials or assembly of the module.

Show a child's module both the target objective and the prerequisite capabilities, as a list or a learning hierarchy, plus a suggested sequence of activities derived from the enabling objectives and making provision for retention and transfer — and design the total menu of modules to meet the needs of fast learners as well as slow.

Compose a module of teaching-learning units each carrying a single objective, opening each with the learning objective, then the learning activities and references, self-test questions, and discussion questions — using pictorial techniques in the early grades — and on completing the activities the student takes the performance test, moving to a new unit if satisfactory and receiving additional work if not.

Provide four management capabilities for individualised instruction: a way to index and store modules, a way to schedule modules for each learner, a way to monitor pupil progress, and a way to assess performance.
Account for differences in learner readiness, pace, and need instead of forcing an identical amount and schedule of content on everyone.

Provide several versions of a module where it is worthwhile — one with simpler vocabulary, one with shorter sentences, one pairing an outline or advance organiser with a technically complex presentation — while treating the size of the advantage against cost as an open economic question needing research.

Give feedback after small increments of study rather than waiting for a test, for young learners and lengthy modules, since that is a built-in feature of text-based and computer-programmed instruction — while for a brief module, or where the learner typically succeeds, a parallel form of the formal test can supply feedback after learning is completed.

Devise some self-testing with corrective feedback for every module, which enhances learning and saves the teacher's time for individual remedial teaching when all other means fail — a valuable activity for which teachers have too little time under conventional group instruction — with the added bonus of time to guide thinking and give individual feedback when most needed.

Intermingle testing with instruction so a learner advances to the next path only after its prerequisites are mastered, and when they still fail after instruction repeat at a finer level of atomicity with step-level feedback, restarting from the last path performed successfully.

Base adult unit evaluation on the appropriateness of the procedures employed, competence in reporting and interpreting data, and ability to defend a rationale for the completed work — supported en route by advisor feedback on draft plans and preliminary reports and by direct instruction on subordinate capabilities such as writing and finding sources.

Undertake formative evaluation while the unit is being developed to provide evidence on feasibility and effectiveness for revision, seeking it from observers, teachers, and students; and undertake summative evaluation once the program is developed, seeking mainly student performance measured on the capabilities the program was intended to establish.

Store each student's prior study, progress, and performance record in a computer-supported system that prints daily information on which objectives were completed and which activities begun, since that record is the essential information base for planning individual programs.

Keep the material for a single objective either physically separate or clearly identified and indexed to match its objective and test, with a system by which student, teacher, and aides can locate it quickly and a numbering scheme convenient for planning, record keeping, locating, and storing.

Use a per-student planning sheet where students have some freedom to choose objectives, and a single class sheet for planning, monitoring, and record keeping where all start at the first module and progress as far as time permits.

Budget for maintenance as a standing task — keeping a sufficient stocked supply of each module, restocking expendable portions after each use, and cross-referencing new material to objectives and test items — since it is this maintenance that sometimes appears to spell the downfall of individualised instruction, with lack of it a probable major factor in past discontinuations despite adequate development funding.

Evaluate a product against a criterion sheet listing the features to look for, with points per feature or a count of satisfactory features, rather than by a single overall judgment — which improves the evaluation and shows the student where improvement is needed — and give the same sheet to the student at the onset of instruction, where it tells him what is expected, suggests how it may be done, and states how the product will be judged.

Cover the full range when evaluating a new educational product — need, market, field-trial performance, consumer appropriateness, comparison with competitors, long-term performance, process fidelity, side effects, causation, statistical and educational significance, costs and cost effectiveness, and extended support — recording the judgment on each factor on a profile that then supports a systematic overall judgment of appropriateness and worth.
Plan both formative evaluation from learner results during development and summative evaluation of impact with cost-benefit at the end, since feature review is otherwise the only quality signal.

Use oral evaluation where depth matters more than standardisation, since it often probes more deeply and can be combined with planning the next work or the remedial work needed, making it convenient and effective with an individual student.

Administer a brief diagnostic test when a student hits a difficulty, to show which prerequisite skills and information were inadequately learned or forgotten and therefore which next or review assignment will re-establish the necessary competence.
Assess attitudes such as cooperation, helping, and control of aggressive acts by teacher checklists completed at periodic intervals, and broader citizenship attitudes by questionnaires.
Expect computer-assisted instruction to be at least as effective as other delivery modes, on the weight of most research.

Reconstruct teacher training curricula alongside any advanced technological solution if it is to have lasting effects on instruction, and temper optimism with the record: the history of technological solutions to educational problems gives no grounds for unusual optimism, what should be emphasised is that the technology has been proved effective, leaving cost of access and maintenance as the remaining problem.

Treat a claim that a new technology will revolutionise or replace existing education as unproven until evidence is shown: film, radio, educational television, and computer-based programmed instruction each produced the same promise-implement- disappoint cycle, and current claims for games and simulations do not yet have strong research support.

Build more of the needed instructional events and conditions of learning into the materials themselves, since that is what makes modules more distinctly self-instructional than conventional lessons — and expect the teacher's role to shift correspondingly from provider of information toward counselling, evaluating, monitoring, and diagnosing.

Include in every module at minimum a performance objective, a set of materials and learning activities whether self-contained or external, a method for self-evaluation of mastery, and a provision for the teacher to verify the learning outcome.
Make self-directed learning products supply the explanation, remediation, and motivation that an unavailable instructor would otherwise provide.

Deliver a discovery approach through the same instructional events as an expository one, changing the stimulus material so it withholds the relationship while keeping the learning guidance largely the same.

Treat an advance organizer — an introduction, an objectives statement, or self-instructional learning hints — as a cue presented ahead of the discriminative stimuli whose purpose is to direct attention across a whole lesson to multiple stimuli, cues or responses, while recognizing that whether its prospective placement adds effectiveness is an open empirical question.
Do not leave evaluation planning to the end, since designing the evaluation requires the same instructional-planning principles used throughout the design process.

Treat evaluation as a continuing process in which information is first delineated, then obtained, then provided, with the primary purpose of guiding decision making — each stage guiding a different decision: context evaluation determining problems and unmet needs for planning, input evaluation weighing alternative solutions' strengths and feasibility for structuring, process evaluation covering the processes actually set in motion for implementing, and product evaluation assessing how well the course works for the decision to continue, drop, or modify.
Do not treat instructional design as one-way application of psychology. Learning, instruction, and assessment inform each other reciprocally, and theory must be revised by incoming evidence.

Keep development procedures — what the designer should do and in what order — distinct from instructional strategies, which state what the instruction will be like; a top-down design procedure says nothing about the resulting instruction.

Make an evaluation answer three questions: to what extent the stated objectives have been met, in what ways and to what degree the unit is better than the one it supplants, and what additional possibly unanticipated effects it has had and whether these are better or worse.

Plan an evaluation by answering what programme is to be evaluated and what population it serves, what the audience's main concerns are, how the information will be used, what type of study will be conducted, and what questions will be addressed.

Add a goal-free pass that examines the effects of the innovation and assesses their worth whatever they are, rather than confining the study to the stated objectives — so that a change such as teacher attitude counts as one of the effects rather than merely an unanticipated outcome — treating it as a valuable supplement to goal-based evaluation rather than a substitute, with formative evaluation serving development decisions and summative providing a basis for accountability.

Undertake summative evaluation when development is in some sense completed rather than ongoing, to permit conclusions about how well the instruction worked and let schools decide about adoption — addressing the summed effects of a set of lessons, with individual lessons evaluated as components rather than separate entities though the evidence may still reveal defects for the next revision.
Localise a shortfall by examining where the mistakes cluster, since errors concentrated on one component point to the subordinate objective that needs revising or a lesson that needs adding.
Run formative evaluation in three stages, each a tryout with a different sample of potential students representative of the target audience.

Have the evaluator sit with one student and watch performance closely in one-to-one testing, with a subject-matter expert thoroughly acquainted with the objectives and performance indicators addressing the validity of objectives and the accuracy and clarity of materials and items — surfacing errors in estimating entry capabilities, lack of clarity in the instruction, unclear test questions and directions, and inappropriate expectations of outcomes.

Accept that every evaluation presents different circumstances forcing compromises — inadequate outcome measures, difficulty achieving equivalence, events affecting one site and not others — and treat judging the severity of these and how they must be taken into account as part of the evaluator's job in reaching convincing evidence.

Analyze learner-by-item-by-objective performance across pretest, rehearsal, and posttest, separating learners by entry readiness and verifying delayed retention when guided practice may mask missing prerequisites.

Frame the summative decision as whether the new course is better than the one it replaced and should therefore be adopted, letting considerations other than effectiveness such as cost decide if it is merely no better — and build the adoption case from several strands at once: objectives met, examination scores against the prior year, student attitude, teacher-reported working conditions, and cost no greater than the old course.

Establish that the new unit met its own objectives as a minimal condition of any summative study, since failure to meet them affects the conclusions drawable from any comparison — and always explore whether the instruction had unanticipated effects, since a topic teaching one subject may affect attitudes in an unrelated area.

Interpret summative measures primarily by comparison with similar measures from an alternative mode of instruction — usually the unit being replaced, sometimes two new units against each other — which requires data-collection methods able to demonstrate that all other things are equal, by no means an easy thing to do.

Control or otherwise account for the setting factors other than the instruction before drawing valid conclusions about instructional effectiveness, since those factors also affect the capabilities the evaluation measures.
Refine an instructional goal from the verified problem, need, context, resources, and an explicit account of the new capability that contributes to the broader outcome.

Confirm the target audience and define whether performance is independent or collaborative, supervised or field-based, and supported by memory or tools before deciding which capabilities instruction must include.

Assess the process variables — whether the specified questioning occurred, the prescribed sequence was followed, the specified feedback was consistently given — rather than assuming the designer's intentions were carried out, since designers of individualised programmes have frequently found the specified operations not executed as intended, and this matters particularly on a first tryout.
Provide the action that ensures the programme operates as planned, such as training teachers in the required operations, while recognising those efforts are not always fully successful.
Assess process variables by systematic classroom observation performed by an observer rather than the teacher, using a checklist or observation schedule normally designed specially for that study.

Distinguish support from process variables: support variables — classroom and library materials, a quiet place to study, classroom climate, parental reinforcement of homework — do not directly influence the process of learning but determine the general environmental conditions and opportunities during the times when process variables act, so a process variable can be fully satisfied while a support variable still differs.

Exploit the fact that process variables are more amenable to direct control than support or aptitude variables — a noisy environment may be unchangeable, but teachers found not to be using the specified operations can be instructed so the next trial starts with a desirable set — and demonstrate equivalence of process variables before attributing unanticipated outcomes to the programme, since favourable attitudes may stem from one teacher's modelling rather than from the instruction.

Contrast the process variables under study deliberately between groups and verify the contrast by classroom observation, holding other process variables equivalent by using the same teachers for both groups.

Demonstrate that the two groups were equivalent to begin with before making any comparison, equivalence in aptitude being most likely where successive classes in the same school drawn from the same neighbourhood serve as comparison groups.

Demonstrate or statistically handle equivalence on support variables even within one school, since two aptitude-equivalent classes can differ in classroom climate, in whether the teacher is liked or disliked, and in how many students seek new learning opportunities.

Read the comparison pattern strictly: where the experimental group's aptitude exceeds the control's, most if not all of the outcome difference is attributable to aptitude and the instruction's effect cannot be expected to show at all; where only support or only process variables differ, the difference may be due to the instruction, to that variable, or to both in unknown proportion, so no attribution is warranted; and only where aptitude, support, and process have all been shown equivalent can the difference be attributed to the instruction itself — which is the situation summative studies aim for.

Prefer randomisation for control because it handles not only the specific variables identified but also others not singled out for measurement because their influence is unknown — while accepting that it is usually hard to arrange, since schools do not customarily draw students randomly from a community or assign them randomly to classes or teachers, so aptitude, support, and process variables must usually be identified and measured instead, or equivalence established statistically.

Use socioeconomic status as a correlated stand-in for aptitude only where direct measures are initially unavailable across participating schools, and verify later by administering standardised aptitude and readiness tests.

Compare this year's experimental class with last year's class under the previous program only where the school's entering classes have been shown to have essentially the same aptitude and socioeconomic status year after year.

Skip individual measurement of support variables only when the same facilities and the same teachers serve both groups and student socioeconomic status is equivalent, since the school and home support variables can then be assumed equivalent.
Require, when two courses are to be evaluated to determine which is better, control over the other variables so that ideally everything is equivalent except the instructional programs themselves.

Activate relevant prior experience as the foundation for new knowledge by directing learners to recall, relate, describe, or apply it; a simple recall of information or an information-oriented pretest is a weak activator.
When learners lack relevant prior experience, provide concrete relevant experience to serve as a foundation before introducing the new material.
Pretraining principle: teach the names and characteristics of the key concepts before the lesson that shows the process or procedure, which redistributes essential processing to an earlier stage.
Pretrain the example's cover content or pick a context already familiar to learners, since knowledge of the example content correlates with acquiring the target skill.
Demonstrate at the portrayal level: show specific examples and cases, not information alone. Examples outperform information alone, and examples combined with practice outperform practice alone.

Make the demonstration consistent with the learning-outcome type (examples/nonexamples for concepts, demonstrations for procedures, visualizations for processes, modeling for behavior), and apply this consistency check first: if the presentation is inconsistent with the goal, learner guidance and media are moot.

Guide the demonstration: direct learners to the relevant information, use multiple representations, explicitly direct learners to compare them (mere presentation of alternatives is not enough), and fade attention-focusing guidance as instruction progresses.
Build a use-procedure presentation as a general description of the process, then demonstrations with specific objects, then performance by the learner on a similar but different object or materials.

Recognize that a demonstration may deliberately carry more motivational strategies than a real application needs, and defer final selection until the lesson is placed in its broader course and unit context.

Support integration and transfer: give learners opportunities to publicly demonstrate their new skill, to reflect on/discuss/defend it, and to create, invent, and explore personal uses of it; rely on the durable motivation of visible progress rather than on glitz, animation, or games.
Motivate and support transfer through an authentic product, audience, or example that gives the capability learner-relevant purpose without distorting the goal or excluding intended learners.

Use the five first principles as a cross-theory completeness checklist: they recur across diverse instructional-design theories (which differ mainly in vocabulary and emphasis), every reviewed theory implements some and none contradicts them, so a design missing a principle signals a likely gap. The set is not claimed exhaustive.

Require both criteria of a design principle before recommending it: theory-grounded (derived from an explicit account of how people learn) and evidence-based (supported by empirical research). Say which criterion is missing when only one holds.

In whole-task practice, use just-in-time information presentation for the recurrent (consistent) aspects and elaboration for the non-recurrent (variable) aspects, keeping information presentation subordinate to and integrated with the practice.
Treat collaboration as one way to implement activation and integration, not as a separate first principle of instruction.
Integrate design and development for a small unified team; separate their iterative cycles when scale, specialists, programming, contracting, or organizational gates make integration impractical.
Compare viable delivery options and combine media and teaching methods according to effectiveness, feasibility, and cost.
Do not justify an e-learning investment by its delivery medium; justify it by the instructional methods embedded in the course, because methods rather than media cause learning.
Learn a design model through a small authentic project and use it as a scaffold until experience supports responsible adaptation.
Preserve a systematic model's logical sequence as a novice scaffold while building iteration into every step and permitting experienced adaptation to project constraints.

Match project ambition to available content, design, technology, delivery, and teamwork capability; let novices learn the process in a familiar domain while experienced designers bridge unfamiliar domains through collaboration and content learning.
Apply explicit criteria and rubrics to intermediate design products and revise them before downstream work compounds their defects.
Delay summative judgment until formative revision is complete, then test whether instruction solved the original problem and transferred to the intended setting.
Conduct independent summative evaluation only after formative revision meets design standards, testing problem resolution, transfer, and value across intended contexts.
Choose instructor-led, mediated, individual, or group delivery from the learning problem and required instructional conditions, not from a preset delivery preference.
Apply pretraining to the learning environment itself, orienting learners to the delivery platform before the instructional content begins.
Use a multidisciplinary team when the project requires several specialties and manage collaboration as part of integrating their contributions.
Assemble multidisciplinary design expertise when project scope requires content, technology, evaluation, and management capabilities that one specialist cannot supply.

Apply four enablers to online collaboration: interdependence via complex-enough assignments, right-sized teams, and incentives rewarding all members' learning; ill-structured cases for groups of three to five; guided designs such as structured controversy; and clear roles and objectives.
Master the full design process before abbreviating it; under routine time constraints, apply it fully to high-value units and select relevant steps elsewhere with informed judgment.
Diagnose performance with open-minded causal inquiry, contrary evidence, direct observation, records, and the perspectives of people inside the work context.

Trace a voiced problem to an organizational outcome, quantify desired-versus-actual result and job-performance gaps, separate controllable factors, and document causal evidence and candidate solutions.
Narrow an organizational problem through performance analysis, needs assessment, and relevant job or task analysis before finalizing the instructional goal.

Diagnose performance with critical distance, multiple perspectives, direct evidence, contrary evidence, and a measurable chain from organizational outcomes through job standards to controllable causes.
Use an explicitly scoped interim goal when one instructional intervention cannot appropriately or feasibly close the entire performance gap.
Match intervention scope to the verified gap: split an oversized goal, extend an undersized goal only with coherent adjacent skills, and do not default to a full course.
Begin detailed goal analysis only when the goal is behaviorally clear and narrow enough for the intended instructional duration.
Establish a need only as a comparably measured gap between desired and actual status; if no gap exists, do not create instruction on that basis.
Permit an explicitly interim instructional goal when constraints make complete closure of a verified performance gap infeasible.

Diagnose whether people cannot perform or can perform but do not; use instruction for missing ability, investigate causes and noninstructional interventions for performance gaps, and keep only goal-related behavior gaps in scope.
Operationalize a vague goal by generating observable positive and negative demonstrations, reaching stakeholder consensus, and testing whether the revised performance preserves the original intent.

Operationalize a vague goal by eliciting observable success behaviors from several knowledgeable contributors, selecting the best indicators, and checking that they jointly preserve the goal's intent.
Iteratively approve and revise a goal only when it is behaviorally clear, feasible, accepted by decision makers, and persuasively linked to a documented organizational gap or opportunity.
Operationalize an ambiguous or value-laden goal with positive and negative behavioral examples, stakeholder review, and enough refinement that independent designers interpret success consistently.
Confirm a real audience, representative tryout access, content stability, expertise, staffing, technology, time, budget, and delivery capacity before committing to development.

Launch authentic projects through a credible example and learner participation, investigate audience and product possibilities before fixing the plan, expose team plans to stakeholder critique, and plan transfer beyond the project.

Make sponsor obligations for expert access, stakeholder feedback, content participation, and acceptance explicit, and make development-team obligations for iterative design, production, quality, testing support, management, and post-acceptance correction equally explicit.
Before adding curriculum, inspect existing learning opportunities and triangulate the gap with learners, faculty, and external practitioners.

After analysis identifies training as viable, triangulate desired and actual performance with experts, records, observation, stakeholder inquiry, and direct assessment, then express the gap as both an operational standard and an instructional goal.
Corroborate curriculum gaps across existing offerings and multiple stakeholder groups, characterize audience variation, and match the instructional unit's size to the bounded verified need.
Ground new learning in the learner's current knowledge, capability, real situations, and recognizable performance gap, and supply missing terminology or prerequisites before relying on them.
Use rapid prototyping when instruction must evolve alongside a new product and waiting for stable, detailed performance documentation would impose unacceptable delay.
Use rapid prototyping and continuous access to emerging product knowledge when training and a new product must be developed concurrently without stable documentation.

Select a prototyper for rapid construction, listening, synthesis, design judgment, and willingness to discard; allow exploratory shortcuts that would be unacceptable in production only when they preserve the tested behavior.

Give a small prototyping unit a short interruption-free build interval and a preset reassembly time; use parallel prototype teams only when an experienced group can coordinate alternatives without fragmenting understanding.
Accept alternate wording or decomposition only when it preserves the complete, essential performance and its required sequence.
Give verbal information an explicit conceptual or spatial organizing scheme when the material has no natural chronology.
Provide repeated physical practice for psychomotor outcomes so learners can calibrate force, timing, coordination, and movement accuracy.
Teach motor skills through visual demonstration of sequence and timing, part-to-whole integration for complex performance, and repeated practice with immediate corrective feedback.
Choose between original development and existing materials by comparing their alignment to outcomes with available development resources.
Treat revision as continuous reassessment throughout design and evaluation, not as a single terminal activity.
Learn the complete systematic process before selectively abbreviating it, so constraints are handled through informed judgment rather than omission by habit.
Treat curricula, standards, expert content, and mandates as evidence to validate against current needs, not automatic proof that a content deficit exists.

Begin performance improvement without presuming instruction, and use proportionate front-end analysis to distinguish capability deficits from accountability, incentive, tool, process, and culture causes.
Observe the actual setting and consult frontline practitioners before prescribing training, distinguishing capability gaps from time, support, resource, workflow, and implementation constraints.
Map each verified cause to a feasible, cost-effective remedy, coordinate remedies for interacting causes, and evaluate initial changes long enough before escalating.

Build and validate a current job-task inventory from observation and incumbent reports, prioritize tasks by prevalence, demand, criticality, and difficulty, and reserve detailed decomposition for high-priority work.
Avoid extensive development for rapidly expiring content unless a critical short-term need justifies the investment.
Schedule post-release update iterations when content, context, technology, or field evidence is likely to shorten the product's useful life.
Let the eventual performance context shape strategy, including access to aids, supervision, collaborators, and opportunities for repeated authentic practice.
Classify a goal as psychomotor only when nontrivial physical execution must be learned and practiced.
Represent verbal-information goals as meaningfully sequenced topic clusters rather than procedural flows.
Analyze an attitudinal goal according to the observable behavior that expresses the choice—procedural flow for intellectual or psychomotor action and topic clusters for verbal demonstration.
Structure summative evaluation as detached expert judgment followed by contextual impact analysis, using an independent evaluator when available and qualified.
Share congruence findings with accountable decision makers and let the verified fit among need, audience, and resources determine whether summative evaluation should continue.
Screen instruction first for congruence with organizational needs, content completeness against validated analysis, and strategy fit to outcomes and transfer before funding an impact study.
Test adoption fit against current organizational goals and job needs, participant characteristics, and total acquisition, implementation, maintenance, facility, and equipment demands.
Test transfer feasibility by checking job aids and guidance, worksite-compatible technology, realistic simulation of critical conditions, and compatible equipment, supervision, and environments.
Give a qualified content expert validated goals and skill frameworks as explicit review standards, converting them into structured coverage criteria rather than requesting an unbounded opinion.
Judge content separately for accuracy, completeness, job relevance, assessment coverage, currency, sequence, prerequisite fit, learner congruence, and cultural and accessibility appropriateness.
Compare worksites and investigate successful outliers to separate weaknesses in instruction from local implementation barriers and transferable support practices.
Report purpose, questions, design, procedures, findings, recommendations, and evidence-based rationale, leading with an executive summary and stating limits introduced by scope compromises.
Baseline scope only after target outcomes, treatment coverage, and design proof approval; analyze, document, and approve every later change and its effects before implementation.

Recognize that breadth and depth of guidance trade off: interrogate a broad framework for what implementation guidance it omits and a narrow one for what outcome types it excludes, and use a broad framework as the container into which deeper theories are subsumed rather than choosing between them.

Measure workplace use separately for each learned capability by degree, frequency, context, and prior use, and diagnose nonuse across relevance, learning, permission, support, resources, and adaptation opportunity.

Tie organizational impact to concrete use of learned capability, investigating adoption perceptions and social exchange while triangulating objective indicators, relevant observers, records, and feasible direct methods.

Compare interventions only after each is mature enough for routine use, center summative judgment on resolution of the originating problem, and use an independent evaluator when stakeholder interests threaten impartiality.
Convert stakeholder opinions into explicit acceptance criteria, separate delivery success from performance impact, and define how ability and behavior change will be measured before treatment design.
Treat abbreviated case-study design artifacts as illustrations of design products, not universal delivery prescriptions.

Maintain an alignment matrix from subordinate skills to condition-response-criterion objectives and parallel assessments, using authentic integrated products and explicit component rubrics for complex performance.
Assess recognition and independent production separately when the learning progression requires both, because identifying a correct form does not establish generative capability.
Evaluate authentic generation in addition to objective component mastery, and monitor individual performance when collaborative production could conceal a learner's gap.
Cluster objectives by skill relationships and dependencies, and anchor unit motivation and orientation in a learner-managed authentic product that visibly combines the component skills.
Document congruence through side-by-side comparison of organizational needs, learners, context, resources, and instruction, retaining both standardized ratings and reviewer rationale.
Teach and assess multiattribute concepts with closely matched examples and nonexamples, immediate error review, and new but strategy-parallel items across pretest, practice, and posttest.
Evaluate a development process by the quality and performance impact of its learning products, team effectiveness, constraint handling, and sustained value—not by phase visibility or mere delivery.
Do not infer individual learning from team product quality; the two outcomes are unrelated, so decide which one you are after and measure it directly.
Define and represent a process precisely enough to expose real effort, dependencies, sequences, criteria, and variations; judge it by evidence rather than familiarity or a broad label.
Work in short, low-cost, reversible cycles that expose the emerging product and use evaluation to correct direction before one approach consumes the budget.
Use a process that produces a usable product early while remaining iterative, collaborative, effective, efficient, manageable, and able to predict change impacts against quality criteria.

Begin and end every cycle with evaluation; keep the first cycle to a thin slice connecting performance goals, behavioral objectives, appraisal, practical media, representative treatments, and representative content.
Select and adapt a process for the organization's desired product, constraints, and performance outcomes; preserve routines only while evidence shows they still work.
Operationalize collaboration with explicit roles, decision authority and timing, documentation, communication, and flow; do not assume adding people automatically improves the work.
Cover breadth before depth by prototyping every materially distinct content or treatment type, while reusing a prototype for equivalent instances.

Map objectives to treatments, reuse treatments where context and criteria permit, draft only enough objectives to prototype representative cases initially, and prototype each distinct objective-activity type rather than every instance.
Alternate whole-solution and component views, cover content and treatment breadth before depth, map connections across blended events and supports, and assign unresolved segments to later cycles.
Test the real delivery mechanism early, including instructor handoff, interface behavior, communications, and platform compatibility as applicable.
Document the delivery platform with operating-performance tests and document the actual assignment, enrollment, use conditions, and support environment that the design must serve.
Review tangible low-investment prototypes, plan for some to be discarded, and avoid early refinement that creates sunk-cost attachment.
Bring key stakeholders and designers together early and use disposable rapid prototypes to expose existing solution ideas, assumptions, priorities, and team values.
Make stakeholder expectations tangible early through an integrated design proof, then sustain alignment with small production chunks, frequent review, and continuous contact.
Begin with readily available background information, then analyze candidate solutions and use prototype review to discover the specific questions worth deeper research.
Build detailed cost, schedule, staffing, scope, risk, and communication plans from initial designs; flag any objective without a prototyped treatment as an estimation risk.
Make budget and deadline constraints explicit before ideation, but do not commit to a firm cost or schedule until plausible treatments have been explored enough for responsible estimation.

Estimate cost and duration from backgrounding, representative prototypes, treatment coverage, and committed resources; when funding is inadequate, reduce to a coherent effective core or phase delivery instead of underfunding the whole solution.

Obtain decision-maker approval of evolved prototypes and validate an integrated design proof built with representative polished components, final tools, and the intended platform before full production.
Record and discuss user-test findings, then consolidate approved discovery, planning, prototypes, and additional design into a whole-application design proof before full production.

Use experiential prototypes rather than specification-only approval to align stakeholder expectations and test timing, transitions, media, interaction, and integration before misunderstanding reaches costly development.

Lead beyond status reporting by setting client expectations, identifying alternatives, negotiating trade-offs, coordinating people, and combining instructional-design, project-management, consulting, and persuasion skills.

Assign one client-side lead or an equivalently complete authority structure, give every interdisciplinary responsibility an owner, assess staffing-change impacts, and document binding sign-off authority by decision domain.
Favor people and interaction, working instructional products, customer collaboration, and response to evidence over rigid process, exhaustive documentation, defensive contracting, and plan adherence.
Adjust activities, design, and project variables without losing momentum, but reverse direction when continuing would compound a fundamental error.
Build schedule contingencies for predictable disruptions and communicate any conflict with concrete resolution options and the client's handling expectations.
Negotiate instructional change by presenting alternative treatments with their learning, budget, schedule, content, media, and staffing impacts, then securing informed agreement.

Elicit the sponsor's performance-gap view, involvement, treatment expectations, and success definition, then test whether tools, communication, incentives, supervision, or another non-course intervention better addresses the need.

Surface organizational values and preconceptions in a prepared collaborative workshop that aligns key players, exposes authority, agrees success measures, and cycles rapidly through alternative prototypes.
Keep the core whole-group brainstorming session small enough for every participant to contribute and respond; use larger groups only with facilitation that preserves equivalent participation.

After the initial workshop, establish a task-focused working team and a separate support, review, and approval network with explicit responsibilities, committed availability, scheduled review dates, prompt response, and openness to other perspectives.

Use a workshop agenda to turn divergent discussion into decisions and artifacts; align at the opening, agree continuation at the close, and shorten activities only after accounting for the prototypes, decisions, or risks left uncovered.
Prepare the collaboration space and tools in advance, open each work period with process and progress alignment, preserve restorative breaks and prototyping time, and close with a wrap-up.

Run several rapid brainstorm-build-review cycles, plan representative-user testing while changes are cheap, and visibly assign ownership for objectives or treatment cells the workshop leaves unresolved.

Use the initial workshop to test project readiness, governance, authority, constraints, information, team fit, and candidate solutions; regroup or redirect when evidence fails, and issue firm estimates only after documenting a credible basis and next actions.

Treat experts and approvers as scheduled resources, plan the workshop-to-project-team handoff, name authority for timely reviews and changes, and reject delegation that leaves an undocumented superior veto.

End early design with an agreed continuation process, feedback method, remaining cycles, responsibilities, and risks; if the workshop is shortened, substitute deliberately and preserve orientation to method, goals, and strong examples.

Keep early reviews brief and alternative-oriented, deepen later reviews, explain only missing mechanics without defending the design, capture reactions first, then classify them against objectives and recheck the solution's assumptions and appropriateness.
Facilitate toward decisions and prototypes rather than equal airtime, with ground rules for concise constructive input, timely dissent, changed minds, psychological safety, and time control.
Gather candid stories from recent learners, instructors, and supervisors about difficulty, utility, engagement, waste, and transfer because they reveal situational detail formal summaries omit.

Build each summarizer from a concise statement of every idea taught, a typical easy-to-remember example, and diagnostic self-test items, distinguishing a lesson summarizer that closes one lesson from a set summarizer covering all lessons that elaborate directly on a single lesson.
Use visibly incomplete sketches for collaborative idea generation and functional prototypes for feasibility and experience testing; redraw sketches freely as ideas evolve.
Build several fast, rough, explicitly disposable prototypes with only the content, art, prose, and functionality needed to compare the target interaction.
Alternate short brainstorming and prototyping intervals on small representative segments, use the prototypes as a safe error sandbox, and defer expected omissions to later design.

Continue unresolved design through the same design-prototype-evaluate loop after an initial workshop, using special-purpose prototypes for consequential questions that rapid brainstorming cannot settle.
Use repeated prototype review as analysis that turns content, pedagogy, stakeholder values, expectations, and technology into testable choices before high-cost development.

Alternate divergent and convergent work, commit to several materially distinct alternatives, force one to escape the first design's anchor, and synthesize only after independent directions have been tested.

Increase fidelity by phase—crude for ideation, functional for interaction, and integrated polished samples for proof—and answer superficial polish concerns with existing examples unless appearance is the actual risk.
Simplify or modularize a simulation when environmental richness obscures the core decision or action learners need to practice.
Let the prototyper fill only minor gaps, implement plausible group concepts fairly before advocating personal alternatives, and use evidence rather than authority to resolve disputed ideas.

Use structured controversy as a proven collaborative design: pro and con pairs build evidence-backed positions, each restates the other's argument to demonstrate understanding, then the team synthesizes a unified position.
Build only enough prototype functionality to enact the activity or witness key inputs and responses; if feedback is indecisive, test a materially different alternative rather than forcing consensus.
Design backward from authentic terminal performance through prerequisite performance and remediation until reaching abilities the target audience already has.

Let performance outcomes, authentic activity, and selected treatments drive content requirements; reuse prior material only when it supports those objectives, and remove or demote unsupported additions to optional reference regardless of sunk investment.
Audit content against the destination delivery mode and budget the time and talent to author missing explanations, demonstrations, context, challenge, activity, feedback, and learner support.
Define meaningful individualization early, vary challenge, sequence, remediation, comparison, modality, or choice from assessed needs, and design the interactions needed to collect that evidence.
Schedule representative-learner validation as a project dependency rather than allowing logistical convenience to defer design evidence until after introduction.

After exploratory design reveals likely content, treatments, delivery, resources, cost, and duration, explicitly fund the plan, resize the goal, or stop; only then formalize what happens, when, by whom, and how.

Rank schedule, budget, media, interactivity, content, design quality, collaboration, localization, and approval speed explicitly, and use the ranking to resolve trade-offs until new evidence justifies a deliberate change.

Establish technical feasibility before design commitment by checking device, network, browser, software, bandwidth, continuity, media, communication, adaptive behavior, and cross-session learner-history requirements.
Do not estimate interactive-content work from material built for another delivery form without auditing whether it contains the required contexts, activities, responses, and feedback.

Use the treatment matrix to connect objectives, sequence, models, budget, and schedule, and describe reusable treatments through learner inputs, system behavior, configurable elements, and evidence or tools.
Treat localization as an early design and resource requirement when language or culture differs, not as a late text substitution.
Let the human and organizational cost of performance errors raise the priority of instructional impact over cosmetic economy.
Test with target users at early prototype, design proof, alpha, and beta, including both untrained and recently trained participants when relevant.

Make quality assurance a user advocate, test component integration continuously, evaluate usability at design proof, defer intensive editing until content stabilizes, and run complete-system functional tests at alpha.
Build milestone dates from expert and user availability, and document each deliverable's purpose, creation process, delivery date, approval date, and shared review location.
Define assessment purpose, data, collection, and analysis in a tracking plan, and distinguish audience groups by role, motivation, prerequisites, conditions, and measurable target performance.
Prepare complete content and media artifacts against the treatment matrix and standards, approve them, then integrate them incrementally into usable modules with internal quality checks.

Name primary contacts, record important verbal agreements, report status and corrective action regularly, confirm material decisions through the agreed binding channel, and update the authoritative plan or design proof.
Prioritize prototype feedback and log every requested post-alpha change through resolution.
Protect schedule-dependent work with a rolling near-term lookahead, early absence notices, and rescheduled reviews, inputs, and handoffs before availability gaps become blockers.
Keep evolving project artifacts in a controlled shared repository with dated versions and change notes so reviewers can identify the authoritative state and reconstruct decisions.
Define issue escalation before disputes occur, beginning with named operational leads and ending with named authorities empowered to resolve impasses.
Maintain an actionable risk register that connects each risk to impact, likelihood, mitigation actions, and a responsible decision owner.
When stakeholders can fragment or delay decisions, establish participation timing, response windows, reviewer preparation, one consolidating lead, and a clear decision authority.
Serve materially different audiences with explicit prerequisites, audience-specific treatments, separate modules, or separate products instead of weakening all solutions into one compromise.
State the target audience and delivery form of a design explicitly, because the same objectives for a different audience or medium yield a different lesson.

Treat learning, willingness to apply, and workplace enablement as distinct implementation concerns, and address transfer with relevant examples, aligned incentives, manager preparation, and barrier removal.
Assign the sponsoring organization responsibility for identifying, preparing, and scheduling representative users when the development team lacks direct audience access.
Prototype consequential experience dimensions in their operative form, including visual treatment, media, enacted role-play, navigation, and integrated platform services.

Converge as evidence stabilizes, resist perfection and unplanned refinements, release a solution fit for responsible use with correction capacity, and reopen approved design only for unacceptable defects or risks.
Build a design proof as an intentionally incomplete but integrated whole that represents every structural component and each distinct event type before full production.
Make design-proof fidelity selective: finalize representative high-risk media and content, simulate low-risk repetition, and implement unique logic, accessibility, consequence, or integration risks.

Before authoring, require a performance-centered content grid that connects each event's objective, context, challenge, activity, actions, consequences, judgments, branches, audience-fit language, learner resources, and focused questions for experts.
Review a design proof for whole-course structure, treatment effectiveness, and representative coverage, not for production completeness unless a particular detail is the risk under test.

Review interactive products across navigation, media, interaction, content, and feedback using explicit criteria tied to learner fit, usability, accessibility, maintainability, and the target behavior.
At interaction-prototype review, require objective alignment, realistic context, sensible challenge, authentic activity, intuitive options, and consequence-based feedback.
Review media prototypes for audience fit, learning contribution, standards compliance, accessible redundancy, and intuitive controls before scaling media production.
Define each review's purpose, eligible elements, criteria, and stage-specific definition of done before preparing the deliverable.
Turn comments from every review pause into an explicit next-iteration action plan, keeping early review broad and creative and later review focused on validation and completion.

Assess quality as distinct dimensions—appropriateness, correctness, operation, usability, design consistency, accessibility, intended effect, and psychological impact—rather than collapsing them into polish.
Review early text for scope and completeness, defer detailed editing until context stabilizes, and stop rewriting once the prose is correct, clear, concise, consistent, and audience-fit.
Approve a project plan only when estimates and treatments are realistic and complete, responsibilities and expectations are named, and material contingencies are explicit.

Use progressive release gates: design proof establishes representative integrated viability, alpha establishes complete testability with disclosed exceptions, and beta establishes corrected release completeness.
Build quality assurance into every iteration with criteria agreed in advance, and keep production increments small enough that correction does not waste large volumes of completed work.
Delay expensive hard-to-change media when alpha changes are likely, but provide scratch media whenever timing or experience is essential to valid evaluation.

Use frequent delivery of coherent working instructional increments as the primary evidence of progress and interruption resilience, segmenting large content bodies when all-at-once integration would make review unmanageable.
Maintain direct collaboration among sponsors, users, designers, and developers throughout iterative work instead of restricting contact to phase gates.
Protect a sustainable pace and technical and design excellence because overextension and accumulated quality debt weaken future adaptability.
Treat late scope change as a resource decision, explicitly choosing added capacity, deferred scope, schedule movement, or displaced effort.
When one segment is blocked, release other coherent completed segments for review if reviewers can act without creating incompatible decisions or false acceptance.

Regression-test every release candidate across navigation, media, interaction, content, and feedback, including unusual inputs, repeated encounters, interrupted scoring, practice sufficiency, and requested corrections.
Where a lesson explains material in words alone, add corresponding pictures: learners understand more deeply from words and pictures together than from words alone.

Design a graphic to be integrated with the words it explains, not to replace them or to repeat them: the benefit comes from the learner building connections between corresponding verbal and pictorial representations.

Do not justify adding graphics on the grounds that two channels simply carry more material than one; that quantitative rationale wrongly treats words and pictures as equivalent. Justify it by the complementary, qualitatively different contribution pictures make.
Redundancy principle: when graphics are present, explain them with narration alone and omit on-screen text that duplicates the narration.

State the generalisation limits when citing this evidence base: most studies are short-term, use immediate tests, run in laboratory settings, and use college students, so long-term effects in authentic training settings are not established.
Weight a recommendation by the strength of its evidence base — replicated experiments and meta-analyses over single studies — and say which level supports the advice given.

Prefer replicated results synthesized across studies — review journals, handbooks, and meta-analyses — over any single study, and note that meta-analysis also pinpoints the conditions under which an effect is strong.
Prefer meta-analytic evidence, which averages effect sizes across many experiments and warrants more confidence than any single study.

Read the retention-and-transfer pattern as a diagnosis: poor-poor means no learning, good-poor means rote learning with inert knowledge, and good-good means meaningful learning with transferable knowledge. Do not report a single score as "learning".

Read good retention with poor transfer as the learner having done only essential processing: they represented the material as presented but never reorganised and integrated it. The remedy is to foster generative processing, not to simplify further.
Direct presentation is not sufficient on its own: an incoherent, disorganised, or overlong presentation will not foster meaningful learning no matter which medium delivers it.

Make relevance visible in the display. Selection is forced by capacity limits and the learner must judge what is most relevant, so a presentation that hides or dilutes the relevant material degrades learning before any other process starts.
Reject the learning-styles hypothesis as a justification for dual-format presentation; a research review found no evidence that visualizers learn better visually or verbalizers verbally.
Pose even a low-level problem before a presentation, since it stimulates information-seeking and can simultaneously clarify a viewing convention the learner will need.

Test a design feature by comparing performance on the lesson with the feature against the same lesson without it, holding the rest constant; a before-and-after or across-media comparison does not isolate the feature.
Prefer use-inspired research that serves theory and practice at once; a finding that only shows what works gives no mechanism, and a finding that only refines theory is untested on realistic tasks.

Answer the one-theory-or-several question by purpose: organize research and principle derivation around a single conceptual system for coherence, while for practice select the theories and techniques that fit the particular situation, since exclusive reliance stretches theories to cover matters never in their scope.

Guard against using the approach you happen to know rather than the one the problem needs, recognizing that practitioners are consistently more eclectic than researchers and that scarce guidance on which theory fits which situation is the gap integrative work exists to fill.
State the scope this evidence base was built on — lessons that explain how something works, presented in words and pictures — and flag when advice is being carried outside that scope.

Define learning as a change in knowledge caused by experience, observable only by inference from performance; therefore choose the assessment that can detect the change you claim, and do not assert learning without one.
Build a perceptible contrast into practice so the effect of the skill is its own reinforcement, such as having learners observe the unaided case immediately after the aided one.

Design against the three assumptions of the cognitive theory of multimedia learning — dual channels, limited capacity, active processing — and reject designs that implicitly assume a single-channel, unlimited-capacity, passive learner.
Design against the three cognitive-science constraints: dual channels, limited capacity per channel, and the requirement that learners actively select, organize, and integrate.

Do not rely on the learner converting material into the other channel; cross-channel conversion happens only when the learner has spare cognitive resources, which is exactly what an overloading lesson removes.

Treat the design target as the five cognitive processes — selecting words, selecting images, organising words, organising images, integrating with prior knowledge — and say which process a proposed change is meant to support.

Treat the design problem as guiding appropriate cognitive processing without exceeding working-memory capacity, and remember that the three demands — extraneous, essential, generative — all draw on the same limited pool.

Classify every design principle by the demand it addresses and match it to the diagnosis: coherence, signaling, redundancy, spatial contiguity, and temporal contiguity reduce extraneous processing; segmenting, pre-training, and modality manage essential processing; personalization, voice, image, embodiment, immersion, and generative activity foster generative processing.

Identify the target knowledge structure before designing the presentation — process (flowchart), comparison (matrix), enumeration (list), classification (hierarchy), or generalization (branching tree) — and let that structure drive the layout.

Fill each presentation form with the information its content type requires: a concept definition naming the concept, its superordinate, the distinguishing attributes and their relationships; a procedure presentation giving goal, steps, order, decisions, branches and response mode; and a principle presentation naming the principle, its component concepts and their relationship.

Make the first design decision the choice of organizing knowledge type — conceptual (what classes exist), procedural (how something is accomplished), or theoretical (why processes occur) — reading it from what the objectives emphasize.

Design so that the three processes can each happen: selecting relevant material, organising it into a structure, and integrating it with prior knowledge activated from long-term memory. A design that blocks any one of the three caps the outcome.

Expect peripheral detail in a complex illustration or animation to be dropped: learners cannot process all parts, so put the instructional load on the elements that carry the explanation and not on decorative detail.

Keep enough spare capacity for integration, the step where verbal and pictorial models are mapped onto each other and onto prior knowledge. Integration is the most crucial and most demanding step, so a design that consumes capacity elsewhere sacrifices it first.
Present material in learner-sized segments and keep corresponding words and pictures together within each segment: the five processes run segment by segment, not once over the whole message.
Integrate a remember-generality objective with the segment teaching the corresponding concept or principle rather than treating it as a standalone segment.

Design for a schematic pictorial model, not a photographic copy: the mental representation the learner builds is a structured spatial abstraction, so visual realism beyond what the structure requires buys nothing.

Prefer simpler visuals with fewer simultaneous details when the goal is understanding a process or principle: line drawings over photographs, reviewable frames over animation, schematic over video-realistic.
Vary practice instances across representational modes — drawings, a recalled instance from an earlier segment, and an imagined real object — so classification is not tied to one depiction.
Place words next to the part of the graphic they describe rather than in a separate caption block; separated captions force back-and-forth visual scanning that wastes capacity.

Treat total extraneous overload as a no-learning outcome: when extraneous processing consumes all available capacity, the learner cannot select, organise, or integrate at all, and both retention and transfer fail.

Diagnose the cause before prescribing a fix: extraneous processing is caused by confusing instructional design, essential processing by the inherent complexity of the material, and generative underuse by an unmotivating communication style. Each of the three scenarios has a different remedy.

Diagnose an overload problem as one of three types and apply the matching fix: cut extraneous processing, manage essential processing by chunking or pretraining, or foster generative processing with engagement techniques.

Manage overload inside whole-task designs by controlling scenario complexity and available help: open with a simple scenario an expert solves, then escalate complexity while the learner does more of the work.

Budget the three demands as one additive total under a fixed capacity ceiling: capacity spent on extraneous processing is unavailable for essential and generative processing, so every addition to a lesson displaces something else.
Budget for the fact that automaticity comes only after many repetitions, and treat it as a stated performance requirement rather than an assumed by-product of a course.

Check learner prior knowledge before applying a design principle: several principles help low-knowledge learners more than high-knowledge learners, so a principle applied blind to expertise level can be ineffective or counterproductive.

Apply the expertise reversal effect as a standing check: an instructional support that helps novices may not help and may hurt high-knowledge learners, so re-evaluate every support against the actual audience.

Present the triarchic three-load model as a useful working categorisation rather than a settled fact: its three-way split has been challenged in the cognitive-load literature and is retained here for its usefulness in classifying interventions.

Map the terminology to cognitive load theory when talking across communities: extraneous processing corresponds to extraneous load, essential processing to intrinsic load, and generative processing to germane load.

Test the causal chain rather than the endpoint alone: measures of learning process such as eye tracking and log-file analysis link the lesson to processing to outcomes, and brain-based measures of this chain are still preliminary.

Keep the constant core of the theory in view when applying it: dual channels, limited capacity, and active processing have held across three decades of revision, while specific components and the motivational extensions have not.
Ground every e-learning design decision in empirical research and cognitive theory rather than in fads, expert opinion, organizational politics, or ideology.

Run performance analysis before design to establish both that training will support organizational goals and that e-learning is the right delivery solution, judged against bottom-line operational indicators.
Judge an activity by the psychological processing it produces, not by the behavioral activity it generates; select methods that drive high cognitive activity even when overt response is low.
Avoid both failure extremes: glitz that overloads the limited cognitive system, and minimalist wall-of-words or page-turner designs that forfeit proven methods.
Classify the training goal first as inform, perform-procedure (near transfer), or perform-strategic (far transfer), because the applicable guidelines differ by goal type.

Match the instructional architecture to goal and learner: receptive for inform goals, directive for near-transfer procedures with novices, guided discovery for far-transfer strategic tasks with more experienced learners.
Use simulated job-realistic scenarios to compress rare or slow real-world experience when proficiency would otherwise take years of on-the-job exposure to accumulate.

Accelerate expertise by supplying compressed, deliberately ordered cases, because the real workplace delivers problems too rarely and in no order of complexity; twenty to twenty-five hours in a coached troubleshooting environment matched four years on the job.
Embed the job context in examples and practice so new knowledge is encoded with retrieval hooks; knowledge stored without contextual cues is retained but fails to transfer.
Mirror the job: derive interactions from a job and task analysis so learners respond during training as they will at work, embedding job-environment features that become retrieval cues.
Apply encoding specificity and transfer-appropriate interaction: make training conditions resemble retrieval conditions, practising on the same system, cases, and interfaces used on the job.
Ask of any technology feature not whether it is good or bad but whether it can be used to support selection, rehearsal, load management, and retrieval.
Match the research method to the question: experimental comparison for whether a method works, factorial comparison for when it works, and observation or interview for how it works.
Accept an experimental comparison as sound only if it shows experimental control, random assignment, and appropriate learning measures reported with mean, standard deviation, and n.

Do not treat a null result as evidence of no effect until inadequate sample size, insensitive measure, weak treatment implementation, insensitive learners, and confounding variables have been ruled out.
Require both statistical significance below p .05 and an effect size of .5 or greater before adopting a method, since large samples make trivial differences significant.
Multimedia principle: present content with words and relevant graphics rather than words alone, the single best-supported multimedia guideline with a median effect size of 1.50.
Extend the multimedia principle beyond static explanation to interactive feedback, graphic organizers, and video examples, where it also produces gains.

Apply the multimedia principles inside worked examples: relevant visuals, audio for complex steps tied to a graphic, integrated text, meaningful step chunks with signalling, and learner-paced progression.

Rank the multimedia principles by their measured strength when they compete for effort: multimedia 1.50, coherence 1.32, personalization 1.30, contiguity 1.11, segmenting .98, modality .97, pretraining .92, redundancy .69.
Plan visuals and words together during job analysis and course design; never select pictures after the text has been written.

Select graphics by function: minimize decorative and bare representational graphics, and use organizational, transformational, and interpretive graphics that help learners understand or organize the material.

Match graphic type to what is being taught: relational graphics for quantitative relationships, transformational for change over time, organizational for qualitative structure, and interpretive for invisible relationships.
Supply coordinated graphics especially to low-knowledge learners; expect the benefit to shrink or reverse for high-knowledge learners, who can generate their own mental images.

Use static illustrations as the default graphic and adopt animation only on a compelling instructional rationale, presenting a series of static frames rather than a lock-step animation when explaining how a system works.
Contiguity principle 1: place printed words next to the part of the graphic they describe, with a pointing line, rather than in a caption, legend, or separate text block.
Contiguity principle 2: present spoken words at the same time as the graphic they describe, never narration before or after the visual and never behind separate media icons.
Modality principle: present words as audio narration rather than on-screen text whenever a graphic is the focus of those words and both appear at the same time.

Eliminate split attention wherever it appears in the interface: scrolling screens that separate text from graphic, feedback on a screen apart from the question and the learner's answer, linked windows that cover what they explain, and exercise directions away from the work area.
Minimize split attention in the response mode itself: prefer on-screen input such as sliders or drag-and-drop over keyboard text entry, which depressed transfer.
Do not run an animation while related printed text is displayed; present the text first and let the learner start the animation with a play button, keeping the text available.
Use rollover text only as a fallback when screen space cannot hold both graphic and text, and prefer a permanent integrated display whenever the learner must revisit the text while acting on it.
Keep words as on-screen text when the learner needs them available over time: technical or unfamiliar terms, non-native language, formulas, step keywords used as organizers, and practice directions.
Keep audio narration brief and clear, since lengthy narration both wastes the modality advantage and leaves learners waiting.

Treat audio infeasibility as a real constraint: bandwidth, sound hardware, ambient noise, cost, and rapidly changing content can all preclude narration, in which case fall back to concise integrated text rather than abandoning the graphic.
Keep narration concise per screen, which serves coherence and keeps learners from waiting through long audio.
Expect the modality benefit to be largest for less-skilled learners and to shrink for the skilled, consistent with expertise reversal.
Apply these principles as guidance consistent with how the mind works, not as unbending rules applied rigidly in every situation; state the boundary condition whenever you invoke one.
State the boundary conditions whenever recommending a principle, since every principle has situations where it does not hold and learner background experience is the standing example.

Recognize that rules for teaching mental operations are conditional rather than absolute: a method that succeeds under one set of conditions may fail under another, so state the conditions with the rule.
Reject the information-acquisition rationale that format does not matter provided the information is delivered; it is the reason words-only and duplicated-format designs seem defensible.
Meet accessibility needs with an audio-off control that swaps narration for on-screen text, never by presenting both at once; compliance is not a licence to duplicate.
If text and narration must both be delivered, sequence the text after the narration rather than concurrently.
Coherence principle: weed out every word, graphic, and sound that does not support the instructional goal — the most commonly violated and most consequential of the guidelines.
Apply coherence most strictly for the most at-risk learners, since extraneous material hurts low-working-memory learners most and draws more of their gaze.

Do not add seductive details — interesting but irrelevant sounds, pictures, or words — to counter boredom or dropout; they reliably reduce learning, and making them more interesting makes learning worse.
Exclude extraneous pictures and video, which damage learning through distraction, disruption of relevant links, and seduction of inappropriate prior knowledge.
Reject the generational argument that learners raised on high-intensity media are immune to overload; the seductive-details experiments used eighteen-to-twenty-two-year-olds.

Do not equate coherence with dullness: stimulate interest through job-relevant examples, practice, and explicit benefits rather than through decoration, since understanding produces enjoyment rather than the reverse.
Exclude background music and environmental sounds, whose combined penalty reached an effect size of 1.66, and which are most damaging when material is unfamiliar, fast-paced, or system-paced.

Cut extraneous words in all three forms — added for interest, added to elaborate key ideas, and added for technical depth — and prefer a concise summary over the same content plus complementary material.
Strip quantitative and computational detail when the objective is conceptual understanding; added formulas depressed conceptual transfer with effect sizes of .69 and .97.
Supply a concrete analogy for a quantitative relationship, mapping the varying attribute onto a familiar contrast, as a memory aid for the direction of the relationship.
Personalization principle: write in conversational style with first- and second-person constructions and active voice, which raises social presence and drives deeper processing.
Voice principle: use a human voice rather than machine-simulated speech for narration.
Deliver agent words as speech, in conversational style, with human-like articulation, since the modality, personalization, and voice effects all apply to agents.
Use polite conversational language as the standing tool for social presence in synchronous delivery, where the instructor's voice is often the only channel.
Keep personalization subtle: a few personal pronouns or one friendly comment is enough, and excessive informality distracts the learner and undermines the material.
Do not select narrator gender, ethnicity, or accent on stereotype grounds; the evidence is conflicting and unsettled, so treat any such claim as unsupported.
Phrase agent and tutor feedback politely — as a suggestion or shared action rather than a command — because politeness helps learners who lack domain background.
Use agents only for instruction — hints, worked examples, demonstrations, explanations, feedback — and never as entertainment mascots, which are seductive details.
