Design pedagogical agents for behaviour rather than appearance: a cartoon works as well as a realistic video person, but human-like locomotion, gesture, and eye-gaze do improve learning.
Make the author visible with a modest amount of personal perspective, stopping well short of self-revelation that becomes a seductive detail; the evidence is preliminary.
Never simplify complex material by deleting elements or steps, which destroys the lesson's accuracy; manage the complexity by segmenting instead.
Segmenting principle: break a complex lesson into learner-paced parts of one to three steps each, with a continue button, rather than presenting it continuously.
Set the segment boundaries in the design rather than relying on a pause button: learners mostly do not pause, so stop the animation at logical points and offer continue or replay.
Synchronize narration with the demonstrated action and pause after each action so the learner finishes watching before the next statement.
Present pretraining components inside the context of the whole interface, equipment, or task rather than in isolation, so parts keep their relation to the whole.
Flag segmenting and pretraining as less-developed guidance: segment size, break placement, concept selection, and pretraining depth are all unresolved.
Use worked examples for strategic as well as procedural skills, including modeling examples in which a person demonstrates the task with commentary.
Never present a worked example without an engagement device, because many learners skip or skim examples; attach self-explanation questions that ask for the principle behind each step.

Use active observing where feasible — learner pairs solving a problem while watching a tutor-tutee video — which matched direct tutoring, while noting the evidence is early and demonstrated only in physics.
Override the audio default with text whenever the learner must re-read steps at their own pace, as alongside a self-explanation question or a faded example.
For far transfer, supply at least two worked examples that vary the surface context while illustrating the same principle, since one analogue is not enough to abstract a general rule.

Span a wide range of difficulty in the situations used to illustrate and practise a principle — some where its application is obvious and others where it is subtle — and draw divergence from systems that each require some modification in how the principle applies, not from surface variation.
Display varied-context examples contiguously and require an active comparison between them; mere exposure to both without a comparison question does not produce the gain.
Do not assume that stacking fading and self-explanation questions is better than either alone; in some complex domains self-explanation questions alone produced the best learning.
Implement adaptive branching from self-explanation responses: a wrong answer routes to another example of the same concept, a right answer to a harder item or the next topic.

Add enough practice interactions to reach the objective, favouring more over less when achievement matters, while recognizing the power law of practice means the greatest gains come from the earliest trials.
Give feedback on every solution step when the steps are interdependent, since an early wrong step derails the rest.

Distribute practice within a lesson, across lessons, and across separate learning events; the spacing effect is among the most reliable findings in experimental psychology and persisted for as long as eight years.
Expect spaced practice to show no immediate advantage and to pay off only on delayed measures, so a program that never measures delayed learning will systematically miss it.

Invert the modality default during practice: keep directions, questions, and anything needed to answer on screen as text, and present feedback in text so learners can review at their own pace without narration.

Apply the consolidated defaults for novices: concise informal narration of relevant graphics where audio exists, concise informal integrated text where it does not, short learner-paced segments in every case, and key concepts sequenced before the process or procedure.
Keep practice free of gratuitous animation, applause, bells, and whistles, and keep the synchronous classroom silent during practice.
Transition from examples to practice gradually via faded worked examples, because completing practice imposes heavy load that fading raises in step with expertise.
Drive adaptive fading of worked examples from the accuracy of learners' self-explanation selections, which needs no extra test items and beat both a standard tutor and fixed fading.

Fade the job aid across successive practice problems on a planned schedule — required, then available only if needed, then forbidden — recognizing that removing it entirely at the last attempt is a large fading jump that must be justified, and that fading may be offered as a learner choice.
Pair each recall exercise with its cued and uncued version — one problem permitting reference to the source table, the next forbidding it — so fading happens within the same skill.

State plainly that experimental evidence on computer-supported collaborative learning is still insufficient for firm guidelines, and that its research base is too heterogeneous to yield universal rules.
Treat cooperative learning as effective only under well-specified conditions; it ranked twenty-fourth of 138 influences with an effect size of .59, and not all comparisons favour learning together.
Base group rewards on the sum of individual learning, not on a single group product; product- based rewards produced a negligible .07 against .32 for individually-summed rewards.
Do not simply tell teams to work together: unstructured assignments produce knowledge-telling and free-riding, so specify structure, roles, and instructions.
Pitch the collaborative assignment between too simple and too vague: simple tasks do not motivate dialog and general ones give too little structure.

Match the tool to the outcome: asynchronous channels for reflection and independent research, synchronous channels for social presence and group synergy, and allow ample working time since CSCL takes longer than solo work.
Recognize that social presence is a property of the delivery medium rather than of the instructional method, and that recording a synchronous session converts it into asynchronous review material.

Expect virtual and face-to-face collaboration to trade off by outcome: chat produced better team products and more questioning, while face-to-face produced better individual post-test scores and easier information sharing.

Do not assume a new social medium helps: its benefit depends entirely on whether its features are exploited to fit cognitive learning needs, so carry over the lessons from in-person and prior online collaboration.
Prefer a representation that externalizes the group's reasoning over a purely chronological discussion thread, which hides agreement, relevance, and outcomes.

Assign explicit roles in collaborative discussion, including a moderator and a designated generator of alternative solutions, since deeper knowledge construction appeared only when both roles were present.
Train argumentation rather than assuming it: use video-modeled examples with stage- identification questions or argumentation templates before expecting quality argument.

Always give pacing control in asynchronous e-learning — forward, back, replay, and exit — even where content control is withheld; learner-paced review produced better transfer at the cost of more time.

Insert questions with feedback to improve calibration and to relieve novices of self- monitoring load, since calibration is more accurate after answering questions and low-prior- knowledge learners lack capacity for planning and monitoring.
Shift control toward the learner as their knowledge base grows: program control was better during initial learning and learner control better at later stages.

Where learner control is granted, route the default navigation through the important instructional events so bypassing practice takes a deliberate choice; this nearly doubled screens viewed and raised test scores.

Use adaptive control to adjust difficulty and support from the program's assessment of learner responses, which is how the expertise-reversal trajectory can be timed to each individual rather than to the average.
Offer learner control at the microstrategy level — how many instances to study, when to receive help, and similar strategy choices.

Assess competence cheaply enough for real-time adaptation: rapid verification, in which learners judge presented solution steps right or wrong, correlated .71 to .75 with a traditional test at over three times the speed.
Substitute a pretest that routes learners to the right session for the dynamic adaptation a live class cannot provide.
Justify adaptive learning by audience heterogeneity or a universal-competence requirement, since it costs extra design of assessments, decision logic, and alternative paths.

Provide navigational support in hypermedia: screen headings combining lesson title and topic, descriptive labels on text segments and visuals, navigation reachable from every display, and a progress indicator.

Use links sparingly for novices and never for essential instructional elements such as worked examples or practice; a link signals the content is peripheral, and heavy link use was negatively related to learning.

Integrate job-specific cognitive and metacognitive skills into the technical training for that role rather than buying a stand-alone generic thinking course, since non-routine problems are always encountered in a specific job context.
Derive job-specific thinking processes through cognitive task analysis rather than by asking experts directly, since most experts cannot articulate their own rationale.

Choose between part-task and whole-task by learner expertise and transfer distance: part-task with a closing case suits novices, whole-task suits more experienced learners and far-transfer goals, and the comparative evidence is mixed.

Expect whole-task designs to buy transfer rather than component skill: part-task and whole-task tied on component tests, while whole-task won the applied test at .71 and a novel transfer task at 1.14, attributed to varied-context practice.
Show the expert's reasoning, not just the expert's actions: expose alternatives considered, the rationale for the choice, and responses to avoid.
Require learners to articulate their own lessons learned from the expert comparison, so reflection lands on the process rather than the answer.

Direct attention within a video model with a focusing statement just before each modelled behaviour or a requirement to identify specific behaviours; without it learners took longer and scored much lower on transfer.

Use cues also to direct attention — to the discriminative stimuli, to isolated features of them, to a problem's requirements, to the required response, or to what makes an answer correct — since directing attention in these ways is central to all forms of instruction, every instance of which combines cues that already elicit responses with stimuli that must acquire that capacity.

Choose the cognitive task analysis method by task and setting: concurrent reporting is rich but obtrusive and impossible for verbal or unobservable tasks, retrospective and critical- decision methods are unobtrusive but memory-dependent, and structured expert sessions pool several experts.

Make a cognitive task analysis deliver four outputs: the scenarios to serve as cases, the criteria separating complex from simple ones, the tools and resources normally available, and the alternative solution paths with their rationale.

Scope thinking-skills work by needs analysis: identify the roles whose thinking most drives competitive advantage, then weigh problem complexity and the stability of the underlying skills before investing.
Supply several diverse problem scenarios plus enough guidance to ensure successful case resolution, so learners build robust rather than brittle problem-solving skill.

State that the games and simulations evidence base is weak: of 155 studies reviewed none met all criteria for sound research, learner ratings of a simulation correlate little with performance in it, and there is little objective evidence of relative merit.

Put explanatory feedback in every game and simulation — the single most cited success factor in medical simulation research — since it doubled transfer at an effect size of 1.87 without reducing motivation or interest.
Separate the well-supported simulation claim from the contested game claim: simulations provide practice unavailable or unsafe at work, whereas the motivational case for games remains unproven.
Ask the value-added question — which features of this game or simulation produce learning — tested by comparing versions that differ in one feature, rather than whether games work.
Align the game or simulation's goals, rules, activities, feedback, and interface to the intended learning outcome, and make the learning required to progress the same learning the objectives demand.
Build proven instructional strategies into games rather than starting from scratch: modality, personalization, and pretraining all show high effect sizes inside game environments.

Add self-explanation prompts to game problems as a selectable checklist rather than free typing; selection improved in-game and transfer performance while typed generation added load and gave no gain.
Avoid open-ended exploratory games and simulations; pure discovery has consistently failed for fifty years, and the belief that mental activity requires physical activity is a teaching fallacy.

Guide inquiry simulations four ways: help identify the relevant variables, offer ready-made hypotheses from a menu, structure the inquiry with concrete assignments, and require reflection on activities and results.
Supply visualization support where success depends on spatial reasoning; diagrammatic aids beat text strategy aids and no aid in a geology simulation.

Insert brief instructional explanations as hints between rounds; without them the learner must chase the game goal and learn at once, and it is the game that wins — hints lifted pretest-to-posttest gain from 13 to 32 points.

Teach the tool before the content: a simulation only beat a text lesson when preceded by a short video explaining how to use it, and access to variable information both before and during the task produced the best performance.

Require the learner's prediction before they may manipulate the simulation, both because it increases the mental effort demanded and because gating access separates the practice display from the example display.

Make workplace relevance immediately visible through objectives, embedded explanations, and an interface mirroring the work environment; high-fantasy themes that motivate entertainment players may reduce motivation for workforce learners.

Diagnose which motivational category actually needs work: an audience may be interested and already convinced of relevance yet lack confidence, and may be driven by extrinsic reward rather than intrinsic enjoyment.

Diagnose a text-heavy procedure screen as a joint multimedia and coherence violation, and repair it with a relevant visual of the actual tool, minimal text, the procedure split into a few steps, and callouts anchoring text to the graphic.

Check every practice item for the three recurring defects: a recall question where application is needed, directions or input boxes separated from the work area, and feedback that confirms correctness without explaining it.
Explain correct answers as well as incorrect ones, since a correct response may be a guess.
Strip congratulatory banners from feedback even when the explanation is good, because praise redirects attention from the task to the ego.
Drop the live instructor video window when the slides carry the instructional message, since it is the voice rather than the image that promotes learning and a second image splits attention.

Run fading live in a synchronous session: the instructor completes the first step of a shared procedure, learners finish it, directions and syntax stay on screen as memory support, and the support is withdrawn as the lesson proceeds.

Constrain the simulation environment as a guidance device — for example refusing an irrelevant tool with an explanatory message — and layer guidance through an advice channel, the real job reference system, intrinsic consequences, and an end-of-case expert comparison.
Blend face-to-face and digital delivery deliberately to realize distributed practice, since face-to-face retains a substantial share of delivery.
Reserve three-dimensional virtual worlds for goals that genuinely benefit from three-dimensional multi-party interaction, and use conventional courseware for the rest.
Reframe every 'is this technology good for learning' question as which of its features best achieve a specific instructional goal for a specific group of learners.
Guard against both failure modes by name: the technophile who overloads learners with sensory stimulus, and the technostic who ports old techniques to new media without adaptation.
Scope each guideline to where it applies: items covering all e-learning, teaching job tasks, collaborative facilities, asynchronous navigation, and problem-solving with simulations and games.

Keep descriptive and prescriptive statements distinct: a descriptive principle or theory states the effects of a component or model under given conditions, while a prescriptive one names what should be used for a given outcome and conditions. Do not read a prescription out of a description.

Treat a set of validated single-component prescriptions as incomplete: it does not account for the full range of components a unit of instruction needs, so a design built only from them will have gaps.

Analyse a phenomenon into manageable components before researching its effects, then synthesize the component findings into progressively more comprehensive models; comparisons framed on broad undifferentiated variables cannot identify reliable causes because within-category variation swamps between-category variation.

Diagnose the relation between two competing prescriptions by testing which of three cases holds: same technique and same situation in different terminology (duplication), different techniques for the same situation (genuine competition), or different techniques for different situations (compatible, and integrable). Most apparent conflicts turn out to be the third case.
When an objective does not fit the approach or is impractical at the available scale, exclude it and state explicitly that it was excluded and why, rather than forcing it in or silently dropping it.
Annotate each point of a design with the specific prescription being implemented there, and mark which parts were the designer's own discretion, so the rationale stays traceable and auditable.
List every prescription used in preparing a design alongside a comment on how it applies, so the design can be checked against the theory prescription by prescription.

Audit a design against each prescription and name its shortfalls — insufficient fading, too narrow a range of representation, missing misconception coverage — rather than presenting it as fully conforming.

Annotate and modify another designer's work to illustrate a supplementary model without implying criticism, stating the audience assumptions the modifications rest on, and apply the model to segments from different theoretical viewpoints to show its prescriptions are not tied to one approach.

Classify the desired learned capability into its outcome category before designing or developing instruction, because the appropriate methods differ by category; a body of prescriptions is a theory of instruction only when it differentiates methods by situation.

Keep the goal of algorithm-based instruction on the algorithmic process rather than the prescription: the prescription is one means of teaching the process, though it makes learners more aware of the operations and speeds their generalization and transfer.

Teach the prescription explicitly when the objective is awareness and faster generalization, or when learners will have to communicate the method to others; omit it when only a particular skill is wanted, since prescription knowledge is unnecessary for solving problems oneself.

Keep a theorist's three contributions separate when applying their work: a theory of how learning occurs, procedures for instructional development, and prescriptions for what the instruction should be like.

Explore the purpose, global goals, specific objectives and delivery conditions of the instruction in depth before selecting a theory, because clarifying those is what makes it possible to recognize which theories match the situation.
Supply remedial instruction — returning to stimulus presentation and learning guidance — whenever the elicited performance is incorrect, rather than moving on after marking it wrong.

Recognize that discriminative stimuli cannot elicit the required responses before instruction — which is why instruction is needed — and supply cues, chosen for their capacity to elicit the responses that need practice, alongside rather than instead of those stimuli.

Plan retention and transfer as design work: additional practice across a wide variety of instances raises retention, spaced reviews are particularly effective for intellectual skills, and practice on divergent instances is what makes the capability likely to transfer to new situations.

Acknowledge that sequencing above the task-analysis level rests on expert opinion, consensus and common sense rather than on a validated rule, and record that basis rather than presenting such ordering as derived.

Allow that a rule may be prerequisite to a concept rather than the reverse, since many complex concepts are defined by the cause-and-effect relationships among other concepts, and derive the order from the actual dependency rather than from category rank.
Express cause-and-effect principles as chained if-then decisions and teach them with the same procedural form used for concept classification.

Support first practice of a multi-step procedure with an explicit written step list the learner consults and a partner uses to guide and give feedback, and prompt with questions that surface the procedure's decision points rather than its steps.
Separate reading a procedure from performing it on the first pass, and key each step of the written aid to a labelled diagram so the learner locates the physical part named while reading.

Let a procedural demonstration be repeated step by step in any order as often as needed, structured as an overview menu of major steps with drill-down to substep detail, and advise viewing the overview before the details.

Make the process description identify the outcome following the procedure produces, every step and its order, and every decision with the branches following each alternative; keep it concise with critical steps separated from elaborative information.

Elaborate a process description with aids for remembering the steps and their order, reviews of the prerequisite concepts any decision depends on, at least two alternative representations, and a single-word label per step so the learner can hold its essential aspect in memory.
Self-test a procedure by having the learner mentally rehearse every step with eyes closed, picturing exactly what they would do, then check the written version for missed steps and wrong order.

Practise a procedure on several different instances of the equipment, not only the demonstrated one, because procedural competence must show regularity across situations and the target is any instance of the class.
Demonstrate a procedure on the same equipment learners will use, so the demonstration is of exactly the performance they must produce.

Provide practice on real equipment of the demonstrated type, since adequate procedural practice is impossible from demonstration alone, and sequence that practice by backward chaining — performing only the last step first and adding the preceding step each time until the whole procedure is done.
Give learners practice across the variety of objects and equipment the procedure will actually be used with; where varying the equipment is impossible, vary the materials instead.
Stage recall of prerequisites even when they were taught minutes earlier in the same lesson, whenever they are essential to the relationship now being learned.
Where efficiency allows, lead learners to combine subordinate rules and concepts themselves through a line of questioning rather than stating the rule outright.

Classify every method as one of three treatment kinds and apply them in that order of precedence: routine treatments always, shaping treatments before them whenever the conditions pose learning difficulty, and specialized treatments to supplement both for particular problems.

Reach for a specialized treatment when a specific difficulty warrants it: concrete examples before abstract ones, deliberate exaggeration of a stimulus or response, practice of errors to sharpen the right-versus-wrong discrimination, backward-order practice of procedural steps, or practice of a procedure's principles before the procedure.

Recognize that a theory may consist of one model with prescribed variations, so the substantive comparison between such theories is how each defines its situations, not how many models it names; and a theory bought depth of guidance at the price of breadth must be interrogated for the outcome types it omits.

Accept that no theory can address every aspect of a setting, so each sets priorities; read a theory's omissions as informative, since what it ignores or treats as peripheral shows where it will not help.

Fade cues deliberately: start with maximum help, move through progressively weaker partial cues, end with none, set the rate by the learners' estimated and increasing capacity, never require a longer jump than they are judged able to make, and remove cues completely only when they can respond unaided.

Analyse any performance into its combination of discriminations, generalizations, associations and chains — classification depending on the first three and equipment operation additionally on chaining — and use that analysis to locate where difficulty will fall.

Spell out the concrete engineering tactics that implement a high-level principle, because directives such as transfer control, fade cues or shape behaviour are too general for practitioners to act on; approaches that share underlying principles differ in these tactics, not in the principles.

Treat subject-matter characteristics as part of the conditions a treatment must accommodate: similarity among stimuli makes discriminations hard, chain length makes procedures hard, and the number of stimulus-response associations makes associations hard.

Ask learners to practise the complete set of skills from the first opportunity where conditions permit, for the efficiency whole-task practice makes possible; where difficulty is anticipated, keep the routine treatments but defer intact full performance to the close of instruction, preceded by easier practice.

State the conditions of a lesson section as concrete performance requirements the learner must acquire — producing each step, producing them in order, recognizing correct outcomes, performing unaided, transferring to unused instances — and pair each with the treatment selected to meet it.
Place simple early exercises to give an immediate sense of accomplishment, and help learners recognize and avoid obstacles to success, since both build confidence independently of the content taught.

Make early practice easier along named levers — the size of the behaviour unit practised, the amount of cuing, the mode of stimulus or response such as recognizing rather than producing, the frequency and variety of practice, and the difficulty of practice content — used singly or together to build a graduated progression ending in the complete performance.
Add nonroutine treatments only as needed, letting the conditions of each objective decide, because placing them before the routine ones lengthens instruction and reduces its efficiency.

Frame learning hints as the specific kinds of information — or the specific questions — the learner should search for in the upcoming segment, since repeated practice at that search is intended to build a self-directed searching habit whose durability is still an open empirical question.

Design how information is displayed as deliberately as what information is presented: display can enhance or detract from effectiveness and efficiency, and a display designed to serve the same goal as its content makes the two work together.

Use display parameters as a nonverbal characterization of the information type and of how it must be used, and reuse the same convention for the same purpose so it becomes a stable tool that reliably elicits the intended response.
Design the relationships between displays deliberately, since they affect learning independently of the displays themselves.

Choose the display form to match the cognitive work required: a numbered list for a sequence of steps, juxtaposition rather than serial presentation for stimuli that must be told apart, and tabular rows and columns to cue comparison for discrimination, similarity for generalization, or pairing for association.

Match the combination of primary presentation forms to the performance level, since achievement and learning efficiency rise when the necessary forms are present and fall when they are absent or inappropriate.

Add secondary presentation forms — attention-focusing help, repeated prerequisite information, alternate representation, mnemonics and feedback — to primary forms, since an enhanced presentation increases achievement and learning efficiency.

Annotate any demonstration design externally, because a lesson by itself cannot testify how it exemplifies a theory: supply reader introductions naming the conditions and chosen treatments per section, itemized comments tied to callouts, and learner-facing hints, keeping reader-facing annotation explicitly separate from what the learner receives.

Have learners self-test on annotated examples by covering the notes and attempting both the classification and the reason before revealing them, requiring an explanation of why each case is or is not an instance before moving to practice.

Build the transfer requirement into practice by varying the equipment across problems and ending with an unaided attempt on an untrained instance, since the final practice must match what the objective calls for.

Treat concept recognition as three conditions at once — discriminating instances from noninstances, generalizing across varied instances, and associating the label — and meet them with the routine treatment of a definition, multiple annotated examples and nonexamples, and attachment of the label.

Build a concept classify-practice item from a new instance with all relevant attributes present, represented in a form that shows them, asking the learner to name it or judge class membership; procedure practice supplies new materials and requires execution, and principle practice supplies a new problem and requires a prediction.

Annotate every example and nonexample with the specific feature that decides the case, using such cues to mark differences for discrimination and similarities for generalization, so learners attend to the criterial attribute rather than to surface appearance.

Lead learners to the criterial dimension by presenting instances that differ on it and asking what makes the difference — including a pair identical on the obvious attribute but differing on the intended one — and have them state the resulting generalization in their own words before moving on.

Encode the criterial attributes in a memorable rhyme or verbal formula and tell learners to rehearse it until it comes easily, and distinguish a confusable term by tying each to a concrete image whose own name carries the cue, so the contrast is self-checking.

Include near-miss nonexamples that satisfy some but not all of the definition's attributes, and present examples in matched pairs, because a controlled contrast is what forces attention to every criterial attribute.
Place exercise answers where confirmation is immediate but cannot pre-empt the response, with an explicit instruction not to look until finished.

Require learners to produce a representation — drawing the predicted result as well as stating it — because producing it elicits the performance while recognizing it does not, and drawing is also an easier alternative practice mode when the full statement is too hard.

Use visual examples concrete enough that learners can respond to individual features, while recognizing that support which almost gives the answer away is heavy cuing appropriate early in a shaping sequence but not as terminal practice.
Use drawing as an active response mode, which both elicits production rather than recognition and varies the response format.

Meet a fact-recall objective with the routine treatment of stating the facts and having learners practise stating them or predicting from them, presenting the facts in a table with the association pairs made explicit and itemizing them as separate points.

Escalate exercise items within a section from recall through explanation to definition, and name for the learner the ideas a required explanation must use, so the explanation exercises the intended relationships rather than any account reaching the right answer.

Drill a fact set with paired-associate cards, recalling the hidden side before turning the card for correct-answer feedback, shuffling between passes so the association is to the cue rather than to position, and repeating to a criterion of no errors and immediate recall.

For a remember-instance fact objective, present the instance and then practise on the same instance, since a fact is an arbitrary association no generality can derive and there is nothing to generalize; feedback is correct-answer information alone.

Set a 100% mastery criterion for fact learning with immediate recall as part of the criterion, because a partial criterion is not meaningful — either an association is needed or it is not — and an association should require minimal processing time even though problem solving does not.
State both directions of a pair of related generalizations explicitly rather than leaving the learner to invert one of them.

Judge chain length against the specific audience before choosing a treatment, because a procedure that is a long chain for that audience cannot be learned from a single reading of a step list and needs routine treatment plus shaping.

Recognize multiple-choice recognition as an easier, altered practice mode than requiring identification of individual instances, and schedule full-blown practice last so the routine element the objective actually requires closes the sequence.
When examples and nonexamples differ by minute features, make feedback annotate the defining characteristics rather than merely marking the answer right or wrong.
Practise facts individually before practising them in combination, treating combination as a later stage rather than the starting point.

For a small set of factual associations with no anticipated difficulty, a routine treatment alone suffices; where even a small set is judged too hard to recall on one read-through for that audience, insert a cued practice before the uncued one, and design the fact display so its look alone cues how many facts there are and what types they are.

Build an explanation objective's routine presentation from the statement of the relationship plus examples it applies to, adding the nonroutine step of presenting the statement's constituent parts individually when the whole is too large.

Distinguish an algorithm — a precise, unambiguous and sufficiently general prescription of what to do to solve any problem in a class — from a heuristic, which indicates what to do to find a solution more easily but carries uncertainty and does not determine the process; intermediate semialgorithmic and semiheuristic forms exist between them.

Select the indicative features to teach on psychological criteria — comprehensible, sufficiently elementary, unambiguous, workable, economical and convenient — and make a feature workable by first teaching the operations that let learners detect it.

Analyse each indicative feature for its logical property — necessary and sufficient, necessary but not sufficient, or sufficient but not necessary — and determine all the sufficient feature sets, because each type is acted on differently and several may give learners alternative identification methods.
Use an algorithm as a means of developing the concept and not only of applying it, because performing the operations on the indicative features teaches those features faster and better.

Determine whether a concept's indicative features are connected conjunctively, disjunctively or in a mixed structure, and express that structure as an implicational if-then proposition with the features in the antecedent and the inference in the consequent.

Recognize that a logical proposition models only the conceptual component of instruction: the operational component of identification can be modelled only by an algorithm, so develop an algorithm directing what the learner should do mentally to decide class membership.

Treat logically equivalent algorithms as psychologically different, since some require more operations or are less comfortable to execute, and make it the designer's task to produce the most efficient one rather than merely a correct one.

Make every instruction in an algorithm comprehensible and unambiguous for the given population, make the instruction set complete so it guides under every logically possible condition, and make each instruction as general as elementariness and comprehensibility allow.
Vary the instances used for algorithmic practice deliberately across the whole range of cases the algorithm must cover, and continue until the task is mastered.

Order an algorithm's tests in a logically reasonable and natural sequence, checking the partitioning attribute before the finer ones, and among the natural orderings choose the one that solves the problem in the fewest mental operations.

Lead learners to discover the prescription when time allows, because independent discovery is educationally much more valuable though much slower; present it ready-made when time does not allow, and mixing the two is legitimate.
Supply a ready-made technique rather than leaving learners to discover it when discovery time is unavailable, since an untaught discovery attempt risks failure rather than learning.

Choose the sequential step-by-step method when the teacher has time for direct interaction, since it makes the process easier to learn and speeds internalization; choose the integral whole presentation when self-learning must carry part of the load, accepting that it lacks those benefits.

Treat internalization and automatization of the learned operations as an explicit instructional objective in its own right, choosing the techniques according to whether the sequential or the integral method introduced the algorithm.

Under a sequential approach use the snowball principle: after each new operation is mastered, practise it together with the block already formed, and join new subalgorithms to those already acquired to build more branched and comprehensive algorithms.

Join each new algorithm to those already taught so that a system of algorithms covering the subject area is built up, each successive system more general, and form interdisciplinary connections between such systems to produce systems of still higher order.
Build the comprehensive algorithm by combining the already-mastered subalgorithms, since synthesis presents no difficulty once the components are internalized and automatized.

Treat the development of general, content-independent cognitive abilities as a distinct instructional task of its own, since systematism and generality across subject matters are what let those abilities be produced purposefully rather than incidentally.

Check that the objective is stated at the right grain for the method: an objective scoped too narrowly may have to be broadened to the whole class of related discriminations before a general-ability approach can show its value.
State explicitly which aspects of a method a given demonstration cannot exercise, rather than letting the demonstration stand for the whole method.
Design the algorithm against the specific difficulties learners have with the existing account, aiming at a general, easy-to-follow method that classifies any instance accurately and quickly.
Motivate a classification topic by showing that class membership predicts the consequence the learner cares about, so knowing the type immediately tells them what to expect.
Teach a relational concept by having learners mentally perform the transformation that produces it, so the concept is defined by an operation rather than by appearance.

Teach the cognitive operations of relating explicitly when the concept is relational, because those who identify relations perform these operations unawares and learners' difficulty with relational classification usually traces to never having been taught them.

Have learners construct the algorithm themselves by asking how they would explain the procedure to someone who does not know it and requiring a numbered step-by-step answer, introduce the term algorithm only after they have produced one, and derive the identification algorithm from the formation algorithm they built.

Take each concept of a contrasting pair through the identical stage sequence — enhance the concept, build a formation algorithm, build an identification algorithm, practise, internalize and automatize, then formulate the search algorithm.

Internalize an operation through staged practice: execute it from the written algorithm, then self-instruct aloud with the text removed, then self-instruct silently reporting only the answer, then execute with no self-instruction, and finally drill against an explicit speed criterion until recognition is immediate on sight.

After identification of a designated element is mastered, pose the harder search problem where nothing is designated and have learners extend the algorithm to it: select a candidate, apply the identification test, move to the next, and continue until all are examined.

Train searching operations separately from identification, since they are not a by-product of identification skill: a learner may recognize a target instantly when it is pointed out yet be unable to find it, and without systematic search a composite object will be misclassified through an overlooked component.
Ask explicitly whether all indicative features are needed to classify an instance or whether one suffices, since that question is what converts a list of attributes into a usable decision rule.

Have learners state each candidate definition in explicit if-then form, then test rival definitions by asking whether each applies to all possible objects of the type and yields the correct conclusion; the more general definition — applying to more instances and correct in more cases — is the better one.
Probe a candidate definition with a constructed edge case that has one indicative feature but not another, so learners discover for themselves which feature is the more general criterion.

Have learners propose names for newly distinguished subtypes and then correct them to the conventional term, and state the naming convention as an explicit rule so learners can generate and interpret unfamiliar compound terms by analogy.
Teach general methods of constructing theories and definitions, including how to decide which of several possible definitions is best and why.

Represent a completed prescription as a branching decision diagram so the sequence of tests and their conclusions are visible at once, and extend it branch by branch: establish the superordinate class first, then add the question that separates one subtype from the rest.
State openly where a theory has no prescription for a step and the step was carried out conventionally, rather than presenting the design as fully derived.
Treat a theory of presentation components as a specification rather than a method: the designer must still choose a method that carries the prescribed components.

Present or have learners identify the basic concept-forming components whose combinations generate the object types, and teach the generating operations that produce them, so learners can actively generate the types rather than receive them; the active generative approach is preferred over the passive receptive one.

Prefer generating a thing over receiving it as the route to knowing it well enough to identify it reliably, whenever generation is possible and time-efficient; transformational operations can generate the very classes learners must recognize.

Expect an operational-generative approach to yield much more general concepts and a much more general identification method than conventional instruction, because learners acquire one procedure whose particular cases cover the whole family of types.

Introduce terms and formal definitions at the point where learners have mastered the generating operations and so already hold the concepts, presenting paired contrasting concepts simultaneously and against each other; definitions grounded in generating operations are operational and easy to apply.

Teach both a generative and an identification algorithm, since the operations that generate an object are not necessarily those that identify it, and prefer having learners discover or reconstruct the identification algorithm over receiving it ready-made.

Use independent or guided discovery when time permits, because it is educationally superior for transfer; comparing two or several objects to identify their common and distinctive features is an effective way to discover criterial attributes.

Teach role assignment as an explicit step of any relating operation — isolate the reference-point object, isolate the object to be related, then perform the relating — because reversing the roles immediately produces the inverse relation and a wrong conclusion.

Associate every concept with a variety of objects whose irrelevant attributes are varied, or the term becomes tied to irrelevant features that narrow its generality; a large and varying empirical basis also speeds generalization.
Distinguish a generality — a definition, principle, or statement of a procedure's steps — from an instance, a specific illustration of the object, symbol, event, process or procedure.
Teach not only the operations for solving a class of problems but also how to become aware of one's own operations and formulate explicit prescriptions from them.

Create the expert format deliberately by transforming sequential conscious operations into simultaneous postconscious ones, with the terminal aim of converting the procedure into a pattern-recognition mechanism that solves the problem on sight.
Uncover and specifically train the small, unnoticeable operations in a skill's terminal mechanism rather than assuming they come along with the visible ones.

Skip explicit algorithm instruction where a definition is simple enough to classify from directly, and invest in it when the objective extends to finer varieties whose identification uses that first test as a subalgorithm.
Teach learners to represent an algorithm in flowchart form as an objective in its own right.
Set an explicit synthesis objective after subskills have been automatized separately: practise the comprehensive algorithm until the whole process is itself internalized and automatized.
Where a theory prescribes representing all content as rules, use higher-order rules in place of lower-order ones wherever possible, and analyse each rule into its domain, range and operation.

For a theoretical course, order principles from the most basic and observable to the most detailed and restricted — an order usually resembling the historical order of discovery — building the sequence by repeatedly asking what you would teach with only one more hour, and finding each principle's elaborations by interrogating it with why, which way, how much, and what else.

Require mastery of each equivalence class of a rule, teaching only the paths for classes a learner has not mastered, and use equivalence classes as the operational definition of the categories across which examples and practice must diverge.
Teach the simplest unmastered path through a rule first and proceed to progressively more complex unmastered paths until the whole rule is mastered.

Define the rule's domain as the full set of situations it must handle, select test items for a path from that domain according to the path, and treat the resulting critical domain attributes as the learning environment for the lesson.
Bridge between paths by describing the similarities and differences of the path just taught and comparing one concrete instance from each path's equivalence class.

Make every teaching and practice instance a specific member of the class or a representation carrying all the relevant attributes as the definition states them, and recognize that diagram-only instances strip the irrelevant characteristics real objects carry, so a diagram-only design overstates what learners can do with real instances.

Decompose a rule to atomic components — single units of behaviour or individual decisions whose further refinement has no distinct behavioural consequence — accepting that atomicity assumes each component is either fully available to the learner or not at all.

Treat atomicity as a population-relative and somewhat arbitrary judgement: steps may legitimately be collapsed when the audience is known to possess them, but the risk is assuming more ability than is justified, so set atomicity at the least common denominator of the target population.

Define a path as the sequence of atomic rules that satisfies an objective at a specific difficulty level, treat each path as an equivalence class of problems, and note that paths differ in the complexity implied by the objective's conditions or the domain elements supplied, with the less complex being subordinate.

Develop a test covering all paths of a solution rule, since precise diagnosis comes from the atomic decomposition plus accurate identification of every subordinate path, and represent the paths as subgraphs of the full solution flowchart.

Select for instruction exactly the paths at which the learner is not competent, beginning at the most atomic failing path, omitting instruction on paths the diagnostic shows they already perform, and testing the component behaviours within the simplest path if even that one fails.

Use interchangeability within an equivalence class to avoid repetition, but never across classes: success on one item implies success on the others in that class only, so coverage across classes remains obligatory.
Recognize automation as the redefinition of a rule to incorporate several atomic rules into a single cognitive step, and use automated rules as the basis for more complex training in the subject.

When learners already perform all paths and complete mastery is wanted, teach and practise the collapsed automated rule at its own level of specificity across the range of outputs, since associating fewer steps with each completion improves long-term retention.
Recognize that content-and-behaviour analysis does not settle medium and delivery strategy: those depend on secondary objectives and require analysis of learner traits and logistic variables.
Expect no single instance of the domain to exercise every variation the analysis identifies, so not every decision or operation in a rule is required to succeed on a given instance.

Derive the test directly from the equivalence classes, one item per path requiring completion of every step in that path, so a rule with four paths needs only four items; where a rule has only one step, vary instances across the range instead, since there is no path structure to exploit.

Begin testing above the most subordinate path of a group and work downward until the competence level is found, using the two adaptive assumptions that competence on a path implies competence on its subordinate paths and failure implies failure on its superordinate paths.
Test each independent group of paths separately, since assumptions established on one group cannot be generalized to another.

Select paradigm cases whose relevant factors all point the same way, giving a clear positive exemplar and a clear negative one, then vary cases systematically so each comparison differs from the previous along a single factor.
Span the qualitatively distinct regions when varying a continuous factor — below the critical value, at it, and above it — so learners see that the outcome is not monotonic.

Ask learners continually to predict how the outcome varies with the factors, naming both what it depends on and in which direction, then have them work out how to test the hypothesis rather than confirming or refuting it yourself.

Have learners consider alternative predictions explicitly — naming the possible outcomes and asking which will occur — both to foster differential diagnosis as a habit and as the way to correct a misconception without stating the right answer.

Entrap learners by deliberately proposing an incorrect hypothesis, including by restating their own vague suggestion as an explicit but wrong one they will assent to, and follow the entrapment immediately with a mini-experiment so observation rather than the teacher's authority does the refuting.

Pause an experiment midway and have the learner revise their hypothesis in light of the partial evidence, and praise a well-reasoned conjecture warmly even when it proves incorrect, saying explicitly that it was a good hypothesis.

Maintain a continuously updated agenda of goals and subgoals in dialogue teaching: high-level goals choose the problems and opening questions, learners' answers reveal misconceptions that spawn diagnostic subgoals, and this diagnosis-driven agenda is the sequencing strategy in place of a pre-fixed order.

Decline a method for material it does not fit and state the reason, since content supplied as bare steps without reasons or as unrelated facts cannot be made into an inquiry dialogue without substantial additional work.
Distinguish systematic case variation, which governs the examples presented, from variety of practice, which governs the practice items.

Open a dialogue by establishing what the learner already knows and settling the terminology the rest will depend on, teaching each distinction by presenting cases and testing classification rather than asserting the criterion, and grounding each new term in an experience the learner has already had.

Have learners draw a representation of each varied case so they can see how the representation changes and acquire the rules for representing new configurations; when a drawing embodies an error, use one of their own earlier representations as the counterexample and trace consequences until they see the contradiction.
When a learner offers a plausible mechanism, neither confirm nor deny it: tell them to draw or model it and see whether it holds.
Design a dialogue strategy set to handle detours, since a naive but perfectly cooperative learner is idealized and real learners lead dialogues astray far more often.

Accept that dialogue teaching is time-consuming but may be the only available method where the goal is to teach creative problem solving or theory invention; make every dialogue move traceable to the strategy it instantiates and the objective it serves, and track goals that stay open across many exchanges.

Build a prescriptive theory inductively from a review of empirical findings across behavioral, cognitive and humanistic perspectives, recognizing that narrowing scope to microlevel strategies buys considerably more detailed designer guidance than a broad theory can give.

Describe and audit any presentation as a sequence of discrete displays plus their interrelationships, where each display is one of four primary forms produced by crossing content mode (generality or instance) with presentation mode (expository or inquisitory).
Supply an alternate representation as a restatement of the generality, an instance in a different context, or the same information in another medium.
Make successive instances divergent in their variable attributes so irrelevant features do not become part of the learned concept, and span a range of difficulty rather than clustering at one level.

Make successive instances divergent in both examples and practice so learners see the variety the class contains, and span a range of difficulty in both stages, with more complex concepts requiring an even greater range.

Match each example with a nonexample sharing the superordinate attributes but differing on the relevant ones, and for procedures and principles show inappropriate applications matched against correct execution.

Match each teaching example to a potentially confusing nonexample from a coordinate concept under the same superordinate, use matched pairs early and fade them later, and never match during practice — present instances and noninstances one by one in random order to avoid unintentional prompts.
Fade the help supplied by secondary presentation forms gradually across displays rather than holding it constant.
Isolate the primary presentation forms so the learner can tell a generality from an example from a practice item, and state at the start of a segment what to do with each part of it.
Combine into one presentation two objectives that rest on understanding the same principles rather than teaching them as separate segments.
Show the wider professional practice a simplified classroom procedure abstracts from and state which parts are unnecessary for present purposes.
Isolate each primary presentation from surrounding text with explicit section labels and visual separation, so learners can tell the main idea from its illustration and from practice.
Govern test items by their own adequacy rules: keep divergence and range, drop matching, fading and help, because the item must measure rather than teach.
Distinguish a new term from the term it is most often confused with at the point of introduction, illustrating both contrasts side by side.
Annotate each matched pair with the specific attributes present and absent that decide the case, rather than only labelling the pair.

Make helped feedback explain for each item why it is or is not an instance, naming the criterial attribute the incorrect options fail, and direct the learner to review the key ideas and examples if any item was missed.

Give feedback on a practice classification that shows why the instance does or does not belong, make it unavailable before the learner responds, and fade its help, because unfaded help makes learners help-dependent and they try less hard knowing an explanation follows regardless.

Supply a mnemonic tying the term's meaning to a reconstructable image when the objective is to remember a generality, practise by having the learner label a diagram from memory before checking it, and use cloze items requiring the right term in a described situation to test the generality in use.
Elaborate a definition with attention-focusing information that identifies the relevant attributes and recalls the prerequisites, and restate it in another mode such as a graphic, chart or diagram.

For a remember-generality objective present the generality, one reference example, and practice recognizing the generality stated in two or more different ways; make the reference example show every critical attribute, since learners remember examples more easily than verbal statements and will use it to reconstruct the definition, and let feedback name the synonyms involved.

Use a manipulable simulation in which the learner varies one factor and observes the change as the set of reference examples, then follow it with a tutorial whose questions direct the learner to state the principle themselves before it is formally stated.

Escalate successive simulations to slightly more complex arrangements of the same components, and before transferring a principle to a system containing a new component type, lead the learner to see that the new component behaves like one they already understand.
When a learner's stated observation is wrong, advise a return to the simulation rather than correcting them, leaving the choice to return or continue under learner control.
Follow right-or-wrong feedback with a display of the mechanism that produced the outcome, so the learner sees why their prediction held or failed.

Show the major steps of a process first for the big picture, then explain each with its own pictures and captions, stating the number of steps before naming them and naming each in imperative form against a still picture.

Show a procedure's complete step order in a procedural synthesizer, preferring a flow diagram to a numbered list for more complicated procedures, and always pairing the steps with a picture of the object being operated so the generality has its prototypical example.

Say why each step matters and what failure the substep prevents — the contamination, damage or wrong reading that would follow from skipping it — because that is what makes the step's constraints memorable.
Interleave demonstration and practice step by step rather than completing all demonstration first, while acknowledging that this arrangement is often difficult or impossible in real school settings.
Recognize that asking a question does not make a display practice: rhetorical questions on an expository generality or example are attention-focusing devices and are legitimate there.
Use a manipulable simulation as a source of automatically matched examples, since only the relevant attribute changes between states while everything else is held constant.

State a principle by naming the component concepts it relates and the causal or correlational relationship between them, and make every instance adequately represent each component concept rather than the outcome alone.

Build a theoretical sequence by brainstorming all the principles, listing those the objectives make obvious, then epitomizing to the simplest principles that are the most basic, observable and representative of the whole set — where a simpler principle is one in which fewer things happen but the things that happen are the essence.
Use a component-classification theory to enforce consistency across the designation of objectives, the presentation of instruction, and the evaluation of outcomes.
Make a represented rather than hands-on demonstration illustrate each step, the proper execution sequence, and the expected consequence of each step.

Identify each step of a demonstration as it is executed and focus attention on the decisions and their consequences, then fade that attention-focusing in a second demonstration so the learner must attend more closely.

Illustrate the full range of a process from simple to complex execution and let learners practise both, showing even advanced variants they will not be required to perform so they see the range of possibilities.
Ground an elaborative sequence in the aim of building stable cognitive structures by assimilating new content to existing ones, which is the rationale unifying its otherwise borrowed strategies.

Expect a well-built elaborative sequence to raise questions, broaden horizons and create realizations that would not otherwise surface, communicating that the more one learns the more one sees remains unknown.

Offer macro-level learner control over content selection and sequencing — which part to elaborate next and how far — distinguishing it from microstrategy control, and allow selection of any lesson whose prerequisites the learner already holds.

Define the scope of strategy-level learner control explicitly: the type, order and number of microstrategy components such as examples, practice items and alternative representations, and the type and timing of macrostrategy components such as summarizers, synthesizers and analogies.

Treat macro-level sequencing and micro-level presentation theories as complementary layers: a sequencing theory gives no guidance for teaching the individual skills that make up a course, and demonstrating one is done with course and lesson outlines rather than a finished lesson.
Complete content selection by allocating supporting content to each elaboration, assigning all content to individual lessons, and sequencing content within each lesson.

Offer learner control over content selection wherever prerequisites allow, even when many lessons elaborate two earlier ones at once and the available options are narrower than usual, and let a learner take a deeper lesson as soon as the specific lesson it elaborates is mastered rather than requiring the whole level be completed.
Elicit the epitome from a subject-matter expert with two questions: which principle they would teach if only one were possible, and which principles were discovered earliest.

Name the dimensions along which simplification proceeds and give the reason each case is simpler — fewer interfaces, fewer interacting variables, or a governing relationship that is precise and intuitive rather than dependent on several factors at once.

Expand the most important and most representative dimension of simplification first, defer any dimension presupposing elaboration of another, and tell learners from the beginning that the deferred contrast exists so the simplification is not mistaken for the whole story.

Check the complex end after simplifying to the learners' entry level, confirming every more complex principle the course should cover has been identified, using the heuristics of asking what else happens and asking why, which way and how much about a principle already placed.
State that a curriculum blueprint built without a subject-matter expert violates the procedure and should not be implemented without further consultation and revision.

Teach a phenomenon's behaviour first through simpler physical analogues that share those behaviours, keeping the same behaviour categories across each successive analogue so the parallel structure itself carries the transfer, and teaching the simplest case of each behaviour so learners can predict it before the cases where behaviours interact.
State explicitly where an analogue breaks down — a behaviour the target has that the analogue lacks or the reverse — rather than leaving the analogy to over-extend.

Have each elaboration lesson carry forward the principles established earlier and add only the new ones, so the accumulating principle set is visible; where cases are structurally adjacent, derive the family from one principle plus one explicitly stated varying condition.
Organize a principle's elaborations by the question each answers — what else happens, why, which way, how much — so the outline shows which kind of complexity each addition supplies.

Open a lesson with an initial synthesizer stating the context — where this topic sits among its siblings, a brief review of each, and which one this lesson explores — followed by demonstrations of the most important causes and effects, posed as questions about each case to be covered.

Open a lesson with a concrete scenario in which the learner must make a consequential decision the skill would settle, framed as an explicit challenge naming the desirable and undesirable outcomes, so the need for the skill is felt before it is taught.

Tag every element in a lesson outline with both its type — prerequisite concept, principle, supporting concept, supporting information, supporting procedure — and the performance level at which it is to be taught.

Teach each prerequisite concept immediately before the principle that uses it, naming in the outline which later items it serves, and set its performance level by what the dependent principle does with it: remember level for some, application level for others.

Teach principles at application level rather than remember level, since a principle exists for prediction and explanation in new cases, and state each in the outline as a complete conditional sentence naming situation and outcome rather than as a topic label.

Assign each supporting element the performance level its use actually requires: classification tasks at use level, a concept needed only for meaningful understanding as remember-level information, and a procedure the learner need only understand rather than execute as information rather than as a supporting procedure.

Pair each case with two complementary principles — what happens to the observable outcome and what happens to the underlying mechanism — teaching the observable one first because the observation-to-deduction order is also concrete-to-abstract, and recognizing the mechanism principle as the more complex elaboration since it explains why, involves many simultaneous elements, and cannot be seen.

Place a conceptual synthesizer-summarizer immediately after a group of coordinate concepts is taught rather than deferring all synthesis to the lesson's end, and close the lesson with a summarizer that includes the synthesizer matching its organizing content type.

Use an initial synthesizer for external synthesis relating the lesson to the larger picture and for a preview of how this lesson's ideas relate, while deferring explicit internal synthesis until the learner has analysed and understood each element, because analysis must precede synthesis.
Show interrelationships at the start of a lesson with demonstrations when the content is principles or procedures, and with a combined summarizer-synthesizer when it is concepts.
Place a summarizer-synthesizer where all the content it covers has already been taught rather than automatically at the lesson's end.
Make a synthesizer show the major relationships among ideas simply and with a minimum of words — for concepts, which are kinds of which.
Make the summarizer-synthesizer accessible on demand at any point during a learner-controlled lesson, and perhaps before or after it.
Build a unit or set summarizer-synthesizer — an expanded epitome — from the same elements as a lesson one, differing only in covering all lessons that elaborate directly on a single lesson.

Give each content type its own review form in a summarizer: a term-and-definition list with a cover-and-reveal drill for concepts, a situation-by-outcome table for principles with a prototypical illustration for each, a labelled numbered step diagram for procedures, and a two-column drill for facts run in both directions.

Write each summarized generality as just enough critical words to stimulate recall rather than a full restatement attempting to create new understanding, and pair it with a prototypical example, preferably a line drawing for concepts, showing every critical attribute.

Order a summarizer by dependency: prerequisite concepts before the principles that use them, remember-level information last, with concept review including classification of new examples and nonexamples rather than definition recall alone.

Expect an elaboration tree to be uneven: what was one lesson at one level becomes a whole unit at the next, each module elaborates a unit of the module before it, some lessons have no further elaboration, and a later lesson may elaborate two earlier ones at once when its subject combines their behaviours.
Choose the epitome for concreteness as well as simplicity: the case that can be seen and touched and that exhibits the fewest behaviours comes first.

State what a sequencing theory does not prescribe — discovery versus expository, inquiry versus non-inquiry, game versus non-game, medium selection, example and practice-item sequencing, management strategy — since a truly comprehensive theory of instruction would need all of them.

Design a summarizer-synthesizer to force active processing and offer a low-risk self-test with immediate feedback, arranging its generalities so they work both expositorily as summary and inquisitorily as self-test; a delivery system that prevents premature peeking and enforces a response is preferable, since a skippable effortful self-test will usually be skipped.

Integrate with a theoretical synthesizer only principles that are parts of the same causal chain; principles that are merely parallel cases can be compared and contrasted but not synthesized, and a dynamic demonstration beats a static diagram because a cause-and-effect process is what is being shown.

Treat inclusion of a synthesizer as a coverage decision rather than a universal requirement, since a slower learner may need extra explanation to benefit from one that a stronger learner does not need at all.

Arouse attention perceptually with novel, surprising, incongruous or uncertain events; arouse inquiry by posing a question or problem or having the learner generate one; and sustain interest by varying the elements of the instruction rather than holding its form constant.

Create satisfaction through natural consequences by giving opportunities to use the new knowledge or skill in a real or simulated setting, through positive consequences that sustain the desired behaviour, and through equity by maintaining consistent standards and consequences.

Run motivational design as four development events — audience analysis, motivational objectives, strategy selection, evaluation — recognizing these as procedures for the designer rather than specifications of the instruction, and analyse the audience first because added motivational strategies increase development length and expense.

Screen every candidate motivational strategy against five constraints: not taking too much time, not detracting from the learning objectives, fitting the development and implementation budget, being acceptable to the audience, and being compatible with the delivery system including the instructor's personal style.

Build on the motivational elements a design already contains rather than replacing them, add strategies judiciously so the original structure and purpose are enhanced rather than altered, and never let motivational strategies overshadow the primary instructional objectives.
Acknowledge that a dramatized scenario is unlikely and then name the real occupations facing the same problem daily, so the artificial hook is anchored to genuine utility.

Offer an optional further-challenge problem so multiple achievement levels exist within the same lesson, and state the scoring criterion before the attempt with the instruction to take the exercise as if it were the quiz.

Embed a short true anecdote about someone the learner's age using the skill for a purpose they care about, and reframe abstract example content in terms the learner already values by naming the ordinary object and why anyone would examine it.
Weight exercise items by the points they carry so a multi-part explanation scores more than a single-choice recall item.
Close a segment by connecting what was learned to the terminal task the learner will perform, stating what they will now understand while doing it.

Close each lesson with a passage tying it to the next and to the greater unit, since restarting the motivation process from scratch each lesson wastes design and learning time and the connection supplies more payoff than merely finishing.

Treat the title as a strategic position in a lesson, revising it to add novelty while carrying learning cues about the content, and use a specific person's name, personal pronouns and a visualizable example so the instruction reads as a relevant human experience.

Use a how-to segment title to stimulate an information-seeking attitude and promise a useful payoff, keep titles consistent with the lesson's promised scope, keep terminology consistent by replacing later synonyms with the earlier term, and give parallel objectives parallel length and phrasing.
Vary format across pages — margin width, text against illustration, white space, type style — to sustain learner attention.

Use an unexpected everyday object as an example to capture attention while supplying another familiar association for the concept, and vary the response format across exercises to maintain the stimulation level.
State cautions positively — that a present success predicts future success because the required performance is the same — rather than warning that shortcuts will cause later failure.
Let a novice rely mainly on one theory, since considering several at once can be overwhelming, while an experienced designer draws comfortably from several.

Treat the selection of a theoretical model as a judgement having no truth character — a personal and professional decision whose appropriateness lies partly but not entirely in the eye of the beholder — and note the close parallel to selecting a therapeutic approach, whose treatment-selection literature is transferable.

Attend to theories' commonalities as well as their unique features, since recognizing commonalities is what makes integration possible, and note which aspects each treats as central and which as peripheral, since that shows where it can contribute.

Do not assume practice maps one-to-one onto theory: similar practical approaches can follow from different theories with different rationales, and the same theories can dictate quite different approaches in other cases.
Recognize that cognitively based theories assume cognitive operations are the necessary and sufficient conditions for appropriate behaviour, reversing the direction behavioral theories assume.

Call a theory eclectic in two senses — addressing a wide range of issues rather than a narrow band of objectives, and drawing on diverse resources rather than one approach — and treat a micro theory of presentation detail and a macro theory of course design as complementary rather than competing.

Extract transferable procedures and decision rules from studying worked applications, so future theories encountered can be evaluated, and treat any collection of demonstrated theories as a representative sample rather than an exhaustive listing.

Draw on findings across instructional contexts, since classroom teacher-effectiveness research and training-context design projects have identified many of the same issues, problems and solutions, and communication across industry, higher education, early childhood and military settings clarifies issues despite local differences.

Treat every point where an application failed to address a relevant aspect as an opportunity to expand the variables a theory covers, and never overlook the limitations of the theory being used however useful its guidelines.

Evaluate a relatively modest implementation before embarking on a more ambitious one, exercising discretion about which ideas to implement and about evaluating the results, whether relying on one theory or several.
